ai_content.transcribed_text:
My dear Jarvis,

Our interpreter here has been spending a month in Mansourah on leave and on his return gave me the following account which may interest you. He says that among the masses of Egypt discontent is soothing and that Zaghloul's name is uncharaterised and cursed. The burdens put on the shoulders of the fellahin are such that they have just about had as much as they can swallow and some bright individuals have seriously discussed the advisability of murdering some one more important Englishman so the English will get angry and take over the country once more to work it as in former days. The corruption in the irrigation service, he states, is astounding and in some parts fellahin have to make collections from several villages to pay for water which should be free, before their sluice gates are opened.

The one cry among the fellahin apparently is now, "Oh for the English times once more".

The interpreter referred to is a most loyal fellow of good standing - his pay here is £27 per month, and has been with us many years so his account is true according to what he saw and heard. He told me much more of very great interest having once served the Egyptian government in a temporary capacity during the better times.

Kind regards both to Mrs Jarvis and yourself.

Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) C.F. Reading.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a personal letter written by C.F. Reading to an official named Jarvis, dated April 23, 1937, from Amman, Trans-Jordan. It relays observations from an Egyptian interpreter who recently returned from Mansourah, Egypt. The interpreter reports widespread discontent among the Egyptian peasantry (fellahin) regarding the current administration, noting that the name of the nationalist leader Zaghloul is now cursed. The letter highlights severe corruption within the Egyptian irrigation service, where peasants are forced to pay bribes to access water. The interpreter claims that the general sentiment among the Egyptian populace is a longing for the return of British colonial administration ('the English times').
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of colonial-era intelligence correspondence from the British mandate period in Trans-Jordan. It provides a contemporary perspective on the political and social climate in Egypt during the late 1930s, specifically highlighting the disillusionment of the Egyptian peasantry with the post-independence government and the persistence of pro-British sentiment among certain segments of the population due to perceived administrative corruption. The document serves as a primary source for studying British perceptions of Egyptian nationalism and the socio-economic grievances of the Egyptian rural class during the interwar period.

ai_content.transcribed_text: MINUTE on Residency paper No. 5649/23. Mr. Smart. Parliament and the Fellahin. It is, I think, worth recording that two (fellah) visitors during the past week have urged that the Government should make some practical move towards preparing a new electoral law, as earnest of its intention to revise Parliamentary life. 2. We run a risk of disappointment if we think that the fellahin are wholly satisfied with the suspension of Parliament. They do not want the same Parliament again, and they differ as to the sort of electoral law they favour; but they have been able to judge of the potentialities for good of the constitutional régime, and they want some democratic body to stand between them and absolute government. 3. If this Ministry delays too long the gesture of reform, however excellent its administration, the people may feel that their security is too precarious to bank upon, and may incline, in self-protection, to the demagogues again. L.B.G.-S. 21.12.28.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an internal British Residency minute discussing the political sentiments of the Egyptian peasantry (fellahin) regarding the suspension of the Egyptian Parliament. The author notes that despite the suspension, the peasantry desires a democratic representative body to act as a buffer against absolute rule and warns that the current Ministry must initiate electoral reforms to prevent the public from turning back to demagogues.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British Residency minute from late 1928, likely originating from the British Residency in Cairo, Egypt. It reflects the colonial administration's assessment of the political climate following the suspension of the Egyptian Parliament. The author, identified by the initials L.B.G.-S. (likely a British official), analyzes the concerns of the 'fellahin' (peasantry) and their desire for a functional, democratic constitutional system. It highlights the British concern that the lack of political reform by the Egyptian Ministry could lead to instability and the resurgence of populist 'demagogues,' illustrating the complex power dynamics between the British Residency, the Egyptian government, and the rural population during the interwar period.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPY.
Cairo, 30th March, 1919.
Under-Secretary of State,
I inspected by aeroplane the center parts of the Delta yesterday afternoon, leaving Heliopolis at 2.45 P.M. and returning at 4.40. The route followed was Heliopolis, Shoubra, Banha, Benha, air plains at Zuhra, Mansoura, sheikh el Kam, then, Belbeis, Zagazig, Bilbeis, Cairo, and returned.
Unfortunately the weather was by no means at its best, being windy and very bumpy, and the visibility not very good. Generally, we had to fly much higher than I should have liked, being usually at about 5000 ft, and hardly ever descending to less than 1000 ft. In addition the time of day is not specially favored by the fellahin for working.
However, I can quite enough to be able to say with some certainty that so far as the districts visited are concerned the political disturbances have had no appreciable effect on the cotton cultivation. Honest in the Benha district where there is a lot of vegetable land, practically all it was recently irrigated.
Where it was not yet ridged, men were at work on it, ploughing and ridging. Unfortunately the plants were already peaking, what proportion of the fields the plants were already peaking. As regards cultivation in general, irrigation is proceeding freely, and men were to be seen at work cutting drains and harvesting flax. In fact there was no visible sign of anything unusual in any of the districts visited.
(signed) G. Storey.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a report from G. Storey to the Under-Secretary of State regarding an aerial inspection of the Nile Delta region conducted on March 29, 1919. The author notes the flight path, the weather conditions, and the altitude. The primary purpose of the flight was to assess the impact of political disturbances (likely the 1919 Egyptian Revolution) on agricultural activities, specifically cotton cultivation. The author concludes that there was no significant disruption to farming, irrigation, or harvesting in the areas observed.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official report from the British administration in Egypt during the 1919 Revolution. It provides a unique perspective on the use of aerial reconnaissance by colonial authorities to monitor the stability of the countryside and ensure that the vital cotton economy remained unaffected by the widespread nationalist uprisings occurring at the time. The mention of 'political disturbances' refers to the Saad Zaghlul-led movement against British occupation, and the report serves as evidence of the British attempt to maintain economic control and normalcy in the agricultural heartland of the Nile Delta.

ai_content.english_translation:
I venture to think that Your Excellency may be interested in seeing telegrams which have passed between this Company and the leading Cultivators in the district of Baliana Province of Girgeh, Upper Egypt. 

'Mr. Carver, Alexandria = 
The notables, mayors, and farmers of the Baliana district request that you kindly order the operation of your Baliana irrigation machine as soon as possible, given the great importance of the summer crop and the volume of maize in the consumption of the broad popular masses. We take the liberty of drawing your attention, sir, to the state of absolute tranquility in our province, so that the operation of your machines can only result in more prosperity for your company. Moreover, the entire population is prepared to give you all the financial and other guarantees you deem necessary to ensure your profits. 
KAMEL BOUTROS, CHOUHDI BOUTROS, AHMAD MOHAMED ABOU STEIT.'

'MR. CARVER, ALEXANDRIA = 
Following our last request regarding the operation of your irrigation machines in Baliana, we draw your attention, sir, to the sufficient quantity of local fuel available in the province. The farmers, who are all interested in the operation of your machines, are prepared to deliver this fuel to you in payment for the water price. We hope that under these conditions you will kindly order the operation of your machines as soon as possible so that the sowing can be done under good conditions. CHOUHDI BOUTROS, KAMEL BOUTROS, AMIN ABOU STEIT'

The correspondence highlights the critical need for irrigation to support summer crops (sefi) and maize production, emphasizing the stability of the region despite the political unrest of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The landowners offer local fuel as payment for water services to incentivize the company to resume operations, reflecting the intersection of colonial-era agricultural infrastructure management and local economic survival strategies.

Loss of water from Aswan Dam.
To The Residency, Cairo.
Sir,
Yours of 23.4.1919 re P.O. telegram No. 471 of April 17th, the reply is as follows:-
"Water drawn from Aswan reservoir for emergency navigation in excess of needs of irrigation will be six hundred and twenty five millions. Stop. Effect on Cotton crop nil. Stop. I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient servant,
[Signature]
UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE.

The text notes that while the cotton crop remains unaffected, the 'Dhura' (sorghum/maize) crop will suffer due to delayed sowing and reduced yields unless the annual Nile flood arrives early.

In reference your circular No. I.19887/D attached.
I have consulted the Agricultural expert, Mr. Heald, who states that about 5% of the cotton crop has been planted late owing to persons having omitted to purchase seed before the disturbances and to disregard of rotations in irrigation. This is not expected to produce any heavy loss.

Political Officer, No. 3 Section.

The economic life of the country in the Province of the Dakahlia has not suffered to any great extent from the outbreaks. Owing to the scarcity of water at the end of March and beginning of April in certain localities the cotton crop has suffered and in some places the Fellahin were unable to sow but the area is not extensive. The wheat and bean crops are disappointing but this is due to outside causes which are not yet known.

Owing to the abundance of water during the past fortnight, resulting from the water which has been let out of the Assouan dam and owing to the impossibility of supervision by the civil authorities, the Fellahin have seized the occasion created by the disturbances to plant rice in areas forbidden by the decree. This will result in a dead loss as they will find out to their cost when the lack of water makes itself felt in the months of June and July.
ai_content.english_translation: The economic life of the Dakahlia Province has not been significantly impacted by the recent unrest. While a water shortage in late March and early April hindered cotton planting in some areas, the affected acreage is small. Wheat and bean yields are poor, though the reasons for this remain unclear. Conversely, the recent release of water from the Aswan Dam, combined with a lack of civil oversight due to the disturbances, has led farmers to illegally plant rice in restricted zones. This will likely lead to significant losses when water supplies dwindle in June and July.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official report from the British military administration in Egypt (2nd Echelon G.H.Q.) dated May 1919, concerning the agricultural and economic situation in the Dakahlia Province following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It highlights the dual impact of political instability: the disruption of normal agricultural cycles due to civil unrest and the breakdown of administrative control, which allowed farmers to bypass government decrees regarding water-intensive crops like rice. The report reflects the British colonial concern for maintaining agricultural productivity and resource management during a period of intense nationalist uprising.

COPY.
Report on damage resulting to the Economic life of
O.C. Barrage Force Area, from the lack of transport facilities,
in accordance with G.S. "I" (d) letter No. I.19887/d of 30.4.19.

The villages included in the area under the Command of O.C.
Barrage Force, with the exception of Galioub, have a population
entirely agricultural.
The Area, discounting the railway, is served by the main
Cairo to Alexandria road, and the Nile.
The land owners round Galioub have always supplied the
Cairo market with vegetables, eggs and poultry and have in
consequence a good service of carts running between the two
places, and other produce is almost entirely consumed locally
(excepting Cotton which is not affected yet).
At the commencement of the outbreak the cotton crop was being
planted and the seed was available in the area, the wheat and
barley crops were well grown and the bean crop was about to be
harvested.
The exports from the area therefore during this period,
excepting vegetables eggs and poultry which are independent of rail
transport, were nil.
The only imports into the area which affects agriculture
seriously is fuel. Owing to the high price of coal cotton sticks
have been used by owners of small irrigation pumping engines, and
areas, so situated that they can irrigate by gravity, have been in
the habit of supplying those not so happily situated, with this
fuel. Lack of transport has prevented this distribution and
small owners of pumping plants are finding some difficulty in
keeping their pumps running.
With the exception of the shortage of cotton stick fuel, the
fellaheen are not affected to any extent by the lack of
communications.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official administrative report detailing the economic impact of transport disruptions on the Barrage Force Area in Egypt following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution (referred to as 'the outbreak'). It notes that while the local agricultural population is largely self-sufficient, the lack of transport has halted exports and created a fuel shortage for irrigation pumps, as the distribution of cotton-stick fuel (used as a coal substitute) has been interrupted.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal military-administrative report dated May 16, 1919, concerning the economic conditions in the 'Barrage Force Area' (north of Cairo) during the immediate aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. The report assesses the impact of the civil unrest and subsequent transport disruptions on local agriculture. It highlights the reliance of the Cairo market on produce from Qalyub, the status of seasonal crops (wheat, barley, beans, and cotton), and the logistical challenges faced by farmers in maintaining irrigation pumps due to the scarcity of fuel and transport. ai_content.transcribed_text:
Dear Cheetham,
I am sorry for being so long in returning you the papers you handed me the other day, but I am waiting for the result of enquiries made concerning the effect of the recent troubles on the prospects of the Cotton crop.
From what I can gather, the crop will not be affected in any way owing to the disturbances. At the same time, however, present reports are not very satisfactory, as it appears that the cold season has affected the growth considerably, and that the condition of the crop may be taken as from 15/25 days late.
It is, however, too early to estimate what the eventual effect of this on the crop will be, for, if we get suitable weather now, it is quite possible that the crop may recover all lost ground.
Yours sincerely,
W. Furner
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter from W. Furner to Sir Milne Cheetham regarding the impact of recent political disturbances in Egypt on the cotton crop. Furner notes that while the disturbances themselves did not damage the crop, the cold season has caused a delay in growth of 15 to 25 days, though he remains optimistic that favorable weather could mitigate the loss.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
DIRECTION GÉNÉRALE
DES
DOUANES ÉGYPTIENNES.

No 3185

Alexandrie, le 29th May 1919.

Export Control re-destination of goods.

Sir,

Referring to your No E/5432 of the 22nd inst., I have the honour to inform you that formerly the M.I.O. working in conjunction with the Censor was able to prevent the despatch of goods to other than permitted destinations. As however, the M.I.O. has now been suppressed, this method of ensuring compliance with the terms of export licences can no longer be used, and I think that in existing circumstances the only effective method of ensuring compliance with the conditions (as to destination) attached to export licences, is that of guarantee given by the exporter, guaranteed to be refunded only if within a defined period the exporter presents to the Egyptian Customs a certificate from the Customs at the destination named in the licence, stating that the goods have been landed there according to the conditions stated in the said licence. I append a suggested form of guarantee and certificate. The guarantee and certificate could be on the same sheet and should be made out in duplicate, the original to be retained by the exporting Customs, and the duplicate marked as such to be given to the exporter who will take the necessary steps to see that the certificate is returned duly signed to the exporting Customs.

The duplicate could be perforated along a line below the guarantee, so that the exporter may retain the latter if he desires.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,

[Signature]
Actg Director General.

The Director,
War Trade Department,
Import & Export Section,
The Residency,
Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: Official letter from the Direction Générale des Douanes Égyptiennes (Egyptian Customs Administration) in Alexandria, dated May 29, 1919, addressed to the Director of the War Trade Department (Import & Export Section) at the Residency in Cairo. The letter, numbered 3185, discusses 'Export Control re-destination of goods' in response to a previous communication (No E/5432 of May 22). The Acting Director General explains that since the Military Intelligence Officer (M.I.O.) working with the Censor has been suppressed, a new method is needed to ensure exported goods reach their permitted destinations. He proposes a system of financial guarantees from exporters, refundable only upon presenting a certificate of landing from the destination customs within a specified timeframe. He suggests a duplicate form system with perforations for ease of use.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official administrative letter from the Egyptian Customs Administration (Direction Générale des Douanes Égyptiennes) in Alexandria to the British War Trade Department in Cairo, dated May 29, 1919. Written in the immediate aftermath of World War I, the letter highlights the transition from wartime military censorship and intelligence controls (specifically the suppression of the Military Intelligence Officer or M.I.O. and Censor system) to peacetime administrative regulations. To prevent the unauthorized re-exportation or diversion of goods to restricted destinations, the Acting Director General proposes a bureaucratic mechanism involving financial guarantees and landing certificates. This reflects the complex Anglo-Egyptian administrative apparatus during the British protectorate era, where trade controls were managed jointly by Egyptian departments and British colonial authorities based at the Residency in Cairo.

The D. G. CUSTOMS,
ALEXANDRIA

May 22nd

No. E/3452
8/65

With reference to your No. 2930 of the 17th inst.
Is there any means of ensuring that goods exported under a licence specifying a particular destination should be shown on the Bill of Lading and Ship's Manifest as consigned to that destination?

Perhaps you would kindly advise me of your views, as, unless some means exist or can be devised of providing for the regularity of shipping documents at the port of embarkation, the objects of export-control - not only from the legal point of view, but also as regards the blockade and distribution controls instituted by the associated Governments - are largely defeated.

for DIRECTOR.
ai_content.english_translation: The Director General of Customs, Alexandria. May 22nd. Reference number E/3452, 8/65. With reference to your letter number 2930 dated the 17th of this month: Is there any method to ensure that goods exported under a specific license are correctly recorded on the Bill of Lading and Ship's Manifest as being destined for the location specified in the license? Perhaps you could advise me on your perspective, because unless a method exists or can be created to ensure the accuracy of shipping documents at the port of departure, the goals of export control—not just legally, but also regarding the blockade and distribution controls established by the associated Allied Governments—are largely undermined. Signed, for the Director.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Alexandrie, le April 12th 1919. The Director, W.T.D. Import & Export Section, The Residency, CAIRO. Sir, I beg to refer to your letter of the 4th inst., No R/5453, granting my application to export to Greece ONE TON OF INDIGO. My application of the 2nd inst., mentioned in error only ONE TON instead of 1 ton 1 cwt 1 qr 9 lb, which equals to Kilos 1088,600 gr. Consequently I was authorised by the Director of Customs to ship only 7 cases (out of the whole of 8 cases) giving the official weight of Kilos 985. - I therefore shall feel greatly indebted if you will instruct the Director of Customs not to object to my shipment of the balance of ONE CASE of the same parcel, weighing Kilos 98, 600 gr. nett. Thanking you beforehand, I am, Sir, Yours obediently, A. B. Israel.
ai_content.english_translation: Alexandria, April 12th, 1919. To the Director, Import & Export Section, The Residency, Cairo. Sir, I refer to your letter of the 4th instant, No. R/5453, regarding my application to export one ton of indigo to Greece. My application of the 2nd instant erroneously stated one ton instead of 1 ton, 1 cwt, 1 qr, 9 lbs, which equals 1088.6 kilograms. Consequently, the Director of Customs only authorized the shipment of 7 cases (out of 8), totaling 985 kilograms. I would be very grateful if you could instruct the Director of Customs to allow the shipment of the remaining case, weighing 98.6 kilograms net. Thank you in advance. Yours obediently, A. B. Israel.

Israel, to the Import & Export Section of the British Residency in Cairo during the post-WWI period (1919). The correspondence concerns a clerical error in an export permit for indigo destined for Greece. ai_content.transcribed_text: A. ISRAEL, COMMISSION, IMPORTATION-EXPORTATION, ALEXANDRIE (EGYPTE), Boite Postale No 980. March 23rd, 1919. The Director, W.T.D. Import & Export Section, The Residency, CAIRO. Sir, Following your advices of your letter of the 15th ult., No 0/53, I hereby beg to apply for permission to export to Greece: ONE TON INDIGO - imported from India, lying now in bond, and originally intended for re-shipment to Greece. The telegrams Nos 1, 2 & 3 herewith will show to you that I insisted that the goods be manifested in transit; however, the prohibition by the Indian authorities to ship in this condition, forced me to conclude the purchase and get the Indigo shipped without the mention 'in transit', and on the other hand, the Egyptian authorities did not exact this condition at that time - to allow re-shipment abroad. I therefore sold the Indigo in question to my Greek clients, as proved by recommendations of the Athens British Legation herewith (Nos 6835, 6782 & 6747) but was unable to effect shipment, from Alexandria to Greece, as the Director of Customs advised me that a fresh order had prohibited export of goods which were not 'manifested in transit'. Five cases of above parcel are stocked by Banque d'Athenes, while the balance of three cases are with the London Bank, the whole for the account of the destinies, by whom I am requested to obtain your licence to export their goods; please note, these are outstanding for nearly one year, and have supported very heavy expenses of storage, insurance &c. I trust above explanations will be a clear proof that the Indigo in question was imported for re-shipment abroad, and that you will see your way to grant my application. Awaiting the favour of your reply, I am, Sir, Yours obediently, A. Israel. Encl: which please return after perusal. N.B. Les renseignements ci-dessus consignés nous ont été fournis par Monsieur Russel, Administrateur Séquestre des biens de la Daira du Prince Abdel Halim Pasha. Il ne nous a pas été encore possible de les faire contrôler par notre service d'inspection.

The author provides evidence of his intent via telegrams and British Legation recommendations. The French note at the bottom clarifies that the information provided was supplied by Monsieur Russel, the sequestrator of Prince Abdel Halim Pasha's estate, and notes that it has not yet been verified by the inspection service.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
A. R. ISRAEL
COMMISSION
IMPORT-EXPORTATION
Alexandrie, le February 25th 1919
Boite Postale No 989
W.T.D. Import & Export Section, The Residency, CAIRO.
In accordance with your letter of the 15th inst., No 0/53, I hereby to apply for permission to export to Greece:
One Ton of INDIGO imported from India and originally intended for re-shipment for Greece.
This parcel, although being ordered for account of my Salonica correspondents, as proved by Recommendation No 5456, was not manifested 'in transit' as the Indian authorities did not allow to do so, nor this condition was exacted by the Egyptian Customs at the time of shipment from India, to authorise reshipment to Greece.
In addition to above Recommendation of the British Legation at Athens which proves that the INDIGO in question was ordered for Greece, I beg to enclose:
LETTER OF BANQUE D'ATHENES, relating to a Bank credit of £ 1800.- opened in my favour to cover my sale of One Ton INDIGO.
LETTER OF COMPTOIR NATIONAL D'ESCOMPTE DE PARIS, relating to my Bk credit in favour of the shippers in India.
INVOICE of the Indian shippers.
6 TELEGRAMS & LETTERS, showing that I insisted so that the INDIGO should be manifested in transit - with intention to re-ship to Greece - but the shippers were not allowed to do so.
The INDIGO in question has been lying in bond at Alexandria for nearly one year, and I trust that in consideration of aforesaid explanations, I will be allowed to re-ship this parcel for Greece.
Looking forward to your favourable reply,
I am, Str, Yours obediently,
[Signature: A. R. Israel]
N.B. Les renseignements ci-dessus consignés nous ont été fournis par monsieur Russel, Administrateur Séquestre des biens de la Daira du Prince Abdel Halim Pacha. Il ne nous a pas été encore possible de les faire contrôler par notre service d'inspection.
ai_content.english_translation: A. R. ISRAEL, Import-Export Commission, Alexandria, February 25th 1919. To the W.T.D. Import & Export Section, The Residency, Cairo. In accordance with your letter of the 15th inst., No 0/53, I hereby apply for permission to export to Greece: One Ton of INDIGO imported from India and originally intended for re-shipment to Greece. This parcel... was not manifested 'in transit' as the Indian authorities did not allow it... The INDIGO has been lying in bond at Alexandria for nearly one year... I trust I will be allowed to re-ship this parcel for Greece. [N.B. The information provided above was supplied to us by Mr. Russel, Sequestrator of the assets of the Daira of Prince Abdel Halim Pasha. It has not yet been possible for us to have them verified by our inspection service.]

Import & Export Section). The merchant is requesting official permission to re-export one ton of indigo from a bonded warehouse in Alexandria to Greece. The document highlights the bureaucratic complexities of wartime trade regulations, specifically the 'in transit' manifestation requirements imposed by Indian and Egyptian customs authorities during the post-WWI period. It includes supporting financial documentation from the Banque d'Athènes and the Comptoir National d'Escompte de Paris, and notes the involvement of the Sequestrator of the Daira of Prince Abdel Halim Pasha, reflecting the administrative oversight of assets during the British occupation of Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION ÉCONOMIQUE & AGRICOLE ACTUELLE (AVRIL 1919)
MOUDIRIEH DE CHARKIEH
district de Héhia
RENSEIGNEMENTS GÉNÉRAUX: Les événements en cours n'ont occasionnés qu'un ralentissement insignifiant sur la marche habituelle des travaux. Sauf quelques rares exceptions où les semailles ont subi un retard d'une quinzaine de jours à peine et sur des surfaces représentant le 1/10 de l'arénage total, les ensemencements de coton ont été faits en temps normal sur toute la surface prévue.
RENSEIGNEMENTS CULTURAUX: Les récoltes chétouie n'ont eu rien à souffrir des événements récents. Mais elles ont été fortement endommagées par les intempéries et des maladies. Le rendement des fèves envahies par l'orobanche sera notablement réduit; celui du blé attaqué par la rouille subira une diminution de 20%.
Jusqu'à présent la culture est son cours normal.
N.B. Les renseignements ci-dessus consignés nous ont été fournis par Monsieur Russel, Administrateur Séquestre des biens de la Daira du Prince Abdel Halim Pacha. - Il ne nous a pas été encore possible de les faire contrôler par notre service d'inspection.
ai_content.english_translation: CURRENT ECONOMIC & AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (APRIL 1919). Moudirieh of Charkieh, District of Héhia. GENERAL INFORMATION: The ongoing events have only caused an insignificant slowdown in the usual progress of work. Except for a few rare exceptions where sowing was delayed by barely a fortnight and on areas representing 1/10 of the total acreage, cotton sowing was done at the normal time over the entire planned area. CULTURAL INFORMATION: The 'chétouie' (winter) harvests have suffered nothing from recent events. But they have been heavily damaged by bad weather and diseases. The yield of fava beans infested with broomrape will be significantly reduced; that of wheat attacked by rust will suffer a decrease of 20%. So far, cultivation is on its normal course. N.B. The information recorded above was provided to us by Mr. Russel, Sequestrator Administrator of the assets of the Daira of Prince Abdel Halim Pasha. - It has not yet been possible for us to have them checked by our inspection service.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official agricultural report from April 1919 concerning the Charkieh province (Moudirieh) in Egypt, specifically the Héhia district. It also provides technical data on crop health, noting damage to winter crops (fava beans and wheat) due to environmental factors and pests rather than political instability. The document is significant for its administrative context, as it references the 'Daira' (estate) of Prince Abdel Halim Pasha, which was under the control of a Sequestrator Administrator (Monsieur Russel) during the British occupation period.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SITUATION ÉCONOMIQUE & AGRICOLE ACTUELLE (AVRIL 1919) MOUTIRIEH DE BEHEIRA. Districts de Teh el Baroud & de Damanhour. Ces renseignements concernent: 1°) La Teftiche de Damanhour de Teh el Baroud dépendant de la Daira du Prince Abdel Halim Pacha. 2°) La région environnant ce teftiche constitue en majeure partie des propriétés Wakfs et quelques propriétaires indigènes. Les récoltes chétouie n'ont eu rien à souffrir des événements récents. La récolte de fèves est bonne; l'orge est bien venu; le bersim a déjà donné en troisième coupe; la culture du blé est généralement satisfaisante sauf quelques champs de blé dans la région de Samia attaqués par la rouille et le charbon. Les étendues prévues pour la culture du coton ont été labourées à temps, un léger retard de quelques jours par suite du manque d'eau. A ce jour le coton a été semé et biné. L'aphis (Nadoua aswalia) a fait son apparition dans quelques cultures près de Teh el Baroud. Il n'a pas été autorisé cette année dans la région. Les renseignements ci-dessus consignés nous ont été fournis par l'administrateur séquestre des biens de la Daira du Prince Abdel Halim Pacha. Il ne nous a pas encore été possible de les faire contrôler par notre service d'inspection.
ai_content.english_translation: CURRENT ECONOMIC & AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (APRIL 1919) MOUTIRIEH OF BEHEIRA. Districts of Teh el Baroud & Damanhour. This information concerns: 1) The Teftiche (estate) of Damanhour of Teh el Baroud belonging to the Daira of Prince Abdel Halim Pacha. 2) The region surrounding this teftiche consists for the most part of Wakf properties and some indigenous owners. The winter (Chetouie) harvests have not suffered from recent events. The fava bean harvest is good; the barley has grown well; the clover (bersim) has already yielded a third cutting; the wheat crop is generally satisfactory except for some wheat fields in the Samia region attacked by rust and smut. The areas planned for cotton cultivation were plowed on time, with a slight delay of a few days due to a lack of water. To date, the cotton has been sown and hoed. Aphids (Nadoua aswalia) have appeared in some crops near Teh el Baroud. It has not been authorized this year in the region. The information recorded above was provided to us by the sequestrator administrator of the assets of the Daira of Prince Abdel Halim Pacha. It has not yet been possible for us to have them verified by our inspection service.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION ECONOMIQUE & AGRICOLE ACTUELLE (AVRIL 1919)
MOUDIRIEH DE BEHERA
districts de Délingate - Kom Hamada & Abou-Hommos
RENSEIGNEMENTS GENERAUX
L'absence & la difficulté des communications ont occasionné dans cette région les préjudices suivantes:
1o) Les gros propriétaires et les Sociétés Européennes ont été empêchées de recruter dans des régions populeuses la main-d'oeuvre qui leur était nécessaire.
2o) Des cultivateurs sont dans l'impossibilité d'écouler les produits de la récolte chétoui et de procéder comme d'habitude à la vente anticipée de leur récolte.
RENSEIGNEMENTS CULTURAUX
Cultures Chétoui: Situation normale. Les événements récents n'ont eu que peu d'influence sur la marche de la culture du coton: cependant la rareté de la main d'oeuvre pourrait rendre difficile dans la suite l'exécution de travaux urgents tels que l'éclaircissage et binage. En raison des événements récents, préjudice insignifiant jusqu'à ce jour.
N.B. Les renseignements consignés ci-dessus nous ont été fournis par les agents de nos domaines dans le Moudirieh de Béhéra, et nous n'a pas encore été possible de les faire contrôler par notre Service d'inspection.

CURRENT ECONOMIC & AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (APRIL 1919)
MOUDIRIEH OF BEHERA
Districts of Delingat - Kom Hamada & Abou-Hommos
GENERAL INFORMATION
The absence & difficulty of communications have caused the following damages in this region:
1st) Large landowners and European companies have been prevented from recruiting the labor they needed in populous regions.
2nd) Farmers are unable to sell the products of the 'Chetoui' (winter) harvest and to proceed as usual with the advance sale of their harvest.
CULTURAL INFORMATION
Chetoui Crops: Normal situation. Recent events have had little influence on the progress of cotton cultivation: however, the scarcity of labor could make it difficult in the future to carry out urgent work such as thinning and hoeing. Due to recent events, insignificant damage to date.
N.B. The information recorded above was provided to us by the agents of our estates in the Moudirieh of Behera, and it has not yet been possible for us to have it checked by our Inspection Service.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative report from April 1919 concerning the economic and agricultural state of the Behera province (Moudirieh) in Egypt, specifically covering the districts of Delingat, Kom Hamada, and Abou-Hommos. The report highlights the disruptions caused by the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, noting that the breakdown in communications and transport hindered labor recruitment for large estates and European agricultural companies, and prevented farmers from selling their winter (Chetoui) crops. It provides a snapshot of the colonial-era agricultural management system, noting that the data was gathered by estate agents and awaited verification by an inspection service.

SITUATION ÉCONOMIQUE ET AGRICOLE (avril 1919)
MOUDIRIEH DE DAKAHLEH
districts de Mansourah & de Dekernès
RENSEIGNEMENTS GÉNÉRAUX
En général préjudice presque nul, sauf pour les cultures en règle. Retard de 20 à 25 jours dans les labours et les ensemencements en coton, occasionné surtout par le manque de main-d'oeuvre; les ouvriers ayant fui les ezbehs et villages. -
Pour les propriétés entièrement louées:-
1°) Retard de 15 à 20 jours pour l'ensemencement, faute de transport à temps de la graine de coton; les communications par voie ferrée et fluviale ayant été interrompues. -
2°) Préjudice, du fait du manque de combustible pour les machines d'irrigation. -
3°) Dans certains cas, pillage, incendie des ezbehs et autres constructions, détérioration des machines d'irrigation et de drainage, désertion de la main-d'oeuvre. - Tel le préjudice dans le rendement des terres pourrait être évalué de 40 à 50%
Même préjudice que pour les grandes domaines européens. -
RENSEIGNEMENTS CULTURAUX
En général pour la culture chétoui de 1919 presque pas de préjudice, sauf pour le besoin qui a souffert du manque d'eau en Mars. -
Retard général de 15 à 20 jours, quant aux labours et à l'ensemencement des terres; l'étendue ensemencée ne sera pas inférieure à celle prévue. -
Retard dans l'ensemencement, dû au manque d'eau et comme conséquence, rendement éventuel médiocre qui sera très sensible.
Le préjudice dans le rendement des terres pourrait être évalué pour le moment de 15 à 20%. -
Les renseignements ci-dessus consignés, nous ont été fournis par les gérants de nos domaines, qui eux-mêmes et recueillis auprès des divers propriétaires, gérants de domaines et autres. Il ne nous a pas été encore possible à faire contrôler par notre Service d'Inspection. -
ai_content.english_translation: ECONOMIC AND AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (April 1919). Moudirieh of Dakahlieh, districts of Mansourah & Dekernès. GENERAL INFORMATION: In general, almost no damage, except for regular crops. Delay of 20 to 25 days in plowing and cotton sowing, caused mainly by the lack of labor; workers having fled the ezbehs (hamlets) and villages. For properties entirely rented: 1) Delay of 15 to 20 days for sowing, due to lack of timely transport of cotton seed; communications by rail and river having been interrupted. 2) Damage due to the lack of fuel for irrigation machines. 3) In some cases, looting, burning of ezbehs and other buildings, deterioration of irrigation and drainage machines, desertion of labor. Such damage to land yield could be estimated at 40 to 50%. Same damage as for large European estates. CULTURAL INFORMATION: In general for the 1919 chetoui (winter) crop, almost no damage, except for the wheat which suffered from the lack of water in March. General delay of 15 to 20 days regarding plowing and sowing of land; the area sown will not be less than that planned. Delay in sowing, due to lack of water and as a consequence, potential mediocre yield which will be very noticeable. The damage to land yield could be estimated for the moment at 15 to 20%. The information recorded above was provided to us by the managers of our estates, who themselves collected it from various owners, estate managers, and others. It has not yet been possible for us to have it checked by our Inspection Service.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative agricultural report from April 1919, detailing the impact of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution on agricultural production in the Dakahlieh province. It highlights the disruption caused by labor shortages, the flight of rural workers from hamlets (ezbehs), the destruction of infrastructure (irrigation and drainage machinery), and the interruption of transport networks. The report specifically mentions the property of Victor Mosséri in the Dekernès district, providing a granular view of how political instability and civil unrest directly affected the economic output and operational capacity of large agricultural estates in the Nile Delta during the post-WWI period.

MOUDIRIEH DE GHARBIEH
DISTRICTS DE KAFR EL CHEIKH, CHERBINE & TALKHA
RENSEIGNEMENTS GÉNÉRAUX
Presque aucun préjudice, sauf pour très peu de cultivateurs, un retard de 10 à 15 jours dans l'ensemencement du coton et qui a été occasionné par l'insuffisance d'irrigation, dû au manque de contrôle dans la distribution de l'eau. -
Pour les cultures en règle, retard de 20 à 25 jours dans les labours et les ensemencements en coton, occasionné surtout par le manque de main-d'œuvre, les ouvriers ayant fui les ezbehs & villages.
Pour les propriétés entièrement louées:
1°) Retard de 15 à 20 jours pour l'ensemencement, faute de transfert à temps de la graine de coton, les communications par voies ferrées et fluviales ayant été interrompues. -
2°) Préjudice du fait du manque de combustible pour les machines d'irrigation. -
3°) Dans certains cas, pillage, incendie des ezbehs et autres constructions, détériorations des machines d'irrigation et de drainage, désertion de la main-d'œuvre. Ici le préjudice dans le rendement des terres pourrait être évalué de 40 à 50%. -
Mêmes préjudices que pour les domaines appartenant à des européens, le préjudice dans le rendement des terres peut être évalué de 40 à 50%. -
RENSEIGNEMENTS CULTURAUX
En général pour la culture Chétoui de 1919 presque pas de préjudice, sauf pour le beraim qui a souffert du manque d'eau en Mars. -
Retard général de 15 à 25 jours: quant aux labours et à l'ensemencement des terres, l'étendue ensemencée ne sera pas inférieure à celle prévue. -
Retard dans l'ensemencement dû au manque d'eau et comme conséquence rendement éventuel médiocre qui sera très sensiblement inférieur à celui de 1918. -

ECONOMIC & AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (APRIL 1919)
MOUDIRIEH OF GHARBIEH
DISTRICTS OF KAFR EL CHEIKH, CHERBINE & TALKHA
GENERAL INFORMATION
Almost no damage, except for very few cultivators, a delay of 10 to 15 days in cotton sowing which was caused by insufficient irrigation, due to a lack of control in water distribution. -
For crops in order, a delay of 20 to 25 days in plowing and cotton sowing, caused mainly by the lack of labor, workers having fled the ezbehs (farm estates) & villages.
For fully leased properties:
1st) Delay of 15 to 20 days for sowing, due to the failure to transport cotton seed in time, communications by rail and river having been interrupted. -
2nd) Damage due to the lack of fuel for irrigation machines. -
3rd) In some cases, looting, burning of ezbehs and other buildings, damage to irrigation and drainage machines, desertion of labor. Here the damage to land yield could be estimated at 40 to 50%. -
Same damage as for estates belonging to Europeans, the damage to land yield can be estimated at 40 to 50%. -
CULTURAL INFORMATION
In general for the 1919 Chetoui (winter) crop almost no damage, except for the berseem (clover) which suffered from the lack of water in March. -
General delay of 15 to 25 days: as for plowing and sowing of land, the area sown will not be less than that planned. -
Delay in sowing due to the lack of water and as a consequence potential mediocre yield which will be very significantly lower than that of 1918. -

It assesses the economic and agricultural impact of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution on local farming operations. The report details how the civil unrest, interruption of transport, labor shortages, and destruction of infrastructure (looting and arson of farm estates/ezbehs) significantly hindered the cotton sowing season. It provides a comparative analysis of the damage sustained by European-owned estates versus local properties, noting that yields were expected to drop by 40-50% in affected areas due to the inability to maintain irrigation and drainage systems during the political upheaval.

SITUATION ÉCONOMIQUE & AGRICOLE ACTUELLE (Avril 1910)
MOUDIRIEH DE BEHERA
districts d'Abou-Hommos, de Délingate & Damanhour

Les travaux de culture se sont fait normalement. Le coton a été semé à temps; le Crédit Foncier Égyptien ayant livré la graine de coton avant les événements. -

En ce qui concerne le chétoui, rien d'anormal dans les travaux, cependant l'absence ou la difficulté des communications, empêchant les cultivateurs, soit comme propriétaires, soit comme cultivateurs de procéder comme d'habitude à la vente anticipé de leur coton, et, soit comme séquestre judiciaire. Ces [?] les rentrées des locations pour les échéances chétoui se feront difficilement. Les domaines sont repartis entre les districts [?] Abou-Hommos, de Délingate & Damanhour. -

N.B. - Les renseignements ci-dessus consignés, nous sont été fournis par les gérants de nos domaines, il ne nous a pas été encore possible de les faire contrôler par notre Service d'Inspection. -
ai_content.english_translation:
CURRENT ECONOMIC & AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (April 1910)
BEHERA PROVINCE
Districts of Abou-Hommos, Délingate & Damanhour

Cultivation work has proceeded normally. Cotton was sown on time; the Crédit Foncier Égyptien having delivered the cotton seed before the events. -

Regarding the 'chetoui' (winter crop), there is nothing abnormal in the work, however the absence or difficulty of communications, preventing the farmers, whether as owners or as cultivators, from proceeding as usual with the anticipated sale of their cotton, and, whether as judicial sequestration. These [?] the receipts of the rents for the chetoui deadlines will be difficult to collect. The estates are distributed between the districts [?] of Abou-Hommos, Délingate & Damanhour. -

N.B. - The information recorded above was provided to us by the managers of our estates; it has not yet been possible for us to have it verified by our Inspection Service. -

SITUATION ECONOMIQUE & AGRICOLE (AVRIL 1919)
MOUDIRIEH DE GHARBIEH
DISTRICT DE KAFR EL ZAYAT
RENSEIGNEMENTS GENERAUX
Retard de 20 à 30 jours dans l'ensemencement des terres en coton, causé par le manque d'eau dans la 2ème quinzaine de mars.
Beaucoup d'indigènes n'ont pu avoir de semence à temps. Déficit de 20% dans le rendement des terres comparativement au rendement de 1918.
Retard de 20 à 35 jours dans l'ensemencement aussi par le manque de main-d'oeuvre et d'eau dans la 2ème quinzaine de mars.
Quelques cas de pillage de vol de bétail et de détérioration de machines d'irrigation.
CAS PARTICULIERS
Dans les domaines appartenant à M. Choueri, Trindafillou d'une étendue totale dépassant 10.000 fed.
et à 3 autres propriétaires
grecs: Pillage des denrées en magasin, vol du bétail, détérioration des machines d'irrigation, désertion de la main-d'oeuvre.
Les mines [sic - mains] faite se sont produits: -
Actuellement la main-d'oeuvre est rare et très exigeante
8 à 10 P. par journée d'homme
4 à 6 P. par journée de fillette ou garçonnet.-
ai_content.english_translation:
ECONOMIC & AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (APRIL 1919)
GHARBIEH PROVINCE
KAFR EL ZAYAT DISTRICT
GENERAL INFORMATION
Delay of 20 to 30 days in the sowing of cotton lands, caused by the lack of water in the second half of March.
Many natives could not get seed in time. 20% deficit in land yield compared to the 1918 yield.
Delay of 20 to 35 days in sowing also due to the lack of labor and water in the second half of March.
Some cases of looting, cattle theft, and damage to irrigation machines.
PARTICULAR CASES
In the estates belonging to Mr. Choueri, Trindafillou, with a total area exceeding 10,000 feddans, and to 3 other Greek owners: Looting of stored goods, theft of cattle, damage to irrigation machines, desertion of labor.
Labor is currently rare and very demanding
8 to 10 Piastres per man-day
4 to 6 Piastres per day for a young girl or boy.

The report highlights social unrest and security issues, such as the looting of estates belonging to prominent landowners like Mr. Choueri and Greek proprietors, as well as the destruction of irrigation infrastructure. The document provides valuable insight into the post-WWI economic climate in rural Egypt, characterized by labor shortages, inflation in wages, and civil instability.

SITUATION ÉCONOMIQUE & AGRICOLE ACTUELLE (AVRIL 1919)
MOUDIRIEH DE DAKAHLIEH
districts de Aga, Simbellawain & Faraskour

RENSEIGNEMENTS GÉNÉRAUX
Situation normale, les façons culturales pour le coton se sont faites en leur temps, l'eau a été suffisante. Cette région n'a eu à souffrir que du manque de moyens de communication par voies ferrées.

RENSEIGNEMENTS CULTURAUX
Culture chétoui: Rien à dire: situation normale
Culture du riz: Aucun retard dans l'ensemencement; l'eau a été suffisante.
Culture du coton: L'étendue ensemencée ne sera pas inférieure à celle prévue; 1/4 retard dans les façons culturales et dans l'ensemencement des terres.

CAS PARTICULIERS
Dans les domaines suivants appartenant à: Sté Foncières 2.600f. C.D. à Kafr El Guenéna, district de Talkha. - Hassan Pacha Foda 2.500f. C.D. dist. Aga & Simbellawain. - Said Pacha Halim 11.000f. à Chawa, dist. Aga & Mansourah. - Dans le district de Faraskour, quelques propriétaires Arméniens & Syriens ont eu à souffrir des dernière évènements du fait des indigènes: vol de denrées et de bétail, détérioration des habitations. - Domaines appartenant à des Arméniens & à des Syriens: soit 30.700 feddans. - Bedraoui Pacha 13.000f. (dist. Talkha).
ai_content.english_translation:
CURRENT ECONOMIC & AGRICULTURAL SITUATION (APRIL 1919)
PROVINCE (MOUDIRIEH) OF DAKAHLYA
Districts of Aga, Simbellawain & Faraskour

GENERAL INFORMATION
Normal situation, cotton cultivation methods were carried out on time, water was sufficient. This region only suffered from the lack of railway communication means.

CULTURAL INFORMATION
Chetoui cultivation: Nothing to report: normal situation
Rice cultivation: No delay in sowing; water was sufficient.
Cotton cultivation: The area sown will not be less than planned; 1/4 delay in cultivation methods and in the sowing of lands.

PARTICULAR CASES
In the following estates belonging to: Land Companies 2,600 feddans at Kafr El Guenéna, Talkha district. - Hassan Pacha Foda 2,500 feddans, Aga & Simbellawain district. - Said Pacha Halim 11,000 feddans at Chawa, Aga & Mansoura district. - In the Faraskour district, some Armenian & Syrian owners suffered from recent events caused by the natives: theft of food and livestock, deterioration of dwellings. - Estates belonging to Armenians & Syrians: totaling 30,700 feddans. - Bedraoui Pacha 13,000 feddans (Talkha district).

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Reference your G.34/16 of 3/5/1919, forwarding Political Officers on the damage resulting to economic life of the country from the recent disturbances, I am now able to reply.
1. Reports agree generally that damage to economic life has been mainly caused by the interruption of railway communication. This has been felt keenly at AIYAT FAYOUM, where Cotton merchants are unable to transport their large supplies of Cotton to ALEXANDRIA and dealers in Fowle, Eggs, etc. are unable to send their produce to CAIRO.
2. The neighbourhood of AIYAT has suffered considerably from the shortage of irrigation water, since the disturbances commenced.
This is attributed to 3 causes:-
(a) By the low Nile.
(b) The damage to the ASYUT Regulator.
(c) Lack of supervision at the hands of Canal.
Of these causes (a) has no connection with the disturbances. (b) has been remedied and (c) will probably continue throughout the summer owing to the lack of British Inspectors.
3. It is reported from AIYAT that the troubles have been followed by a period of general lawlessness, encouraged by inactivity on the part of the police, with the result that thieves have not improved the economic situation nor those persons who have burned their enemy's corn.
4. Merchants at WASTA whose shops were looted have retreated to CAIRO and have not replaced their stocks, thus causing a shortage and increased prices in such articles as linen, cotton, shoes, and grocery.
At WASTA commodities such as Paraffin Oil and Methyvated Spirits hardly exist. The exhorbitant price of four piastres a litre as against 18 milliemes before the outbreak is being charged for Paraffin Oil.
In this district the crop is practically nil. The Onion crop in the district is practically nil. Barley, beans, and Beerseen.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official report from the British military headquarters in Egypt to the Residency in Cairo, detailing the economic impact of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It outlines how the disruption of railway lines paralyzed the transport of agricultural goods (cotton, poultry, eggs) from rural areas like Aiyat and Fayoum to major urban centers. It further notes the failure of irrigation infrastructure due to the Asyut Regulator damage and the lack of British oversight, alongside reports of local lawlessness, looting of shops in Wasta, and the resulting hyperinflation of essential goods like paraffin oil.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal administrative report dated May 1919, written in the immediate aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. It provides a granular assessment of the economic paralysis caused by the uprising, specifically focusing on the breakdown of transport infrastructure, the failure of irrigation systems, and the resulting supply chain crises in rural districts. It serves as a primary source for understanding the British colonial administration's perspective on the 'disturbances' and their efforts to restore economic order and agricultural productivity in the Nile Valley.

TELEGRAM.
No. 452.
Mr. Walter Davies, Contractor, was murdered in his house in Cairo last night and his wife seriously injured by two natives who have not yet been arrested. There is no reason to suppose this has any political significance. Mrs. Davies doing well. Please inform son Warwick Davies whose telegraphic address is Traffic, Birmingham.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a diplomatic telegram sent from the High Commissioner for Egypt to the Foreign Office in London. It reports the murder of a British contractor named Mr. Walter Davies in Cairo, the injury of his wife, and the status of the investigation. It explicitly notes that the incident is not believed to be politically motivated and requests that the victim's son, Warwick Davies, be notified.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal diplomatic telegram sent from the British High Commissioner for Egypt to the Foreign Office in London, dated March 29, 1918. It serves as an official notification of a violent crime involving British subjects in Cairo during the period of the British Protectorate over Egypt. The document highlights the administrative priority of distinguishing between criminal acts and potential political unrest or nationalist agitation during the First World War era, as well as the standard consular procedure for notifying the families of British citizens involved in incidents abroad.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
To His Excellency
THE HIGH COMMISSIONER,
The Residency,
Ramleh.

C.H. PERROTT,
Cairo.
28, Sharia El Magraby,
July 20th, 1920.

Sir,
I am instructed by Mrs. Amelia E. Davies, the widow of Mr. Walter W. Davies, Contractor, who was murdered on the 28th, March 1919, to ask if you could see your way to recommend the Egyptian Government to award her a sum by way of pecuniary compensation for the losses she has sustained arising out of the murder in question.
The matter has been before the Indemnities Commission, and her case was argued by me, but the Commission rejected the claim for compensation on the ground, that the losses occasioned were not the direct result of the disturbances.
It is not my purpose to criticize the finding of the Commission, or to appeal to you against its decision, but rather to suggest that this is a case where the Egyptian Government might well see fit to award an indemnity, even if such indemnity were not considered to be within the scope of the powers conferred by the Proclamation upon the Indemnities Commission.
I beg to enclose for your information a copy of the claim made by Mrs. Davies and addressed to the Indemnities Commission, which, in fact, is a statement of her case.
I have, Sir, the honour to remain,
Your humble servant,
C.H. Perrott
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official letter written in English from C.H. Perrott to the British High Commissioner in Egypt. It requests that the Egyptian Government provide financial compensation to Mrs. Amelia E. Davies, whose husband, Walter W. Davies, was murdered during the unrest in Egypt on March 28, 1919. The letter notes that the official Indemnities Commission had previously rejected the claim on the technicality that the losses were not a 'direct result of the disturbances,' and asks the High Commissioner to consider an ex-gratia payment outside the Commission's formal mandate.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of legal correspondence from the post-WWI period in Egypt, specifically following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British occupation. It highlights the administrative challenges faced by British authorities in dealing with claims for damages and loss of life resulting from the widespread civil unrest. The letter illustrates the intersection of private legal advocacy and the British High Commissioner's discretionary power in Egypt during the protectorate era, specifically regarding the limitations of the Indemnities Commission established to process claims arising from the 1919 disturbances.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPY.

23, Sharia Antikhana,
Cairo.
May 26th, 1920.

TO
THE SECRETARY,
Indemnities Commission,
14, Sharia Abdin,
Cairo.

This claim is for the sum of L.E. 12,000, and is brought in respect of the murder of my late husband WALTER W. DAVIES on 28th March 1919.

The circumstances of the murder are related in the accompanying 'Resumé et Extraits des Procès-verbaux de Police'. A translation (in French) of the judgment of the Court of Assize sentencing Mustapha Shebata Kamar (our former servant) to penal servitude for life for complicity in the murder, is also enclosed.

I am convinced that the murder of my husband and the attempted murder of myself were due to and arose directly out of the political disturbances which at the date of the murder were at their height. It will be remembered that it was in the same week that the attack on Assiout took place, while the assassination of Mr Smith and our notorious train murders occurred only a few days earlier.

It is obvious that robbery was not the motive, or at least was not the sole motive for the crime. The key of my husband's safe was on a chain which he was wearing, and it was not taken, nor was his watch or money, and nothing was taken from the flat. The evidence of premeditation shows, I think, conclusively that the assassins had another purpose than robbery in view. Otherwise why did they not in connivance with Mustapha, the servant, enter the flat and carry out the robbery at dead of night, instead of deliberately choosing the dinner hour when I was certain my husband and I would be in the house and about?
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal claim for 12,000 Egyptian Pounds regarding the murder of Walter W. Davies on March 28, 1919. The document references attached police reports and a French translation of a court judgment sentencing a former servant, Mustapha Shebata Kamar, to life imprisonment. The claimant argues that the murder was politically motivated, citing the 1919 Egyptian Revolution disturbances, the attack on Assiout, and the assassination of Mr. Smith, rather than a simple robbery, as valuables were left untouched.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal claim for financial indemnity submitted to the Indemnities Commission in Cairo in 1920. It pertains to the murder of Walter W. Davies during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, a period of intense anti-British nationalist unrest. The claimant, the widow of the deceased, provides evidence to argue that the crime was a politically motivated assassination rather than a common robbery, linking the event to broader insurrectionary activities in Assiout and Cairo. The document highlights the intersection of personal tragedy and the volatile political climate of post-WWI Egypt under the British Protectorate.

The Court of Assize have found that there was premeditation to commit murder, and for the murder no other motive can be discovered than hatred of the British which at the date in question had reached fever pitch.
It was stated at the time that the attempt was being made by the worst elements among the revolutionaries in Cairo to persuade native suffrage to assassinate their British employers. It is suggested that the police hold reports from their agents proving this. The tragedy of my husband's death and the attempt upon my own life lend strong support to this view. Moreover, Mustapha's conduct had changed for the worse since the disturbances began. He lived in the Ablin quarter, and on one occasion I remember hearing him say that he spent part of the afternoon at cafés there, discussing matters with his friends, and I conclude he came under the influence of the agitators who, as I believe reports in the possession of the police will show, were endeavouring to organize a concerted movement of murder against the British.
After the terrible events of 28th March, I spent a month in hospital, and incurred expenses amounting in all to £320.200. as per statement at foot.
My left arm and right thumb are practically useless owing to injuries sustained by me in my struggle with one of the murderers.
My husband had for many years been in business as a merchant and Commission Agent. The business was a purely personal one, and is now in process of being closed down.
I attach Balance Sheets for the 3 3/4 years, 1915-1918, 1918-1919, 1917-1918 and 1918 to March 1919, which were prepared by a Chartered Accountant, and which show a net profit for each of the undermentioned periods as follows:-

ai_content.transcribed_text:
MINUTE on Residency paper No. 8958/7.
Mr. Selby.
The attached correspondence concerns a murder which took place at the time of the riots in March last year. It was a particularly atrocious affair, the man and his wife being attacked with knives while in bed and the assailants escaping undetected.
With all the sympathy in the world, I cannot imagine that Mrs. Davies has any claim to financial compensation from the Egyptian Government.
The first explanation which naturally occurred to everybody, I remember, was that the crime was a political one and I have no doubt that the Indemnities Commission approached their enquiry with this presumption strongly in their minds. They were however unable to find any grounds for attributing the affair to such motives.
Mr. Perrott, as you will observe, recognises the fact that she has little claim and his letter merely amounts to a suggestion that the Egyptian Government might be willing to give her something as an act of charity.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal internal minute regarding a request for financial compensation for a murder victim's widow. The author notes that the murder occurred during the riots of March 1919, but despite the brutal nature of the crime, the Indemnities Commission found no evidence that it was politically motivated. Consequently, the author argues that Mrs. Davies has no legitimate claim for compensation, though Mr. Perrott suggests the Egyptian Government might consider a payment as an act of charity.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an internal British Residency minute from 1920 concerning the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It discusses a claim for financial compensation by a Mrs. Davies, whose husband was murdered during the civil unrest. The document highlights the administrative process of the 'Indemnities Commission,' which was tasked with distinguishing between political crimes (eligible for state compensation) and common criminal acts. The author concludes that since the murder was not deemed political, the claim lacks legal standing, reflecting the British colonial administration's cautious approach to financial liability during the volatile post-war period in Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Chancery, The Residency.

I regret that it is quite out of the question to advise the Egyptian Government to consider the claim submitted by Mrs. Walter W. Davies and forwarded under cover of your 8956/8. In the first place it is arguable that responsibility for the outbreak of the disturbances last spring attaches at least as fully to His Majesty's Government as to this Government. In the second place, this Government, acting under legal advise and upon precedent, has expressly repudiated liability for loss even directly and un-questionably arising from riot and pillage occurring during the said disturbances, and although it has provided certain sums to be applied to the recoup-ment of certain of such losses, they are expressly accorded ex gratia and are being distributed under stipulated conditions at the sole discretion of the Indemnities Commission.

The Egyptian Government consequently cannot possibly be asked to entertain claims for indirect loss, particularly a claim the connection of which with the disturbances is so hypothetical. It is further to be noted that upon Mrs. Davies' own showing her husband had adequate means to make proper financial provision for his family in the event of his death, a contingency which any prudent man must envisage.

[Signature]
ACTING FINANCIAL ADVISER.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal rejection of a financial claim submitted by Mrs. Walter W. Davies. The Acting Financial Adviser explains that the Egyptian Government cannot accept liability for losses incurred during the spring disturbances of 1920. The letter argues that the British Government (His Majesty's Government) shares responsibility for the unrest, and that the Egyptian Government has already legally repudiated liability for riot-related damages. Any payments made by the Indemnities Commission are described as 'ex gratia' (voluntary) rather than a legal obligation. Furthermore, the claim for 'indirect loss' is dismissed as hypothetical, and the official notes that the deceased husband should have made adequate financial provisions for his family.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official memorandum from the British Residency in Egypt, dated August 3, 1920, addressed to the Ministry of Finance. It concerns the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution (often referred to as the 'disturbances last spring'), a period of intense anti-colonial uprising against British rule. The document highlights the administrative and legal friction between the British-controlled Residency and the Egyptian Government regarding financial reparations for foreign nationals. It illustrates the British policy of denying legal liability for damages caused by the nationalist uprising, framing any compensation as a discretionary act of grace rather than a right, while also reflecting the colonial-era bureaucratic dismissal of claims deemed 'indirect' or 'hypothetical'.

HIGH COMMISSIONER
FOR EGYPT
8988/10
August 4th, 1920.

8988/10.
August 4th, 1920.

Sir,

With reference to your letter of July
20th, I am directed by the Acting High Commissioner
to inform you that the possibility of awarding
Mrs. Amelia Davies an indemnity in respect of the
murder of her late husband was duly referred to
the competent authorities of the Egyptian Govern-
ment.

The latter, while fully sympathising
with the loss which Mrs. Davies has sustained,
regret that, after careful consideration of the
circumstances of the case, they can find no ground
to justify recommendation of any such award.

I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,

Third Secretary.

Garrett Esquire,
S. Sharia El Magraby,
CAIRO.

It is addressed to Garrett Esquire at S. Sharia El Magraby, Cairo. The letter acknowledges Garrett Esquire's communication of July 20th. It states that the Acting High Commissioner referred the possibility of granting an indemnity to Mrs. Amelia Davies, whose husband was murdered, to the relevant authorities of the Egyptian Government. The Egyptian authorities, while expressing sympathy for Mrs. Davies' loss, regret that, after careful review of the case, they found no basis to recommend such an award. The letter concludes with the formal closing 'I am, Sir, Your obedient servant,' and is signed by the 'Third Secretary.'

The communication, sent by the Third Secretary to Garrett Esquire, details the administrative process of referring the claim to the Egyptian Government. Sir, 
As a result of a conversation with Mr. Amos this morning, His Excellency the High Commissioner directs me to inform you that this morning he received a visit from a certain Miss Lilian M. Davies of 13 Sharia Antikhana. This lady brought to Lord Allenby's notice the question of her father's murder which took place at their house in March 1919 and desired to know whether it would be possible for her to secure any compensation from the Egyptian Government in view of the possibility of the murder having been actuated by political motives. 
His Excellency would therefore be glad to be informed if, in your opinion, any such compensation can be paid, as Miss Davies would appear to be in considerable [need]. 

[Handwritten note on insert]: 
I have only recently returned to Egypt, again in the event of my mother's death. 
Yours very respectfully, 
Lilian M. Davies 

[Signature]: H. Hughes Esq., 
[Title]: of Inspector, Native Parquet.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Caire 12 March 1921. With reference to your letter of the 7th inst. received yesterday. I have the honour to report: The murder of late Mr Davies took place during the March troubles of 1919. At that time I was working in the Legal Office at G. H. under Judge Percival. The case came to the Legal Office. I read the evidence and exposed the case to Judge Percival. We concluded that though the murder would probably not have taken place in normal times yet there was no evidence to show that it was actuated by political motives. The evidence pointed to theft being the object of the murderers. General Pulfin and Judge Percival therefore decided to leave the case to the Native Court by which the accused were eventually tried and convicted. Your obedient servant, [Signature], Chief Inspector. To the Private Secretary, The Residency, Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official report from a Chief Inspector in Cairo to the Private Secretary at the British Residency, dated March 12, 1921. It clarifies the circumstances surrounding the murder of a 'Mr. Davies' during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution (referred to as 'March troubles'). The author explains that while the murder occurred during a period of political unrest, the legal investigation—conducted by the author and Judge Percival—determined that the crime was motivated by theft rather than political insurgency. Consequently, the case was referred to the Egyptian Native Courts, where the perpetrators were subsequently prosecuted.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British colonial administrative correspondence from the High Commissioner's office in Cairo, Egypt, shortly after the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It serves as a post-facto legal clarification regarding the death of a British subject, Mr. Davies. The document highlights the British colonial administration's efforts to distinguish between common criminal acts and politically motivated anti-colonial violence during the 1919 uprising. By categorizing the murder as a theft, the authorities justified transferring jurisdiction to the Native Courts, thereby distancing the British military administration from the specific criminal proceedings while maintaining oversight of the broader political narrative.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Sir, With reference to your letter of the 7th inst., received to-day, I have the honour to report: The murder of late Mr Davies took place during the March troubles of 1919. At that time I was working in the Legal Office at G. H. Q. under Judge Percival. The case came to the Legal Office. I read the evidence and exposed the case to Judge Percival. We concluded that though the murder would probably not have taken place in normal times yet there was no evidence to show that it was actuated by political motives. The evidence pointed to theft being the object of the murderers. General Bulfin and Judge Percival therefore decided to leave the case to the Native Court - by which the accused were eventually tried and convicted. Your obedient servant, G. W. W. W. Chief Inspector. To The Private Secretary, The Residency, Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is written in English. It is a formal report from a Chief Inspector to the Private Secretary at the British Residency in Cairo, clarifying the circumstances surrounding the murder of a Mr. Davies during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The author explains that while the murder occurred during a period of political unrest, the legal assessment at the time—conducted by the author, Judge Percival, and General Bulfin—concluded that the motive was theft rather than political, leading to the case being handled by the Native Court.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official administrative report dated 12 March 1921, originating from the British authorities in Cairo, Egypt. It provides a retrospective legal analysis of a murder case involving a 'Mr. Davies' that occurred during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution (often referred to as the 'March troubles'). The document is significant for its administrative context, illustrating how British colonial officials (such as Judge Percival and General Bulfin) categorized crimes during the nationalist uprising, specifically distinguishing between politically motivated acts of rebellion and common criminal acts like theft to determine jurisdictional authority between British military oversight and the Egyptian Native Courts.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
April 1st, 1921.

Miss Lillian M. Davies,
13 Sharia Antikhana,
Cairo.

Madam,

With reference to your recent letter to and subsequent interview with His Excellency on the subject of the murder of your father in March 1919, I am directed to inform you that Lord Allenby has caused careful enquiries to be made as a result of which it has been ascertained that there is no further evidence to show that the case was actuated by political motives. Lord Allenby regrets therefore that it is not possible for him to hold out to you any hope of compensation as suggested in your interview.

I am therefore to return to you with the compliments of His Excellency the personal MS record of the case which you were good enough to place at His Excellency's disposal.

I am, Madam,
Your obedient servant,
First Secretary.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter from the British High Commissioner's office in Cairo to Miss Lillian M. Davies. It addresses her request for compensation regarding the murder of her father in March 1919. The letter states that after an investigation, Lord Allenby concluded the murder was not politically motivated, and therefore, the British government would not provide compensation. The letter concludes by returning a personal manuscript record of the case that Miss Davies had previously provided to the High Commissioner.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of official British colonial correspondence from the High Commissioner's office in Egypt, dated April 1, 1921. It reflects the administrative handling of claims following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, a period of significant civil unrest and violence against British personnel. The letter demonstrates the British authorities' efforts to categorize acts of violence—specifically distinguishing between 'political' and 'non-political' motives—to manage financial liability and diplomatic pressure during the transition toward the 1922 Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence.

I am directed by the High Commissioner to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of January 2nd.

As you will be aware, the circumstances of the unfortunate death of your father were carefully reviewed two years ago by the competent British legal authorities, who gave their considered opinion that there was no evidence that the case had been motivated by political motives.

There was, therefore, no ground upon which Lord Allenby could then properly base a claim for the payment of an indemnity by the Egyptian Government, and while His Excellency greatly sympathises with you, he regrets that he does not see his way to re-open the case or reverse the previous decision.

I am, Madam,
Your obedient servant,

FIRST SECRETARY.

[Handwritten note on right page]: as perusal to keep the case
M.S. Amos
20.1.23
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter from the British High Commissioner's office in Egypt to a female correspondent, acknowledging her letter dated January 2nd. It informs her that the circumstances surrounding her father's death were reviewed two years prior by British legal authorities, who concluded there was no evidence of political motivation. Consequently, Lord Allenby (the High Commissioner) could not pursue an indemnity claim against the Egyptian government and declined to reopen the case. A handwritten note by M.S. Amos dated January 20, 1923, suggests the document was filed for reference.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official piece of diplomatic correspondence from the British High Commission in Egypt, dated January 29, 1923. It reflects the British administrative stance during the period of the Egyptian Protectorate, specifically addressing a request for an indemnity regarding a past death. The mention of Lord Allenby, who served as the British High Commissioner in Egypt from 1919 to 1925, places this document within the volatile political context of post-WWI Egypt, where the British authorities frequently had to navigate claims and grievances from foreign nationals and local subjects while maintaining colonial control.
