Davies, a merchant, contractor to the War Office, Cairo, and H.M. Postmaster General, who was assassinated in Cairo on March 28th. I beg to ask if it would be possible to obtain information from the £500,000 indemnity paid to your Excellency, this must be by the British Government.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Sir, The recent troubles in Egypt have brought about agitation for compensation to the relatives of several military and civilians killed in the riots between 1919 and 1924, and as one of these, I would like to put forward a claim for the outrageous murder of my father, Walter W. Davies (government contractor) and dangerously wounding my mother, in 1919. Brief details of the case are as follows - On March 28th 1919, at 8 o'c.p.m. in his house at the dinner table, two men gained access to the flat of Walter W. Davies where they stabbed him and cut about Mrs Davies and left her for dead also, and fled away without touching a thing in the way of thieving, etc. Lady Allenby went to my mother's bedside at the Anglo-American Hospital and tried to console her in her awful agonies, and also assured her that she would be compensated. My Mother recovered, but died a few months later. Nothing has been done to compensate the family, and I have been waiting my time to see more of these murders take place, and now perhaps with the £500,000 compensation can be spared to civilians and military victims, other than government officials. Any further information I will gladly give you, if required, and I have every confidence in your power to bring about. The Right Honourable Stanley Baldwin, M.P.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter written in English from Witley, Surrey, dated November 30th, 1924, addressed to Stanley Baldwin, M.P. The author is seeking financial compensation for the murder of their father, Walter W. Davies, a government contractor, and the wounding of their mother during the 1919 riots in Egypt. The letter details the violent home invasion on March 28th, 1919, where the father was stabbed and the mother severely injured. It mentions that Lady Allenby visited the mother in the Anglo-American Hospital to offer condolences and promises of compensation, which were never fulfilled. The author is now petitioning the government for a share of the £500,000 compensation fund designated for victims of the Egyptian riots.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal petition for compensation sent to the British Prime Minister, Stanley Baldwin, in the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. The period between 1919 and 1924 was marked by significant civil unrest and anti-colonial violence in Egypt. The letter highlights the personal tragedy of a British government contractor's family and reflects the administrative challenges the British government faced in addressing claims for damages and loss of life during the transition toward Egyptian independence. It provides a primary source perspective on the human cost of the British occupation and the subsequent political efforts to manage reparations for victims of the riots.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
FOREIGN OFFICE, S.W.1. 8th December, 1924.
Madam,
In reply to your letter of November 30th, addressed to the Prime Minister, suggesting that a portion of the five hundred thousand pounds recently paid by the Egyptian Government should be devoted to the payment of compensation to relatives of officers and civilians killed in Egypt since 1919, and in particular calling attention to the case of your father who was murdered in that year, I am directed by Mr. Secretary Chamberlain to express to you his regret that such a suggestion cannot be entertained in view of the public declaration recently made by His Majesty's Government respecting the allocation of this indemnity.
2. This declaration was to the effect that His Majesty's Government had decided that the fine of five hundred thousand pounds paid by Egypt should, subject to the provision of compensation to the victims of the outrage of November 19th, be applied as they might hereafter direct, to benevolent objects in the Sudan, for which country Sir Lee Stack laid down his life.
I am &c.,
(Signed) D.G. Osborne.
Lillian Lane,
The White Hart,
Witley,
Surrey.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official letter from the British Foreign Office dated December 8, 1924, addressed to a Ms. Lillian Lane. It responds to her request that a portion of the £500,000 indemnity paid by the Egyptian government (following the assassination of Sir Lee Stack) be used to compensate families of British victims killed in Egypt since 1919, including her own father. The Foreign Office, under Secretary Chamberlain, rejects this request, stating that the funds are strictly earmarked for benevolent projects in the Sudan, the country where Sir Lee Stack served and died.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British diplomatic correspondence regarding the aftermath of the assassination of Sir Lee Stack, the Governor-General of the Sudan and Sirdar of the Egyptian Army, in Cairo on November 19, 1924. The assassination led to a severe diplomatic crisis, resulting in the British government imposing a £500,000 fine on the Egyptian government. This letter illustrates the British administration's firm policy of utilizing these punitive funds specifically for projects in the Sudan to honor Stack's legacy, while explicitly denying requests from other British families seeking compensation for earlier losses in Egypt, thereby maintaining the political focus on the Sudan mandate.

FOREIGN OFFICE, S.W.1.
31st December, 1924.

Mrs. Lillian Lane,
The White Hart Hotel,

SURREY.

Madam,
With reference to your letter of December 10th requesting that compensation should be paid in respect of the murder of your father in Egypt in 1919, I am directed by Mr. Secretary Chamberlain to inform you that he regrets that, as stated in the Foreign Office letter of the 8th of December, His Majesty's Government are unable to comply with your suggestion that a portion of the indemnity recently paid by the Egyptian Government should be allocated to this purpose.

(Signed) D.G. Osborne.

It addresses her request for compensation regarding the 1919 murder of her father in Egypt. The letter clarifies that the death of Mr. Davies in March 1919 was not considered a 'political outrage' in the same category as later incidents for which the Egyptian government had provided compensation.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official administrative response from the British Foreign Office during the interwar period. ai_content.transcribed_text:
The White Hart Hotel,
Witley, Surrey.
10th December 1924.
Sir,
With reference to your letter No. E 10896/10439/16
In reply to mine of November 30th. I fail to see why
compensation should not be paid to the relatives of the late
Walter W. Davies who was murdered in Cairo during the riots of
1919 and am not satisfied with the reasons given.
I would like to remind Mr. Chamberlain that compensa-
tion has been paid in other cases, and what is justice for one,
is justice for another. The British Government presumes to
protect its citizens, and the late W.W. Davies was for many
years, a resident in Egypt with his wife and family, honoured
and respected by all and he undertook many contracts for the
Government and he contributed by all means in his power to the
honour and prestige of the British Administration in Egypt.
An immense sum of money has been allocated to the
victims of the outrage of November 19th, and a further large
sum to the native policeman, who only conformed to his duty.
The late Sir Lee Stack was not murdered in the Sudan,
but by Egyptian fanatics, as was the late W.W. Davies. Any
amount of compensation cannot replace the loss of Father and
Mother, but at the same time, the financial distress caused
to the near relatives, and dependents, is a matter which must
be attended to before the Benevolent objects in the Sudan.
The murderers of Sir Lee Stack and W.W. Davies are
still at large. It is now high time to warn Zaghlul and his
associates....
Under Secretary of State,
FOREIGN OFFICE, S.W.1.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal letter written from the White Hart Hotel in Witley, Surrey, on December 10, 1924, addressed to the Under Secretary of State at the Foreign Office. The author is protesting the British government's refusal to provide compensation to the family of Walter W. Davies, who was killed during the 1919 riots in Cairo. The author argues that since compensation was provided to victims of the November 19th outrage (the assassination of Sir Lee Stack) and to a native policeman, the government is obligated to provide similar justice to the family of Mr. Davies. The letter concludes by criticizing the government's handling of the situation and demanding action against Zaghlul and his associates.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of private correspondence addressed to the British Foreign Office regarding the political instability in Egypt during the early 1920s. It highlights the British government's administrative response to the assassination of Sir Lee Stack, the Sirdar of the Egyptian Army and Governor-General of the Sudan, who was killed in Cairo on November 19, 1924. The author uses this high-profile event to draw a parallel to the earlier, unresolved death of Walter W. Davies during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, illustrating the ongoing tensions between British expatriates and the nationalist movement led by Saad Zaghlul.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
From
Mrs. Lillian Lane,
The White Hart Hotel,
Witley, Surrey.
7th January 1925.
Reference your No. E 11201/10439/16 dated 31st December 1924.
Sir,
I have the honour to request that you will kindly inform me what facts influence your decision that the outrage on my father was non-political.
There was no evidence to prove theft, intention of theft or to substantiate the suggestion of the crime being perpetrated through a grudge against my father.
I therefore insist that my case should be sympathetically reviewed for compensation.
I maintain that I am entitled to this compensation unless you can produce evidence to prove that the crime was non-political and not one of the series of atrocities committed in Egypt in 1919.
I have etc.,
(Signed) Lillian M. Lane.
To the Secretary of State,
Foreign Office,
LONDON.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal letter from Mrs. Lillian Lane to the British Foreign Office, written from Witley, Surrey, on January 7, 1925. She is referencing a previous communication from the Foreign Office dated December 31, 1924. She is challenging the official classification of an 'outrage' committed against her father in Egypt in 1919. The Foreign Office had apparently categorized the incident as 'non-political' (likely to deny compensation claims related to political unrest), whereas Mrs. Lane argues that it was part of a series of political atrocities during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution and demands a review of her claim for compensation.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of diplomatic correspondence from the British Foreign Office archives, reflecting the administrative aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. Following the widespread anti-colonial uprisings in Egypt, the British government faced numerous claims for compensation from British subjects or their families who were victims of violence. The document highlights the bureaucratic process of 'classifying' violent incidents as either 'political' (often eligible for state compensation or diplomatic intervention) or 'non-political' (common criminal acts). Mrs. Lillian Lane’s letter serves as a primary source for understanding the personal and legal struggles of British expatriates seeking redress for losses incurred during the turbulent period of Egyptian decolonization efforts.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Sir,
I have the honour to submit the following letter, on the subject of my father's death in Cairo, and in support of one recently written to you by my sister (Mrs. James Lane, White Hart Hotel, Witley, Surrey) on our behalf, and request you to afford same your most kind and considerate attention.
On the 28th March 1919, at Cairo, Egypt, my father (Walter William Davies) was assassinated and my mother severely wounded, at our late residence, 12, Charia El Antikhana el Masria, in consequence of which an appeal was lodged at the Cairo Court for indemnity. The case, however, was 'turned down' for reasons best known to those who failed to consider it.
How could mother, in her then weakened state and distracted mind, barely out of hospital, have expected to give clear evidence, as witness in the case, as to the motive, etc., for the crime?
Since, therefore, the Egyptian Government could not - or would not - accept responsibility and compensate to the best of their power, I appeal to you, in the name of our British Government, to hear and consider our case.
It has been suggested that a portion of the £500,000 fine imposed on the Egyptian Government, should be distributed among...
Right Honourable
Stanley Baldwin, M.P.,
10, Downing Street,
LONDON.

Maison Rêve,
274, Thimble Mill Road,
Warley,
15th January, 1925.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal petition addressed to British Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin regarding the assassination of the petitioner's father, Walter William Davies, in Cairo on March 28, 1919. The author argues that the subsequent legal claim for indemnity in the Cairo courts was unfairly dismissed, citing the mother's inability to provide testimony due to her physical and mental trauma following the attack. The petitioner requests that the British government intervene to secure compensation, specifically suggesting that funds be drawn from the £500,000 fine previously levied against the Egyptian government.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1925 petition sent to British Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin concerning the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The assassination of Walter William Davies occurred during a period of intense anti-colonial unrest in Egypt. The document highlights the personal grievances of British subjects who felt abandoned by the legal processes in Cairo and sought redress through the British government, referencing the collective fine imposed on Egypt by the British authorities as a potential source for private compensation.

among the relatives of Britishers killed in Egypt, and there are certainly a number of those (even more so than we) to whom even a small compensation would prove beneficial.
Should any supplementary information relating to the facts of our particular case be required, I am quite prepared to furnish same in detail to the best of my knowledge.
If the circumstances of our sad loss do not appear to justify indemnity in the eyes of the British Government, or to warrant further enquiry, then I would like to mention and recall to their mind a mistake made by the War Office in connection with my demobilisation from the Army, but for which I should have returned earlier to my home in Cairo (whence I came to England expressly to join the Forces in November 1914), at a time when my mere presence in the house would most probably have thwarted the assassins in their purpose, as I should have taken proper precautions in view of the political unrest extant at that time.
The mistake alluded to was that the War Office (or those officials responsible for the addresses of individual soldiers and Units in France) lost my address and at the same time confounded the "B" schedule with the "A" of the repatriation scheme, for whereas I had applied for same under "A", I was afterwards informed that my name appeared under "B" by mistake. This fact and the losing - or mislaying - of my address delayed my release from the Army by at least two months.
I may add in conclusion that Lady Allenby saw my mother at the hospital in Cairo and "assured her that she would be compensated as far as possible".
Of course, mother has since died, and it is for us children that I now plead, and I hope that you, Sir, may see fit to consider our case favourably.
I am, etc.,
(Signed) Victor W. Davies.

He argues that his delayed demobilization from the British Army, caused by a War Office administrative error regarding his repatriation status, prevented him from returning to Cairo in time to protect his mother from political assassins. He references a promise of compensation made by Lady Allenby to his mother and appeals for the government to reconsider his family's case.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a personal petition written by Victor W. It highlights the administrative chaos within the British War Office regarding the repatriation of soldiers and the personal toll of the political violence in Cairo during that period. The mention of Lady Allenby (wife of Field Marshal Edmund Allenby, the British High Commissioner for Egypt) provides a specific historical context, linking the personal tragedy of the Davies family to the broader British colonial administration in Egypt.

Sir,

No. 126/66/16,

respectfully submit that the explanations required
should be submitted directly by that Government

(Signed) Lillian M. Lane.

Under Secretary of State,
Foreign Office,
London, S.W.1.

She is requesting a copy of an official report from 1919 regarding the murder of her father in Cairo. She further challenges the British government's classification of the murder as 'non-political,' arguing that the government bears responsibility for the safety of British subjects and should provide a direct explanation for their stance rather than redirecting her to other authorities.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
FOREIGN OFFICE
2nd February, 1920.

Madam,
In reply to your letter of the 16th ultimo and previous correspondence, relative to the murder of your father in Egypt in 1919, I am directed by Mr. Secretary Chamberlain to state that it seems possible that you may be under some misapprehension as to the degree of responsibility which attaches to foreign governments in the case of such crimes.

2. I am to point out that a foreign government cannot be called upon to pay compensation to the victims of crimes committed within its borders unless some ground exists upon which the government can be held responsible for the commission of the crime in question. Should, for instance, a foreigner be murdered in this country, His Majesty's Government could not be called upon to pay compensation to the representatives of the victim unless valid reasons could be adduced for maintaining that the government were in some way responsible for the commission of the crime or its non-prevention by the taking of proper precautions.

3. Hitherto His Majesty's Government have been unable to find any adequate ground upon which the Egyptian Government can be held responsible for the murder of your father in 1919. If His Majesty's Government had been aware of any evidence on which they could base such a claim, the Secretary of State would have presented a claim for compensation in pursuance of the general care which he exercises over the welfare of British subjects.

[Address:]
11 Elm Lane,
Southwick,
Brighton.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official letter from the British Foreign Office to a woman regarding the murder of her father in Egypt in 1919. The letter explains that the British government cannot demand compensation from the Egyptian government for the murder unless there is evidence that the Egyptian government was negligent or complicit in the crime. It clarifies that the same standard of international law would apply to the British government if a foreigner were murdered in Britain. The letter concludes that the Foreign Office has found no grounds to hold the Egyptian government responsible for the specific murder of the recipient's father.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal diplomatic response from the British Foreign Office, dated February 2, 1920, addressing a claim for compensation following the murder of a British subject in Egypt during the political unrest of 1919. The document serves as a legal clarification of the limits of state responsibility under international law during the period of the British Protectorate in Egypt. It illustrates the bureaucratic process of handling claims from British citizens against foreign governments, emphasizing that the British government would only pursue such claims if there were clear evidence of state negligence or failure to provide security, thereby setting a precedent for how the Foreign Office managed individual grievances within the context of imperial administration.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPY.
[J 432/68/16.]

SOUTHWICK RECTORY COTTAGE,
SOUTHWICK,
BRIGHTON.
10/2/25.

Sir,
With reference to your No. J 227/68/16 dated February 2nd, I have before me a passport issued by the Foreign Office to my father which requires that the Egyptian Government "should afford him every assistance and protection of which he may stand in need."
I submit, therefore, that I am under no misapprehension as to the degree of responsibility which attaches to the Egyptian Government in this matter and I look for the support of the Foreign Office in this my application for compensation for the murder of my father.
The murder of a British subject by an Oriental in an Oriental country is an extreme outrage and seldom perpetrated. When no less than nineteen such outrages occur it is very obvious that influences, other than ordinary crime, were at work amongst the population to induce them to commit such outrages.
These influences were well known to be political and there is no doubt that the murder of my father was the first of these political murders. He was murdered during the first political riots in Cairo in 1919. The murderers decamped at once, as usual in all political crime, after committing the outrage; they stole no thing.
Grounds therefore do exist upon which the Egyptian Government can be held responsible and I regret, the Under Secretary of State, Foreign Office, London.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal letter written by a child of a British subject murdered in Cairo in 1919. The author is writing to the British Foreign Office in 1925 to demand compensation from the Egyptian Government. The author argues that the murder was not an 'ordinary crime' but a 'political murder' linked to the 1919 riots, and cites the protection clause in their father's passport as the basis for the British government's obligation to intervene and secure compensation.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a copy of a 1925 diplomatic appeal regarding the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It highlights the tensions between British colonial officials and the Egyptian government regarding the safety and compensation of British subjects during a period of intense nationalist unrest. The author frames the murder of their father as a political act rather than a criminal one, attempting to leverage the British Foreign Office's diplomatic weight to extract reparations from the Egyptian state, reflecting the broader geopolitical friction during the transition of Egypt toward nominal independence.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Dear Chancery, (1904/25) Your despatch No. 108 of the 12th February: list of Englishmen murdered in Egypt since 1916. We are repeatedly pestered by the children of the late Mr. W. Davies with requests for the reasons which led His Majesty's Government to consider that the murder was non-political. In Lord Allenby's telegram No. 452 of the 29th March, 1919, he stated that there were no reasons to suppose that the crime had any political significance. We have replied to the children of the deceased and to a Member of Parliament who has enquired on their behalf that by international practice His Majesty's Government are bound to consider that a foreign Government cannot be called upon to pay compensation to the victims of crime committed within its borders unless some ground exists upon which the government can be held responsible. I will speak to Mr. Hughes (1/13) and perusal can't remember any details. A.T.W. 14/5.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal diplomatic communication from the Foreign Office in London to the Chancery in Cairo. It addresses the persistent inquiries from the children of a Mr. W. Davies, who was murdered in Egypt. The Foreign Office explains that, based on a 1919 telegram from Lord Allenby, the murder was deemed non-political. Consequently, the British government maintains that, under international law, they cannot demand compensation from the Egyptian government for crimes committed within its borders unless there is evidence of state negligence or responsibility. A handwritten note at the top indicates a follow-up action by an official named Mr. Hughes.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British diplomatic correspondence from 1925 regarding the aftermath of political instability in Egypt following the 1919 revolution. It highlights the British government's policy of distancing itself from individual compensation claims for British subjects murdered in Egypt, provided the crimes were classified as 'non-political' by the High Commissioner (Lord Allenby). This reflects the delicate balance of the British Protectorate era, where the British sought to maintain order while limiting their financial and legal liability for the safety of British nationals in a volatile post-war Egyptian political climate.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Dear Wiggin,
Murder of Mr. Walter Davies.
I have run through the dossier of this case. I understand that you merely wish to know if there is anything in the enquiry pointing to the crime being a political one, and that you do not require a summary of the evidence.
I find that Mr. Walter Davies was a contractor living with his wife in a flat in Cairo. They employed one servant a cook who slept out. The cook had been obtained 6 months before the crime from a registry office. He had at first given satisfaction but shortly before the crime had become unsatisfactory and given trouble.
On the evening of the 29th March 1919 Mr. & Mrs. Davies returned from a walk about 7.20 and finding the cook was not in Mrs. Davies began to get ready the dinner. The cook came in shortly afterwards. Mr. & Mrs. Davies then sat down to dinner. The cook brought in the soup and retired closing the door after him but Mr. Davies rang for him and ordered him to leave it open as the night was warm. Shortly after the cook had again retired two men came in one of whom stabbed and killed Mr. Davies and the other attacked and wounded Mrs. Davies who however managed to defend herself and to scream for help on which the two men fled. After the men had gone the cook came in and Mrs. Davies sent him for assistance.
Mrs. Davies in her statement evidence ed that 3 days before the crime an attempt had been made as if with a diamond to cut a piece out of one of the panes of glass of the front door and on the night of the crime they noticed that the lock had been oiled.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter addressed to Mr. Wiggin regarding the murder of Mr. Walter Davies. It summarizes the investigation into the crime, specifically addressing whether there was a political motive. It details the events of the evening of March 29, 1919, in Cairo, where Mr. and Mrs. Davies were attacked by two men while dining, resulting in the death of Mr. Davies and the wounding of his wife. The letter notes that the couple's cook, who had recently become problematic, was present at the time of the attack. It also mentions suspicious activity prior to the murder, including an attempt to cut the glass of the front door and the oiling of the lock.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal report from the British High Commission in Egypt, dated June 2, 1925, concerning the 1919 murder of a British contractor named Walter Davies in Cairo. The correspondence serves as an administrative review of the case file to determine if the murder was politically motivated—a significant concern during the period of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British occupation. The text provides a detailed eyewitness account of the home invasion and murder, highlighting the security concerns of British expatriates in Cairo during a time of intense civil unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
2.
PARQUET
DES
TRIBUNAUX INDIGENES.
AVOCAT DU PROCUREUR GENERAL

Mr. Davies kept a safe in the flat for money etc.
After the murder a witness spoke of his knowledge of
an attempt having been made by certain bad characters to
enter the flat by cutting out a pane of glass in the front
door in order to steal the contents of the safe. Evidence
was also produced showing that the cook had been seen with
these same bad characters.
Mrs. Davies stated that in her opinion the object of
the criminals was theft and that the murder was committed
in order to facilitate the theft but that the criminals
were frightened at her screams.
The cook was sent to trial, sentenced to penal servitude
for life.
There is nothing in this case either from the researches
of the police or from the Parquet enquiry to suggest that
the murder was in any way connected with politics and Mr.
Davies was not an official. In fact it bears all the marks
of an ordinary case of murder committed for theft and
clumsily carried out.
I can only recall one other case of an Englishman since
1914 being murdered in his flat that of captain Foster of
the Khedivial mail in 1914 and that case was clearly non-
political but theft.
Our experience of political murders in Egypt shows that
they are not carried out in this way. All that could possibly
be urged to give a political flavour to the case is that in
normal times the case would probably not have happened.

Yours sincerely,
G. H. Hughes
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal report from the Parquet of the Native Courts (Tribunaux Indigènes) in Egypt, written by an official (likely an Advocate to the Prosecutor General). It details the investigation into the murder of a man named Mr. Davies. The author argues that the murder was a botched robbery rather than a political assassination, citing evidence such as a previous attempt to break into the victim's safe and the involvement of the cook, who was subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment. The author compares this to the 1914 murder of Captain Foster to establish a pattern of non-political crimes against foreigners in Egypt.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a page from an official legal report originating from the Parquet of the Native Courts in British-occupied Egypt. It provides a rare glimpse into the administrative and judicial handling of criminal cases involving foreign nationals during the early 20th century. The text is significant for its explicit attempt to distinguish between 'ordinary' criminal activity (theft/murder) and 'political' violence, a distinction that was crucial for the British colonial administration in Egypt to maintain order and manage public perception during a period of rising nationalist sentiment.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
British Consulate
Dear Sir,
I have the honour to inform you, that according to your order to make my communication in writing about Mohamed Hassan Ellawi who is prisoner at Police Office from 15th March 1919.
After enquiring well I found that Hassan Ellawi his father has sent him to (musta-hader) to get him some goods, and while the boy going in way he saw at a distance - people crowded opposite the Hulk Caffe place near the station. Before he arrived, he saw a man running back with some Cognac bottles, and he pulled one of him, and returned back to get what his father order him. When he got near to his father shops another boy took the bottle from him and drank it all. And near the shops of his father a person called Ali reported give notice to the Police that he saw that Mohamed Ellawi got Cognac bottles, the police has pitched the house & the shops, did not find any thing, because Mohamed Ali reported gives this news to Police, because he is enemy to the boy father. -- Ali is inspired sir, he is from the persons whom pulled down the Consul (arma) yesterday. I therefore beg of your kindness to give order.
ai_content.english_translation: British Consulate. Dear Sir, I have the honor to inform you that, in accordance with your order to provide my communication in writing regarding Mohamed Hassan Ellawi, who has been a prisoner at the Police Office since March 15, 1919. After conducting a thorough inquiry, I discovered that Hassan Ellawi, his father, had sent him to a 'musta-hader' (attendant/porter) to fetch some goods. While the boy was on his way, he saw a crowd of people gathered opposite the Hulk Cafe near the station. Before he arrived, he saw a man running away with some bottles of Cognac; he took one from him and then returned to complete his father's errand. When he neared his father's shop, another boy took the bottle from him and drank it. Near his father's shop, a person named Ali reported to the police that he saw Mohamed Ellawi with Cognac bottles. The police searched the house and the shops but found nothing, because Mohamed Ali provided this false report to the police as he is an enemy of the boy's father. Ali, sir, is one of the individuals who pulled down the Consular emblem yesterday. I therefore request your kindness to issue an order.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal report from a British Consular official, likely in a Middle Eastern context (given the mention of the 'Consul arma' or emblem and the Arabic script on the facing page), dated March 1919. It details an investigation into the arrest of a youth, Mohamed Hassan Ellawi, who was accused of possessing alcohol (Cognac). The author argues that the arrest was a malicious fabrication by a local rival named Ali, who had a personal vendetta against the boy's father and was also involved in the politically charged act of vandalizing the British Consular emblem the previous day. The document highlights the intersection of local personal disputes and anti-colonial political unrest in the immediate post-WWI period.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
BRITISH CONSULAR AGENCY
MANSOURAH
EGYPT
2nd, April 1919
Dear Mr. Gout,
I hear a disturbance took place yesterday afternoon in the secondary portion of the Rashad School and speeches were made in the school insulting to Great Britain Teachers aiding and approving the speakers sentiments and insulting language.
I enclose a letter from the Egyptian Engineering Company concerning one of their clerks stranded at Luxor and if you can indicate any means whereby they can send him money about E.10 and facilitate his return either by boat, or rail to Mansourah they will be much obliged.
The anual Sports of the Government Primary School and Technical School are generally held during the month of April, and these are attended by probably 800 to 1000 Europeans and Native.
The Head Master Mohamed Bey Obeid called here yesterday to ask me for the list I usually give him of the British Subjects having special knowledge of Sports who are nominated by me to act (gratuitously of course) as Starters, Time Keepers, Judges &c.,
I told him that, taking into consideration the bad feeling caused in Mansourah by the conduct of the Students of the Government Schools, joining in these demonstrations, and subsequent destruction of life and property, I thought the best thing he could do would be to abandon the Sports for this year. I consider it highly undesirable for such a large number of people Europeans and Natives to gather together owing to the bad feeling aroused by the conduct of the Students taking part in these disturbances. He agreed with me in this and there will be no public sports at the Government School here this year. He informed me he had written a report of the conduct of his students on the 15th, March, he had written a report of the Daniel) and, (if I may be permitted to suggest it) you would probably find the contents of this report interesting if you can obtain a copy from the Ministry of Public Instruction.
I also enclose the copy of a letter in Arabic I have just received concerning Mahmoud Bey Abou Nosseir who has gone to Cairo, as he knows he will be arrested if he returns here. He frequents the Splendid Bar, Cairo.
The writer of this letter in known to me and he is willing to give evidence when called upon provided that his testimony is heard secretly not in open Court as he and several others fear reprisals.
I enclose a leaflet which is being distributed to day in the Streets and Cafes here.
I am surprised to notice that Abdellatif Bey El Kakabaty had the impertinence to go to the Residency on the 31st, March, with the Notables of Cairo. This man is a member of the Legislative Council one of the principals of the Nationalists here, and one of the most important Nationalists in Mansourah. How much he is implicated in the organisation of the recent disturbances I cannot say, but he took the precaution to be absent at his farm about 8 or 10 miles from Mansourah while the riots were taking place. Mahmoud Bey Abou Nosseir is one of his puppets, and is a stupid fanatical person. Probably Mahmoud Bey Abou Nasr is a misprint of Nosseir, in the list of persons who were present at that function.
There are far too many of these Nationalists at liberty here at present and they are very active in their propaganda witness the present leaflet. I have a list of these persons but my informants are afraid to give evidence before open court.
I hope to receive authority to arrest these vile wretches, and as soon as I obtain it I shall not lose much time in putting it in force.
I am, Yours truly,
[Signature]
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official report from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, dated April 2, 1919, addressed to a Mr. Gout. It details the political unrest in the region following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The author reports on anti-British sentiment in local schools, the cancellation of annual sports events due to security concerns, and provides intelligence on local Nationalist figures, specifically Abdellatif Bey El Kakabaty and Mahmoud Bey Abou Nosseir, whom the author characterizes as agitators. The author requests authorization to arrest these individuals and notes the difficulty of obtaining testimony due to fear of reprisals.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a primary source from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. It provides a vivid account of the administrative and security challenges faced by British officials during the uprising, including the monitoring of Nationalist activities, the suppression of student demonstrations, and the reliance on local informants. The document highlights the tension between the British colonial administration and the Egyptian Nationalist movement, illustrating the use of intelligence gathering and the desire for summary arrests to maintain order during a period of widespread civil unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Mansourah, Egypt. 3rd, April 1919. Dear Mr. Gout. I was unable to complete my letter of yesterday, and send it to you to reach the post at 3.30 p.m. and I send it with this one to-day. These agitators are becoming bolder by their apparent immunity from arrest and my futile order to arrest Mahmoud Bey Abou Hossein is a sign of public ridicule, and regarded by them as a sign of weakness. Hassan Nofal made a speech yesterday at the Café of Mathieu near the Hospital concerning the intended strike of the Government and other employees to take place to-day and Saturday. From enquiries I have made to-day I learn that this strike is not quite a success because some of the employees are working. There is serious trouble ahead unless a very strong and peremptory order is as soon as possible issued by the Ministry of the Interior to the authorities here to arrest:- Hassan Nofal Native Lawyer Abdel Wahab El Borray Native Lawyer the men mentioned in my oval despatch of 20th, December last. This letter has taken an active part in the agitators making speeches ag. against the British Rule in Egypt. This person has been in hiding for the last week at Kafr Badaway and I was wrongly informed when I told Lieut Harper that Abou Hossein was there. Borray returned to Mansourah yesterday and with characteristic impudence he went to one of the Civil Permit Officers, and demanded a Permit to travel to Cairo and this thing he did not know him) refused the Permit unless he produced a note from the Koudir stating he was a fit and proper person to receive a Permit. Needless to say he did not bring the letter. I am, yours truly, Fred. H. Murdoch. I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient servant, Fred. H. Murdoch, BRITISH CONSULAR AGENT. EDGAR GOUT ESQUIRE H. B. M's Acting Consul Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from the British Consular Agent in Mansourah, Fred H. Murdoch, to Edgar Gout, the Acting British Consul in Cairo. It details the political unrest in Mansourah during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. Murdoch expresses frustration over the perceived weakness of the British administration in failing to arrest local agitators like Hassan Nofal, Abdel Wahab El Borray, and Mahmoud Bey Abou Hossein. He reports on a strike organized by government employees and describes the movements of the agitators, specifically noting that Borray attempted to obtain a travel permit to Cairo despite being a wanted individual.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a primary source from the period of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. It captures the anxiety and administrative frustration of British consular officials stationed in the provinces (Mansourah) as they struggled to maintain order against a rising nationalist movement. The correspondence highlights the breakdown of British authority, the use of strikes as a tool of resistance by Egyptian government employees, and the specific efforts of local British agents to suppress nationalist lawyers and agitators through arrests and travel restrictions.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
BRITISH CONSULAR AGENCY
MANSOURAH
EGYPT
3rd April 1919

Sir,
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your despatch dated 1st April and in accordance with the instructions therein contained, I sent this morning to the Police Station and examined the Consular Coat of Arms. It is absolutely useless, and cannot be used again as a Consular Coat of Arms, because it has been bent horizontally across its width for about 5" or 6" and the letters round the edge of the oval are also damaged, and some of the rest of the enamel splintered off on various parts of the shield. It measures about 4' high X 3' feet wide.

Moreover when it was new in 1887 I had a most substantial oval wooden frame and cornice made to fit the enamelled shield, and strong iron rods to secure it by dowels in the wall so that, a considerable amount of force was required to remove it from its position. Not a vestige of this wood work or the iron rods are now at the Police Office Store where it is now lying.

In ordering a new one please note the old one has the words "VICE CONSULATE" on it whereas this is only "CONSULAR AGENCY".

This wooden frame will now be very costly indeed to make owing to the high price of timber, and I take the liberty to suggest that if a new shield is sent here that the Head Master of the Government Technical School should be instructed to make a completely new frame for it with iron rods, and dowels to secure it to the wall, as I do not now have any workshop or workmen capable of making it.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Jas. H. Murdoch
BRITISH CONSULAR AGENT
EDGAR GOUT ESQUIRE
H. B. M's Acting Consul
Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter from the British Consular Agent in Mansourah, Jas. H. Murdoch, to Edgar Gout, the Acting British Consul in Cairo, dated April 3, 1919. The author reports on the damaged state of the Consular Coat of Arms, which had been removed from its original location and was being held at a police station. He describes the physical damage to the enamel and the loss of the original wooden frame and iron mounting hardware. He requests a replacement shield, noting that the old one incorrectly read 'Vice Consulate' instead of 'Consular Agency', and suggests that the Government Technical School be commissioned to build a new mounting frame due to the high cost of timber and lack of local skilled labor.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, during the immediate post-WWI period. It highlights the logistical challenges faced by British diplomatic outposts in provincial Egyptian cities, specifically regarding the maintenance of official symbols of state authority. The letter provides insight into the material culture of British colonial administration, the reliance on local technical institutions (the Government Technical School), and the bureaucratic process of replacing damaged official property in the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
BRITISH CONSULAR AGENCY
MANSOURAH
EGYPT.
9th, April 1919
Dear Mr. Alban,
A huge demonstration took place here yesterday and passed off peaceably.
The release of Zaglou and his companions instead of having the effect of calming the natives here, has had the opposite effect, and they are all to-day in a state of great excitement and there is an influx of a large number of fellaheen into Mansourah, and I am told that the leaders, and some of those fellaheen are armed.
Yesterday about 10-30 to 11 A.M. a so called peaceful demonstration took place at Aga about 6 miles from Mansourah where there were 25 or 30 Australian Cavalry soldiers, and the demonstrators threw stones at them.-Then one of the mob rushed up to them and grasped the bridle of a horse.-A soldier was shot and he was given me by a resident at Aga and is not official.-Then the Mamour came with the native police and dispersed the crowd.-Some time ago the Government and a private telephone line to Mansourah was cut at Aga, but the former has since been repaired.
I hear that some trouble has arisen this morning at the Provincial Council Girls School, and some Australian Soldiers have been sent there to protect Miss Johnston, Miss Handley and Miss Hughes, 3 British heads of the School, but I have not heard if any damage other than breaking some glass has been done.
I called this morning at the Australian Head Quarters, to pay my respects to two Generals who have come here.
The European shop-keepers here are very doubtful about the result of the so called peaceful demonstration to take place here to-day, as they learn that the leaders and some of the fellaheen who have come into the town are armed, and a large number of fellaheen who have come in to-day doubtless in the hope of getting some loot if any of the shops are looted.-One of these shop-keepers a British Subject asked me if he should close his shop, but I advised him he must do as he thinks proper about the shop, but I advised him he must frequent the streets, and that his family would do well to remain in doors while the demonstration was passing.
I learn that as the leaders are now coming out in the open, and boasting of what they are going to do, that one of them is to post an insulting placard on my house, and if they do me no more harm than that I do not mind.
The whole country is now in a state of unrest, and it looks as if there will be a good deal of serious trouble in the near future and I am afraid it will be accompanied by bloodshed, before tranquility is again restored, but this is my opinion without anything to support it except the aggressive attitude of the whole population and their hatred of any British rule or control of any kind whatever.
I enclose a copy of the Procès Verbal of the meeting held at the Greek Consulate on the 16th March 1919. - Also a programme of the demonstration to take place to-day.
I am,
yours truly,
Fred. J. Murdoch
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal report from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, dated April 9, 1919, addressed to Mr. Alban. The author, Fred J. Murdoch, describes the volatile political climate in Egypt following the release of Saad Zaghloul and his companions. He details civil unrest, including a violent incident at Aga involving Australian cavalry and local fellaheen, the cutting of government telephone lines, and threats against British nationals and property in Mansourah. The document reflects the colonial administration's anxiety regarding the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, noting the arming of protesters and the general anti-British sentiment among the population.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a primary source report from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It provides a granular, on-the-ground account of the civil disobedience and anti-colonial unrest that swept Egypt after the British authorities exiled Saad Zaghloul and his Wafd Party colleagues. The letter highlights the intersection of local nationalist fervor, the presence of Australian imperial troops, and the precarious position of British consular officials and expatriates during the uprising.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Dear Mr. Alban,
The demonstration of yesterday afternoon passed off quietly and nothing happened although I learn that it is intended to have another to-day. These demonstrations cause nearly all the shops in Ismail Street to be closed while it is passing their premises and the shopkeepers are complaining about the frequency of these huge processions.
One of the leaders of the Nationalists has ordered the native shop-keepers in the Suk El Hawgate to close their shops to-day and to-morrow. This is done openly, and as they are docile people they have obeyed this order and they are closed to-day.
I learn that the Armenians and Syrians are very much afraid to-day, and I learn that the Moudir is sending them some extra policemen arranged for their protection.
I learn that the Commandant of Police is warning the people that if they make any demonstration to-day it will be very dangerous for them because the British Soldiers may shoot the demonstrators.
I enclose a copy of some more nonsense concerning the new Ministry.
I am, yours truly, Fred. J. Murdock
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, reporting on civil unrest and nationalist demonstrations in April 1919. It details the closure of shops on Ismail Street and Suk El Hawgate due to political pressure, the fear among minority communities (Armenians and Syrians), the protective measures taken by the local Moudir (governor), and a stern warning issued by the Commandant of Police regarding the potential use of lethal force by British troops against demonstrators.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a primary source record from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, dated April 1919. It provides a contemporary account of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919, a countrywide uprising against the British occupation. The correspondence highlights the intersection of local nationalist agitation, the economic impact of strikes on commercial districts like Ismail Street and Suk El Hawgate, and the escalating security measures employed by British colonial authorities and local officials to suppress dissent. The mention of the 'new Ministry' and the threat of British military intervention underscores the volatile political climate during the transition period following the First World War.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Dear Mr. Gout, 1st April 1919. All is quiet here now, and everything is now assuming normal conditions. Please excuse the errors in spelling and defective composition in my despatches, and letters sent you lately as they were written in great urgency principally with the object of keeping you informed of events here. I am greatly pleased to receive your letter of the 29th March and thank you for its contents. I hand you herewith enclosed a copy of the Official Report sent me by the O.C. (Lieut. Harper) in charge of the British Soldiers here, and I may add to it that it was owing to his prompt, and decisive action, and the clever manner in which he arranged and directed his men that a serious riot, destruction of property and possibly massacre of Europeans was arrested, and peremptorily stopped. I am informed by the other Consular Officials that in their reports to their respective superiors in Alexandria, and Cairo, they are unanimous in their appreciation of the conduct of Lieut. Harper, who, by his prompt, and efficient action doubtless prevented a wholesale destruction of life, and property of Europeans, and I agree with this expression of their opinion regarding the conduct of Lieut. Harper, I wish to emphasise this because I learn he has been blamed for exceeding his authority, and if blame is to be attached to him I am afraid that the more guilty of the two is myself, who authorised him to arrest Mahmoud Bey Abou Nosseir, and I did not at the same time advise H.E. the Moudir because it is useless to send such an order through his subordinates 3/4 of whom are Nationalist and the person to be arrested seems to get notice in good time to change his residence hiding place before the police come. Rumours occasionally reach me of the fabrication of bombs, but so far the investigations I have carried out have not been successful in finding any trace of the manufactory of any bombs, I am still pursuing my enquiries in this matter. Yours truly, [Signed] Murdoch, British Consul, [Location illegible/M...]
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from a British Consul (Murdoch) to a Mr. Gout, dated April 1, 1919. It discusses the restoration of order following civil unrest, praises the decisive actions of Lieutenant Harper in preventing a riot and potential massacre of Europeans, and defends Harper against accusations of exceeding his authority. The author takes responsibility for ordering the arrest of Mahmoud Bey Abou Nosseir, explaining that he bypassed the local Moudir (governor) because the Moudir's subordinates were Nationalists who would warn the suspect. The letter also mentions ongoing investigations into the rumored manufacture of bombs.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of diplomatic correspondence from the British Consulate in Egypt during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It provides a primary account of the British administrative perspective on the unrest, highlighting the tension between British military/consular authorities and local Egyptian officials (the Moudir and his subordinates). The text illustrates the 'Nationalist' sentiment prevalent among local officials and the British reliance on military force (Lieut. Harper) to maintain order and protect European interests during a period of intense anti-colonial agitation.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPY
Report on proceedings in Menoufia for 13th March 1919

Huge demonstrations took place early in the morning. I received information that the people were going to attempt to disarm the Egyptian Police who would not fire. I immediately despatched one officer with twenty other ranks to the Police Station. This force was sent in the main street by thousands of demonstrators carrying flags and sticks; they were also followed by thousands of other demonstrators.

The troops were forced to fire in order to disperse the crowd and to prevent the police have reported seventy five casualties including the Armour of Police.

I consulted the Governor and decided to disarm the Egyptian Police who would probably have allowed their arms to fall into the hands of the rebels.

A meeting of the European Consular Agents was held and they decided that the Europeans should all be transferred to a central locality, where they could be guarded, as no attempt had yet been made on any Europeans lives.

The British however agreed with one proposal, and gathered together at one central point, and I was able to supply them with the necessary weapons with which to protect themselves until the arrival of the troops.

The Armoured Train arrived about 14.30 hours and Capt. Hughes (Essex Regt.) met the Moufti and two of the Chief Nationalists. He he would have them and other ringleaders arrested and shot.

During the remainder of the day nothing unusual occurred.

(Signed) J.W. Harper Lieut.
O.C. Troops
Menoufia
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official report detailing the civil unrest in Menoufia on March 13, 1919, during the Egyptian Revolution. The author, Lieutenant J.W. Harper, describes the mobilization of thousands of demonstrators, the decision to disarm local Egyptian police to prevent weapons from falling into the hands of protesters, the consolidation of European residents for protection, and the arrival of British military reinforcements via an armoured train to restore order.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a contemporary report from the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, a pivotal period of anti-colonial uprising against British rule. The text provides a first-hand account of the British military response to nationalist demonstrations in Menoufia. It highlights the breakdown of trust between British authorities and the local Egyptian police, the strategic use of armoured trains to suppress unrest, and the protective measures taken for European expatriates. The mention of 'Capt. Hughes' and the threat to arrest and execute 'ringleaders' illustrates the harsh, militarized nature of the British administration's response to the nationalist movement during this period.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Dear Mr. Gout,
The Australian Troops arrived here on the 3rd, and the Officers are to take charge of all matters concerning the Province of Dakahlia.
The New-Zealand Officers are in charge of matters of Gharbia.
Mr. de Smidt, Inspector of Agriculture informed Mr. Smith, Inspector of Irrigation that his (Mr. Smith's) employees were afraid to come to their work because they had been warned by the "Black Hand" that if they did go to work, sulphuric acid would be thrown in their faces. Mr. de Smidt promised to send me a copy of the leaflet but so far I have not yet received it.
I enclose the copy of an arabic poem which has been posted up at the Moudirieh, and the Mixed Tribunals, and I send you the original very quaint translation of the poem.
I am told these leaflets are being distributed by the Students of the Government Schools.
I am receiving anonymous letters more or less concerning this "Black Hand" and I enclose one herewith which has just arrived.
The sooner these Courts Martial begin their work and some drastic punishment is inflicted including a good deal of the application of the lash, and the sooner they hang the better. As soon as these punishments are begun the whole thing will collapse.
I am, yours truly, Mrs. J. Murdock
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter written in English from Mrs. J. Murdock to Mr. Gout, dated April 5, 1919, in Mansourah, Egypt. It details the arrival of Australian and New Zealand troops to manage the provinces of Dakahlia and Gharbia during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It reports on intimidation tactics used by a group identified as the 'Black Hand' against government employees, specifically mentioning threats of sulphuric acid attacks. It also discusses the distribution of anti-British leaflets by government school students and the circulation of an Arabic poem posted at the Moudirieh (provincial administrative headquarters) and the Mixed Tribunals. The author advocates for harsh military justice, including corporal punishment and executions, to suppress the unrest.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a primary source from the period of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. It provides a colonial perspective on the civil unrest, documenting the British military response (the arrival of ANZAC troops) and the administrative anxiety regarding the 'Black Hand'—a clandestine group associated with the nationalist movement. The letter highlights the breakdown of civil order, the role of students in the resistance, and the reliance on Courts Martial to maintain control in the Nile Delta provinces of Dakahlia and Gharbia.

The proclamation issued by the Egyptian Ministry on April 14, 1919
The Council of Ministers met and decided the following:
First: That the Egyptian Government requests His Excellency the British High Commissioner to lift martial law from the country.
Second: That the Egyptian Government also requests His Excellency the British High Commissioner to lift the protectorate over Egypt and recognize its complete independence.
Third: That the Egyptian Government requests His Excellency the British High Commissioner to stop all demonstrations in the streets of Egyptian cities.
Fourth: That the Egyptian Government requests His Excellency the British High Commissioner to maintain security and order in the country.
This proclamation continues to stir Egyptian public opinion.

ai_content.transcribed_text: BRITISH CONSULAR AGENCY, MANSOURAH. 13th, April 1919. Lieut-Col. Bailey, D.S.O. Australian Mobile Column, Mansourah. Sir, I hand you herewith enclosed the copy of an anonymous letter I received yesterday afternoon, and which had the Alexandria post mark on it, of yesterday's date. The letter gives the names of some people presumably residing at the Markaz AGA, who apparently intend to kill as and all are said to possess ARMS. I do not attach much importance to the contents of the letter; but I do not think it prudent to ignore the information therein given, especially in the matter of a KAB said to be in possession of these people, for which they are not likely to have a 'ROKEAS, OR PERMIT, to possess any them? It is absolutely useless to advise, or show H.E. the Moudir the contents of this letter, because he is now 'A NATIONALIST'. Moreover three fourths of his subordinates are the same. Consequently, if I were to send, or show the letter to him; the arms would be removed, before any search, or inspection could be made, the arms would be removed, and the search would be rendered useless. I take the liberty to suggest that, if you think it expedient; might send H.E. the Moudir an official notice that you require 10, or 12 Policemen preferably mounted, to go with your men with a British Officer because you may require to go into some native houses, this precaution is necessary in order that you should not be accused of INVASION OF DOMICILE. You might give the insignificant village of SANDOUP as the place you desire to search, then after a search there, continue on the way to AGA by continuing upstream on the left bank of the Mansourah Canal to AGA about 5 or 6 miles away. At Sandoup the first thing to be done is to get control of the telephone and before leaving to render it useless for communicating with Mansourah, some of your men should be posted at the Police Station, in order that the village may be duly reported and if AGA is put temporarily out of connection before your men start, I think it would be a wise precaution. I shall call upon you this afternoon and discuss the matter; possibly you may devise a more effective manner in which to accomplish the same object, viz: if these people are found to have arms in their possession without a 'ROKSA' they may be imprisoned for infringement of MARTIAL LAW. I have the honour to be, Sir, your obedient servant, Fred. J. Murdoch, British Consular Agent.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from the British Consular Agent in Mansourah to Lieutenant-Colonel Bailey of the Australian Mobile Column. It details intelligence received via an anonymous letter regarding individuals in the Markaz of Aga who are allegedly armed and planning violence. The author expresses distrust of the local Egyptian official (the Moudir) and his subordinates, labeling them 'Nationalists' who would tip off the suspects if warned. The author proposes a tactical ruse: requesting mounted police for a search of the village of Sandoup as a cover, then proceeding to Aga to seize arms and enforce Martial Law, while also neutralizing the local telephone lines to prevent communication.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British colonial administrative correspondence from April 1919, a period of intense political unrest in Egypt known as the 1919 Revolution. It illustrates the deep suspicion held by British consular officials toward local Egyptian administrative authorities (the Moudir and his staff), whom they viewed as compromised by the Nationalist movement. The letter provides a rare, granular look at the intersection of British military intelligence, colonial policing tactics, and the use of Martial Law to suppress perceived anti-colonial activity in the Nile Delta region.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Mansourah, 25th May 1919. Dear Mr. Alban, I have received the enclosed letter from Mr. Anis Nasr the lessee of the Municipal Theatre whose lease expires on the 31st May current. The lease was lately the subject of an adjudication, and if the statements in the letter are correct the Municipal Councillors have leased it to a criminal, by the use of a fictitious person's name. This is no business of mine to whom the Councillors let the Theatre, but when I hear on what I regard as fairly good authority that it is intended to be used for political meetings and propaganda against the British Authorities in Egypt, I consider it my business to do what I can to prevent the Theatre being used for such a purpose the more especially as I learn from the contents of the letter sent me by Mr. Anis Nasr that the real lessee is a criminal. I think it my duty to try and prevent such a person obtaining a lease of the Theatre. Judging by the leaflet I enclose, and from the name of the first play to be produced 'THE HEROES OF MANSOURAH' I have not the least doubt about the object of this pretended lease who I learn is absolutely incapable of managing a Theatre and is only a puppet of Mahmoud Bey Abou Honeth a most fanatical person who is alleged to have been very active in instigating the students in their demonstrations during March last teaching them to call out in the streets 'Yaish El Osmanly' 'Yaish El Afondina' 'Fatsh Zagloul' &c. This Nosseir is the same person who escaped to Talkha in a carriage fearing arrest, when I ordered the re-arrest of Shoukri Sadek the person who is alleged instigated the removal of the Consular Coat of Arms. The Municipal Council have granted the lease to this fictitious person provisionally but the lease must be approved and ratified by Dr. Batta, and I writing this letter in duplicate an order that you may, if you consider it expedient send the copy to him as Director of Municipalities so that he may know the object of this criminal in leasing the Theatre with funds probably furnished by Nosseir. He is not a fit, and proper person to be a member of the Municipal Council. I am, yours truly, Fred. J. Murdoch.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter written in English by Fred J. Murdoch in Mansourah, Egypt, on May 25, 1919, addressed to Mr. Alban. It concerns the lease of the Municipal Theatre in Mansourah, which Murdoch alleges has been fraudulently obtained by a criminal using a fictitious name to facilitate anti-British political propaganda. The letter details concerns regarding the involvement of local figures like Mahmoud Bey Abou Honeth in student demonstrations and anti-British slogans, and requests that the Director of Municipalities, Dr. Batta, intervene to prevent the ratification of the lease.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British consular correspondence from the immediate post-WWI period in Egypt (1919), a time of intense nationalist agitation against British occupation. The letter highlights the British administration's anxiety regarding the use of public spaces (like the Municipal Theatre) for nationalist propaganda. It provides a window into the administrative tensions between local Municipal Councils and British officials, as well as the specific political climate in Mansourah, where local figures were actively organizing against the British presence through demonstrations and political theater.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
British Consular Agency
Mansourah 23rd, August 1919.
Sir,
FORCIBLE REMOVAL OF THE BRITISH CONSULAR COAT OF ARMS FROM MY HOUSE DESTROYING, THROWING IT INTO THE RIVER, AND SUBSEQUENTLY INSULTING IT.
I send you herewith enclosed the copy of a letter received from the CHPF du Parquet, Mansourah, in which he gives the names of two persons, who have been sentenced to one year, and six month's imprisonment respectively, in connection with the forcible removal of the CONSULAR COAT OF ARMS from my house, by a mob, on the 15th, March last, destroying, and throwing it into the river, and subsequently insulting it, until it was rescued by H. F. the Moudir from the mob at the POLICE STATION.
He mentions that the PARQUET have made an appeal, asking that these sentences be increased and should be quadrupled, as they are out of all proportion with the gravity of the offence, and gross insult to HIS MAJESTY'S GOVERNMENT.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal diplomatic report from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah to the British High Commission in Cairo. It details a criminal incident occurring on March 15th, 1919, where a mob forcibly removed the British Consular Coat of Arms from the agent's residence, destroyed it, threw it into the river, and insulted it before it was recovered by the local Moudir (governor/official) at the police station. The document notes that two individuals were sentenced to one year and six months in prison respectively, but the local Parquet (public prosecutor's office) has appealed these sentences, seeking to have them quadrupled due to the perceived severity of the insult to the British government.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British colonial administrative correspondence from the immediate post-WWI period in Egypt (1919). It reflects the heightened political tensions and anti-British sentiment prevalent during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The destruction of the British Consular Coat of Arms was a symbolic act of defiance against the British Protectorate. The document highlights the British diplomatic efforts to ensure harsh judicial penalties for acts of civil disobedience and anti-colonial protest, framing the destruction of property as a 'gross insult' to the British Crown.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Monsieur le Consul,
J'ai l'honneur de porter à votre connaissance que l'affaire No. 1117 Bandar de Mansourah année 1919 concernant la (Coat of Arms) de Sa Majesté Britannique à Mansourah a été jugée le 10 courant par devant le Tribunal de Mansourah.
Le nommé Aly Mohamed Megahed a été condamné à une année d'imprisonnement avec travail et le nommé Mohamed Aly Hussein a été condamné à six mois d'emprisonnement avec travail.
Le Parquet a interjeté appel demandant l'aggravation de la peine et l'affaire sera vue au appel le 22 Septembre par devant la Cour d'appel à Mansourah.
Veuillez agréer, Monsieur le Consul, l'assurance de ma toute considération.
signé, Kamel Ibrahim
Chef du Parquet de Mansourah.
ai_content.english_translation: Mr. Consul, I have the honor to bring to your attention that case No. 1117 Bandar of Mansourah, year 1919, concerning the (Coat of Arms) of His Britannic Majesty in Mansourah, was judged on the 10th instant before the Tribunal of Mansourah. The individual named Aly Mohamed Megahed was sentenced to one year of imprisonment with labor, and the individual named Mohamed Aly Hussein was sentenced to six months of imprisonment with labor. The Public Prosecutor's Office has filed an appeal requesting an increase in the sentence, and the case will be heard on appeal on September 22nd before the Court of Appeal in Mansourah. Please accept, Mr. Consul, the assurance of my highest consideration. Signed, Kamel Ibrahim, Chief of the Public Prosecutor's Office of Mansourah.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal communication from the Chief of the Public Prosecutor's Office in Mansourah to the British Consul in Cairo, dated August 1919. It details the judicial proceedings of a criminal case (No. 1117) involving the desecration or misuse of the British Coat of Arms in Mansourah. The document outlines the initial sentencing of two individuals, Aly Mohamed Megahed and Mohamed Aly Hussein, and notes that the prosecution has appealed for harsher sentences, with a follow-up hearing scheduled for September 1919. It reflects the administrative and legal oversight maintained by British consular authorities over British interests and symbols in Egypt during the British Protectorate period.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
British Consulate, Cairo
October 24th, 1919.

Sir,

I have the honour to forward herewith copy of a communication which I received from Mr. Rose, who was temporarily acting as Consular Agent at Mansourah and has now been replaced by Mr. Warner, Manager of the Agricultural Bank of Egypt at Mansourah until Mr. Murdoch's return.

I should be glad to know whether the ceremony suggested by Mr. Murdoch is considered desirable.

I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Arthur Alban

The Acting High Commissioner
The Residency
Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal diplomatic letter from the British Consulate in Cairo, dated October 24, 1919. The author, Arthur Alban, is forwarding a communication from Mr. Rose, who had been serving as the acting Consular Agent in Mansourah. Mr. Rose has been replaced by Mr. Warner, the manager of the Agricultural Bank of Egypt in Mansourah, who will hold the position until Mr. Murdoch returns. The letter concludes by asking the Acting High Commissioner whether a ceremony previously suggested by Mr. Murdoch should proceed.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of official British consular correspondence from the post-WWI period in Egypt, specifically during the British Protectorate era. It reflects the administrative management of consular affairs in provincial cities like Mansourah, highlighting the reliance on local bank managers (such as those from the Agricultural Bank of Egypt) to fill temporary diplomatic roles. The mention of a 'ceremony' suggests ongoing efforts to maintain British administrative presence and local relations during a period of significant political unrest in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
British Consular Agency,
Mansourah, Egypt,
Sept. 29th, 1919.

Sir,
I have the honour to advise you that the new Consular Shield has reached me safely. It was Mr. Murdoch's intention to have a demonstration in connection with the British troops stationed here on the occasion of the erection of the sign. I propose to simply erect the shield in the position indicated by Mr. Murdoch i.e. on the balcony of the Nile House well out of ordinary reach and to defer any ceremony that may be necessary until the return of Mr. Murdoch himself. I think it would be nicer and more effective so. Kindly let me have your instructions.

I have the honour
etc.
signed; S. Rose.
Act. British Consular Agent.

Arthur D. Alban Esqr.
British Consul
Cairo.

[Handwritten note]: A shield was delivered by riders -
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from the Acting British Consular Agent in Mansourah to the British Consul in Cairo. It confirms the receipt of a new Consular Shield and proposes a change in the installation plan, suggesting that the formal ceremony be delayed until the return of a Mr. Murdoch, while the shield itself be installed immediately on the balcony of the 'Nile House' to avoid public interference.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative communication from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, dated September 1919, shortly after the end of World War I and during a period of significant political unrest in Egypt (the 1919 Revolution). The correspondence highlights the symbolic importance of the 'Consular Shield' as a marker of British authority and the caution exercised by local consular officials regarding public demonstrations in the presence of British troops. The mention of 'Nile House' and the concern for the shield's security reflect the tense atmosphere of the British protectorate era in Egypt.
