ai_content.transcribed_text:
PRIVATE.
August 29th 1919.

Dear Albin,

I submitted your letter of the 28th
instant relative to the sentences imposed by the
native court on the two natives found guilty of
the removal and destruction of the Coat of Arms
on the Consular Agency building at Manbourah to
His Excellency, who is not prepared to take
any action in the matter. I may add that Amos,
who has also seen the correspondence, is of opinion
that the Parquet is acting quite correctly.
The sentences imposed seem to him, however, to be
inadequate punishment for the offence committed.

Yours sincerely,

(Signed) EDWARD HOPE VERE.

CAIRO.
The Agency, Manbourah.

(Stamp on left margin)
HIGH COMMISSIONER
EGYPT
28 OCT 1919
COVERT
8954
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official letter, typed in English. It is a private communication dated August 29th, 1919, from Edward Hope Vere in Cairo to an individual addressed as 'Dear Albin.' The letter states that Vere submitted Albin's letter of the 28th instant, which concerned the sentences handed down by a native court. These sentences were for two 'natives' found guilty of removing and destroying the Coat of Arms from the Consular Agency building in Manbourah. Vere informs Albin that 'His Excellency' (likely the High Commissioner) is unwilling to take any action on the matter. He further adds that 'Amos,' who has also reviewed the relevant correspondence, believes that 'the Parquet' (the public prosecutor's office) acted correctly. However, Amos also feels that the sentences imposed were 'inadequate punishment' for the offense. The letter concludes with 'Yours sincerely,' and the signature of Edward Hope Vere, with the location 'CAIRO. The Agency, Manbourah.' A stamp on the left margin indicates receipt by the 'HIGH COMMISSIONER EGYPT' on '28 OCT 1919,' with a 'COVERT' marking and reference number '8954.'
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of official correspondence from August 1919, originating from the British administration in Egypt, specifically from Edward Hope Vere in Cairo to 'Albin.' It details a legal case involving two 'natives' convicted by a local court for the removal and destruction of the Coat of Arms from a Consular Agency building in Manbourah. The letter reveals an internal discussion regarding the appropriateness of the sentences. Edward Hope Vere reports that the High Commissioner is not inclined to intervene, while another official, 'Amos,' concurs with the Public Prosecutor's (Parquet's) handling of the case but deems the imposed sentences insufficient. This document provides insight into the administrative and judicial oversight exercised by British authorities in Egypt during the post-World War I period, highlighting their engagement with local legal proceedings and their assessment of offenses against symbols of foreign presence. The receipt stamp from the High Commissioner's office in October 1919 indicates its official processing within the British administrative structure.

The proposal was to install the new British Consular Shield at the Consular Agency in Mansourah without any formal ceremony.

ai_content.transcribed_text: BRITISH CONSULATE, CAIRO. 13th November 1919. Sir, With reference to your despatch No. 8954 of October 20th, I have the honour to transmit, herewith, a letter from the Acting British Consular Agent at Mansoura, in which he proposes that the Consular shield should be restored with due ceremony. It references a previous dispatch (No. 8954) from October 20th regarding a request from the Acting British Consular Agent in Mansoura. The agent is seeking permission to hold a formal ceremony for the restoration of the Consular shield. The author, A. M. Geary, is forwarding this request to the High Commissioner's office for approval.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence from the British occupation period in Egypt. It highlights the formal protocols maintained by British consular officials in provincial cities like Mansoura. The request to restore a 'Consular shield' with 'due ceremony' reflects the importance of symbolic displays of authority and diplomatic presence during the post-WWI period, shortly after the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, when British officials were keen to reassert their status and visibility in the Egyptian provinces.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
No. 398.

Mansoura, 12/11/1919.

Dear Mr. Geary,

I was sorry to miss you when I called at the Consulate in Cairo the other day.

As regards the erection of the consulate shield with 'due ceremony' I would suggest that on the return of Mr. Mirdooh the shield should be publicly erected - that the various Consular Agents and the leading government officials, and notables, should be invited to attend and that the Post Commandant should be requested to supply a guard of honour of British soldiers.

It would also be a case of poetic justice if the two men who were imprisoned for the destruction of the old consular shield should personally erect the new one.

Apart from the gross outrage to the British nation by the forcible removal and destruction of the consular shield I think that there was also a considerable amount of personal spite and vindictiveness shown against Mr. Mirdooh in the action of the so-called Egyptian Nationalist party in the removal and destruction of the consular shield.

It is submitted that the Egyptian is a great believer in the outward display of stone of authority and that if the outrage had been committed
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter written from Mansoura on November 12, 1919, addressed to Mr. Geary. The author discusses the protocol for re-erecting a British consular shield in Cairo following its destruction. The author proposes a public ceremony involving local officials, consular agents, and a British military guard of honor. Furthermore, the author suggests that the individuals previously imprisoned for destroying the original shield should be forced to install the replacement as a form of 'poetic justice.' The text concludes by analyzing the political motivations behind the act, characterizing it as both an affront to the British nation and a personal attack on Mr. Mirdooh by the Egyptian Nationalist party, noting the importance of symbols of authority in the Egyptian context.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of diplomatic correspondence from the immediate post-WWI period in Egypt, a time of intense political unrest and the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. The letter reflects the British administrative perspective on maintaining 'prestige' and 'authority' through symbolic acts, such as the public re-installation of a consular shield. It highlights the tension between British consular officials and the Egyptian Nationalist movement, specifically referencing the destruction of property as a form of political protest and the British desire to use public humiliation (forcing the perpetrators to reinstall the shield) as a deterrent and a display of imperial power.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The Adviser, Ministry of Interior.

8954.

During the disturbances at Mansourah on March 16th last, the British Consular Coat of Arms on Mr. Murdoch's house was forcibly removed by the rioters, destroyed and thrown into the river.

Two persons were sentenced to one year, and six months' imprisonment respectively for their part in this affair.

The new Consular Shield has now reached Mansourah, and I enclose the copy of a letter from His Majesty's Consul at Cairo covering a despatch from the Acting British Consular Agent at Mansourah, suggesting that this shield should be erected with ceremony.

I should be glad to receive your observations upon the advisability of giving effect to this proposal at the present time, before replying to Mr. Henry's letter.

First Secretary.

November 17th, 1919.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official memorandum from the First Secretary to the Adviser of the Ministry of Interior, dated November 17, 1919. It references a previous incident on March 16, 1919, in Mansourah, where rioters destroyed the British Consular Coat of Arms at the residence of a Mr. Murdoch. Two individuals were subsequently prosecuted and sentenced for the act. The letter notes that a replacement shield has arrived and discusses a proposal from the Acting British Consular Agent in Mansourah to hold a formal ceremony for its installation. The First Secretary is seeking the Adviser's opinion on whether such a ceremony is advisable given the political climate before responding to a letter from a Mr. Henry.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British colonial administrative correspondence from the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It highlights the sensitivity of British diplomatic symbols during a period of intense nationalist unrest. The destruction of the Consular Coat of Arms in Mansourah was treated as a significant affront to British authority, leading to criminal prosecutions. The document illustrates the cautious approach of British officials in Egypt, who were weighing the symbolic importance of re-erecting the shield against the risk of provoking further civil disturbances.

BRITISH CONSULATE.
CAIRO.
17th March 1920.
Sir,
I have the honour to report that in accordance with the instructions contained in Despatch No. 6 (K.3943/555/216) of March 2nd from the Foreign Office, I am issuing a letter of authority constituting and appointing Mr. Frederick James Templeton thereto as British Consular Agent at Mansourah.
I have the honour to request that the necessary steps may be taken to secure his recognition by the Egyptian Government and that sanction may now be given for the replacing, with due formality, of the Consular Shield, which was torn down by the rioters last year.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your most obedient servant,
A. S. Henry.
The Residency,
Cairo.

Henry, informs the recipient that, following Foreign Office instructions from March 2, he has appointed Frederick James Templeton as the British Consular Agent in Mansourah. He requests that the Egyptian Government formally recognize this appointment and grant permission to replace the British Consular Shield, which had been destroyed by rioters during the previous year's unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Ref. Residency file 7200/5. 16th April 1920. BRITISH CONSULATE, CAIRO. Sir, With reference to previous correspondence on the subject of the re-erection of the Consular Shield at Mansourah and your memorandum of April 6th, I have the honour to report that Mr. Murdoch states that the shield will be ready in a few days' time. He is anxious that the formality should not be purely local and that the two prisoners, who tore the shield down, should be compelled to uncover it. He asked me whether I could attend in uniform at the ceremony and whether the Ministry of the Interior could be represented and a guard of British troops be present, to prevent any attempt at a demonstration. If His Excellency the High Commissioner approves I could be present on that occasion on Sunday May 2nd. I should add that Mr. Murdoch fears that, if only local officials are present, it will be thought that he himself has arranged for the ceremony to redound to his own glory and honour and I am inclined to agree with him. I have the honour to be, Sir, Your most obedient servant, O. W. Geary, H.B.M. Consul, The Chancery, The Residency, Cairo.

The letter outlines a request from a Mr. Murdoch to ensure the re-erection ceremony is formal and includes British military and official representation to prevent public unrest. Geary seeks approval from the High Commissioner to attend the event on May 2nd, noting concerns that a purely local ceremony might be perceived as a personal political maneuver by local officials.

CAIRO.
April 26th, 1920.

Sir,

With reference to your letter of the 14th instant, I am directed to inform you that the High Commissioner approves the arrangements proposed, for the formal re-erection of the British Consular Shield of honour, except that the P.W.D. I am, Sir,
Your obedient servant,

George Ogilvie,
First Secretary.

MINISTRY OF THE INTERIOR.
ADVISER'S OFFICE.

Cairo, 29th April, 1920.

I have been directed by the High Commissioner to make with H.M.'s Consul in Cairo the arrangements necessary to give effect to the programme of the ceremony of the formal re-erection of the British Consular shield at Mansoura. I understand that you have received from the Residency copies of the correspondence which has passed on this subject.

H.M.'s Consul in Cairo will call upon you and discuss the arrangements required for the ceremony. When the details have been arranged between you and him, I should be grateful if you could inform me of them in order that I may instruct the Mudir regarding his share in the arrangements and the assistance which he will be required to give.

(Signed) : G.P. CLAYTON.
ADVISER.

ai_content.transcribed_text: I have the honour to report that the new consular shield, which was sent to replace the escutcheon torn down by the rioters in March 1919 at Mansourah, was unveiled with due ceremony on Sunday May 9th, under the directions and with the sanction of His Excellency, the High Commissioner. Owing to the whole hearted co-operation of the Army and Local authorities, the little ceremony was carried through with great success. The Mudir or Local Governor, the Local Commandant and the representatives of all Foreign Powers at Mansourah as well as the whole of the small British community were in attendance. The Local Police maintained excellent order while the Guard and Band supplied by the Highland Light Infantry lent dignity to the proceedings. I was present in uniform and after inspecting and receiving the salute of the military guard, unveiled the shield after a brief speech, which was well received. I referred briefly to the fact that the old shield had been torn down by certain ignorant and misguided individuals, whose violence could never be approved by the best Egyptians. I then pointed out that Egypt was never more prosperous and that the continuation of her prosperity depended on the discovery of the bridge of sympathy over which the British and Egyptian nations might march in a spirit of co operation rather than antagonism, and I added that, when deeds of violence and disorder ceased, the Egyptian nation would show that

The author describes the event as a success, noting the attendance of local Egyptian officials (the Mudir), foreign representatives, and the British community, supported by the Highland Light Infantry. The author recounts his speech, which emphasized the need for cooperation between the British and Egyptian nations and condemned the violence of the previous year, framing it as the work of 'misguided individuals' rather than the Egyptian people as a whole.

ai_content.english_translation: This document is a confidential report detailing the political climate in Mansourah regarding a planned visit by the Sultan of Egypt in December 1920. The author reports on the organized opposition to the visit, led by local professionals and landowners, and notes the influence of the Central Committee in Cairo and Prince Omar Toussoun. It highlights the tension between the Sultan and the public, exacerbated by the breakdown of negotiations between Saad Zaghlul and Lord Milner, as well as economic hardships caused by the cotton market.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British intelligence or administrative report from late 1920, a period of intense political unrest in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution. It captures the fragile legitimacy of Sultan Fuad I, who was viewed by many nationalists as a British puppet. The report illustrates the 'non-cooperation' tactics employed by the Wafd party and local notables to undermine the Sultan's authority by organizing boycotts of his official visits. The mention of the breakdown in negotiations between Saad Zaghlul and Lord Milner refers to the failed attempts to reach a settlement on Egyptian independence, which ultimately led to the British unilateral declaration of 1922.

ai_content.transcribed_text: (Copy). STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL. No. RS. 45. Adviser, Ministry of Interior. Nov. 28, 1920. (1). I proceeded to Mansourah on November 22nd according to instructions received, and remained there until November 26th. I went thoroughly into the question of the Sultan's visit to Mansourah on December 11th. (2). It appears that the opposition to the visit is mainly the work of the lawyers and doctors of the town, who are very possibly acting under instructions from the Central Committee in Cairo. It is also rumoured that Prince Omar Toussoun is at the back of the movement. He has considerable influence in the districts round Mansourah and this may have suggested this idea. Some of the most important notables among the landowners in Daqahlia have also declared themselves opposed to the Sultan's visit. Chief among these are Hassan Pasha Foda and Mahmud Pasha Atriba. It is most probable that they have been bullied into this attitude by the lawyers, etc., of Mansourah. Shemnawi Pasha is the most important of those who are willing to receive the Sultan, but he is not a man who takes an active part. (3). The official reasons given for the withdrawal of the invitation to the Sultan are (1) the break in the negotiations between Saad Pasha Zaghlul and Lord Milner, (2) the fact that cotton has not yet been sold and money is in consequence short. The real reasons appear to be that the Sultan is genuinely disliked and that very few people have any good thing to say for him. He is considered to be neither an Egyptian nor an Englishman and yet he has thrown in his lot with the English. It is thought that he is primarily responsible for the break in negotiations and that he is backed up in this by his ministers.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a strictly confidential report from an adviser at the Ministry of Interior regarding the political climate in Mansourah. The author details their visit to the town to assess the opposition to a planned visit by the Sultan on December 11th. The report identifies key figures, including lawyers, doctors, and prominent landowners like Hassan Pasha Foda and Mahmud Pasha Atriba, who are opposing the visit, potentially under the influence of the Central Committee in Cairo or Prince Omar Toussoun. It contrasts this with the stance of Shemnawi Pasha, who is willing to receive the Sultan. The document concludes by analyzing the underlying political reasons for the withdrawal of the invitation, citing the failed negotiations between Saad Pasha Zaghlul and Lord Milner, economic distress due to cotton prices, and a general public dislike for the Sultan, who is perceived as being too closely aligned with the British.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential intelligence report from the British-led Egyptian Ministry of Interior, dated November 1920. It captures the volatile political atmosphere in Egypt during the post-WWI nationalist movement. The report highlights the tension between the Egyptian nationalist aspirations (represented by the Wafd party and Saad Zaghlul) and the British-backed Sultanate. The document provides a granular look at how local notables and professional classes in Mansourah were organizing resistance against the Sultan's authority, reflecting the broader national struggle for independence and the deep unpopularity of the Sultan's perceived collaboration with the British administration.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
(4). In dealing with Egyptians, it is almost impossible to forecast what is likely to happen. At present the line of action would seem to be as follows: All lawyers and doctors, even those belonging to the Municipality and other such bodies, are certain to absent themselves on the occasion of the Sultan's visit. Great pressure is being brought to bear on all notables not only of the first but also of the second class, not to attend the reception. I do not think that this will have much effect on the second class, but some of the leading notables, such as the two I have previously mentioned, may be bullied into not attending. I am rather of the opinion, however, that they may in the end attend. Efforts are also being made to induce all shopkeepers to shut their shops on the day of the visit. A more likely event is a strike on the part of the students in the schools, who will not attend when the Sultan visits the schools. I consider this probable unless steps are taken. The only precautionary step would seem to be a threat of dismissal. Unfortunately such threats have been made again and again and, not having been carried out on this occasion, the Government would have to be prepared for sympathetic strikes on the part of the schools throughout Egypt.

I might mention, in connection with the students, that some schools struck on November 20th in sympathy with the resignation of the Mudir. Some demonstrations took place and stones were thrown at the Police. I am not certain whether this was reported by the Mudiria authorities, but it certainly should have been.
ai_content.english_translation: The text is already in English. It describes the political climate in Egypt regarding a planned visit by the Sultan, noting widespread opposition among professional classes (lawyers, doctors), notables, and students. It details tactics of civil disobedience, such as boycotting the reception, closing shops, and student strikes, while noting a specific recent incident involving the resignation of a Mudir (provincial governor) and subsequent police clashes.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official report from the Ministry of the Interior in Cairo, likely authored by a British colonial official or advisor during the period of the British occupation of Egypt. It provides a candid assessment of the public's hostile sentiment toward a visit by the Ottoman Sultan. The report highlights the fragility of the government's control, noting that threats of dismissal against striking students and civil servants have lost their efficacy. It serves as a primary source for understanding the intersection of Egyptian nationalism, anti-colonial sentiment, and the waning influence of the Ottoman Sultanate in early 20th-century Egypt.

I am informed that a students' committee exists in the Training College, which issues instructions to all the other schools as to their actions under different circumstances. This Committee should be broken up, if possible.
I consider that demonstrations in the town are possible on the day of the visit, but it is more likely that nothing will occur except, perhaps, some shouts of "down with the Sultan." The possibility of an attempt on the life of the Sultan must always be considered. This is not likely to originate from Mansurah, but might come from somewhere outside. The very narrow main street of Mansurah would be very suitable for such an attempt.
(5). Five hundred extra Police have been asked for. A considerable proportion of these should be mounted.
(6). I have discussed the question with very many Egyptians and I find that my principal difficulty is entire ignorance as to the intentions of His Majesty's Government as to the Protectorate. I have heard that the High Commissioner has, in the course of conversation with Egyptians who have seen him, stated that Great Britain will not do away with the Protectorate, owing to the difficulty of inducing the other powers to abolish the Capitulations.
The general lines of argument that I have employed are that negotiations have not been broken off, that Lord Milner's mission was not sent out to negotiate but only to report, that the conversations between Lord Milner and the Wafd were merely an exchange of views, that the Wafd is not considered official by the British Government, who will, after receiving Lord Milner's report, negotiate with the Egyptian Government.
If any directions could be given to those who like myself are continually discussing politics, it would be most helpful and would, incidentally, prevent Englishmen expressing very divergent views.
(7). The resignation of Kutry Pasha appears to be genuinely regretted by the Government officials, with whom he was very popular owing to his personal integrity.

It discusses the British Protectorate status, the role of the Milner Mission, the Wafd party's lack of official standing, and the resignation of Kutry Pasha.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
FOREIGN OFFICE.
No. 1164.
15.12.20, 1 pm.
The Sultan paid a formal visit to Mansurah on the 11th instant. Great preparations had been made and he received an enthusiastic reception. Extremists had for some time previous tried to deter notables from attending and to influence local opinion against the Sultan. These efforts failed. The Sultan had even a better reception than on the visit he lately made to Damanhour. Along the whole route crowds turned out and greeted him with acclamation. This I regard as very gratifying. It shows that the people appreciate the interest which the Sultan is taking in them and that they are grateful for what we are doing to improve economic conditions in the country. The Sultan's next visit will be to Benoufin.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a diplomatic cable from the Foreign Office dated December 15, 1920, reporting on the Sultan's recent activities. It notes that the Sultan visited Mansurah on the 11th of the month, where he was met with great enthusiasm despite attempts by extremists to discourage local notables from attending. The report highlights that the reception was even better than a previous visit to Damanhour, with crowds cheering along the route. The author expresses satisfaction, noting that this demonstrates public appreciation for the Sultan's efforts and gratitude for the economic improvements being implemented in the country. The cable concludes by mentioning that the Sultan's next planned visit is to Benoufin.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British Foreign Office cable from December 1920, documenting the political climate in Egypt during the transition period following the 1919 revolution. It reflects the British colonial administration's efforts to bolster the legitimacy of Sultan Fuad I (later King Fuad) against nationalist 'extremist' opposition. The report serves as a piece of intelligence regarding the success of the Sultan's provincial tours in garnering public support and countering anti-monarchical sentiment, while simultaneously framing the British presence as a benefactor of economic development in the Egyptian countryside.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO, 14th MAY 1921. With reference to your correspondence of the 9th instant, I beg to inform you that the play mentioned in Mr. Murdoch's letter (returned herewith) was submitted to the Censor and passed by him about a year ago. It is quite harmless as you see from the résumé which I also attach. The question of the maintenance, in case of trouble, of public security in general and precautions for the life and property of foreigners in particular is being dealt with by the G.O.C., Egypt.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official communication from The Residency in Cairo, dated May 14, 1921. It addresses a previous inquiry from the 9th regarding a play mentioned by a Mr. Murdoch. The author confirms the play was reviewed and approved by the Censor a year prior and is considered harmless, with a summary attached. It further notes that the General Officer Commanding (G.O.C.) in Egypt is handling security protocols regarding the safety of foreigners and public order.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British colonial administrative correspondence from the Residency in Cairo during the British Protectorate era in Egypt. It reflects the bureaucratic oversight of cultural production (the censorship of plays) and the heightened security concerns of the British authorities in 1921, a period marked by significant Egyptian nationalist agitation and political instability following the 1919 Revolution. The mention of the G.O.C. (General Officer Commanding) underscores the military-backed nature of British governance in Egypt at the time.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
AHMED AND HANNA
----------
Ahmed is a clever & nice young fellow witn an inventive
aind and an enterprising spirit.
Hanna is a young man with a very sensitive and temperamental
disposition also very keen and interested in antiquities.
For the purpose of getting the financial support of Hanna
for launching his threshing machine (Norag), Ahmed succeeds in
getting introduced to have through the good offices of a Priest.
In order to get Hanna interested in his enterprise, Ahmed
takes Hanna round the different ancient Egyptian Museums. Hanna
sees the statue of Queen Nefart and admires it so much that he
becomes infatuated with Queen Nefart.
Ahmed who is an expert hypnotist throws Hanna in a trance
and shows him the Pyramide and other Ancient Egyptian antiquities
etc. He also shows him King Ramases & Queen Nefart.
Hanna asks if he could take Queen Nefart for a wife, but
Ramases tells him that could have been possible had you followed
in the paths of your forefathers, had you kept your unity and
supported agriculture & industry. Hanna promises to do all that
and wakes up from his trance.
Hanna greatly influenced by what happened to him joins hands
with Ahmed and ends by the realization of Ahmed's enterprise.
The whole piece tends to urge the nation to support agri-
culture & industry especially sculpture.
The author is the owner of a Sculptural Museum and the
inventor of an agricultural machine.
R.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a synopsis of a story titled 'Ahmed and Hanna'. It describes Ahmed, an inventive young man, seeking financial backing from Hanna, a sensitive man interested in antiquities, to fund his threshing machine. Ahmed uses his skills as a hypnotist to show Hanna ancient Egyptian sites and figures, including Queen Nefart and King Ramases. After a moral lesson from Ramases about supporting agriculture and industry, Hanna agrees to fund Ahmed's project. The text concludes by stating the author is a museum owner and inventor, and that the story serves as a nationalistic appeal to support Egyptian agriculture and industry.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a typewritten synopsis for a didactic literary work or play, likely written in mid-20th century Egypt. It serves as a promotional or conceptual piece by an author who identifies as both an inventor of agricultural machinery and a proprietor of a sculptural museum. The narrative uses a blend of Egyptian nationalist sentiment, historical romanticism (involving Ancient Egyptian figures), and a moralizing tone to advocate for the modernization of Egyptian agriculture and the preservation of national industry. The mention of the 'Norag' (a traditional Egyptian threshing sledge) highlights the transition from traditional to mechanized farming methods.

Mr Innes.

7.15 p.m. message from M.T.A. to say that they had received a call from the Consular Agent Mansourah asking for British troops which M.T.A. could not provide.

7.25 p.m. Reported to Seu Herbert who said he would ring up Mansourah, ask the Mudir if he wanted troops & tell him that if he did he could have assistance from Zagazig as soon as the troops could get from there to Mansourah. He would also...
ai_content.english_translation: Mr. Innes. Mansourah. The following is the sequence of events this morning relative to the state of public security at Mansourah. At 7:15 PM, a message was received from the M.T.A. stating that they had received a call from the Consular Agent in Mansourah requesting British troops, which the M.T.A. could not provide. At 7:20 PM, I informed Mr. Monteith Smith at Kafr, who asked me to report to Seu Herbert. At 7:25 PM, I reported to Seu Herbert, who said he would call Mansourah, ask the Mudir if he required troops, and inform him that if he did, he could receive assistance from Zagazig as soon as the troops could be transported there.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official minute from the British High Commission in Egypt, dated May 1921. It records a series of urgent communications regarding civil unrest or security concerns in the city of Mansourah. The text details the administrative coordination between the Consular Agent, the M.T.A. (likely a military or transport authority), and local British officials (Monteith Smith and Seu Herbert) regarding the potential deployment of British troops from Zagazig to stabilize the situation under the authority of the local Mudir (provincial governor). The document reflects the British colonial administration's reliance on rapid communication and military contingency planning during the volatile period following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
BRITISH CONSULATE
CAIRO
23rd May 1921.

Sir,

I have the honour to refer to you an enquiry from the British Consular Agent at Mansourah which I first passed on to the Residency but I have now referred to you. 
He writes "In view of the unrest at present prevalent in the country and especially in regard to recent events at Tantah I should esteem it a favour if you would kindly inform me what precautions are going to be taken for the safety of the British Subjects in my province in the event of dangerous riots and demonstrations."

I do not know if there is anything to tell him, but I pass on his enquiry as a matter of form.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient Servant,
(sd) W.S. WARD
ACTING CONSUL.

General Sir W. Congreve,
General Officer Commanding,
Egypt, Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from the Acting British Consul in Cairo to General Sir W. Congreve, the General Officer Commanding in Egypt. The Consul is forwarding an inquiry from the British Consular Agent in Mansourah regarding the safety of British subjects in that province. The agent is concerned about the prevailing unrest in Egypt, specifically citing recent events in Tantah, and is requesting information on what military or security precautions are being planned to protect British citizens in the event of riots or demonstrations. The Acting Consul notes that he is passing this request on as a matter of administrative procedure.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document reflects the volatile political climate in Egypt during the post-World War I period, specifically in May 1921. Following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, the British administration faced significant civil unrest and nationalist agitation. The correspondence highlights the anxiety of British consular officials stationed in provincial towns like Mansourah, who were seeking clarification from the military authorities (General Officer Commanding) regarding security protocols for British nationals in the face of potential anti-colonial demonstrations and civil disorder in cities like Tantah.

My Lord,
I transmit herewith, for Your Lordship's information a copy of a despatch from the Acting British Consul at Cairo reporting the resignation of the British Consular Agents at Mansourah and Birkat-el-Sab.
2. I request that I may be furnished with Your Lordship's observations in regard to the necessity or desirability of retaining the Consular Agencies in question, having regard not only to the volume and nature of the Consular business requiring to be transacted, but also to the possible effect upon the extremist section of the Egyptian Nationalist party of the closing of the posts, in view of the incident in March 1919 when the Consular shield at Mansourah was destroyed and thrown into the river and the subsequent conditions on which it was defaced.
I am, with great truth and regard,
My Lord,

Sir,

I am directed by the High Commissioner to inform you that H.M. Acting Consul in Cairo has recently raised the question with the Residency of the safety of the various Consulates and Consular Agencies throughout the country in the event of their being attacked in time of riot. Captain Heard suggested that each Consulate should be given a stand of arms and a supply of ammunition which would be under the sole control of the Consulate and used solely for the defence of Consular buildings and of such British Nationals as had taken refuge therein in time of stress. He had in mind particularly the case of the small British Consular Agencies at Mansourah and Zagazig which would in time of riot become the assembly point of the small British Colonies in those two towns.

His Excellency would be grateful if you would furnish him in due course with your views on Captain Heard's suggestions on receipt of which he will communicate on the subject with the General Headquarters of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force.

I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient servant, H.M. Consul-General, Alexandria.

It discusses a proposal by Captain Heard to arm British Consular Agencies in Egypt (specifically Mansourah and Zagazig) with firearms and ammunition to protect British nationals during potential civil unrest or riots. The High Commissioner is seeking the Consul-General's opinion on this security measure before consulting with the General Headquarters of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force.

The British administration, operating under the Residency, was concerned about the vulnerability of isolated British personnel and consular staff in provincial towns like Mansourah and Zagazig. ai_content.transcribed_text: BRITISH CONSULAR AGENCY. MANSOURAH, EGYPT. Mansourah, 27th December 1921. CONFIDENTIAL. Sir, I have the honour to inform you that yesterday afternoon (Monday) I rang up on the telephone the Consulate, three times and each time there was no answer. The reason I rang up was that the Demonstrations were getting rather excited and the Police had to fire. I should be glad if you would inform me what measures are to be taken for the safety of the British Community in this town. Although we have not had as yet any serious events I should not be surprised if we have some trouble in the near future and should feel more at ease if I knew that British Troops were handy. As you are no doubt aware, I, in conjunction with General Cassels, got out a scheme for the defence of the Community including the foreigners. The first part of this scheme was that an Officer should come from Ismailia on the slightest sign of trouble and report on the situation. I regret to inform you that although things were getting serious on Monday this officer has not yet put in an appearance and secondly I have not yet received the Very pistols and cartridges to enable me to signal to the aeroplanes, although they have been signalling to me. If the scheme has been shelved for another one, I should like to know what it is, so that I can do the right thing when the occasion arises. Although Zaghloulists were very noisy yesterday they are...
ai_content.english_translation: This is a confidential report from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, dated December 27, 1921. The author reports an inability to reach the Consulate by telephone during civil unrest, noting that police had to fire on demonstrators. The author expresses concern for the safety of the British community and requests clarification on defense measures, specifically noting the absence of a promised officer from Ismailia and the lack of signaling equipment (Very pistols) for communication with aircraft, as part of a defense scheme previously coordinated with General Cassels.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential dispatch from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, written in the immediate aftermath of the 1919-1922 Egyptian Revolution. It highlights the precarious security situation for British nationals during the height of the Wafd Party's (Zaghloulists) anti-colonial agitation. The text provides a rare glimpse into the logistical failures of British colonial defense schemes, specifically the breakdown in communication and coordination between local consular outposts and military authorities (General Cassels) during periods of civil disorder.

31st December, 1921.

Sir,

I should like to say a few words about the Mudir here MAHMOUD PACHA RACHAD. From the beginning he has been untiring in his effort to prevent trouble and has taken a very strong stand against the Demonstrations and it is due to him that we have not had serious trouble so far.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd). F. JAMES MURDOCH.
BRITISH CONSULAR AGENT.

(Seal)

BRITISH CONSULATE.
CAIRO.

Acting British Consul.

With reference to your letter of December 28th with which you communicated to His Excellency copy of a letter from the British Consular Agent, Mansourah, relative to the state of public security in that town, I am directed by the High Commissioner to inform you that he has caused copies of Mr. Murdoch's letter to be communicated to O.B.Q. and to the Director of Public Security for their information and for such action as they consider necessary with regard to the security of Mansourah.

I am, sir,
Your obedient servant,

FIRST SECRETARY.

B.B. Acting Consul,
CAIRO.

COPY OF REPORT FROM MAJOR GAYER ANDERSON OF JAN. 4/22.

I have been in communication with Col. Stafford on the subject of Mr. Murdock's letter to you dated Dec. 27th, 1921. (Forwarded through Col. Ryder); he informs me that when new Defence Schemes were in process of construction for all provinces during June, July, last, he held a meeting at Mansura of responsible Officials there, to consider that for Dakahlia; to this meeting Mr. Murdock was invited but did not attend.

Col. Stafford made a point however of seeing him later and fully explaining how matters stood. There would seem little excuse therefore for Mr. Murdock's lack of information on this head. He may however, be re-assured that full provision has been made for the safety of the British & Foreign Communities in Mansura. Particulars of which he can obtain from H.E. the Mudir or Col. Stafford.

Sir,

In continuation of my letter No. 9954/2 of December 31st 1921.

January 7th, 1922.

THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO

ai_content.transcribed_text: INFORMATION TELEPHONED BY MR. TONNOR, MANSOURAR. 23.11.34. All was quiet until 9 a.m. when the newspapers arrived. Then there was a good deal of shouting amongst the students 'Yehia Saad' but no cries against England were heard. The Head Master came out and asked what was the matter and was told by the students 'You have the newspaper, go and read it.' The students then formed demonstration and left the school and as they departed one of the staff heard 'Down with England' is out and as they passed through the town were heard to shout 'Down with Britain'. The attitude of the Egyptian masters is quiet and reserved, they are unwilling to discuss the situation. Is not aware if any special instructions have yet been received by the Head Master from the Ministry. He is informed from a source which he believes to be reliable that a threatening attitude was adopted towards an English lady by a demonstrator passing his finger across his throat. He hears an unconfirmed report that 25 students have been put in prison. The students are wandering about the streets of the town. There are now about 300 of the Govt. Secondary School out, but he cannot say how many students of other schools are out. If he hears anything more of interest he will telephone.

The Mamur, Kailub Markas, in a letter (No 382), 'Confidential' dated 16th written as follows :-
On the 15th inst., at 8 a.m., on being informed that a demonstration was held by villagers of Kailub, the school-boys & spinners, etc., the Mamur at once left for the scene, with the Moawin of Police & a force of mounted men. On arrival at the village, they found the demonstrators (about 2000 persons) carrying pieces of timber; or else, thick sticks. Though good advice was given, yet the rioters would not listen. In fact, the crowds were so excited as to attempt at assaulting the Mamur & his men. They asked that the Parquet & the Monkomen Sharia be closed, afterwards proceeding, in separate parties in the direction of the Ry. station
This state of things reported to the Mudir, the latter issued the necessary instructions to the Mamur, detailing the Commandant of Police, with the necessary force of men, to leave for the scene.
Meantime, the demonstrators made for the civil court & the Monkomen Sharia & compelled the officials to leave, afterwards proceeding with devastating the Station & the destruction of the Telephone & the Telegraph lines. The small Police force on the spot, did its utmost to keep the rioters at bay. At about 10.30 a.m., the Comt. of Police arrived by the Express & saw, with his eyes, the demonstrators scattered about the Station, a police guard was set up to protect the Express train, inasmuch as, it was perceived that some of the rioters were going to attack it.
ai_content.english_translation: The Mamur of Kailub Markas, in a confidential letter (No. 382) dated the 16th, reported the following: On the 15th of this month, at 8:00 AM, upon being informed that a demonstration was being held by the villagers of Kailub, including schoolboys and spinners, the Mamur immediately departed for the scene with the Moawin of Police and a mounted force. Upon arriving at the village, they encountered approximately 2,000 demonstrators carrying timber or thick sticks. Despite receiving good advice, the rioters refused to listen and attempted to assault the Mamur and his men. They demanded the closure of the Parquet and the Sharia Court, then proceeded in separate groups toward the railway station. This situation was reported to the Mudir, who issued instructions to the Mamur and dispatched the Commandant of Police with a force to the scene. Meanwhile, the demonstrators headed to the civil court and the Sharia Court, forcing the officials to leave, and proceeded to devastate the station and destroy the telephone and telegraph lines. The small police force on-site did its best to hold the rioters back. At approximately 10:30 AM, the Commandant of Police arrived on the Express train and witnessed the demonstrators scattered around the station; a police guard was established to protect the Express train, as it was perceived that some rioters intended to attack it.

The report highlights the escalation of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule, noting the specific targeting of symbols of authority and the subsequent deployment of police forces to restore order and protect railway assets. ai_content.transcribed_text: Also, on a train from Sharkia by which were travelling some British officers & men approaching the Station, a guard was set up, to protect it. These two trains did not actually entered the station, but stopped at about 200 metres. In the interval, the Mamur arrested four persons, among the rioters. On learning of that, a great number of the demonstrators, carrying levers, axes, screw-wrenches, etc., which they had obtained possession from the Ry. stores at the Station, attacked the Markaz, surrounding it. As they began to destroy the doors & windows, the Mamur threatened with firing at them, but without result. However the Mamur & the Commandant of Police obtained from carrying out their threats, with object of avoiding adding fuel to the fire. At the persistent demand of the demonstrators, the four persons, already arrested, were released, in-as-much as, their ringleaders (Ibrahim el Arfas, by name, & student of Law & a certain Kamel Abdel-Wahhab) undertook to disperse the rioters, provided that the four persons be released. In fact, when the release was granted, the demonstrators began to return to their normal work, The Mudiria was therefore advised of that. Half an hour later, the train from Sharkia entered the Station, when the Mamur, the Commandant of Police proceeded thither. Before reaching the quay, however, they heard shots & were told that it was Mr. Brayen (Inspector, plate-layer) & one of the British passengers who fired. As the quay was found thronged with the rioters, some of whom, in conjunction with the Commandant of Police, to open fire, when the demonstrators were dispersed. A certain Yehia Abdel-Rahman, who was standing near a British soldier (found thrown on the ground of the level-crossing) was arrested, for the Commandant heard him say: 'Here you are, we have killed a Briton'.

It details the escalation of violence, the arrest and subsequent release of four rioters under the mediation of ringleaders Ibrahim el Arfas and Kamel Abdel-Wahhab, and the eventual arrival of a train carrying British personnel. The report notes that shots were fired by a British inspector and a passenger, leading to the dispersal of the crowd and the arrest of Yehia Abdel-Rahman for allegedly inciting violence against a British soldier.

Taha Hassanein Ahmed Helal was arrested, for he was found carrying a blood-stained knife, the knife & his clothes being retained at the Markaz. CASE NO 47 OF 1913

PLATTICE & CO., LIMITED, Plaintiffs.
-v-

Dated this 26th day of June 1913.
1. The Plaintiffs are an English Corporation with limited liability carrying on trade in cotton at Alexandria.
2. The Defendant was their agent for the purchase of cotton, carrying on business at Berka.
3. By a verbal agreement entered into between the Plattice Company and the Defendant on the 18th March 1913, confirmed by a letter of the same date written by the Defendant to the Plattice Company, it was agreed between the Plaintiffs and the Defendant that the Defendant should supply the Plattice Company with ginned cotton from the districts of Galioubieh and Gizeh Kenoufieh delivered free at Alexandria station, any difference between the original weight of the cotton despatched by the Defendant and the weight of the same cotton at Alexandria was to be borne exclusively by the Defendant, after deduction of a bonification of 1 1/2%.
4. By the same agreement any dispute which might arise between the parties as to the conformity of the qualified supplied with those sold was to be decided in accordance with the Regulations of the Alexandria General Produce Association and the customs of the market at Minet el Bassal.

It specifies terms regarding weight loss during transit, a 1.5% bonification (allowance), and the arbitration process for quality disputes, which were to be governed by the Alexandria General Produce Association and local market customs at Minet el Bassal.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 'Statement of Claim' from a case (No. 47 of 1913) heard before His Britannic Majesty's Consular Court in Cairo. It provides significant insight into the legal and commercial infrastructure of the British presence in Egypt during the early 20th century. The document illustrates the mechanisms of the cotton trade—the backbone of the Egyptian economy at the time—and demonstrates how British extraterritorial courts handled contractual disputes between British-registered firms and local agents. It highlights the role of the Alexandria General Produce Association and the importance of the Minet el Bassal market as the central hub for cotton commerce in the Mediterranean.

CRIMINAL JURISDICTION.
In His Britannic Majesty's Provincial Court at Cairo.

Case No. 52 of 1913
___ day, the ___ day of May 1913
Mohammed Moursi el Skandarani, Coffee Keeper of Mansourah being first duly sworn complains that Spiro Zonello of Mansourah on the 25th day of April last did enter his coffee shop causing disturbance which led all the customers to leave his place without paying for their drinks, he also did throw twice empty bottles on the crowd and the singers & caused the breakage of a looking glass worth £.10 He also did assault him by taking him by the throat and threatened to strike him with a stick.
Taken before me, this twentysecond day of May in the year one thousand nine hundred and thirteen.

Cairo, May 24, 1913
[Signed] Arthur H. [illegible], Consul
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official English legal document. It is a formal criminal complaint (Form No. 31) filed within the Criminal Jurisdiction of His Britannic Majesty's Provincial Court at Cairo, originating from the local district of Mansourah. The complainant, Mohammed Moursi el Skandarani, a coffee shop keeper in Mansourah, states under oath that on April 25, 1913, the defendant, Spiro Zonello, entered his establishment and caused a disturbance. This disruption forced all customers to flee without paying for their beverages. Furthermore, the defendant threw empty bottles at the crowd and the performing singers, broke a mirror valued at 10 pounds, physically assaulted the complainant by grabbing him by the throat, and threatened him with a stick. The complaint was sworn before Consular Agent T. Dunlop on May 22, 1913, and a summons was subsequently issued in Cairo on May 24, 1913, ordering the defendant to appear in court on Friday, May 30, 1913, at 10:00 AM.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document illustrates the operation of the Capitulations and extraterritorial legal systems in Egypt during the British protectorate era. Under this system, foreign nationals or protected subjects (such as the defendant, Spiro Zonello, likely of Greek origin or holding foreign protection) were subject to the jurisdiction of foreign consular courts rather than local Egyptian tribunals. The record details a local dispute in a provincial coffee house in Mansourah, highlighting the daily social and economic interactions—and occasional friction—between local Egyptian business owners and foreign residents. Administratively, it shows how legal complaints initiated in provincial towns were sworn before local consular agents and then processed through His Britannic Majesty's Provincial Court in Cairo, which held the authority to issue formal summonses and try criminalizing local disturbances.

British Consular Agency
Mansourah
(Egypt)

June 1st 1913

Sir,

Further to my letter of the 28th ult, I enclose a note received from the woman Faika Ahmed el Masria acquitting Spiro Bonello of all blame in the Record No. 648 which she brought against him; this will show how the man intimidates this woman. And further to my letter of the 29th all the persons concerned in this action have been duly advised to appear on Saturday next at 10 AM, Mohamed Moursi having been subsequently found in this town.

I am
Your most obedient and humble servant
[Signed: J. Rawlings]
Acting Consular Agent.

Arthur D. Alban Esq
H.B.M.'s Consul
Cairo.

Alban, regarding a legal case (Record No. 648). He forwards a note from an Egyptian woman named Faika Ahmed el Masria, who has acquitted Spiro Bonello of blame, suggesting this acquittal was obtained through intimidation. He notes that all parties, including Mohamed Moursi, have been summoned to appear the following Saturday.

Alban, His Britannic Majesty's Consul in Cairo. Signed by the Acting Consular Agent, J. Rawlings, the correspondence concerns a legal dispute or criminal complaint (Record No. 648) involving an Egyptian woman, Faika Ahmed el Masria, and an individual named Spiro Bonello (likely a British subject or protected person under the Capitulations system). The agent expresses concern that Bonello has intimidated the complainant into withdrawing her charges. This document illustrates the administrative and judicial functions of British consular courts in Egypt during the period of the British Veiled Protectorate, highlighting how local disputes involving foreign nationals or protected subjects were managed under extraterritorial jurisdiction.

TO Mr. Mullings Esq.
ACTING BRITISH CONSULAR AGENT,
MARSOUMAH.

Sir,

With reference to your letter of the 28th April
last, I am directed by His Majesty's Consul to send you
herewith a Form of complaint drawn up according to the
statement of the above mentioned prosecutor and to
request that you will kindly have it signed by the
said prosecutor and return it to this Consulate with
as to enable us to issue the summons for the defendant
and fix a date for the hearing of the case.

The prosecutor should, on signing the complaint
deposit the sum of £.3 to cover the cost of the case - I
this sum will be refunded to him if his case is proved.

I am, Sir,
Your obedient Servant,
H. HOLSTROM,
CONSUL.

ON PROSECUTION MOHAMED HOURAI EL MOURABY.
v/s
SPYRO MOURTZO.

CAIRO
May 8th 1913.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal letter written in English. It is a communication from the British Consulate in Cairo to the Acting British Consular Agent in Marsoumah. The letter refers to a previous communication from April 28th and instructs the agent to facilitate a legal process. It states that a complaint form, drafted based on the prosecutor's statement, is enclosed. The agent is requested to have the prosecutor sign this form and return it to the Consulate. This is necessary for the Consulate to issue a summons to the defendant and set a date for the case hearing. The prosecutor is also required to deposit £3 to cover the costs of the case, with the assurance that this sum will be refunded if the case is proven in their favor. The letter is signed by H. Holstrom, Consul, and identifies the parties involved in the prosecution: Mohamed Hourai El Mouraby as the prosecutor and Spyro Mourtzo as the defendant.
ai_content.historical_summary: This letter, dated May 8th, 1913, from the British Consulate in Cairo to the Acting British Consular Agent in Marsoumah, details the administrative steps for initiating a legal case. It highlights the extraterritorial jurisdiction and judicial functions exercised by British Consulates in Egypt during the early 20th century. The Consulate is directing its agent to process a complaint filed by Mohamed Hourai El Mouraby against Spyro Mourtzo. This involves obtaining the prosecutor's signature on a formal complaint and collecting a deposit of £3 to cover court costs, which would be reimbursed if the prosecutor's case was successful. The ultimate goal is to enable the Consulate to issue a summons to the defendant and schedule a court hearing. This document provides insight into the consular administration of justice, particularly concerning disputes involving individuals under British protection or jurisdiction in Egypt, reflecting the broader context of British influence and legal mechanisms in the region prior to the First World War.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Dear Mr. Alban,

26th, April, 1913.

It appears to me that Spiro Bonello is incorrigible, and if it were possible to have him deported, it would be a good riddance of an intolerable nuisance from this town. He has terrorised the Police and some Café keepers here that they practically allow him to do what he likes, as frequent brawls would endanger the issue of their license, they are afraid to give evidence against him, and Mohamed Skenderani the proprietor of the "Alateea" where the last brawl took place told me that the statement he made about that incident was done under a threat that if he stated anything against Spiro he would do some damage to his Café. I do not know how much truth there is in this statement but there may be something in it.

Notwithstanding the fact that I told Spiro in his Father's hearing that I was making a report to you about his bad behaviour, and advised him to keep away from the "Alateea", as any further misdemeanour would probably be punished with great severity, he promised not to go there again, and to show how much his promise is worth, I hand you herewith enclosed a complaint of Mohamed Skenderani, in which he is accused of throwing two beer bottles at one of the girls employed at the "Alateea". They both missed the girl and smashed a large mirror, fixed on the wall behind her, and in the melee which followed some chairs and other things were broken in the place.

I hope you will be able to take up this matter as I I do not consider myself competent to deal with it.

I am,
yours truly,
Fred. J. Murdoch
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from Fred J. Murdoch to Mr. Alban at the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, dated April 26, 1913. It details the disruptive and criminal behavior of an individual named Spiro Bonello, who is described as an 'intolerable nuisance' terrorizing local café owners. The letter specifically recounts an incident at the 'Alateea' café involving the smashing of a mirror and property damage, and requests that the Consul consider deporting Bonello due to his incorrigible nature and the fear he instills in local witnesses.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of consular correspondence from the British Consular Agency in Mansourah, Egypt, during the period of the British occupation. It provides a rare, granular look at the administrative challenges faced by consular officials in managing the conduct of foreign nationals (likely Levantines or Europeans under consular protection) in provincial Egyptian towns. The letter highlights the intersection of local law enforcement, the protection of commercial interests (cafés), and the exercise of extraterritorial consular authority, where the Consul is asked to intervene in a local criminal matter involving public order and intimidation.

British Consular Agency
Mawanah (Egypt)
May 8th, 1913

Sir,

In order that you may see what a perpetual nuis-
ance the Bonello family is, I enclose the following:
No. 642 Record against Spiro Bonello for striking
No. 640 Record against Nouri Bonello for striking
public woman Fatma Ahmed el Kassria.
No. 646 Record against Ibrahim Mohamed el Shewih.
With reference to the first I also enclose a letter
of July 5th 1912 which I wrote to Mr Murdoch, and I would
also draw your attention to Mr Murdoch's letters to you of
March 24th and April 8th last.

I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your most obedient and humble servant

J. D. Dalglish
Acting Consular Agent.

Arthur D. Alban Esq.
H.M.'s Consul
Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal letter from the British Consular Agency in Mawanah, Egypt, dated May 8th, 1913. It is addressed to Arthur D. Alban, H.M.'s Consul in Cairo. The Acting Consular Agent, J. D. Dalglish, is writing to highlight the 'perpetual nuisance' caused by the 'Bonello family'. To illustrate this, Dalglish encloses three records: No. 642 against Spiro Bonello for striking, No. 640 against Nouri Bonello for striking 'public woman Fatma Ahmed el Kassria', and No. 646 against Ibrahim Mohamed el Shewih. Dalglish also refers to a letter he wrote to Mr. Murdoch on July 5th, 1912, concerning the first record, and directs Alban's attention to Mr. Murdoch's letters of March 24th and April 8th (presumably 1913).
ai_content.historical_summary: This consular correspondence from 1913 provides insight into the administrative and judicial functions of British consular agencies in Egypt during the British Protectorate era. The letter from the Acting Consular Agent in Mawanah to the Consul in Cairo details ongoing issues with a specific family, the Bonellos, who are described as a 'perpetual nuisance'. The enclosed records pertain to incidents of assault, specifically involving Spiro Bonello and Nouri Bonello, the latter striking a 'public woman' named Fatma Ahmed el Kassria, and another incident involving Ibrahim Mohamed el Shewih. The reference to previous correspondence with 'Mr Murdoch' and the Consul highlights the bureaucratic process of reporting and managing cases involving British subjects or those under consular jurisdiction in Egypt. Such documents are crucial for understanding the daily challenges faced by consular officials, the legal framework governing foreign residents, and social dynamics in early 20th-century Egypt.

The document serves as a record of an alleged assault by a local government official against a police officer, processed through the British Consular Court in Cairo, reflecting the complex legal landscape of early 20th-century Egypt where consular courts held significant authority over legal disputes involving foreign nationals.

ai_content.transcribed_text: The Adviser, Ministry of the Interior, Cairo. 31st May, 1913. Dear Alban, Please see and return the enclosed report, regarding a certain Spiro Bonello. I think that if this family does not mend its ways, we shall have to ask for more drastic action. It is evident from the attached, that Spiro Bonello, when at the 7th March 1913 to a café called Murex. At 12:40 a.m., I.E. when the owner of the café told him that the regular hour of closure was before, attempted to bring the police, and in spite of the opposition of the café, whom he assaulted, Spiro broke into the café, and tried to settle the dispute, where-upon he was conducted to the police station where the officer on duty enquired into the affair; but Spiro refused to make any statement to the said officer. In the meanwhile Spiro's brother arrived, and both reviled the policemen, using impertinent language. Three days afterwards, he submitted a complaint to the Consulate alleging that he was insulted, and that P30 were stolen from him. The enquiry, however, proved that this charge was unfounded. With reference to El Sayed Mohamed Agha and Mohamed Ali Asfahani, who deposed in favour of the foregoing Spiro, and whose friends they are, the former came to the police station, after the incident, and endeavoured to dismiss the matter; the latter, a lad employed by El Sayed Mohamed Agha, was not present at all. It will be seen from the above that Spiro Bonello and his brother assaulted the police. In addition to this offence Spiro assaulted the proprietor of the café, and committed other...
ai_content.english_translation: The Arabic text on the right page is a handwritten summary or translation of the events described in the English report. It details the incident involving Spiro Bonello at the Murex café, his refusal to comply with closing hours, the subsequent altercation with the police, the false accusation of theft made to the Consulate, and the involvement of Mohamed Agha and his employee in providing false testimony.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document consists of an administrative file from the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior, dated May 1913, concerning the disruptive behavior of a foreign national named Spiro Bonello. The file includes a typed memorandum from an official (likely a British adviser) to a colleague named Alban, detailing a specific incident on March 7, 1913, where Bonello assaulted a café owner and police officers. The document highlights the colonial-era administrative tension regarding foreign subjects (often protected by Capitulations) who frequently used Consular complaints to evade local police authority. The accompanying Arabic text serves as an official record or translation of these events for the local Egyptian authorities.

ai_content.transcribed_text: With reference to the attached, it is evident from the enquiries made into this affair that Spiro Ronello, when drunk, went on the night of the 7th March 1913 to a café belonging to a certain Mohamed Murai. At 12:40 a.m., I.E. 20 minutes before the regular hour for closure, he asked one of the dancers to dance, and that the owner of the café told him that there was no time and that the regular hour of closure had approached. Spiro, therefore, attempted to bring the dancer from her room by force; and in spite of the opposition made by the owner of the café, whom he assaulted, Spiro broke open the door, and sought to force his way to her. A police-man on beat duty, arriving, tried to settle the dispute, where-upon he was assaulted by Spiro. Eventually, the latter was conducted to the police station where the officer on duty enquired into the affair; but Spiro refused to make any statement to the said officer. In the meanwhile Spiro's brother arrived, and both reviled the policemen, using impertinent language. Three days afterwards, he submitted a complaint to the Consulate alleging that he was insulted, and that £30 were stolen from him. The enquiry, however, proved that this charge was unfounded. With reference to El Sayed Mohamed Agha and Mohamed Ali Asfahani, who deposed in favour of the foregoing Spiro, and whose friends they are, the former came to the police station, after the incident, and endeavoured to dismiss the matter; the latter, a lad employed by El Sayed Mohamed Agha, was not present at all. It will be seen from the above that Spiro Ronello and his brother assaulted the police. In addition to this offence Spiro assaulted the proprietor of the café, and committed other...
ai_content.english_translation: The English text provides a detailed account of a public disturbance involving an intoxicated individual named Spiro Ronello at a café on March 7, 1913. The Arabic text on the right page appears to be a corresponding administrative report or summary of the same incident, detailing the altercation with the café owner and the subsequent police intervention.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative report from the 'Secretariat' of the 'Ministry of the Interior' (Public Security) regarding a public order incident in 1913. It documents a case of assault and disorderly conduct by a man named Spiro Ronello against a café owner and police officers. The report serves as an official rebuttal to a subsequent complaint filed by Ronello at his consulate, where he falsely claimed to have been insulted and robbed. The document highlights the colonial or administrative oversight of public conduct and the investigative process used by local authorities to verify claims against police conduct during the early 20th century.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Cairo
March 29, 1913
Dear Graham,
I understand that the Agency are sending you the report from Mansourah about the Bonello family. At the present time there is a charge of [illegible] force on disant [illegible] le Chaouiche [illegible] que il y a un grand Seigneur avec elle et on n'a sortit dehors après avoir enlevé un Napoléon qui était annexé dans ma chaine et P.T. 430 en poche et en allant au Police pour prendre mon argent je trouve l'officier et malheureusement il n'a pas voulu d'entendre ma plainte et il m'a chassé dehors en sortant j'ai trouvé le Chaouiche Abdel Hafez avec les deux soldats sont venus et on m'a arrêté quand on a terminé son procés à H. et de suite on m'a mis en prison.
Je l'ai bien expliqué que on m'a voler mon argent, on m'a frappé sans raison.
ai_content.english_translation: Cairo, March 29, 1913. Dear Graham, I understand that the Agency is sending you the report from Mansourah about the Bonello family. At the present time there is a charge of [force]... that there is a great Lord with her and they did not let me out after taking a Napoleon [gold coin] that was attached to my chain and 430 piasters in my pocket, and while going to the Police to get my money back, I found the officer and unfortunately he did not want to hear my complaint and he chased me out. While leaving, I found the Chaouiche [police sergeant] Abdel Hafez with two soldiers who had come, and they arrested me when they finished his trial at H. and immediately they put me in prison. I explained clearly that they stole my money, they hit me for no reason.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document consists of a personal letter written in English, attached to a typed French deposition or statement regarding a legal grievance in Egypt. The text details an incident involving the Bonello family and a subsequent altercation with local police (the Chaouiche Abdel Hafez) in which the author claims to have been robbed of a gold Napoleon coin and cash, only to be arrested and imprisoned after attempting to report the theft to the authorities. It reflects the administrative and legal tensions in early 20th-century Egypt under British influence, where consular agencies often acted as intermediaries for foreign nationals seeking redress against local police actions.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Monsieur le Consul, Le soussigné Spiro Bonnelo a l'honneur de vous informer qu'à la requête présenté par moi le 6 Mars 1913. Je me suis entré au Palais Cristal le 3 Mars écoulé pour voir la meilleure artiste Asia qui a été venu du Caire pour passer quelques jours à notre ville et comme je n'ai pas vu cette artiste j'ai demandé le patron qui s'appelle Mohamed Moursi il m'a dit qu'elle est assis la dedans d'une autre chambre, alors je me suis allé pour le voir et j'ai commencé d'ouvrir la porte j'ai trouvé un certain Abdel Hafez le Chaouche avec deux soldats on m'a empêcher par force en disant que il y a un grand Seigneur avec elle et on m'a sorti dehors après avoir enlevé un Napoléon qui était annexé dans ma chaine et P.T. 450 en poche et en allant au Police pour prendre mon argent je trouvé l'officier et malheureusement il n'a pas voulu d'entendre ma plainte et il m'a chassé dehors en sortant j'ai trouvé le Chaouche Abdel Hafez avec les deux soldats sont venus et on m'a arrêté quand on a terminé son procédé il H. et deule on m'a mis en prison. Je l'ai bien expliqué que on m'a voler mon argent, on m'a frappé sans raison.
ai_content.english_translation: Mr. Consul, The undersigned Spiro Bonnelo has the honor to inform you that following the request presented by me on March 6, 1913. I entered the Palais Cristal on March 3rd to see the best artist Asia who had come from Cairo to spend a few days in our city and as I did not see this artist I asked the owner whose name is Mohamed Moursi, he told me she was sitting inside another room, so I went to see her and I started to open the door, I found a certain Abdel Hafez the Chaouche [guard/officer] with two soldiers, they prevented me by force saying that there is a great Lord with her and they threw me out after having removed a Napoleon [gold coin] which was attached to my chain and 450 piasters in my pocket and while going to the Police to get my money back I found the officer and unfortunately he did not want to hear my complaint and he chased me out, while leaving I found the Chaouche Abdel Hafez with the two soldiers, they came and arrested me when he finished his procedure... they put me in prison. I explained clearly that they stole my money, they hit me without reason.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal written complaint addressed to a Consul by an individual named Spiro Bonnelo, dated shortly after March 1913. The narrative details an incident at the 'Palais Cristal' in a city (likely in Egypt or a French-influenced territory given the currency references like 'Napoléon' and 'P.T.' for Piastres). Bonnelo alleges that he was physically barred from seeing an artist named Asia, robbed of his gold coin and cash by a guard (Chaouche) named Abdel Hafez and two soldiers, and subsequently arrested and imprisoned without cause after the local police refused to hear his complaint. It serves as a primary source for the study of consular protection, local policing, and social tensions in the early 20th-century Levant.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Mr J. Murdock
British Consular Agency
Mansura

Sir
I have the honor to inform you that
I am Spiro Bonello British subject:-
At four hours night I went to Cafe Chantant
in Abassi street as a new woman arrived to this
Cafe, but when I went I did not found this woman
I asked the owner of this Cafe about her, he told
me that she is in a special room, but when I
entered this room I found with her one soldier
Constable named called Aziz & his Assistant Ahmed
when they saw me they caught & struck me,
My chain cut in five pieces & one found with
it lost & also 430 Piastre was in my pocket
All this happened before Adel Hadi Mohamed,
Adela Dario, Mustafa El Recca, Francis Coto,
the soldiers when struck me did not like to go
to the police, but I went alone, & told the [illegible]
about all happened but also they wrote against
me & left me till 1, 30 A.M. next day, & at the
same time, 1, 30 A.M. came my brother Victor
to ask about me & was his luck that he had been
prisoned with me till the next day also.
I wrote this to you sir to see this case by your
self & call me & oblige.

Your obedient servant
Spiro Bonello
6. 3. 18
ai_content.english_translation: Mr. J. Murdock, British Consular Agency, Mansura. Sir, I have the honor to inform you that I am Spiro Bonello, a British subject. At 10:00 PM (four hours night), I went to the Cafe Chantant on Abassi Street because a new woman had arrived there. When I arrived, I did not find her. I asked the owner of the cafe about her, and he told me she was in a special room. When I entered, I found a soldier, a constable named Aziz, and his assistant, Ahmed. When they saw me, they caught and struck me. My chain was cut into five pieces and lost, and 430 Piastres were taken from my pocket. All this happened in front of Adel Hadi Mohamed, Adela Dario, Mustafa El Recca, and Francis Coto. The soldiers who struck me did not want to go to the police, but I went alone and reported what happened. They wrote a report against me and held me until 1:30 AM the next day. At 1:30 AM, my brother Victor came to ask about me, and it was his misfortune that he was also imprisoned with me until the next day. I am writing this to you, sir, so that you may look into this case yourself. Please call me. Your obedient servant, Spiro Bonello. March 6, 1918.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal complaint written by a British subject, Spiro Bonello, to the British Consular Agency in Mansura, Egypt, during the British Protectorate period. It details an incident of alleged police brutality and arbitrary detention involving a constable named Aziz and his assistant. The document provides a rare, granular look at the social tensions and the interaction between local law enforcement and foreign subjects in provincial Egyptian cities during the First World War era, highlighting the role of the Consular Agency in providing legal protection to British subjects.
