ai_content.english_translation: This document is a summons issued by His Britannic Majesty's Consular Court in Cairo, operating under its civil jurisdiction. It is addressed to the defendants, The Egyptian Delta Land & Investment Co. Ltd. and Reginald G. Henriques, commanding them to appear in court in Cairo on the 25th day of July 1913, at 10 AM. They are required to answer a claim brought by the plaintiffs, A.J. Wakeman Long and B.A. Britain, the specific details of which are attached to the summons. The document explicitly warns that if the defendants fail to appear, the plaintiff may proceed with the case, and judgment may be rendered in their absence. The summons itself was officially issued and signed by the Consul at Cairo on the 2nd day of June 1913. Handwritten annotations on the document indicate the case reference number as 596/1913, a summons amount of £11.10.0, costs of £1.5.0, totaling £12.15.0. An attached slip provides an administrative instruction, stating that the summons should not be served unless 'Paragraph 6 becomes Paragraph 9' and specific words 'from and including 'further,' on the 17th February' are considered, suggesting a procedural amendment or clarification.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British Consular Court summons from Cairo, issued on June 2, 1913, with a court appearance scheduled for July 25, 1913. It exemplifies the extraterritorial legal jurisdiction exercised by the British Empire in Egypt during the early 20th century, a period when Egypt was under de facto British control prior to its formal declaration as a British Protectorate in 1914. The case involves A.J. Wakeman Long and B.A. Britain as plaintiffs against The Egyptian Delta Land & Investment Co. Ltd. and Reginald G. Henriques. The summons demands the defendants' appearance to answer a claim, with a clear warning of default judgment if they fail to attend. The financial details of the claim and associated costs are noted on the document. The existence of a British Consular Court in Cairo underscores the system of capitulations, which granted foreign nationals legal immunity from local Egyptian laws and allowed their home countries to administer justice through their own consular courts. The attached note, detailing a procedural condition for service related to specific paragraphs and wording from a February 17th document, highlights the meticulous administrative and legal framework governing such extraterritorial judicial processes. This document provides valuable insight into the legal and administrative mechanisms of British imperial power in Egypt and the specific legal disputes that arose within this complex framework.

The return to Egypt on the 4th instant of Saad Zaghloul will be celebrated by the local authorities at Alexandria and Cairo by demonstrations etc., and the General Officer Commanding directs that officers and other ranks shall be confined to barracks, etc., as under:-
1. Alexandria on the 5th April.
2. Cairo on the 5th April.
All Military Police will be withdrawn from duty on 4th and 5th April respectively. This will include police-men on duty at the various Railway stations between Alexandria and Cairo.
No despatch riders, motor cars or ambulances will be sent on duty during the time the troops are confined to barracks. Arrangements will be made for drawing rations both at Alexandria and Cairo which will enable these orders being adhered to.
The Colonel Commanding Alexandria District and Cairo Brigade will take such precautions as they may consider necessary, with the view to rendering assistance to the Civil authorities if called upon to do so.
In the event of celebrations taking place at Port-Said all troops will be confined to camps etc., and the 14th Infantry Brigade making the necessary arrangements for rendering assistance to the Civil authorities if called upon to do so.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official military circular issued in April 1921 regarding the return of the Egyptian nationalist leader Saad Zaghloul. It mandates that British military personnel in Alexandria and Cairo be confined to their barracks on April 5th to avoid conflict with public demonstrations celebrating his return. It further instructs military police to be withdrawn from railway stations and restricts the movement of military vehicles, while ensuring that logistical needs like rations are met. The Colonel Commanding is tasked with maintaining readiness to assist civil authorities if the situation escalates.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British military circular from April 1921, reflecting the tense political climate in Egypt following the return of the Wafd Party leader, Saad Zaghloul, from exile. The British colonial administration, fearing that the public celebrations of his return would lead to anti-British unrest or violence, issued these strict confinement orders to keep British troops off the streets of Alexandria and Cairo. The document highlights the administrative measures taken by the British military to minimize friction with the Egyptian populace while maintaining a state of readiness to support civil authorities during a period of significant nationalist agitation.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Colonel Stafford, from Tanta, has reported as follows on the incidents of yesterday:-

Early in the morning meetings were held and speeches made in favour of Saad Pasha Zaghloul and subsequently the mosques were the scene of further political speechifying. After prayer was over, demonstrations were formed and paraded the town shouting in the majority of cases for Saad though there were also some who shouted for Adly. The demonstrations got out of hand and the Police interfered, and on their warnings to disperse not being obeyed, they were ordered by the Mudir to fire in the air to disperse the crowd. One policeman, however, fired low killing one if not two persons. Subsequently the mob got infuriated and attacked the Markaz pelting it with stones. The hostilities continued off and on all day. It is thought that in the defence of the Markaz the Police may have fired again, but this fact is not confirmed. The mob cut the electric light but not the telephone.

In the evening 150 Egyptian Troops arrived but they did not fire. The demonstrations were organised by the notorious Zaghloulist, Hassan Bey Kemel. The mob were, no doubt, infuriated over the firing and the life of the Mudir was threatened. There were no signs of anti-European feeling in the morning. Colonel Stafford anticipates further demonstrations when the burial of the persons killed takes place, possibly on Monday being Shem el Nessim. Colonel Ryder's Office has a further report, which is not confirmed, that the Mudir tried to interfere unsuccessfully when the mob were attacking the Markaz, and that his motor-car was burnt.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a report from Colonel Stafford in Tanta detailing civil unrest. It describes political demonstrations in favor of Saad Zaghloul, the escalation of violence when police fired on crowds, the subsequent attack on the Markaz (administrative center), and the arrival of Egyptian troops. It notes the involvement of Hassan Bey Kemel and mentions the potential for further unrest during the upcoming Shem el Nessim holiday.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a diplomatic intelligence report from the British High Commission in Egypt, dated May 1, 1921. It provides a detailed account of political unrest in the city of Tanta, reflecting the volatile atmosphere in Egypt during the struggle for independence against British colonial rule. The report highlights the tension between the supporters of Saad Zaghloul and the administration, the role of local police in suppressing demonstrations, and the administrative challenges faced by British officials like Colonel Stafford and Colonel Ryder in maintaining order during the nationalist movement.

Traffic Manager, Cairo.
I beg to report that yesterday the 29th of April at about 4.30 p.m. at Tanta, I was returning on foot from the Tennis Club to the station.
When I got to the Clock's Square I was attacked by a large number of natives with sticks and stones within 50 yards of the Police Station.
Owing to the fact that none of the Egyptians came to my assistance I managed to reach the station where the mob clamoured at the gates for me to be given up to them.
While this was taking place, not a single policeman was in the streets, they had all retired inside the Police Barracks and left the town at the mercy of the mob.
I may add that I saw a policeman stationed on the roof of the Police Station in the Clock's Square at whom some of the people were throwing stones, and he must have seen what was happening, but inspite of this no effort was made by the Police to render me any assistance.
Saad Zaghloul & Dominih the Mudiria Authorities. Colonel Stafford considers that if today can be weathered, the situation will improve tomorrow.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION IN EGYPT
THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO
May 1st, 1921

The celebration of May day in Alexandria was confined to one small demonstration of about 40 people which dispersed without trouble. In Cairo, an equally small demonstration at Ezbekieh faded away without trouble.
SCHOOLS' REPORT
Tanta Secondary School all out strike, and one quarter of the Primary schools.
In Alexandria, Mansourah, and Zagazig, all schools are normal.
In Cairo the Khedivial School which was on strike yesterday is normal today, but the Saidia School is not working. (Colonel Willie, an official who works in Col. Ryder's office, and who also lectures at the Saidia School, tells me that it is true that the school are out, but that some students told him that they did not want to strike, but they were only intimidated into their present action.)
All the Technical schools in Cairo under the Ministry of Education are normal with the exception of Boulak Technical School. There the students are in class, but are not doing any work as a protest.
COL. STAFFORD'S REPORT FROM TANTA
He considers the situation today as critical. The mudir is doing his best and there are enough troops but there are signs of an absence of authority, and demonstrations are going round the town shouting "Long Live Saad Zaghloul & Down with the Mudiria Authorities". Colonel Stafford considers that if today can be weathered, the situation will improve tomorrow.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The following is a rough report received over the telephone from Russell Bey of the incidents of yesterday in Cairo. A fuller report will be received in due course.

From 11 o'clock onwards the town was restless and disturbed by demonstrations. In the morning a large crowd of 800 assembled in the vicinity of Ezbekia and when the Mamour of Ezbekia with a party of Policemen went out to oppose them the crowd attacked with all kinds of weapons and missiles, sticks, bottles filled with sand and road metal from the streets. The Mamour of Ezbekia was knocked out together with some of the Police and the party had to retire. A party of the Guard Company was sent out but on arrival on the scene found that the crowd had moved down Kasr-el-Nil and Soliman Pasha and made their way towards Saad Pasha Zaghloul's house. On their way they demonstrated and tore down some of the trees in order to make sticks. The European shops all put up their shutters. The Guard Company reinforced by twenty men of the mounted Troop went to Saad's house and found that the mob had crowded in some waste ground close to his house. They tried to disperse the mob who however attacked them and two troopers were injured and the Officer nearly unhorsed. He retired with his men, reformed and went through the crowd twice with sticks finally dispersing them.

There were further demonstrations in the evening outside the Mohammed Ali and I think elsewhere.

At about 8 o'clock last night, a bomb was thrown at Shubra as the last tram was entering the tramyard; it exploded and injured a number of people.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The following is information which I have just received by telephone from Ingram Bey with regard to events at Alexandria yesterday.

In the morning AHMED PASHA YEHIA, leader of the Zaghlulists there, was sent for and interviewed by the Governor and Commandant. He promised to go to the ABUL ABBAS mosque and dissuade the congregation assembled there for the midday prayers from making a demonstration. He took entire responsibility for the maintenance of order. Nevertheless a demonstration took place. It appears that AHMED PASHA YEHIA actually urged the people to make a demonstration and merely advised them not to throw stones. There was a much larger crowd than usual, both on account of the announcements with regard to the Official Delegation and also because there were wild rumours as to cavalry charges in Cairo the previous day. The crowd numbering probably more than 5 or 6000 people marched into the town. Students and rabble made up the large proportion of them. As they passed the British Main Guard they threw some bricks at them. Troops at the request of the police officers refrained from firing and the crowd passed on to attack the Attarine Caracol with stones. A British Military policeman coming out of their quarters close by was hit on the head with a brick and was killed. The police managed to drive the mob away from the caracol and it then went on and attacked the Manshiet caracol. Here they had greater success and rushed the ground floor. Police reinforcements turned them out again. They then went on to the Gumruk caracol, cut the telephone wires and surrounded it in thousands. They completely overpowered the police among whom were 24 casualties and again rushed the ground floor of the caracol. They set fire to the building, meanwhile information had come to the Governorate and the guard company arrived and the mob from the rear down one of the main streets. They had now received permission to shoot and had no difficulty in restoring order. As a result of their firing, 7 of the mob were killed or died of wounds and 20 wounded. The quarter was soon completely pacified. At some time after this collision General Blake took charge of the town. Commandant of Police having received orders from the Adviser to hand over the caracol. These orders were subsequently cancelled, the police were sent an armoured car which, however, was not used. It is incorrect to say, as the Gazette states, that British troops were called upon to quell the mob. At night the mob attacked the caracol. They had barricaded the road. The mob was soon got under control however.

This morning the town is absolutely quiet. The caracols are well guarded the guards being armed with rifles. The police are arresting wellknown agitators etc.

21.5.21.

6 p.m. Cairo: All quiet up to the present. The funeral of the two men killed yesterday was orderly and attended by about 400 students and there marching in military formation.

6 p.m. Alexandria: A battalion of S.A. troops has arrived and have taken over all guards and the custody of the Police from the Police barracks. The town is calm and the funerals of those killed yesterday passed off without incident. The Italian and French consuls called on Grantley yesterday to ask for assurances that their colonies would be protected. He reassured them. He asked me to ask H.E. to reconsider the order to withdraw the armored cars from the police. I told him I would ring him up at 7 p.m. with H.E.'s decision. He was not anticipating any definite trouble but thought that the funeral parties might create disturbances later in the evening.

The city is calm, and the funerals for those killed yesterday occurred without incident. The Italian and French consuls visited Grantley yesterday to request assurances regarding the protection of their respective colonies. He provided them with reassurance. ai_content.transcribed_text: I have the honour to report to Your Excellency that renewed attacks were made on the Police yesterday the 16th instant by large crowds armed with missiles of all sorts. The Demonstration was first reported from Midan Khazindar; the Mamur of Ezbekieh at once proceeded to the spot with Thirty Guard Company men in a motor lorry. He found a mob of some 600 men, mostly roughs but led by students, they were all carrying clubs and boughs of trees. As soon as the mob saw the Police they rushed to attack them throwing stones and bottles filled with sand; the attack was very severe and the Thirty Guard Coy: men could do nothing. The Mamur of Ezbekieh was hit three different times and was knocked down, he was taken into a shop which the mob attacked but did not enter. Most of the Guard Coy: men and Police on beat duty had to take refuge in shops etc from the crowd as they were armed only with canes and could not stand up against the determined attack of the crowd. The Mamur of Police was hit and one Policeman, who stood over the Mamur to protect him when he fell, was badly hit in the head with a stone and knocked out. On hearing of the size and savageness of the crowd I sent a second lorry-load of Guard Company wearing steel helmets and armed with shot guns and rifles; by the time they reached the spot the crowd had gone on and had got into Sharia El Nil before I got news of it again. On their way the mob tore down branches off the street trees to use as weapons; the European shopkeepers were filled alarm and hastily pulled down their iron shutters. I had previously sent out all the available mounted Troop under Yuzbashi Azab Selim; this force of 30 men got into touch with the mob in Sharia Khairat at the same time as the Guard Coy; Lorry again effected contact with the crowd. Here again the Guard Coy; could do very little the crowd being so big and the rain of missiles being so severe; several times they had to withdraw to reform and return to the attack. When the attack was at its hottest a Corporal of the Guard Coy; fired his rifle off in the air and the mob ran away at top speed. By 1 PM. all crowds had dispersed with the exception of a group of roughs near the Ministry of Agriculture; these were dispersed by the Mounted Troop.

It details the escalation of violence, the inability of standard police units to contain the mob, the injury of the Mamur of Ezbekieh, and the eventual dispersal of the crowds after the use of firearms and mounted troops.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
-2-
The total casualties to the Police were three officers wounded, four Guard Coy. men, one Mounted Troop and one qiam man wounded.
There can be no doubt that this mob had been deliberately formed and amed by Zaghlulist agents with the definite purpose of attacking the Police.
I had information on the 17th Instant that the students in future intended to use bottles filled with sand and this was one of the weapons used yesterday; the stones also had been brought with them.
Prompt all the evidence I have yet collected I consider that this armed mob was organised by students of the Madia School; earlier in the morning the Amout of Walli heard that 40 boys of that School had left the School and came into the Midan Khazindar from the direction of El Daher, i.e., of the school in question.
The only force that I have at my disposal for dealing with such crowds is 400 conscripts of the Guard Coy; of this force yesterday about 100 were employed on the daily routine duties of escorts from prisons to the Courts etc.; 60 were employed in protecting trams and 40 were in reserve at Boulac in anticipation of trouble in the railway workshops; another 50 must be written off for certain guards which I cannot hand over to the Egyptian Army, orderlies, etc. Leaving me with an effective force of only 150 men; at the end of yesterday morning I had a hundred men out on demonstrations and 60 left to protect the Barracks.
It is quite clear that this force cannot disperse the mobs of seven and eight hundred strong unless they use something more effectual than sticks.
The situation is made doubly difficult by the probability that these attacks on the Police are expressly organised to drive the Police to using fire-arms: if the Police shoot anyone, enormous propaganda will be made out of it here and in England and the inevitable funerals will be made the occasion of monster demonstrations.
The Guard Company is in possession of a certain number of ordinary shot guns with modified charges of small shot: if driven to it, I propose to use these on the crowd before resorting to rifles.
The fact remains, however, that these murderous attacks on the police continue, I shall not be able to get the Police to face them unless they are allowed to shoot.
If I call in the Egyptian Army infantry to help me, they equally will not stand being stoned in the face and will demand to be allowed to fire.
I would ask that it be made quite clear to the Public through the medium of the Press that such attacks on the Police will not be tolerated and that the crowd will have no one except themselves to blame if the Police make use of fire-arms.
If yesterday's events are going to repeat themselves, I foresee that I shall have to use my Guard Coy. to defend my Police Stations. I shall, be unable to deal with the demonstrations except with my Mounted men who will be insufficient; the result will be that these armed mobs will have the run of the town to the great danger of the Ministries and eventually of life and property generally.
I have reason to believe also that students of certain schools intend to make individual attacks on certain Police officers.
P.T.O.

The author outlines the severe shortage of manpower, noting that out of 400 conscripts, only a small fraction are available for riot control after accounting for routine duties. The report argues for the necessity of using shotguns as a deterrent to prevent the need for lethal rifle fire, while warning that if the police are not empowered to defend themselves, the mobs will threaten government ministries and public order.

Following report on the situation of the schools has been received from the special section, Cairo:

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Alexandria.
Information as to the situation received up to 10 a.m. on 4.5.21.
The night of the 2nd to 3rd passed quietly. The town is now very quiet. Armoured cars are patrolling the streets, and British troops in charge. Very few were present at evening prayers at the Abou Abbas Mosque last night and they went home quietly.
Most of the shops have their shutters closed, but business is going on. A good many Europeans are walking about and the people are calming down.
The history of the trouble is as follows:
After the firing on Friday, the native rabble were cowed, but at the same time they were fervent towards Europeans where they could safely be so. As a result the Europeans in the lower quarters were very nervous.
The trouble began on Sunday night by some rabble marching through the Attarine quarter shouting 'Down with the Greeks etc'. Low class Greeks and Italians fired at them from the houses, the natives replied by trying to set the houses on fire etc, and events proceeded as already reported.
Trouble began yesterday with 500 Italians who went to their consul to ask for protection.
The Italian Consul marched them to the Governorate, as a demonstration of protest. Both the Consul himself and the crowd outside were in an extremely excited condition. The Commandant and sub-Commandant endeavoured to calm them down but without success. A group of natives on their way to their work passed at the end of the street, and the men of the Italians outside the Governorate, without any provocation, rushed at them firing their revolvers. The news spread to the Attarine quarter and the events of the previous evening were repeated in a much worse form, the excitement rapidly spreading to the whole town.
European shops, except in the best quarters, were in almost every case sacked, and very often set on fire. Natives knocked Europeans on the head whenever they met them. The Europeans retaliated by shooting.
The British Colonel Commandant, having taken charge, the British troops were firing pretty constantly the whole day, protecting fire engines, preventing hose cutting, looters and incendiaries. (A considerable amount of firing done by persons other than the troops, which must have accounted for a very large proportion of the casualties, it may be presumed that the troops were firing as a warning rather than to kill, many cases at least).
The Egyptian Army and Egyptian Police were not the object of any particular hostility by any of the parties engaged. One policeman was killed by a Greek. The other two police casualties were the result of an accident with an armoured car. There are a few reports, at present unverified of Egyptian Army and police having fired at Europeans, and perhaps under provocation, as the latter appear to have fired at them from windows. There is one authenticated case where an Egyptian private was seen by a British officer to shoot a Greek.
The revised list of casualties is: 36 Egyptians killed, 12 Europeans killed, 91 Egyptians wounded, 60 Europeans wounded. The Alexandria Police have made arrangements for the funerals today, and British cavalry are going to assist to maintain order.

SITUATION REPORT FROM G.H.Q. ALEXANDRIA 12 NOON.
May 24th, 1921.

SITUATION REPORT FROM G.H.Q. ALEXANDRIA 12 noon.
May 24th, 1921.

British Troops during the last 24 hours have been forced to fire in (1) in self-defence on being stoned (2) to prevent looting and incendiarism (3) to protect the fire brigade, engine and hose which was attempting to deal with the fires. Altogether 48 shots were fired by the two companies on picket duty.
The most ugly situation which the Troops had to deal with occurred in Sister Street last night 9.20, on which occasion the troops fired and dispersed the mob.
A party of six Greeks dressed in Khaki are going round the town in a motor-car shooting. Attempts are being made to capture them which have not succeeded up to 12 noon.
36 funerals will take place this afternoon. By order of General Blake, no processions will be allowed.
The Italian and Greek Consuls have protested to General Blake against the employment of Egyptian Army on picket duty in the European Quarter.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Cairo R. Information by telephone from Bimbashi Ablitt... The only signs of trouble as yet are that the Railway Workshops and Government Arsenal employees have struck work. The strike is nominally due to the 20% reduction of bonuses, but a lot of political feeling also undoubtedly enters into it. The Police authorities are afraid that the political motive may lead to the strike developing, and to attempts at sabotage which in the present excited condition of the public might serve as a match which would start serious trouble. Most of the shops are shut. Cairo R. Information from Bimb. Ablitt 9.50 a.m. With regard to one of the rumours that had caused trouble, i.e., that there had been a large influx of demonstrators from the provinces yesterday, investigation shows that 100 persons arrived from Tanta and 60 from Mansourah, in addition to the ordinary passengers, in order, as they said, to go and see the Sultan. It is not known whether they attempted to see the Sultan, but they are known to have gone to Zaghloul Pasha's house. There were also more than usual from Upper Egypt. Wollaston 25.5.21. Seen by all concerned.
ai_content.english_translation: The document consists of two intelligence reports relayed by telephone from Bimbashi Ablitt to the Residency in Cairo. The first report details a strike by Railway and Arsenal workers, noting that while the official cause is a 20% bonus cut, political unrest is the primary driver, raising fears of sabotage. The second report addresses rumors of provincial demonstrators arriving in Cairo; it confirms that 160 individuals from Tanta and Mansourah arrived, ostensibly to see the Sultan, but were observed visiting the residence of the nationalist leader Zaghloul Pasha. The document is signed by Wollaston and dated May 25, 1921.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British intelligence report from the Residency in Cairo, dated May 1921, during a period of intense nationalist agitation in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution. It captures the British colonial administration's anxiety regarding the intersection of labor unrest (strikes in the railway and arsenal sectors) and the broader Wafd-led nationalist movement headed by Saad Zaghloul Pasha. The report highlights the British authorities' surveillance of provincial movements and their concern that economic grievances were being weaponized to destabilize the British-backed Sultanate.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Telephone message from Mr. K.B. at 10.45 Mr. Patterson informed me that he had received a report from Russell showing that Russell had at his disposition as a striking force the following numbers: Guard Company 150, Egyptian Army Inf. 250. Telephone message from Trent Bey - 11.15 a.m. 25.5.21. At 9.30 the Colonel Commandant took charge of the town, and planted troops down the main guard to take up picket posts. Very heavy indiscriminate firing has been going on between Arabs and Europeans since 9.30 a.m. Europeans are firing from their windows. Evidence at present is insufficient but the Commandant believes that the Europeans started it. They certainly started it last night, and order had been restored shorting previous to the recommencement. A considerable number of casualties have taken place. Three policemen have been killed - one shot through the neck. It is believed by a General looting is going on. Armoured cars are controlling the streets. The Egyptian Army has not done well. The Commandant believes; he has been told they got their hands and fired at the Europeans in the windows. This has not been verified. There are many fires in the town. The Wardian quarter is said to be ablaze. The Fire Brigade find it difficult to get down there because of the mob. At the moment of telephoning fires at the Ghomas were reported. Nevertheless, the Commandant believes that the military arrangements made are likely to result in an early restoration of order. I have not been able to get through yet to ask whether British troops have fired. Strike is political and it is necessary to bring the situation to a head.

It records the deployment of security forces, including the Egyptian Army and Guard Company, to manage violent clashes between Arabs and Europeans. The reports describe heavy firing, looting, casualties among the police, and significant fires in the Wardian quarter, while noting the difficulty of the Fire Brigade in reaching affected areas due to the mob.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Telephone message from Mr. K.B. [High Commissioner Egypt 26 MAY 1921 No 8828]
At 10.45 Mr. Patterson informed me that he had received a report from Russell showing that Russell had at his disposition as a striking force the following numbers :-
Guard Company 150
Egyptian Army Inf. 250
Egyptian Cavalry 70
Mounted Police 40
All other men are engaged on Guard work.
Russell wished for instructions as to the use of British Troops. Under instructions transmitted by me to Mr. Patterson, the latter sent Wellesley to G.H.Q. with Russell's report to say that the High Commissioner wished the British Troops to stand by ready to intervene if mobs began to look menacing in European quarters. The Military authorities have been told that it would be a good thing if they would keep in touch with Russell.
The danger is that the men from the Boulac workshops may come down into Cairo.
A railway strike is probable to-morrow. It will be possible to send one train a day to the Forts. Nothing can be done for Upper Egypt.
Blakeney to-morrow will look out the Boulac workshops
He has up to the present been more than conciliatory: things were going well but it is now clear that to-day's strike is political and it is necessary to bring the situation to a head.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a record of a telephone communication regarding civil unrest and security measures in Egypt. It details the military and police forces available to Russell, the deployment of British troops as a standby force to protect European quarters, and concerns regarding potential labor strikes at the Boulac workshops and the railway, which are perceived as politically motivated.

It captures the tense administrative and security atmosphere in Cairo during a period of nationalist agitation. The text highlights the British colonial administration's reliance on military intelligence and the strategic deployment of troops to maintain order in European districts amidst fears of labor strikes at the Boulac workshops and the broader Egyptian railway network. It reflects the transition of labor disputes into political resistance against the British presence.

CAIRO: All quiet and no incidents - A report of the attendance at the Schools will be supplied later.
ALEXANDRIA: During the night a telephone message was received at 9.30 p.m. from Colonel Grant to the effect that he was apprehensive of further severe trouble and that he required the assistance of the armoured car. At 10.30 p.m. he reported by telephone that he no longer felt so anxious as the small demonstrations throughout the town had dispersed separately instead of as he had anticipated combining for joint action. The town is quiet this morning.
TANTAH: On Friday it was generally rumoured in the town that the Mudirieh would be attacked on Saturday. The Inspector of the Interior Mr. Graves and the Mudir saw Dr. Hassan Kamel, the leading Zaghloulist who organised the riots three weeks ago and apparently frightened him by impressing on him the serious consequences which would attend anything like a general attack on Government property and servants. As a result Tantah remained quiet on Saturday. Egyptian Troops are being drafted into the town and it is hoped in four days' time a full Battalion will be stationed there.
Reports from ZAGAZIG, MENOUFIA and DAMANHOUR state that the towns are quiet and report no incidents.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
ALEXANDRIA CITY POLICE
Public Security Division
Branch
THE GOVERNORATE ALEXANDRIA
26th May 1921.
J.R.E. Monteith Smith Esq
Ministry of Interior
CAIRO

No.-DAILY REPORT

A diary of the events since the last report dated 21st.
By last report gave details up to the speeches in the
Mosque and the departure of the demonstration.
At 12.30 on Friday the Mamur reported that
Sheikh Zaki had arrived at the Mosque at 11.45 a.m. and that
there was about 1000 people inside & 500 outside also a number of
youths with carts of stones, waiting to join the demonstration.
At 13.00 it was reported that a crowd with stones & sticks
held a demonstration about 5000 strong proceeded by carts loaded
with stones was going towards Manshia.
At 13.30 Manshia reported that a crowd with stones & sticks
clogs were passing but were quiet, they were followed by the
demonstration which shouted Long live Zaghloul.
They entered the square & proceeded up Sherif Pasha
street but were quiet except a few hostile cries against
the civilian, from the rest of the crowd.
At 14.41 without warning stones were thrown at the
building but the guard did not at that moment fire.
The demonstration then went on to the crowd Elum
breaking the reserves from Ram el Dik with the Mounted Troop
Police who dashed out to attack them.
At 15.15 the crowd attacked Elum Manshia xxxxxx
windows & round the ground floor. By 15.40 the
Mounted Troop arrived & drove off the crowd.
The situation was so serious that permission was
asked to open fire.
At 15.15 The Ministry of Interior said he would consult
Prime Minister re firing & inform us.
At 15.55 it was reported that the mob was in charge of
Elum. At 16.05 I informed G.O.C. that it might be necessary
to take over town but not to do anything till I communicated with
him again. G.O.C. replied that troops were standing by.
At 16.30 it was reported that crowd was on fire.
I left decision to the man on the spot. I gave them left
with armed reinforcements & attacked the crowd from the rear
under heavy firing. He was compelled to open fire & picked shots
selected the ringleaders.

P.S.O.

At 07.00 the Goumrok reported that Europeans were being assaulted on the trams in Marina & some Guard Company were sent off & dispersed them. They were only small boys throwing stones.
The telephone service was very bad owing to the absence of most of the operators & when I rang up in the morning I could not get any reply.
He tried to get on to me without avail getting no answer from the Central Station, so he hurried down & found that they had arrived at the Governorate in a state of wild excitement waving revolvers.
Knowing that any failure to control that crowd would lead at once to bloodshed & riot, the Asst. Commandant tried to get through to me again but failed so he rang up the G.O.C. & informed him that it might be necessary to take over.
Every effort was made to calm them, but they rushed off firing. At this time messages arrived from the Governorate & hurried to the G.O.C. received a communication from the Governorate & that Europeans and other Europeans were opening fire on a mob of rabs who were approaching the Governorate.
Between 08.30 & 09.30 the G.O.C. arrived & informed him that the town was out of control.
At 09.40 the reports strong & Natives & Greeks fighting in the streets.
At 09.45 Lebhan situation very serious. Houses being broken into.
At 09.55 Greeks firing in Goumrok.
At 09.55 Native reports shops being looted.
At 09.55 Ramleh reports shops being looted.
At 09.55 Greeks firing in Goumrok.
After this time the troops had begun to take over the town & all further incidents were reported to the Main Guard for such action as they considered necessary.
(Signed) Ian C. Evans, Commandant, Alexandria City Police.

It chronicles the breakdown of order, starting with minor incidents involving stone-throwing youths, progressing to the arming of Europeans at the Governorate, and culminating in widespread rioting, looting, and gunfire between various ethnic and social groups (Natives, Greeks, and Europeans) across the city, necessitating military intervention.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Communiqué to the Press. 23 S. 21. 2 pm. The following information has been received from the Director General, Public Security. Yesterday evening serious collisions occurred between low class Europeans and natives in the Musull quarter, the exact cause of which is as yet unexplained. Firing took place, and several houses were set on fire. The police with the help of the Egyptian Army were engaged until late last night in quelling the disturbance. Order was re-established about 3 a.m. and the quarter placated. Early this morning further trouble took place, and at 8.30 a.m. the Colonel Commandant of the British forces in Alexandria took charge of the town. Host intercommunication between natives and Europeans continued in the early morning hours of the morning. The casualties as yet reported are: 49 injured and 3 killed, admitted to the Government hospital; 31 injured and two killed admitted to the Greek hospital. 8 policemen were badly injured but no other casualties to police or troops are reported. Some looting took place and a certain number of fires were started in the town, more especially in the Wardian quarter. Most of these fires were put out before mid-day, and the others were then under control. The police have made a large number of arrests and at 12.30 p.m. the condition of the town was approaching normal, except for a few bands of roughs who paraded the outskirts of the city.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official press release issued by the British High Commission in Egypt regarding civil unrest in Alexandria. It details violent clashes between European residents and local Egyptians in the Musull quarter, the subsequent intervention of the British military, casualty counts from local hospitals, and the status of order in the city as of May 23, 1921.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a contemporary record of the civil disturbances that occurred in Alexandria, Egypt, in May 1921. It serves as an official communiqué from the British High Commission to the press, documenting the escalation of violence between European and native populations, the intervention of the British military under the Colonel Commandant, and the administrative efforts to restore order. The report provides specific details on casualties, the involvement of the Egyptian Army and police, and the geographic spread of the unrest to the Wardian quarter, reflecting the volatile political climate in Egypt during the period of the British Protectorate and the rise of the Wafd movement.

ai_content.transcribed_text: The Director, Special Section, Public Security Dept., War Office, CAIRO. 26th May 1921. Summary of the events since the last report dated that. 12.00 as the Mosque at 11.45 am, and that there are about 1000 people inside & 500 outside also a number of youths with carts & stones, waiting to join the demonstration. 13.00 it was reported that a policeman on foot only that a demonstration about 2000 strong proceeded by carts loaded with stones was going towards Manshia. 14.00 the streets were quiet, they were followed by the shops that were closed, except a few hostile demonstrations against the police. 15.00 the crowd gathered up near the Police building but the guard did not fire at any cost. 15.45 witness seeing heavily armed the General & the unit of the Military Police, killing a number of the English mounted police who dashed out to attack them. 15.55 the crowd attacked the British troops breaking the line of the crowd. 16.00 the situation was no serious risk remaining, asked from Cairo to open fire. 16.10 the Ministry of Interior said he would consult the Minister on firing & inform us. 16.15 it was reported that the mob was in charge of the town but not so doing still I consulted with him again. I replied that troops may then left. 16.35 the officer had gained to fire if necessary a left decision to the men on the spot. In my opinion they were under heavy stoning & advanced the crowd from the rear by firing. He was compelled to open fire & killed those who were the ringleaders.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
D.G.P.S. report as follows on the incidents yesterday in Cairo :-
There was a very slight demonstration in the morning outside the Finance, mostly corner-boys and quickly dispersed by the Police.
The meeting at the Continental Hotel lasted from 3.30 to 7 o'clock and was well attended. (Numbers were estimated by Dr. Hafez Bey Afifi at 1500). There was no undue incident outside the Hotel and everything passed off quietly. The tone of the speeches was for Unity. A vote at the end of the day was passed to the effect that should Egypt not receive complete independence from His Majesty's Government, Great Britain would be faced by a united and orderly nation.
The Zaghloulist meeting passed off uneventfully and was well attended. When it broke up, some of the crowd threw stones at the Policemen who charged them and dispersed them.
In the evening at 10.30 a crowd of 300 came into Opera square from Imad el Din Street. The 16 policemen on duty in the square tried to disperse them by charging with canes. They, however, were not strong enough and accordingly fired two shots in the air whereupon the crowd fled.
The tramstrike is over and the attendance in the schools is reported to be normal, although yesterday there was a partial strike.
Port-Said reported yesterday that no incidents had occurred, and Alexandria with whom arrangements had been made that they would ring up in the afternoon if anything happened, did not telephone to the D.P.S. from which it is inferred that the situation is normal.
Attach the A.C.P. daily report for the 14th inst. Which shows that the situation was not calm on that date. Inprouky was rather nervous on Saturday as their were signs of bad feeling in Panic. 16.11.24. Qui.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a daily intelligence report from the Director General of Public Security (D.G.P.S.) detailing civil unrest and political meetings in Cairo, Port Said, and Alexandria. It describes a demonstration at the Finance Ministry, a large political meeting at the Continental Hotel addressed by Dr. Hafez Bey Afifi regarding Egyptian independence from Great Britain, a Zaghloulist meeting, and a skirmish between police and a crowd in Opera Square. It also notes the end of a tram strike and school attendance, concluding with a summary of the situation in Alexandria and a note regarding the 14th of November.

(Director General of Public Security) underscores the British oversight of Egyptian internal affairs during the period of the British Protectorate and the subsequent transition to a constitutional monarchy.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
ALEXANDRIA CITY POLICE
Public Security Division
Branch 'A'
THE GOVERNORATE ALEXANDRIA
13th November 1921
DAILY REPORT

Ahmed Yehia Pasha has made an appeal to the public, by way of the press, to refrain from demonstrations & all celebrations of any description which might lead to incidents on the 12th inst. The Pasha at the invitation of Zaghloul Pasha will leave for Cairo with a delegation of leading Alexandria notables to celebrate the 13th at Cairo.

There is a turbulent spirit amongst the natives at Gurnel and Gabari this morning. It is the general opinion that if the police officers do not take it not unlikely that trouble will occur.

Instructions have been given to all police officers to break up all demonstrations whether so called 'mufti' or otherwise with the utmost rigour. The whole police force is standing by, and the Colonel Comdt. has been requested to take precautionary measures.

Insurance Companies have been doing brisk business during the last two days insuring against civil disturbances.

It should be borne in mind that the majority of the Europeans in the mixed quarters now possess fire arms & that therefore the smallest incident will set the match to the powder.

There are still many rumours afloat & the Europeans are gradually working themselves into a panic.

One of the extremes of one of their comrades who are very excited about the 12th, the Red Death is which will take place on Monday morning next, the Red Death is said to be determined to stop the execution & will march en masse to the prison & liberate all prisoners.

Police - A printed & unsigned circular has been found in Alexandria in this morning's post suggesting that all police officers should send telegrams to H.E. the Prime Minister complaining of their wretched condition & threatening by the same that, should there be a strike forthwith, steps are being taken to discover the authors of this circular.

ABU EL ABBAS - No speeches were made after the noon prayer today. The audience dispersed without incident.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a daily intelligence report from the Alexandria City Police, dated November 13, 1921. It details the political climate in Alexandria, specifically mentioning the appeal by Ahmed Yehia Pasha to avoid demonstrations, the movement of notables to Cairo to meet with Zaghloul Pasha, and the general anxiety among the European population regarding potential civil unrest. It notes the police's readiness to suppress demonstrations, the increase in insurance policies against civil disturbances, and rumors of a planned prison break by radicals. It also mentions a circular inciting police officers to strike and reports on the peaceful conclusion of prayers at the Abu el-Abbas mosque.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
CAIRO. November 26th, 1921.
D.G.P.S. report this morning that the situation is not quite so good as it was two days ago. Signs of unrest are reported from the three towns, Cairo, Alexandria and Port-Said.
CAIRO : The students are reported to be anxious to demonstrate against Adly Pasha on his return, though Saad Pasha himself has advised them to await the publication of the three documents.
PORT-SAID : The Police report that there is an appreciable amount of talk to demonstrate against Adly Pasha and also to organise strikes and a boycott of British shops and goods.
ALEXANDRIA : There are many rumours, but the general opinion is that it will be best to await the publication of the three documents.
Information from a reliable source states that the Gabbari workmen are again restless on economic grounds.
Colonel Hyder emphasised that this report gave the impression that the situation was worse than he actually believed to be the case. Such unrest as there is at present is undefined and so far not important, though it will have to be closely watched by the D.G.P.S.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is written in English. It summarizes intelligence reports from the Director General of Public Security regarding civil unrest in Cairo, Alexandria, and Port-Said on November 26, 1921, specifically concerning political opposition to Adly Pasha and the anticipation of the publication of three documents, alongside labor unrest in the Gabbari district.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British intelligence summary from late 1921, a period of intense political volatility in Egypt following the end of WWI and the rise of the Wafd Party. The text highlights the tension surrounding the political figure Adly Pasha, who was attempting to negotiate a treaty with the British, and the opposition led by Saad Zaghloul Pasha. The mention of 'three documents' refers to the ongoing diplomatic negotiations between the British government and the Egyptian delegation. The report reflects the British colonial administration's anxiety regarding student demonstrations, labor strikes in industrial areas like Gabbari, and the potential for a boycott of British goods, all of which were key tactics of the Egyptian nationalist movement during this era.

SITUATION REPORT: For Monday evening - 12-12-21

CAIRO, ALEXANDRIA and PORT SAID - All quiet.

PROVINCES - All quiet. One of the men hurt in the disturbances at ZAGAZIG died yesterday, his funeral was largely attended but there was no disturbance.

THE SCHOOLS - About half the boys at the Saidia (where they were on strike yesterday), returned to work today. But at the Khedivial school on the other hand which was working yesterday, there were only a few boys present at the beginning of the morning and they subsequently left. At ZAGAZIG the boys have returned to work and all other Government schools are normal.

At Alexandria three of the smaller schools went out on strike and the police officer on duty expressed it as his opinion that they had come to some arrangement whereby the schools should take it in turn to go out, one or two doing so each day.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a situation report dated December 12, 1921, detailing civil unrest and student strikes in Egypt. It notes that Cairo, Alexandria, and Port Said are calm. In the provinces, a man injured during disturbances in Zagazig has died, though his funeral proceeded without incident. Regarding schools, attendance is mixed: some students at the Saidia school returned, while the Khedivial school saw students leave after arriving. In Zagazig, students returned to work. In Alexandria, police suspect that smaller schools are coordinating rotating strikes.

ai_content.english_translation: Situation Report EG.36 for Wednesday evening, December 14, 1921. In Cairo, Alexandria, and Port Said, the police report that the situation at 7:00 PM is normal. In the provinces, there is nothing to report. The Khedivieh School went on strike this afternoon. In the provinces, specifically in Assiout, the Secondary School was closed by the Headmaster because political speeches continued inside the building despite a warning. Copies of this report are directed to: The Chancery, The Residency; The Adviser, Ministry of the Interior; Chief Inspector, Ministry of the Interior; Commandants of Cairo, Alexandria, and Port Said Police; G.S.I., G.H.Q.; G.S.O., Egyptian Army; and the Sudan Agent.

It highlights a dispersed demonstration by private school pupils in Cairo, a strike at the prominent Khedivieh School, and the closure of a secondary school in Assiout (Asyut) due to political speeches. ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT
For Sunday evening - 18.12.21

CAIRO: A crowd of about 2000 collected outside SAAD PASHA ZAGHLOUL's house in the morning, and consisted chiefly of Dar el Alum students and "outside" students. A demonstration was formed which proceeded in the direction of the Ministry of Public Works. It was soon broken up by the Police, the first lorry load of whom were stoned by the crowd on their arrival at the scene.
In the afternoon another demonstration was formed outside SAAD PASHA ZAGHLOUL's house, but this was at once broken up. Some 18 persons were arrested during the morning and afternoon.

ALEXANDRIA: No demonstrations. All Schools, Government and Private, on strike, except RAS EL TIN COLLEGE.

PORT SAID: Small demonstration about 50 persons in the morning, mostly students. In the afternoon, a larger demonstration of about 500 persons consisting of local Zaghloulist supporters, workmen, and others took place in the native quarter of the town. It was quite orderly and easily controlled by the police.

PROVINCES: Quiet. No demonstrations anywhere except a small one at FAYOUM where some of students and others were arrested.

SCHOOLS: All Government Secondary schools on strike in CAIRO, ALEXANDRIA and elsewhere, except SULTANISH TRAINING COLLEGE and BOULAC MODEL WORKSHOPS in CAIRO. A number of private schools also on strike in various parts of the country.

Copies to: The Residency, The Adviser, Min. of Interior, Chief Inspector, Min. of Interior, G.O.C., G.H.Q., S.D.O., Egyptian Army, Sudan Agent.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT
For Monday evening, 19th Dec. 1921
CAIRO, ALEXANDRIA and PORTSAID: All quiet.
At Alexandria the boat containing WILLIAM MAKRAM OBEID arrived at 6.30pm and a large number of people assembled to meet him.
PROVINCES: All quiet since 1pm yesterday except Tanta where there were demonstrations by roughs and school boys in the afternoon, the police being seriously stoned. The police dispersed the mob with sticks and made 12 arrests, one a sheikh from the religious school and the others street roughs. Today all is quiet and a company of the Egyptian battalion has been called in to help in the police work.
SCHOOLS: Tanta, Zagazig and Saidia (Cairo) secondary schools are on strike. At Abbasia (Alexandria) secondary school about a quarter of the students were present. Zagazig secondary school is being closed and Assiut secondary school will be closed until Dec. 24th.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT
for Tuesday Evening, December 20th, 1921

CAIRO. A crowd estimated at 3000 assembled at the station to greet William Makram. When Makram and the students who followed him in cars had passed the Opera Square, the streets leading in to it were closed in order to divide up the mob. Another considerable crowd assembled round Zaghloul's house after his arrival. At 6.30 p.m. they were already rapidly dispersing. No damage or disorder had been reported up to that time.

ALEXANDRIA. A fairly big crowd saw William Makram off at the station, and there were a certain number of spectators along the railway line most of the way to Hadra. There was no disorder and the town was normal throughout the rest of the day.

PORT SAID. All quite quiet.

PROVINCES. Considerable numbers of people greeted William Makram at Kafr el Zayat, Tanta and other stations with a good deal of enthusiasm.

SCHOOLS. Most of the Government Secondary schools, through the country, apart from two closed by order, were wholly or partially on strike.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal situation report detailing the public reception of political figure William Makram (Makram Ebeid) upon his return to Egypt. It describes crowd sizes, the movement of supporters in Cairo and Alexandria, the lack of civil disorder, and the status of student strikes in government schools across the provinces.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT for December 21st 1921. 

CAIRO: Shooting British Soldiers. At about 7.30 P.M. yesterday, the 20th inst., two British soldiers, both from Infantry Regiments, were shot from behind when walking together along Sharia Saptieh in the neighbourhood of the Mankimet Charia. One was killed instantaneously, shot through the back and chest, the other was seriously wounded in the lower part of the back. As usual in such cases no eye-witnesses have been discovered and the perpetrator or perpetrators evidently escaped down an unlit side street opposite the mouth of which the crime was committed. Today, 21st inst., all quiet.

ALEXANDRIA: All quiet.

PORT SAID: All quiet.

PROVINCES: UPPER EGYPT: All quiet. LOWER EGYPT: All quiet except Tanta where last evening the Police were again stoned. Up to mid-day today TANTA has been quiet. 7.20 p.m. The Mudir at TANTA reports 'no disturbances'.

SCHOOLS: ABBASSIA, ALEXANDRIA - About one-third present. KHEDIVIA, CAIRO - About one-sixth present. TEWFIKIA, CAIRO - About seven-eights present. SAIDIA, CAIRO - About 60 on strike. MUSHTOHOR, College - On strike. ZAGAZIG - Still out. ASYUT - Closed.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a daily situation report detailing civil unrest and security incidents in Egypt. It records a specific shooting of two British soldiers in Cairo on the 20th of December 1921, noting the lack of witnesses and the escape of the perpetrators. It provides a status update on various Egyptian cities, noting that while most are quiet, Tanta experienced police stoning. It also tracks student attendance and strike activity at various educational institutions across Egypt, indicating significant unrest in the school system.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SITUATION REPORT for Thursday evening 22.12.21. CAIRO. Serious demonstrations, mostly in the neighbourhood of ZAGHLOUL'S house, occurred in Cairo today during the afternoon. The Police were stoned on more than one occasion and had to fire. Egyptian troops which lent assistance were also stoned. At 6.35 pm the police report that the demonstrations had been broken up but that a crowd numbering about 3000 persons which had been gathering during the afternoon, were at and around Zaghloul's house. Casualties among the crowd, admitted to Kasr el Aini Hospital: 2 dead and 6 wounded.

It notes that demonstrations occurred near the residence of Saad Pasha Zaghloul, leading to clashes between the police, Egyptian troops, and a crowd of approximately 3,000 people. The police were forced to use firearms, resulting in two deaths and six injuries among the protesters. The report also lists the status of various schools and provinces, noting that authorities have ordered specific political figures to refrain from political activity.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SITUATION REPORT 24.12.21. The British Military authorities took over from the police at 8 a.m. this morning. SAAD ZAGHLOUL Pasha was arrested this morning and was taken under escort by motor car to Suez where he arrived at 400. this afternoon. The following persons were arrested this afternoon: ATIF BARAKAT, FATHALLAH BARAKAT, SINNOT BEY HANNA, MUSTAFA EL NAHAS, WILLIAM MAKRAM OBEID. SADIK HENEIN will obey the order made against him. AMIN EZZ EL ARAB is reported by his relatives to have left for his ezbeh. During the day a great deal of damage has been done by parties of roughs, a large number of street lamps broken, trees pulled up and windows smashed. There has been a certain amount of sabotage on the Helouan line where railings and gates have been damaged. The following casualties are reported by the authorities of Kasr-el-Aini hospital. 23-12-21, 2 dead and 9 wounded. 23-12-21, 3 dead and 2 wounded. // ALEXANDRIA After the midday prayer at the mosque there was a small demonstration of about 500 persons which was dispersed without difficulty by the police. Revolutionary pamphlets were distributed and two persons concerned in the distribution were arrested. Further arrests will probably be made tomorrow. PORT SAID All quiet. PROVINCES All quiet except Tanta where there were a few demonstrations but none of a serious nature. 300 British troops proceeded to Tanta this afternoon.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a situation report dated December 24, 1921, detailing the British military takeover of police duties in Cairo at 8:00 AM. It records the arrest of Saad Zaghloul Pasha and his transport to Suez, along with the arrests of several other prominent political figures. It notes civil unrest in Cairo, including vandalism and sabotage on the Helouan line, and reports casualties at Kasr-el-Aini hospital. It also summarizes minor demonstrations in Alexandria and Tanta, noting the deployment of British troops to Tanta.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British military situation report from December 1921, documenting the immediate aftermath of the second arrest and subsequent exile of the Egyptian nationalist leader Saad Zaghloul Pasha. The report highlights the transition to British military control in Cairo, the suppression of the Wafd party leadership, and the resulting civil unrest across Egypt. It serves as a primary source for the escalation of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 and the British colonial administration's efforts to maintain order through martial law and the detention of nationalist figures.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SITUATION REPORT. Saturday Evening - 24.12.21. CAIRO: The students of nearly all Schools went out on strike. Those at GIZA entered the Ministry and Survey Department and either forced or induced the officials to leave their work. Later in the morning the officials of the PUBLIC WORKS Department, WAR OFFICE and Ministry of EDUCATION were for the most part induced or intimidated into leaving their Ministries. An attempt was made to set on fire the stores of the Ministry of Education near the Domains office. Very slight damage was done. An early train on the HELOUAN line was brought to a stand-still near SAIDA ZEINAB. The trains were running again soon after noon. 150 British Troops took over protection of the line at 2 p.m. There was an attempt at an attack on the Railway Workshops at 10 a.m. The attackers fled on the approach of the police and the shops were undamaged. The afternoon was quiet, the hooligan element was not in evidence. One or two small demonstration near AL AZHAR dispersed before the Police arrived. ALEXANDRIA: 8 p.m. Commandant reports all quiet. There were two or three attempts at demonstrations by gutter-snipes and hooligans in the morning, quickly dispersed by Police. A good many large were broken. 165 boys have been arrested. Police arrangements have been made to make more arrests tomorrow morning. Police morale quite good at present. Certain amount of panic amongst Europeans. PORT SAID: At 12 o'clock a demonstration from the native quarter got round the Police cordon. The assistance of the military authorities was called for, and the demonstrators were dispersed and returned to the native quarter. In the afternoon as the SUEZ CANAL workmen left work 150 of them attempted to demonstrate, but the others refused to join. The demonstrators were dispersed by the Police with the help of the military, and driven to the native quarter. SUEZ: 6.45 p.m. Commandant reports demonstrations continued in the native quarter but no damage is being done. ASSIOUT - Interior Inspector reports there were demonstrations during the day but all was quiet in the evening. He says the town knows of the arrival of SAAD Pasha ZAGHLOUL and he thinks that further demonstrations are probable tomorrow.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a daily intelligence summary report detailing civil unrest and student-led strikes across major Egyptian cities on December 24, 1921.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British intelligence situation report from December 24, 1921, documenting the widespread civil unrest and student strikes in Egypt following the political agitation surrounding the nationalist leader Saad Zaghloul. The report provides a city-by-city breakdown of the day's events, highlighting the disruption of government ministries in Cairo, the arrest of students in Alexandria, and the intervention of British military forces to maintain order in Port Said and along the Helouan railway line. It reflects the tense political climate of the period, characterized by the British colonial administration's efforts to suppress nationalist demonstrations and maintain control over public infrastructure and European residents.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
BENI SUEF. Inspector Interior reports MOHAMED KAMEL HUSSEIN the Lawyer arrived from CAIRO on the evening of the 23rd. He made a two hours speech in the mosque after this there was a big demonstration chiefly composed of roughs. It was dispersed by the Police, but only after two hours. The Egyptian Army are patrolling the town and all was quiet at 6.20 p.m. An order has been issued for the arrest of MOHAMED KAMEL HUSSEIN.

LOWER EGYPT.
TANTA. 7 p.m. Interior Inspector reports all quiet. Students have dispersed to their villages and it is probable that they may try to raise the fellaheen. The Omdehs have all been warned, to watch these students and report any sign of trouble at once to Headquarters.

DAMANHOUR. Demonstrations in the morning by roughs and school boys, described by the Mudir as somewhat serious, were dispersed by the Police. Further demonstrations of Railway to leave work finally succeeded.

MENOUFIA: SHERBIN EL KOM: Mudir reports a certain amount of tension in the Mudirieh. 4.35 p.m. reported all was quiet. 100 Egyptian Army troops are being sent to SHERBIN EL KOM.

ZAGAZIG: Reports in the morning the Railway line was out near ZAGAZIG. Later Inspector of Interior reports that the motive was not political. The break was made by a workman out of revenge against a foreman of the line, who had dismissed a friend of the workman's.
6.10 p.m. situation all quiet. 100 Egyptian Army troops are being sent to ZAGAZIG.
ai_content.english_translation: The document provides a status report on civil unrest across various Egyptian provinces. It details the arrival of political agitator Mohamed Kamel Hussein in Beni Suef, the dispersal of student-led demonstrations in Tanta and Damanhour, the deployment of Egyptian Army troops to Menoufia and Zagazig to maintain order, and the clarification that a railway disruption in Zagazig was a personal grievance rather than a political act.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an intelligence summary report from the British military administration in Egypt, likely dating to the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It serves as a daily situation report (SITREP) tracking civil disturbances, the movement of political agitators, and the deployment of security forces to maintain British control over the railway and administrative centers. The document highlights the British concern regarding the spread of nationalist sentiment from urban students to the rural fellaheen (peasantry) and the reliance on local officials (Omdehs) and the Egyptian Army to suppress unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SITUATION REPORT for Sunday evening 25th December 1921. CAIRO. The ABBAS Girl's School was the subject of an attack by demonstrators this morning. One of the Assistant Mistresses gives the following account of what happened:- At about 9.20 a.m. the Boys School broke into the Girls School and made a demonstration. At about 10 a.m. they were joined by a large number of roughs, but Egyptian Cavalry arrived and every one disappeared. The Cavalry then went off and the 'Mob' returned shortly after bringing stones and petrol. They threw both stones and petrol into the School and tried to fire the School. The Police (she described them as 'Secret Police') arrived and fired to clear the mob who went away from there. The girls remained in their play-ground throughout the whole of this disturbance until they were sent away in vehicles sometime after 12. The English Mistresses were not on duty owing to Xmas, and took care not to show themselves as stones were being thrown at the flat which they occupy. Their flat was not in any way singled out for demonstration or attack. Miss Lovegrove and her Colleagues were shortly afterwards taken away in a Lorry under a strong Military English guard.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal situation report dated December 25, 1921, detailing civil unrest in Egypt. It describes an incident at the Abbas Girls' School in Cairo where male students and agitators attacked the school with stones and petrol, necessitating intervention by Egyptian Cavalry and police. It also notes broader unrest in Alexandria and Port Said, including strikes and demonstrations following the arrest of Zaghloul, and mentions the deployment of British troops to maintain order.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SITUATION REPORT CONTINUED for 25.12.21. PORT SAID continued: The leaders. Casualties among the demonstrators: 1 killed, 3 wounded. An Armenian shot a native from his balcony. His arrest was ordered but he has not yet been found. 6.40 p.m. The Commandant reports that a crowd attacked the Armenian's shop and would not desist. They were fired on and two persons were wounded. The town is not quiet. SUEZ. Five of Zaghloul's principal followers who were recently arrested, arrived at 1 a.m. There were demonstrations all last night up to 2 p.m. this morning. O.C. British Troops took over at 5.50 p.m. on 24.12.21. On instructions from O.C. British Troops this morning, the Governor informed the Notables and People that if demonstrations occurred and the demonstrators did not disperse they would be fired on. A demonstration took place in the morning and the demonstrator's refused to disperse. Troops had to fire. One man was killed and 3 wounded. PROVINCES. UPPER EGYPT. Assiout - quiet. Minieh - quiet. Leading agitator has been arrested. Beni Suef - Tribunal clerks on strike. Fayoum - quiet. Giza - quiet. 75% of the Mudiria officials at work. LOWER EGYPT. Qalubia - quiet. Menufia - quiet. Sharkia - marked demonstrations. Forcibly dealt with by Camel Corps with whips with good results. Behera - small demonstrations early. Later all quiet. Gharbia - quiet. (Tanta) Reports have been received from more than one source that Emissaries are being sent from Cairo to the Provinces to stir up trouble. All Mudirs have been warned and instructed how to deal with this move. MOHAMED KAMEL HUSSEIN arrested at Beni Suef last night is now under detention in Cairo. The statement in Zagazig's report that the motive of the line-cutting incident at Zagazig yesterday was non-political is incorrect. The motive was almost certainly political.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT
Monday evening - 26.12.21
CAIRO: at 10 a.m. a crowd attacked Darb el Ahmar Police Station. A Military car with a Lewis gun proceeded to the spot. It was pelted with stones and shots were fired at it. The Officer in charge replied with several rounds of Lewis gun and 5 natives were killed and 4 wounded. It is probable that there were further casualties.
Late in the afternoon in Giza GIDDA and in the side streets barricades were erected and demonstrations made. A Lorry patrol was sent to deal with it and were obliged to fire. Two of the demonstrators were killed and 4 wounded.
Of the eight immediate followers of SAAD ZAGHLOUL against whom an order was made recently to cease all political activities and proceed to SUEZ, 5 as has already been reported, 5 were sent to SUEZ. The remainder ALI EZZ EL ARAB, SADIK HENEIN, and FAKHRY are respectively in QALUBIA province and at ZIFTON and MAZUA, where they are under strict supervision.

It describes violent clashes between police/military forces and demonstrators in Cairo and Giza, including the use of Lewis guns against crowds. It also tracks the administrative detention and forced relocation of political associates of the nationalist leader Saad Zaghloul.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
PORT SAID (Contd): afternoon the town was normal, except that work had ceased in the various Offices and by the Canal side. Notables were again warned by General Lawson that they would be responsible for seeing that work should start tomorrow and a normal state of affairs be resumed. Commandant does not expect any trouble tomorrow.
THE PROVINCES: LOWER EGYPT:
TANTA: All the administration on strike except the Mudiria. In the afternoon a small demonstration took place led by the women of the town, but it was dispersed by the Police.
ZAGAZIG: A small demonstration took place which was put down. In the evening, 7.40 p.m. the Mudir reports all quiet.
ZIFTA: A mob attacked the Markaz building. The Egyptian Army troops fired, the casualties were one killed and two wounded and some ghaffir and police were knocked about. A platoon of British troops from TANTA were called for.
UPPER EGYPT:
MINIA: The 11.10 train from TANTA was delayed by a demonstration for 17 minutes.
BENI SUEF: strike of telegraph officials for three hours. About a third of the officials in the Mudiria on strike.
MINIA: Situation calm and officials are returning to work. The telegraph operators went on strike from noon to 3 p.m. today.
ASYUT: p.m. Mudir Minia states he has telephoned to ASYUT and reports the situation there is good. Strike of telegraph officials took place today.
SINA: Mudir in the morning that a demonstration took place and stones were thrown at the police who fired in reply. He asked for more assistance as his present forces he thought inadequate should anything serious happen.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SITUATION REPORT. Wednesday evening - 28.12.21. GENERAL SITUATION: Decided improvement in tone of reports received both from towns and provinces. CAIRO: Quiet, nothing to report with regard to AL AZHAR University, but a meeting is expected tomorrow. Small demonstration in the Faggallah quarter in the afternoon which was dispersed. Five persons were arrested, otherwise all quiet. ALEXANDRIA: quiet. PORT SAID: Quiet, five persons concerned in the recent disturbances have been arrested. PROVINCES: UPPER EGYPT: All quiet. LOWER EGYPT: All quiet with the exception of FUA (on western Nile Branch south of Rosetta). Inspector Interior at TANTA reports that the Mamur at FUA went this morning to make two arrests in connection with disturbances there. Considerable violence ensued in which the Mamur of Police and Mamur of Idara were badly knocked about. A small detachment of Egyptian Troops proceeded from DAMANHOUR to FUA and after their arrival further disturbances took place, and they had to fire. Details have not at present been received. The following Extracts are quoted from reports received from the DELTA:- DAMANHOUR: Inspector Interior reports all quiet and that this state will continue if CAIRO and ALEXANDRIA remain quiet. MUDIR DAKHALIA: Says he is not anxious at present and things are fairly normal. Markazes are proceeding with elections of Omdahe Commissions, and no untoward incident has taken place. TANTA: Interior Inspector reports all quiet both there and in markazes, except FUA. All administrations at work and most of the schools back. It is reported that a demonstration will take place at KAFR SHEIKH tomorrow. The Mamur has been warned. MUDIR GHARBIA: Reports all quiet at BENHA and in the Markazes. MENUFIA: Mudir reports everything quiet and normal. CASUALTIES: Correction to last night's Report: Authorities at Kasr-el-Aini Hospital report that 2 persons were treated for bullet wounds yesterday.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a daily situation report issued by the Director General of Public Security in Egypt, dated December 28, 1921. It summarizes the civil unrest and security status across various Egyptian provinces. It notes a general improvement in the situation, despite specific violent incidents in Fua involving the police and the deployment of troops. It also tracks minor political activities at Al Azhar University and the Faggallah quarter in Cairo, as well as administrative updates regarding local elections and school attendance.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 'Situation Report' issued by the British-administered Egyptian Public Security department during a period of significant political volatility in Egypt (1921). Following the 1919 Revolution, the British authorities maintained strict surveillance over nationalist activities, student protests at Al Azhar, and local administrative functions. The report highlights the tension between the colonial administration and the local population, specifically documenting the use of force by Egyptian troops in Fua and the monitoring of 'Omdahe' (village headman) elections, which were critical for maintaining rural control. The document serves as a primary source for understanding the mechanics of British security intelligence and the localized nature of anti-colonial resistance in the early 1920s.
