ai_content.transcribed_text: STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL. SITUATION REPORT. Thursday evening - 29.12.21. GENERAL SITUATION: Improvement maintained but AL AZHAR may possibly become a centre of unrest. No definite information at present whether Government officials intend striking at beginning of January. CAIRO: Quiet. A large meeting takes place at AL AZHAR University at 8 p.m. ALEXANDRIA: Quiet. Cab strike proved abortive. Many cabs already back at work. Two small meetings one of students the other of teachers at the Nebi Daniel Mosque today failed to materialize owing to precautions taken by police. PORT SAID: Quiet. All employees back at work. PROVINCES: UPPER EGYPT: Situation generally quiet. LOWER EGYPT: All quiet except FUA where a disturbance again occurred and the Mamour asked urgently for help from DAMANHOUR. Fifty men were sent by special train and situation was got in hand. Casualties said to be 5 killed and 16 wounded; this has not been confirmed, whether this covers today or today and yesterday is at present unknown. MINISTRIES: All working normally. CASUALTIES: FOR FUA see above. Elsewhere nil. The "MINBAR" published this morning a statement that the Egyptian Army Officers resident in CAIRO had protested against their being employed in putting down demonstrations. Headquarters, Egyptian Army report there is no foundation for this statement. PRESENT INFORMATION with regard to rumoured STRIKE of GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS after January 1st: It is reported that a Committee of Egyptian Government officials has been formed for the purpose of deciding whether Government officials should strike at the beginning of next month. Each Ministry is stated to have a delegate and the names of some of these are known. Particular Reporter: Ministry of FINANCE, 28.12.21 Pressure is being brought to bear from outside. No unanimity amongst officials themselves. No leaders so far as can be ascertained.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a strictly confidential intelligence report dated December 29, 1921, detailing the civil and political situation in Egypt. It notes a general improvement in stability, though Al Azhar University remains a potential flashpoint for unrest. It tracks labor strikes (cab drivers in Alexandria, general government official strike rumors), reports on a violent disturbance in Fua involving casualties, and dismisses a newspaper report regarding Egyptian Army officers protesting their role in policing demonstrations. The document concludes with administrative notes regarding the potential for a government-wide strike in January.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 'Strictly Confidential' situation report issued by the British High Commission in Egypt, dated December 29, 1921. It provides a snapshot of the volatile political climate in Egypt during the period of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 and the subsequent negotiations for independence. The report highlights the British colonial administration's anxiety regarding labor unrest, the influence of nationalist institutions like Al Azhar, and the potential for a coordinated strike by Egyptian government officials. The mention of the 'Minbar' newspaper and the specific incident in Fua illustrates the ongoing struggle between the British authorities and the Egyptian nationalist movement during this transitionary period.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT
31.12.21.
Friday evening - 30-12-21
GENERAL SITUATION: Improvement on the whole maintained despite the occasion for disorder which Friday often provides.
CAIRO: Last night's meeting at Al Azhar passed off without disturbances. No details to hand yet of what was decided. At 8.0am. Mr. Hatton, District Inspector of Locomotives, was shot dead outside his house in Geziret Budran, Shubra. No arrest has been made and there is at present no evidence to show if the motive was personal or political.
ALEXANDRIA: At the midday prayer at the Abu el Abbas Mosque inflammatory speeches were made: 3 of the speakers were arrested. Afterwards a demonstration took place and the police were stoned but dispersed the crowd without firing. Six policemen were injured and several demonstrators were arrested. Otherwise all quiet.
PORT SAID: UPPER EGYPT: situation improving. Lower Egypt: all quiet.
GHARBIA: Further details have been received of the incident at Fua reported yesterday. The trouble arose over the arrest of two agitators, who were to be sent to Tanta. On the way to the station the mob attempted their rescue and they had finally to be taken back to the markaz. This building was then attacked by the mob and the police were obliged to fire. The Mamur thought the situation serious and asked for help from DAMANHOUR: 45 Egyptian Army troops were sent and the town is now fairly quiet. Casualties: 4 killed and 15 wounded.
CASUALTIES: Cairo: Kasr el Aini Hospital reports that one of the persons wounded on the 26th died on the 29th.
Copies to: The Chancery, The Residency, The Financial Adviser, The Adviser, Min. of Interior, The Commandant, Cairo, Min. of Interior, The Chief Inspector, Min. of Interior.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a daily intelligence situation report issued by the British authorities in Egypt on December 31, 1921, summarizing civil unrest and security incidents across various Egyptian provinces on the previous day, Friday, December 30, 1921.

The report details localized unrest, including the assassination of a British railway official (Mr. Hatton) in Cairo, demonstrations at the Abu el Abbas Mosque in Alexandria, and a violent confrontation in the Gharbia province involving the arrest of agitators and the subsequent deployment of Egyptian Army troops. The document reflects the British administrative preoccupation with maintaining order through the Ministry of Interior and the Residency, highlighting the precarious security environment in Egypt during the transition toward the 1922 Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
G.H.Q. I.E.F. D: - 31-1-22
ALL ZONES and provinces indicate that country is quiet.
Four incidents are reported today, two undoubtedly being cases of incendiarism.
1) Twenty students attempt to set on fire a signal cabin near MAALIAH (a very short distance from Port Yammouneh) this noon, they also cut the telephone instrument and the wires. The fire was quickly extinguished and the wires were made good.
2) A fire broke out in a reserve train in the SAIDA WHARF this morning, it was extinguished and a certain amount of damage was done.
3) A small demonstration took place in the IDA ZIAD quarter this morning, owing to the arrival of a lorry it quickly dispersed.
4) The Delta Light Railway train was delayed for five minutes at ZIADIA (half way between BALLOUNOU and I.E.F) owing to a piece of iron having been placed on the line.
THE MINISTRIES: No definitive information has been received that officials intend striking. Posters were put up in the SAIDA district this morning calling on Government officials to strike after they had received their pay, on pain of having their houses burnt.
AL AZHAR: Nothing of any great importance has happened in the AL AZHAR in the last 24 hours. 6 persons who have recently made inflammatory speeches have been arrested.
ai_content.english_translation: General Headquarters Intelligence Expeditionary Force report dated January 31, 1922. The report summarizes security conditions across various zones, noting general quietude despite four specific incidents: an attempted arson by students near Maaliah, a fire on a reserve train at Saida Wharf, a minor demonstration in the Ida Ziad quarter, and a railway obstruction at Ziadia. It further reports on the status of government officials in Saida, who were threatened with arson if they did not strike, and notes the arrest of six individuals at Al Azhar for inflammatory speech.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British military intelligence report (G.H.Q. I.E.F.) from the Mandate period in the Levant, specifically dated January 31, 1922. It provides a snapshot of civil unrest and security concerns in the Saida region, reflecting the colonial administration's preoccupation with monitoring nationalist sentiment, labor strikes among government officials, and potential sabotage of infrastructure like the Delta Light Railway. The inclusion of the 'Director General Public Security' stamp and the specific mention of Al Azhar highlights the British effort to track both secular political agitation and religious-based dissent during a period of significant post-WWI regional instability.

SITUATION REPORT for Monday evening - 2-1-22
CAIRO: Quiet.
In the morning Egyptian troops dispersed with their sticks some school boys of the Boulac Technical School, who were trying to persuade their schoolfellows to join them on strike.
Feeling remains high among the students, and frequent meetings are held at Al AZHAR which appears to be the most likely source of future trouble.
ALEXANDRIA: Quiet except for one trifling incident, when 25 Egyptian boys of the Lycee Francais attempted to demonstrate. 5 were arrested.
The police have returned to their normal routine.
PORT SAID: Quiet.
PROVINCES: UPPER EGYPT: All quiet.
DELTA: The Delta Light Railway line and telegraph wire were re-orted to be cut at GIZA during the night.
MINIA: One case of telephone wire cutting is reported. The delinquents were caught and arrested.
GIZA: An attempted demonstration at E. TAWIA on January 1st was prevented by the police, with the assistance of the notables.
MINIA: All officials have been working normally.
ASSUIT: Some of the higher schools are again at work. No attempt has been made to open the government secondary schools.
30/1000 of BRITISH GOODS: A certain number of reports that this is contemplated still come in.

It details student strikes in Cairo, minor demonstrations in Alexandria, infrastructure sabotage (wire cutting) in the Delta and Minia, and the status of government schools and British goods boycotts.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT
Tuesday evening - 3.1.22
GENERAL SITUATION: Quiet, reports however still indicate that the AL AZHAR may prove a source of trouble.
The movement in favour of boycotting all British goods and British commercial undertakings is still actively on foot.
The position with regard to the schools is less satisfactory and there is little doubt that considerable propaganda is going on to make those students strike who have hitherto remained at work.
CAIRO: Last night two bundles of cotton waste soaked in paraffin etc., were dropped on the roof of the Railway stores. No damage was done as the roof is of concrete.
Students of the Sultania Training College attended a meeting at the School of Medicine yesterday afternoon, as a result a large proportion of the students at both schools failed to attend today.
A Greek, described as a Senior Inspector of the Tramway Company was shot last evening, in the leg. The motive was not political.
PROVINCES: A movement in favour of a boycott of the Egyptian Markets Coy., inspired by students, is reported from TANTA. One similar report has previously been received from elsewhere in the Delta.
MINISTRIES: The officials of the Ministries are still working normally, efforts are, however, being made to get them out.
PRESS: The MIMBAR paper has been suspended from tomorrow for a period not yet decided.

It covers the boycott of British goods, student strikes at the Sultania Training College and School of Medicine, an incident involving incendiary materials at the Railway stores, a non-political shooting of a Greek tramway inspector, and the suspension of the newspaper 'Al-Mimbar'.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT
Wednesday evening - 4-1-22
GENERAL SITUATION: Quiet.
The Ministries are working normally. The boycott movement is producing much talk but no results of much consequence yet.
CAIRO: Speeches in AL AZHAR have produced no definite action as yet.
ALEXANDRIA: A small demonstration yesterday evening resulted in an affray and 18 street boys being arrested.
PROVINCE: In GHARBIA some of the fellahin appeared in some attempts to prevent the fellahin from bringing their cattle to the markets. Police were sent to protect the fellahin.
THE SCHOOLS: At the School of Medicine and the Veterinary School the majority of the students were present and the attendance at the Model Workshops in Bulaq was almost normal. At the Sultania Training College more than half were still absent. The attendance at the rest of the Higher Colleges was practically nil, while the Schools of Law and the Government Secondary Schools are all closed.
THE PRESS: The reason for the suppression of AL MINBAR (reported yesterday) was that articles appeared in it of a nature calculated to provoke disturbance and to incite to disorder.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SITUATION REPORT.
Thursday evening - 5th Jan. 1922
CENTRAL SITUATION: Quiet.
The boycott campaign appears to be meeting with little practical sympathy.
CAIRO: At the meeting at AL AZHAR on the 3rd inst., only about 500 persons attended and the speakers deplored the lack of interest in the present movement.
This morning, MOHAMED BADR EL DIN Bey, of the PUBLIC SECURITY DEPARTMENT, was shot in the back while walking from his house to the Ministry of Interior. He was taken to Kasr el Aini Hospital; the medical report at noon stated that he was shot in the right lung and if the bullet has not gone further, his recovery is probable. The evening report gave his condition as fair.

TELEPHONE MESSAGE FROM IBRAHIM BEY, ALEXANDRIA.
Date: 21st March, 1922. Time 11 a.m.
There were several large demonstrations and a number of smaller ones yesterday. In only one case was there direct conflict with the Police. This was at 12.30 p.m. when the crowd attacked the Police in a box car and managed to set it on fire. Help was immediately forthcoming and 16 arrests were made. Three policemen were injured, one rather badly, his helmet being knocked to pieces with stones.
There was another big demonstration in the evening, when the crowd tried to get into the square with the object of smashing up the decorations, this was dealt with successfully. No decorations suffered during the day. The help of British Troops was not called in, a few of the Egyptian Army troops assisted in patrolling certain beats. In one case the Europeans showed anxiety to help the Police and did so with considerable effect. Roughly about 75% of the population were entirely hostile to decorations and there were frequent cries for ZAGHLOUL.
Some 300 hooligans and riff-raff were arrested during the day but most of these were released this morning, as no definite charge could be made against them.
Copy to: The Residency, The Advisor, Ministry of Interior, D.G.P.S.
Telephoned to G.H.Q.
Int. [Signature] 21.3.22.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Dear Furness,
A large number of school-boys and students collected this morning in front of the Ministry of Interior with banners and made a demonstration of protest against the statement recently made by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald to the effect that His Majesty's Government considered themselves bound by the Declaration of February 28th, 1922. Graves, whose room is just below the Prime Minister's windows and who witnessed everything that passed, tells me that he heard many cries of "Down with the British Cabinet! Down with the Declaration of February 28th! Long live Zaghlul Pasha! etc."
After a little while Zaghlul Pasha came to his window, listened to the shouts for a minute or two and then addressed the crowd. He said approximately "there is nothing in the statement of Mr. MacDonald that calls for protest. I am the guardian of the rights and interests of Egypt and that if I see them in danger, I shall protest." (A voice - "What about the reserved subjects?") Zaghlul Pasha: "I am not going to talk politics with you."
"I repeat that I alone am responsible for the interests of Egypt as the chief of the people and the head of the Government. In coming here you interrupt my work for the country and I wish you to go back to your schools."
Most of the crowd cheered Zaghlul Pasha's speech, but a few isolated cries of protest continued to be heard after the Prime Minister had retired from the balcony. Graves thought that an appreciable proportion of the demonstrators were dissatisfied with what the Prime Minister had said. A good number of the demonstrators seemed to be young men of 19 to 20.
It is possible that an early report of the Prime Minister's words may interest the Foreign Office.
Yours,
[Signature: R. Kerr/Boyd]
F. Furness, Esq.,
The Residency,
Cairo.

It describes students protesting against British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald's reaffirmation of the 1922 Declaration, which maintained British control over certain 'reserved' areas of Egyptian governance. The text recounts the Prime Minister Zaghlul Pasha's attempt to disperse the crowd by asserting his own authority as the sole guardian of Egyptian interests and urging the students to return to their studies.

The report documents a public demonstration by students against the British government's insistence on maintaining 'reserved subjects' (such as the protection of foreign interests and the Suez Canal). It highlights the delicate political balancing act performed by Saad Zaghlul Pasha, the first democratically elected Prime Minister of Egypt, who sought to maintain nationalist support while managing the volatile expectations of the Egyptian public and the constraints imposed by the British colonial administration.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
With reference to the attached;
Dear Furness,
(1) Generally, my impression of yesterday's incidents is that the students and others were in a very excitable frame of mind, due to intensive and carefully arranged propaganda on the Sudan question. This spirit would, I believe, have made the crowd actually dangerous had they not been given to understand that Saad, by mentioning in the speech the Sudan, had finally put forward Egypt's claim to that country. Had no mention of the Sudan been made in this speech, I consider that disturbances would certainly have occurred and acts of violence might have been committed.
(2) No mistake should be made as to the reason of the occasional applause with which Lord Allenby and some British Officials were greeted. This applause was certainly an expression of satisfaction at the declarations which Saad was supposed or reported to have made, and had no relation to the personalities.
(3) The attitude of the Egyptian Army should be taken note of. Although orders were issued to the troops to keep the crowd back and the road clear before and after the passage of the King, they made no attempt to carry out these orders.
(4) Before the King passed on his way to the Parliament, the crowd were allowed by the troops to flood the road at the corner of the Ismailia Palace, and a complete block was only averted by the action of the Police.
(5) After the King had returned to Abdin, the troops made no attempt to prevent the people from overrunning the streets, and in some instances were seen to invite persons behind them to pass through the ranks into the street.
(6) The deduction is that, in case of difficulties, the troops could not be relied upon to give any real support to the Police.
Yours sincerely,
Arthur Boyd

The author highlights the unreliability of the Egyptian Army in supporting the Police, noting their failure to maintain order or clear the streets for the King's passage, suggesting a potential security risk for British interests.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Incidents of March 15th 1924. (Reported by Commt. C.C.P.)

The temper of the people was, on the whole, good. The element of organised roughs did not get seriously to work.

The success of the day turned on the Sudan question; the people were on the 'qui vive' to know what Saad Pasha had put into the Speech from the Throne on the subject of the Sudan. As soon as they heard that he had - as they supposed - claimed complete independence for the Sudan, they were happy; otherwise the crowd would probably have been nasty.

At the corner of the old Ismailia Palace, just before the King was due to pass there, a man who had climbed into a tree began to make a speech. The crowd pressed round, broke the cordon and blocked the road, which the police only just succeeded in clearing before the King reached the spot.

The applause which greeted Lord Allenby on his exit from the Parliament-House was not intended for him personally, but only to express appreciation of the sentiments expressed in the Speech from the Throne on the subject of the Sudan.

It is estimated that between 10,000 and 12,000 people got into the Ezbekia Gardens, regularly and irregularly. At one time, Mounted Police were obliged to force the crowd back, and the Guard Company were obliged, at times, to use rough methods. Sughlul Pasha was taken by a couple of police officers surrounded by a detachment of the Guard Company beating the people off.

Shahin Bey had been on duty at Abdin Palace in the morning, and later went to Abbassia Barracks. On the way he was the object of some hooting, and a few stones were thrown without causing any damage. In view of the attitude of the crowd, he sent one of his men to report by telephone from a neighbouring shop; the crowd then threw some stones at the shop, without causing serious damage.

Between 1 and 2 o'clock, a crowd of some 500 people gathered round Shahin Bey's house (he himself was not there, but at the barracks) and threw stones, breaking many windows and causing a great deal of damage. The proprietor of the house, who lives in the flat below Shahin Bey, was hurt by a stone. Some of Shahin Bey's family were injured, and one of the police also thrown at a Heliopolis tram which happened to pass. Abbassia-Heliopolis tram which was damaged. It is believed that a British Sergeant-Major, who had followed the King's procession and was returning, was attacked by the crowd, and that this disturbance was caused by a group of roughs, from the Abbassia and Gamilla quarters, who had followed the King's procession and back to Abbassia. A lorry-load of police, and 30 mounted police were sent up, and dispersed the crowd. An enquiry is proceeding.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Hi Ken, Hi Anthony drew my attention to this extract from the Bourse & notice. It is the sort of fracas which he anticipated for the early days of Ramadan. [Newspaper clipping text]: MANIFESTATION D'APACHES. Du journal 'Al Akhbar' - Le 12 de ce mois d'avril, à 10 h. p.m., à Nabarrô, grand village de la Dakahlia, non loin de Talkha, s'est déroulée une manifestation sans exemple. Elle était composée d'une foule innombrable d'apaches et de voyous. Les derniers étaient tous, sans exception, armés de grosses massues ou de nababouts. Durant leur course à travers les rues, ils lancèrent de grosses pierres contre les maisons, brisant portes et vitres, frappant ceux qu'ils rencontraient sur leur passage. Un chahut a été gravement blessé; le mamour du district de Talkha envoya deux soldats pour maintenir l'ordre. L'armée, de son côté, se multiplia pour essayer d'arrêter ce torrent furieux. Ce ne sont pas là des manifestations politiques, mais simplement une exhibition totale de haine profonde. On ne sait ce que cela veut dire. Le ciel est toujours sombre de menaces. Le correspondant de 'Al Akhbar' demande avec force, au président du Conseil de rétablir l'ordre et publier les promoteurs de ce mouvement.
ai_content.english_translation: Hi Ken, Anthony drew my attention to this extract from the Bourse & notice. It is the sort of fracas which he anticipated for the early days of Ramadan. [Newspaper clipping translation]: APACHE DEMONSTRATION. From the newspaper 'Al Akhbar' - On the 12th of this month of April, at 10 p.m., in Nabarro, a large village in Dakahlia, not far from Talkha, an unprecedented demonstration took place. It was composed of an innumerable crowd of apaches and thugs. The latter were all, without exception, armed with large clubs or nababouts. During their run through the streets, they threw large stones at the houses, breaking doors and windows, striking those they met on their way. A chahut [policeman] was seriously wounded; the mamour of the Talkha district sent two soldiers to maintain order. The army, for its part, multiplied its efforts to try to stop this furious torrent. These are not political demonstrations, but simply a total exhibition of deep hatred. One does not know what this means. The sky is still dark with threats. The correspondent of 'Al Akhbar' strongly asks the President of the Council to restore order and publish the names of the promoters of this movement.

The incident involved a large mob attacking property and individuals, which the newspaper characterized as a display of 'deep hatred' rather than political protest. The document highlights the colonial administration's concern regarding public security during the sensitive period of Ramadan in 1924, reflecting the volatile socio-political climate in Egypt following the establishment of the Kingdom of Egypt and the rise of the Wafd Party.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Dear Furness,
Ingram tells me that during the big demonstration which took place yesterday there was a certain amount of stone-throwing in the neighbourhood of the Zewa and the Azhar. The demonstration was attended by a goodish number of roughs who seemed anxious for trouble and Ingram expects that there will be more of it at the big workmen's demonstration which is arranged for Saturday unless the government tell the police definitely that they want order to be preserved.
M. d'Avierino was interrogated for several hours to-day, but I don't know if they got anything interesting out of her. Holmes was present as acting Crown Prosecutor but he did not ask any questions. I shall find out from him to-morrow if her evidence was of interest and let you know.
The minister having become alarmed at the rumours that further assassinations have been planned the police are going to provide them with large escorts.
I enclose a cutting from the Journal du Caire in case you have not seen it. I imagine it has been translated into Arabic and inserted in the native press. The article in the Journal is so outrageous (as well as being dangerous in this country) that I expect H.M. would like the F.O. to have something said about it in Paris or to approach d'Aumale direct.
Do you care for me to go on giving you news from here everyday or two? I have not heard from you and so am not sure whether you are interested.
Yours ever,
H. M. GRAVES.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a personal letter written by H. M. Graves from the Turf Club in Cairo to a colleague named Furness. It details civil unrest in Cairo, specifically mentioning stone-throwing near the Zewa and Azhar districts during a demonstration. It discusses the interrogation of a woman named d'Avierino by the acting Crown Prosecutor, Holmes, and notes the government's concern regarding potential future assassinations, leading to increased police escorts for ministers. Graves also expresses concern over an inflammatory article in the 'Journal du Caire' and suggests that the Foreign Office (F.O.) should intervene diplomatically with the French authorities in Paris or directly with d'Aumale.

It provides a contemporary account of the volatile political climate in Egypt during the post-independence period (following the 1922 Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence). ai_content.transcribed_text: No. 666. CONFIDENTIAL. Cairo, 16th Nov 1924. His Excellency The Under-Secretary of State, Ministry of the Interior. I beg to forward a copy of the Report by Bimbashi HENN on the disturbance caused on yesterday evening by students outside the Parliament. I myself arrived on the scene just as the Prime Minister was leaving the Parliament. I am sure that when His Excellency the Minister understands the circumstances he will agree with me that, so far from any blame attaching to the Police, Bimbashi HENN and the force under him Command prevented with the minimum of violence what might otherwise been a disaster. The means he used were the only means possible to prevent the mob of students from crushing the Prime Minister and invading Parliament. Had I been on the spot myself I should have given exactly the same orders as were given by Bimbashi HENN. Sgd. T.W. RUSSELL. COMMANDANT CAIRO CITY POLICE.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a confidential report from T.W. Russell, Commandant of the Cairo City Police, to the Under-Secretary of State at the Ministry of the Interior, dated November 16, 1924. Russell forwards a report regarding a student disturbance outside the Parliament building the previous evening. He defends the actions of Bimbashi Henn, stating that Henn's intervention was necessary to protect the Prime Minister from a mob of students and to prevent them from storming the Parliament. Russell asserts that he would have issued the same orders had he been present, and argues that the police actions prevented a potential disaster with minimal violence.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential administrative report from the British-led Cairo City Police during the period of the British protectorate in Egypt. It highlights the volatile political climate in Cairo in November 1924, specifically regarding student activism and the security of the Parliament. The report serves as an internal defense of police conduct, justifying the use of force by Bimbashi Henn against student protesters to protect the Prime Minister. The document provides insight into the hierarchical reporting structures within the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior and the role of British officials in maintaining public order during a time of heightened nationalist tension.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPY.
Cairo City Police
#2 Division.
Abdin Qism.
15th November, 1924.
Sir,
With reference to the disturbance at the Parliament House this afternoon :-
At about 3-45 pm. I received a telephone message from the Mawin of Parliament saying that a demonstration of about 200 students had gathered in the street opposite the gates. As he expected more to gather, I at once telephoned to the Guard Company to send him 60 men, and also to Mr. Frazer to go down there. I then informed you of what had done, and went myself to the Parliament House.
On arrival I found the Guard Company in position round the gates under Mr. Frazer. The crowd had increased very much, and I reckoned about 2000 were present. According to Standing Orders, I did not interfere with them, merely putting a strong guard inside each gate, and a few Officers and N.C.Os. outside to keep a narrow lane open for the motors etc. of the members. As a precautionary measure, I rang up the Mounted Troops and asked for 12 men to be sent.
The crowd, which was almost entirely composed of students, continued to increase, especially on the Sh. Palaki end, where it was almost solid.
At about 5 pm. the car of H.E. the P.M. appeared round the corner of Sh. Palaki. It was entirely covered with students, and proceeding very slowly. About 70 yards from the Parliament gate it came to a dead stop, entirely unable to proceed. I reckoned that the crowd of students round it was about 30 deep.
I managed to reach the car, alone, and endeavoured to clear a way in front. I spoke to the driver who asked me to stand on the running board, which I did. I managed to clear off some of the students on my side, but their places were at once taken, and I was struck several times from behind on the shoulders. At that moment Mr. Frazer came up with 10 Guard Company, and we managed to get the car going slowly. The P.M. was lying back in his seat apparently exhausted. The crowd was entirely out of hand, and getting dangerous from sheer weight of numbers. At one moment I feared that the whole car would be overturned, as it rocked badly after a rush.
I know that the crux would be at the gate, where the crowd was very heavy indeed. All semblance of discipline was lost, I noticed that some students who had been trying to keep the others back before the P.M.'s arrival now join in mobbing the car themselves. The car turned slowly into the gate I jumped off and ran round behind it, checking for a moment the solid crowd that was following.
As the car entered, still covered with students, Mr. Frazer got the Guard Company reserve of about 30 men across the gate as a cordon. The crowd, however, was far too heavy and excited to be checked by a passive barrier, and for a moment almost broke in. I then, to save the situation, led a charge outwards, and after a few minutes' struggle we got the crowd back about 15 yards. As they forming up for another rush, I went for them again, and cleared the street back about 50 yards.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official report from the Cairo City Police, Division #2 (Abdin District), dated November 15, 1924, detailing a student demonstration at the Parliament House. The officer describes receiving a call about 200 students gathering, his deployment of the Guard Company and Mounted Troops, and the arrival of the Prime Minister's car, which was mobbed by a crowd of approximately 2,000 students. The report details the physical struggle to clear a path for the Prime Minister's vehicle, the exhaustion of the Prime Minister, and the eventual use of a police charge to disperse the crowd from the Parliament gates.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a contemporary police report documenting a significant political protest in Cairo during the mid-1920s, a period of intense nationalist agitation in Egypt. It provides a granular, eyewitness account of the tactics used by the Cairo City Police to manage large-scale student demonstrations and protect high-ranking government officials (the Prime Minister) during civil unrest. The mention of 'Abdin Qism' (Abdin Police District) and the Parliament House situates the event in the heart of Cairo's political center, reflecting the volatile relationship between the student body and the government during the post-1919 revolution era.

Stones then began to be thrown from the south trottoir, and I cleared it. Two men of the Guard Company were struck, and I was hit by a stone on the side of the head. The crowd was very excited and hostile, but afraid to close, and the stone throwing ceased. I then withdrew the men inside the gates, and closed them.
The crowd continued to line the railings, shouting. I telephoned for more Guard Company, and for the balance of the Mounted Troop.
At about 5-20 H.E. the P.M. left by the West gate. On getting outside his car was mobbed again, and I informed that the windows were broken during the passage from the Parliament to his house. Yuzbashi Rifaat El Hoteibi and Atef Barakat were with him on the car.
The Guard Company used no unnecessary violence to my knowledge, in spite of great provocation. I saw no one being hit, although the Guard Company waved their sticks about. On the other hand I saw several students strike men of the Police, and try to seize their sticks. I am convinced that only the vigorous action of the Police when the P.M.'s car entered the whole Parliament building from being rushed by a mob of several thousands.
(signed) W.F.HENN.
Bimbashi.
A/C 'B' Division.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Director-General
Ministry of the Interior
European Department
Archive S.P. 213

I telephoned this morning to Mr. Keleher, Manager of Sours Unvers Factory at Ismailia-el-Kubra. He informed me that he believed the disturbance which had taken place there yesterday was rather serious, but that neither he himself nor any of the other Europeans living at Ismailia had been in any way inconvenienced. He stated that he had noticed that a number of policemen standing on the other side of the Canal had been passive spectators of the incident.

Ain Pasha Galal El-Din informed me that the disorders at Ismailia had arisen out of the annoyance of the Zaghloulist party, none of whom had been elected as members of the electoral committees at Ismailia, when it was announced that the members of the Constitutional party, the Zaghloulists had created an uproar and caused a lot of damage to the furniture, they broke up the ballot boxes and tore up all papers connected with the election. Similar scenes were enacted at the Omda's house and the Irrigation Department offices, at both of which electoral committees were sitting. The crowd also broke all the windows in the Omda's house and caused a lot of damage to the furniture. They also, as above reported, destroyed the Omda's carriage. Very considerable damage was also done at the Irrigation office, and there were many important documents destroyed or stolen and certain machines belonging to the Government smashed.

The Chef du Parquet of Tanta arrived not long after the first outbreak at the Omda's and opened an enquiry. The crowd did not allow him to proceed with this for long and began to bombard the Omda with stones. They also invaded the premises, broke all the windows and damaged a good deal of Government property including the canons which with salutes are fired. They attempted to get hold of the police rifles but failed to do so.

The Commandant of Police, Rippas Bey, who arrived from Tanta, I think with the mob, a few of whom were wounded. The rumour, the Commandant, the Omda and all the members of the election committees were injured, most of them not seriously, and the Omda was robbed of his pocket book.

The Under-Secretary of State, who went to Ismailia yesterday, took with him a detachment of troops from Tanta. The letter have been patrolling the town which is now quite quiet.

The above account requires to be substantiated and amplified by details which no doubt be shortly available from the official reports.

R.M. Graves
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official report written in English by R.M. Graves regarding civil unrest and election-related violence in Ismailia and Tanta. It details the destruction of government property, the targeting of electoral committees by the Zaghloulist party, and the failure of local police to intervene.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal report from the European Department of the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior, authored by R.M. Graves. It provides a detailed account of political violence and civil unrest occurring in Ismailia and Tanta, likely during the early 1920s (archival stamp dated 1924). The report describes the frustration of the Zaghloulist party following their exclusion from electoral committees, leading to the destruction of ballot boxes, government offices, and private property. The document highlights the fragility of local order, the passivity of the police force, and the subsequent deployment of troops from Tanta to restore calm, reflecting the volatile political climate in Egypt during the transition toward independence.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
In the Egyptian Gazette of 30/5/1929, a report appears with the caption "Battle in Main Street" - "Bottles and Bloodshed". The account magnifies the true facts and the following is a correct report.
On May 29th at 8 a.m. a case of murder between Saidis, was being heard by the Committing Magistrate at the Minet el Bassel area.
At the opening of the case the following force was present for the maintenance of order: 1 N.C.O. and 3 policemen. Nothing untoward occurred during the hearing, either in Court or in the courtyard of the Tribunal.
At about midday, the Shawish 1/c Police Escort heard a disturbance in the street outside the Tribunal when the prisoners were brought before the judge. Seeing that the disturbance was growing, he immediately informed the Qism by telephone, whereupon the Mamur of the Qism accompanied by the Moawen, proceeded to the scene of the disturbance, having previously ordered the dispatch of reinforcements.
On his way to the Court, the Mamur encountered, in Shereh Kom el Dick, a wounded man and subsequently saw a crowd of women in Rue Césr (a side-street in the vicinity of the Court). A European pointing out to the Mamur a woman as being one of the ringleaders, the Mamur had her arrested.
13 arrests were made (three Alexandrians and ten Saidis; all in the streets neighbouring the Court, partly by the Police on beat duty in Rue Césr and partly by the force which was hurried to the scene.
The incident resulted in four casualties, two of which were serious.
The brawl spread to three spots in the neighbourhood of the Court and would have assumed considerable proportions had it not been for the prompt intervention of the Police. It certainly caused a temporary panic, but not to the extent indicated by the press reports.
The incident was mainly provoked by female members of the rival factions.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official report written in English, correcting a sensationalized newspaper account of a violent disturbance in Cairo. It details a police response to a brawl that broke out outside a tribunal during a murder trial involving Saidi factions on May 29, 1929. The report clarifies that the police successfully contained the incident, which resulted in 13 arrests and four casualties, and notes that the conflict was largely instigated by women from the opposing groups.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official administrative report from the British Residency in Cairo, dated June 11, 1929, signed by R.M. Graves. It serves as a corrective to a sensationalized article in the 'Egyptian Gazette' regarding a public disturbance. The report provides a sober, bureaucratic account of a violent clash between rival Saidi factions outside a court in the Minet el Bassel area. It highlights the colonial administration's concern with maintaining public order and managing the narrative of civil unrest in interwar Egypt, specifically documenting the police response, the number of arrests, and the role of female participants in the conflict.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SYNDICAT DES EMPLOYES DES TRAMWAYS DU CAIRE
Copie de la décision de l'Assemblée Générale prise le 31 Mars 1919
Le Caire, le 31 Mars 1919
Mon cher Greg,
Le Directeur des Tramways, sur la demande du Général Watson a fait hier matin toutes les concessions possibles aux grévistes; en fait il a cédé sur tous les points et leur a accordé au delà de ce que demandaient les autorités militaires: une piastre d'augmentation (les watmen et receveurs gagneront donc jusqu'à 19 P.T., la moyenne 16) - travail de demi-journée, jusqu'à 2 h. ou depuis 2 h. - deux jours de congé payés par mois avec droit d'accumuler - bureau d'enquête pour les punitions, etc, etc. On ne peut pas aller plus loin. Or hier soir ils ont simplement déclarés qu'ils refusaient quand même de travailler, malgré les objurgations de leur avocat qui s'était engagé à leur faire reprendre le travail.
ai_content.english_translation:
SYNDICATE OF CAIRO TRAMWAY EMPLOYEES
Copy of the decision of the General Assembly taken on March 31, 1919
Cairo, March 31, 1919
My dear Greg,
The Director of Tramways, at the request of General Watson, made all possible concessions to the strikers yesterday morning; in fact, he gave in on all points and granted them more than the military authorities requested: a one-piastre raise (the motormen and conductors will therefore earn up to 19 P.T., the average being 16) - half-day work, until 2 o'clock or from 2 o'clock - two days of paid leave per month with the right to accumulate - an inquiry office for punishments, etc., etc. One cannot go any further. However, last night they simply declared that they still refused to work, despite the pleas of their lawyer who had committed to making them resume work.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative record from the British High Commission in Egypt, documenting a labor dispute involving the Cairo Tramway employees in March 1919. It details the concessions offered by the Tramway Director, under the mediation of General Watson, to end a strike. Despite the management meeting or exceeding the strikers' demands—including wage increases and improved working conditions—the workers refused to return to their posts, highlighting the volatile socio-political climate in Egypt during the period of the 1919 Revolution against British colonial rule.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SYNDICAT DES EMPLOYES DES TRAMWAYS DU CAIRE
Copie de la décision de l'Assemblée Générale prise le 18 août 1919 par 2033 voix.
---//---
L'Assemblée Générale du Syndicat des employés du Tramway du Caire a décidé d'ajouter les articles dont la teneur suit et de les considérer comme partie complémentaire de ses statuts:
= Article I =
Le syndicat des employés du Tramway du Caire tiendra lieu et place de chacun de ses membres dans ses relations avec la Société des Tramways du Caire. Les droits et avoirs du dit membre seront transférés au syndicat.
= Article II =
Le Président du syndicat ou celui qui le remplacera faisant fonctions de président, aura le droit entier de procéder à l'encaissement de ce qui serait dû aux membres du syndicat en argent par la Société des Tramways du Caire.
L'encaissement sera fait par l'intermédiaire de l'une des Banque de la Capitale que choisira le Conseil du syndicat.
Cette Banque procédera au paiement sous la surveillance du président du syndicat de ce qui serait dû en argent aux membres du syndicat.
La convention qui interviendra entre le syndicat et la Banque ne sera exécutoire qu'après ratification par le Conseil du syndicat.
---==---
Je soussigné, membre au syndicat des employés des Tramways du Caire travaillant N°
Je reconnais avoir pris connaissance de la décision de l'Assemblée Générale à la date du 18 août 1919 dont les termes précèdent et j'ai donné mandat général et mandat particulier au syndicat en lui conférant les droit et l'autorité
ai_content.english_translation:
SYNDICATE OF CAIRO TRAMWAY EMPLOYEES
Copy of the decision of the General Assembly taken on August 18, 1919, by 2033 votes.
---//---
The General Assembly of the Cairo Tramway Employees' Syndicate has decided to add the following articles and to consider them as a complementary part of its statutes:
= Article I =
The Cairo Tramway Employees' Syndicate will take the place of each of its members in their relations with the Cairo Tramways Company. The rights and assets of the said member will be transferred to the syndicate.
= Article II =
The President of the syndicate or whoever replaces him acting as president, will have the full right to proceed with the collection of what would be owed to the members of the syndicate in money by the Cairo Tramways Company.
The collection will be done through one of the Banks of the Capital that the Syndicate Council will choose.
This Bank will proceed with the payment under the supervision of the president of the syndicate of what would be owed in money to the members of the syndicate.
The agreement that will be reached between the syndicate and the Bank will only be enforceable after ratification by the Syndicate Council.
---==---
I, the undersigned, member of the Cairo Tramway Employees' Syndicate working No.
I acknowledge having taken note of the decision of the General Assembly dated August 18, 1919, the terms of which precede, and I have given general mandate and special mandate to the syndicate, conferring upon it the rights and authority.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal record of a decision made by the Cairo Tramway Employees' Syndicate on August 18, 1919. It outlines a significant shift in labor relations, where the union assumes the legal and financial agency of its members in their dealings with the Cairo Tramways Company. By transferring the rights and assets of individual employees to the syndicate, the union centralized the collection of wages and dues, likely as a strategy to strengthen collective bargaining power and ensure financial oversight during a period of labor unrest in post-WWI Egypt. The document includes a template for individual members to sign, formally granting the union the authority to act on their behalf.

Il en résulte:
1°) La Société s'engage à accepter l'article premier de cette décision et de traiter avec le syndicat pour tout ce qui concerne chacun de ses membres sans qu'elle ait la moindre relation avec les membres du syndicat.
2°) La Société s'engage à payer les salaires des membres du syndicat; le paiement sera fait à la Banque choisie par le syndicat comme étant sa Banque, soit le Banco di Roma.
Cette Banque donnera à la Société décharge de ce qu'il connaîtra de sa Caisse conformément à l'état détaillé contenant l'indication des appointements.
3°) C'est le syndicat qui donnera à la Société le cautionnement pécuniaire demandé de chacun des membres du syndicat après accord sur le montant de ce cautionnement. La Banque choisie par le syndicat payera ce cautionnement au nom et pour compte du syndicat contre quoi la Société restituera au syndicat le montant des cautionnements déjà à elle payés par les membres du syndicat.
Cette décision ne porte aucune atteinte au droit de la Société de prendre les mesures qu'elle croit nécessaire pour la conservation de l'ordre nécessaire pour le fonctionnement de son service à la condition qu'il ne résulte de cet ordre aucune injustice pour l'un des membres du syndicat.
Nous prions Votre Excellence de transmettre copie du présent à Monsieur le Directeur de la Société afin que celui-ci prenne la décision préconisée soit de reconnaître le syndicat après connaissance de la nature et des limites de cette reconnaissance.
Nous sollicitons que cette reconnaissance soit accompagnée de son mandat de la Société, mandat lui conférant le droit de faire pareille reconnaissance à la place de la Société.
ai_content.english_translation:
It results from this:
1) The Society agrees to accept the first article of this decision and to deal with the syndicate for everything concerning each of its members without having the slightest relationship with the members of the syndicate.
2) The Society agrees to pay the salaries of the syndicate members; the payment will be made to the Bank chosen by the syndicate as its Bank, namely the Banco di Roma.
This Bank will give the Society a discharge of what it will know from its Cashier in accordance with the detailed statement containing the indication of the salaries.
3) It is the syndicate that will give the Society the financial security deposit requested from each of the syndicate members after agreement on the amount of this security deposit. The Bank chosen by the syndicate will pay this security deposit in the name and on behalf of the syndicate, against which the Society will return to the syndicate the amount of the security deposits already paid to it by the members of the syndicate.
This decision does not in any way infringe upon the Society's right to take the measures it deems necessary for the preservation of the order required for the functioning of its service, on the condition that no injustice results from this order for any of the members of the syndicate.
We request Your Excellency to transmit a copy of the present to the Director of the Society so that he may take the recommended decision, either to recognize the syndicate after knowledge of the nature and limits of this recognition.
We request that this recognition be accompanied by its mandate from the Society, a mandate conferring upon him the right to make such recognition in place of the Society.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Après lecture de ce projet, le président a demandé aux membres présents de prendre leur décision par scrutin secret pour adopter ou refuser le projet.
Celui d'entre les membres qui accepte le projet doit inscrire sur le papier blanc à lui délivré après y avoir inscrit son numéro et ses fonctions ce qui indique son acquiescement; celui qui n'est pas d'accord ce qui indique son refus.
Les bulletins réunis, le scrutin a donné le résultat suivant:
2033 bulletin contenant acquiescement avec indication des N° et de la fonction et un seul bulletin blanc ne contenant rien et un bulletin contenant le N° et la fonction seulement et et 2 bulletin contenant le N° et la fonction et le nom. Le conseil n'a pas pris en considération ces 5 bulletins.
Ainsi le Conseil a décidé à l'unanimité l'acceptation du projet des notes et de considérer ceux-ci comme partie complémentaire du statut du syndicat.
De même les contrôleurs et chefs de gare ont choisi par scrutin secret trois d'entre eux comme délégués et ce par le procédé plus haut indiqué.
Ont eu la majorité après dépouillement du scrutin par le Conseil les 3 inspecteurs, 73, 74 & 7, le 1er Jean Pervinaki a obtenu 61 voix, le 2e Bellerio Vantarolo 39 voix, le 3e Carmelo Barboglio par 38 voix.
Il a été décidé de les considérer comme délégués des Inspecteurs et chefs au Conseil du syndicat.
Les bulletins de vote des Inspecteurs ont été placés sous enveloppe séparé.
ai_content.english_translation: After reading this project, the president asked the members present to make their decision by secret ballot to adopt or reject the project. The member who accepts the project must write on the white paper issued to him, after having written his number and functions, what indicates his acquiescence; the one who does not agree, what indicates his refusal. The ballots gathered, the vote gave the following result: 2033 ballots containing acquiescence with indication of the numbers and function, and a single blank ballot containing nothing, and one ballot containing the number and function only, and 2 ballots containing the number, function, and name. The Council did not take these 5 ballots into consideration. Thus, the Council decided unanimously to accept the project of notes and to consider these as a complementary part of the union's statute. Likewise, the controllers and station masters chose by secret ballot three of their own as delegates, using the procedure indicated above. Having obtained the majority after the counting of the votes by the Council, the 3 inspectors, 73, 74 & 7, the 1st Jean Pervinaki obtained 61 votes, the 2nd Bellerio Vantarolo 39 votes, the 3rd Carmelo Barboglio 38 votes. It was decided to consider them as delegates of the Inspectors and chiefs to the Union Council. The ballots of the Inspectors were placed in a separate envelope.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document consists of the minutes of a union council meeting, detailing the procedural conduct of a secret ballot regarding the adoption of a new project or set of administrative notes. It outlines the strict voting protocols, including the invalidation of ballots that failed to follow specific formatting requirements (such as including names instead of just numbers/functions). Furthermore, it records the election of three delegates—Jean Pervinaki, Bellerio Vantarolo, and Carmelo Barboglio—to represent the inspectors and station masters within the union's governing body, reflecting the formal organizational structure of a labor or professional syndicate.

Chancery, Cairo Tramway Strike. 
I am informed that on Sept 1st, Madhour Pasha, Bey of the merchants of Cairo (and undoubtedly a member of Saad Pasha Zaghloul's delegation) intervened, as he said, to persuade the strikers of the Cairo Tramway to return to work. The delegates of the strikers appeared before the Governor of Cairo in the evening, accepted the temporary arrangement proposed to them, agreed to resume work on Wednesday morning 3rd. 
On Tuesday 2nd Sept, the tramway lines were cleared of the dirt which had accumulated, but on the same day a group of the strikers left a letter at the Governorate saying they did not intend to resume their work unless all their demands were at once granted. 
A certain number of the strikers have handed in their names to the Company as being willing to resume work. 
The situation at present is as follows: 
The Company states it is ready to resume work on part of its itinerary with the men who have returned, or with newly recruited staff. They will require effective police protection, especially as a rumour is current that the more violent of the strikers will direct the attacks against passengers in the trams. 
It is decided to support by force the strike-breakers of the Company, it must be clearly understood that any failure to carry out such protection to its complete success would have a very unfortunate result by encouraging violence in other strikes. 
Yesterday 3rd, at a meeting at the Governorate it was...
ai_content.english_translation: The document is written in English. It details the mediation efforts of Madhour Pasha (a merchant and associate of Saad Zaghloul) to end the Cairo Tramway strike. It notes that while strikers initially agreed to return to work on September 3rd, they reneged on September 2nd by demanding all conditions be met. The Company is preparing to resume operations with new staff and is requesting police protection due to threats of violence against passengers. The author emphasizes the necessity of protecting strike-breakers to prevent the spread of labor unrest.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British consular or chancery report regarding a labor strike at the Cairo Tramway system in early September. It highlights the political intersection of labor disputes and the nationalist movement in Egypt, specifically mentioning the involvement of Saad Zaghloul's delegation. The text provides insight into the colonial administration's approach to labor unrest, emphasizing the use of police force to protect 'strike-breakers' to maintain public order and prevent the contagion of strikes in other sectors of the Egyptian economy.

ai_content.english_translation:
COPY
ALEXANDRIA 711 100 6:15 AM VMLTE T C
T C ECONOMIQUES 54 Rue de Namur Brussels

The Syndicate maintains as a prerequisite for the resumption of work its recognition by authentic act by the company, implying the substitution of the syndicate for the employees in all their relations with the company, the latter no longer having any relations with its personnel... Consequently, salary payments would be made by the syndicate, the company limiting itself to depositing the sums due at Banco di Roma. Guarantees to be revised according to agreement with the syndicate. We foresee that unexpressed claims could obviously, in our opinion, be refused absolutely and completely and cease all discussion, cable response.

VANDERHECHT.

It concerns a labor dispute involving a company and a labor syndicate. The syndicate is demanding formal recognition and the right to act as an intermediary for all employee relations and salary disbursements, with funds to be held at the Banco di Roma. The cable reflects the volatile labor relations in the post-WWI era, specifically in the context of European-owned enterprises operating in Egypt, where syndicalist movements were seeking to formalize their power against corporate management.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The Residency, Ramleh.
On the 25th and 26th of August, the Labour Conciliation Board was sitting in Cairo and was hearing the statements of the strikers of the Cairo and Heliopolis tramways.
One of the mens demands was, as stated by Mr Van Der Hecht, the recognition by the Companies of the newly established Syndicate of Tramway Workers.
This was refused by the Tramway Company, but eventually a compromise was proposed by the Board, which was acceptable by both sides.
"La Societe (Tramways) ne s'oppose nullement et ne fait aucune objection a ce que ses agents forment des unions ou groupements professionnels entre eux, sans toute fois s'engager a les reconnaitre officiellement.
La Societe ne leur tiendra aucun grief de ce chef, et ne prenara aucune mesure disciplinaire contre eux a ce sujet."
The proposed arrangement of which this was aclause was not, however accepted by the men.
During the discussion the men's delegates put forward the demand that all salaries should be paid into a bank, which would undertake to pay each man his due.
When asked what bank was proposed, it was replied, "the Banco di Roma"-to the question if the Bank had agreed, an affirmative answer was received, and at the demand of the Board the delegates promised to produce a letter to that effect.
The letter was not however produced, and at subsequent meetings nothing more was said about the offer of the Banco di Roma.
18-5-15
ai_content.english_translation: The French text translates to: "The Company (Tramways) does not oppose in any way and makes no objection to its agents forming unions or professional groups among themselves, without, however, committing to recognize them officially. The Company will hold no grievance against them on this account, and will take no disciplinary action against them on this subject."
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official report from the British Residency in Ramleh, Egypt, detailing labor unrest and negotiations involving the Cairo and Heliopolis tramway workers. It documents the mediation efforts of the Labour Conciliation Board in August 1913, specifically addressing the workers' demand for union recognition and a proposal to have salaries paid through the Banco di Roma. The report highlights the tension between the tramway company and the newly formed workers' syndicate, noting the failure of the delegates to substantiate their claims regarding the bank's involvement, which ultimately undermined their bargaining position.

NOTE ON THE STRIKE OF THE CAIRO ELECTRIC TRAMWAYS.
Strike began 10.8.19 Set led & work resumed 5.10.19 Duration 56 days.
The Cairo Electric Tramways have a concession from the Egyptian government made in 1894 and which terminates in 1978.
They pay 5% of their gross receipts to the Egyptian government. Their ordinary fares are limited by the concession to a charge of 5 mill. per line.
The Company has a certain number of ordinary shares and 80,000 joules a reger no fixed nominal value. It has paid considerable dividends on these shares.
There had been a previous strike of the Tramways employés in March-April 1919 and the Company had made certain concessions to the men, and work was resumed.
On the 4th. August the men presented a series of demands to the company. These were:
1. That the normal rate of increase of pay which had been stopped in 1914-1918, for war reasons, should be made up.
2. That an Enquiry Office, which would investigate punishments given to the staff, should be established by the company; that a delegate of their "Syndicate" should be present, and that a lawyer should be allowed to defend.
3. They ask for half pay when sick, & full pay when off duty for accidents due to service & that the war allowance should be counted in with the pay.
4. All deposits of guarantee to receive 4% interest for the past, & at the rate of 5% from 1st. January 1919.
5. That one month pay should be given for each completed year of service as a retiring allowance.
6. No reprisals by the Company against the strikers.
7. They ask for a 30% increase of pay.
The workmen subsequently asked that, the company should recognize their syndicate (Union) and pay for the days they had...

It outlines the financial structure of the company, its concession agreement with the Egyptian government, and the specific list of seven demands made by the workers' syndicate, including wage increases, sick pay, and formal recognition of their union.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal administrative report, likely prepared for the British High Commission in Egypt (as indicated by the 'High Commission' stamp), detailing the labor unrest within the Cairo Electric Tramways in 1919. It provides a concise history of the company's concession, which began in 1894, and documents the specific grievances of the workforce during a period of significant post-WWI social and political upheaval in Egypt. ai_content.transcribed_text: On the 9th, August, the workmen feared that the Managers of the Company were preparing to engage fresh staff in case of a strike and to meet this they decided on immediate action and came out on the 10.8.1919. Various attempts were made by the Governor of Cairo to bring about an understanding between the company and its men, but with no success. One of the main reasons was that the company only had an assistant manager in Egypt and every point had to be referred to Brussels, to the head office of the company. This lead to great delay. On the 25th August the Conciliation Board were asked by the Prime Minister to take on the discussion. Massive difficulties were met with - an absolute board. When finally the Manager arrived with greater powers, he at once countered the men's proposals by asking for leave to increase the fares, so he said, to cover the extra expenses incurred. This entailed a detailed examination of their accounts by accountants of the government. The result was that it was considered that the Tramway Company could meet the extra charges on revenue resulting from the men's demands, without any increase of fares. The Conciliation Board then again intervened and after considerable difficulties arrived at the following agreement between the Company and the men. This condition even only reasonable from the European point of view, but it must be remembered that until this year, Labour was voiceless in this country and companies & that directors imposed whatever conditions they wished on labour. But the workmen in Egypt, have realised their weakness, and have formed unions (syndicates) & have thus acquired the power of making themselves heard and felt. At first, four, and later, three, lawyers assisted the men in formulating their demands. They were not unreasonable and when the final agreement was prepared, used their best efforts to persuade the men to accept the terms offered.
ai_content.english_translation: The text describes a labor dispute involving the Tramway Company in Cairo in August 1919. It details the timeline of the strike, the intervention of the Governor of Cairo and the Conciliation Board, the administrative hurdles caused by the company's headquarters being in Brussels, and the eventual resolution of the dispute, noting the emergence of labor unions in Egypt as a significant socio-political development.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a historical account of a 1919 labor strike involving the Cairo Tramway Company. It provides a rare glimpse into the early 20th-century labor movement in Egypt, highlighting the transition of Egyptian workers from a 'voiceless' labor force to an organized body capable of forming syndicates. The text illustrates the friction between foreign-owned utility companies (with headquarters in Europe, specifically Brussels) and local Egyptian workers, as well as the role of the Egyptian government and the Conciliation Board in mediating industrial disputes during a period of significant nationalistic and social upheaval in post-WWI Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text: D'accord avec son Excellence le Gouverneur du Caire et la Commission de Conciliation du travail du Gouvernement Egyptien, la Direction de la Société Anonyme des Tramways du Caire et son personnel ont décidé de résoudre les questions pendantes, d'une façon définitive, comme suit: 1. La Société ne s'oppose nullement et ne fait aucune objection à ce que ses agents forment des Unions ou Groupements professionnels entre eux, sans toutefois s'engager à les reconnaître officiellement. 2. La Société ne leur tiendra aucun grief de ce chef et ne prendra aucune mesure disciplinaire contre eux à ce sujet. 3. La Société accepte à partir du 1er Octobre 1919, de porter les salaires des receveurs et wattmen aux taux qu'ils auraient atteints à cette date si les augmentations de salaires n'avaient pas été suspendues durant deux ans au cours de la guerre.
ai_content.english_translation: In agreement with His Excellency the Governor of Cairo and the Conciliation Commission for Labor of the Egyptian Government, the Management of the Cairo Tramways Joint-Stock Company and its personnel have decided to resolve the pending issues, in a definitive manner, as follows: 1. The Company does not oppose in any way and makes no objection to its agents forming Unions or professional groups among themselves, without, however, committing to officially recognizing them. 2. The Company will hold no grievance against them on this account and will take no disciplinary action against them on this subject. 3. The Company accepts, starting from October 1, 1919, to bring the salaries of conductors and motormen to the rates they would have reached by that date if salary increases had not been suspended for two years during the war.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal labor agreement dated October 4, 1919, between the Cairo Tramways Company (Société Anonyme des Tramways du Caire) and its employees, mediated by the Egyptian Government's Conciliation Commission. It reflects the post-WWI socio-political climate in Egypt, where labor unrest and the push for unionization were rising. The agreement is significant for its recognition of the employees' right to form professional associations (unions) while simultaneously maintaining a cautious stance on official recognition, and for its commitment to adjusting wages to compensate for the suspension of raises during the war years.

Cette avance sera remboursable par des retenues de P25 échelonnées sur les quinzaines de paie. La 1ère retenue sera faite sur la première quinzaine de paie.
9. La Société reprendra tous les agents qui étaient à son service, le 9 août 1919 sauf les agents qui sont sous le coup de procès verbaux dressés à leur encontre par la Police. Ces agents resteront suspendus jusqu'après le prononcé du jugement définitif à leur égard.
10. Un règlement général des conditions de service sera établi, imprimé en arabe et en français et distribué personnel.
11. Il est entendu que les agents qui ne se seraient pas mis à la disposition de la Société à la date du 5 octobre seront considéré comme démissionnaires, sauf motifs légitimes.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
With reference to Brussels despatch No. 326, of August 30th, last, relative to the apparent connection between the Banco di Roma and the syndicate of the Egyptian Tramway employees during the strike, I have the honour to report that although we have never had definite proof of any definite connection between this bank and the extreme nationalists, there is little doubt that facilities were freely offered by the Banco di Roma for extremists and strikers to bank their funds and subscriptions. Of course, the part played by several members of the Italian colony here, and the sympathy extended by them towards extremists and agitators may have something to do with it. On the other hand, the bank never has been in a very flourishing condition in this country, and it is more than likely that the directors were only too pleased to have an opportunity of handling big subscriptions, whether they were strike funds or nationalist donations.

I have the honour to be,
My Lord,
Your Lordship's most obedient, humble servant,
(Signed) MILNE CHEETHAM.

The Right Honourable
Earl Curzon of Kedleston, K.G., G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a diplomatic report from Milne Cheetham to Earl Curzon of Kedleston regarding the alleged financial support provided by the Banco di Roma to Egyptian Tramway strikers and nationalist agitators in 1919. Cheetham notes that while there is no definitive proof of a formal connection, the bank likely accepted these funds due to its poor financial standing in Egypt and a general sympathy among the local Italian community for anti-British nationalist movements.

The correspondence highlights the British colonial administration's efforts to monitor and suppress the financial lifelines of the Egyptian nationalist movement by linking them to foreign interests.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. 25th February, 1930.
I attach herewith copy of a letter from the Commandant, Cairo City Police, which shows the measures taken to enable the Tram Company to continue a limited service during the period of the strike. It will be observed that the maximum number of trams to which protection can be given is six per day for each of the four main dépôts, that is to say, 24 trams in all. Should protection continue to be necessary, it is impossible to extend it beyond the above figure. Any further increase in traffic would require to be protected by the Military and I am doubtful as to the expediency of enlisting Military assistance in this case at the present stage. It will be realized that the general situation does not permit of withdrawing more than a limited number of police from their ordinary duties in order to afford assistance to the Tramway Company.
The Company were unable to arrange even a limited service yesterday, but today they are running a certain number of trams. These trams are being driven by inspectors for the most part, though a few drivers are still working. It remains to be seen whether the next few days will see the men begin to come back or not.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official memorandum from the Residency in Cairo, dated February 25, 1930. It discusses the ongoing tram strike in Cairo and the police's capacity to provide security for the Tram Company. The author notes that the police can only protect 24 trams total (six per depot) and expresses hesitation about involving the military to increase this capacity, citing the need to keep police on their regular duties. It concludes by noting that the company is currently running a limited service using inspectors as drivers.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official administrative communication from the British Residency in Cairo during the 1930 tram strike. It highlights the colonial administration's concern with maintaining public order and essential services while balancing the limited resources of the Cairo City Police. The document provides insight into the labor unrest in interwar Egypt and the British authorities' cautious approach to using military force to break strikes, preferring to limit the scope of operations to avoid escalation.

ai_content.transcribed_text: CAIRO CITY POLICE, Office of Commandant. CONFIDENTIAL. (COPY) No PO/3/79(7)3. Cairo, 23rd Feb, 1920. The Adviser, Ministry of the Interior. Subject: Tramway strike. Reference your letter re trams. I can see no way of providing Police protection to break the strike. There are three tram depots in Cairo, i.e. Boulak, Shubra and Abbassia (besides the Ginah Depot). To guard these will need not less than 15 men each, i.e. 45 men to be relieved by another 45, i.e. 90 men. It will also be necessary to guard trams running from all four depots: if they run a reduced service of, say, six trams only from each depot, i.e. 24 trams in all, it will need three men per tram i.e. 72 men to be relieved by another 72, i.e. 144. i.e. total number of men needed is 234. At this present moment today, I have available for duty 65 men of the Guard Company, all the rest are employed on essential work which cannot be stopped. It is impossible to provide Qism men for escorting trams, unless I take them off beat. I am also being called upon daily for police to keep order at flour distribution centres. The Governor informs me today that no strike of trams is expected, anyhow, for the present. If in the future, it is decided to try to break a strike, I am afraid the British Military are the only people who can give the necessary protection. true copy! (Sgd) T.W. RUSSELL, Commandant, Cairo City Police.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a confidential memorandum from the Commandant of the Cairo City Police to the Adviser of the Ministry of the Interior regarding a potential tramway strike. The Commandant explains that he lacks the manpower to provide police protection to break the strike, detailing the specific number of men required to guard depots and trams (234 men total), noting that he only has 65 men available. He states that he cannot pull men from their beats or from essential duties like guarding flour distribution centers. He concludes that the British Military would be the only force capable of providing such protection if a strike were to occur.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1920 confidential communication from T.W. Russell, the Commandant of the Cairo City Police, to the British Adviser at the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior. It provides a rare administrative insight into the logistical constraints of the Cairo police force during the volatile post-WWI period in Egypt. The document highlights the reliance of the British colonial administration on the British Military for maintaining order during labor unrest, as the local police force was severely under-resourced and overstretched by essential civil duties such as guarding food distribution centers during a time of economic instability.
