ai_content.transcribed_text:
RAPPORT CONCERNANT LE SABOTAGE.
SUPPRESSION DU MATERIEL.
Vern la fin de novembre le matériel roulant commença à faire défaut, il a manqué sur un total d'environ 160 motrices nécessaires pour assurer les services réguliers :
Le 2 Décembre 4 motrices
Le 4 Décembre 7
Le 6 19
Le 8 25
Le 10 34
Le 11 39
Le 12 47
Le 13 62
En outre, 20 à 30 motrices de celles restant en service doivent journellement rentrer aux dépôts pour réparation sommaire d'avaries souvent dues à des actes de sabotage.
REDUCTION DES SERVICES.
La situation aujourd'hui se résume comme suit :
Lignes Sakakini Ataba, Vieux Caire, Ghamrah Abattoirs, Rod-el-Farag, Citadelle, Khasindar, Imam, Sporting Club, Gare Qanater sont entièrement supprimées, faute de matériel.
GREVE PERLEE.
La "grève des bras croisés" qui se pratique notoirement aux ateliers est assistée d'autre part par le sabotage du matériel sur le réseau.
SABOTAGE.
Un wattman, le 13 Courant, reconnait avoir avarié volontairement son train. Un autre est surpris brisant l'automatique de sa voiture. De toute part, les agents du contrôle signalent des faits d'avarie volontaire du matériel.
ACTES CRIMINELS.
En 16 endroits, dans le cours des journées du 13 et du 14, des boulons sont retirés de la gorge des rails où ils avaient été encastrés pour provoquer des déraillements.
Des hommes du Service Technique sont signalés voyageant sur les motrices et donnant des conseils aux conducteurs sur la façon d'avarier les voitures.
ai_content.english_translation: REPORT CONCERNING SABOTAGE. SUPPRESSION OF EQUIPMENT. Towards the end of November, rolling stock began to be in short supply; out of a total of approximately 160 motor cars necessary to ensure regular services, the following were missing: [List of dates and numbers]. Furthermore, 20 to 30 motor cars of those remaining in service must return daily to the depots for summary repairs of damage often due to acts of sabotage. REDUCTION OF SERVICES. The situation today is summarized as follows: Lines [List of locations] are entirely suppressed, for lack of equipment. SLOWDOWN STRIKE. The 'crossed-arms strike' which is notoriously practiced in the workshops is assisted on the other hand by the sabotage of equipment on the network. SABOTAGE. A tram driver, on the 13th instant, admits to having voluntarily damaged his train. Another is caught breaking the automatic [mechanism] of his car. From all sides, control agents report acts of voluntary damage to equipment. CRIMINAL ACTS. In 16 places, during the days of the 13th and 14th, bolts were removed from the rail grooves where they had been embedded to cause derailments. Men from the Technical Service are reported traveling on the motor cars and giving advice to the drivers on how to damage the cars.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal intelligence report detailing the systematic sabotage of the Cairo tramway network during a period of intense civil unrest in Egypt, likely December 1951. The report documents a 'slowdown strike' (grève perlée) by workshop staff, the deliberate destruction of rolling stock by drivers, and criminal acts such as tampering with rail tracks to cause derailments. The document highlights the administrative collapse of public transport services in specific districts of Cairo, reflecting the broader political instability and anti-colonial sentiment prevalent in Egypt immediately preceding the 1952 Revolution.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
PROVOCATIONS. - Alors que, par suite du manque de matériel pour les causes ci-dessus, le chômage forcé augmente parmi les receveurs et wattman, le syndicat affiche dans les dépôts un avis donnant d'abord copie d'une lettre adressée à la Direction de la Société par l'avocat Kamel Hussein, lettre dans laquelle ce dernier prétend que la Société s'est engagée à donner du travail à tous les agents et doit les payer et les traîner ne sortent pas, de la même façon que s'ils travaillaient. L'avis ajoute ensuite que tous les agents doivent se présenter en masse et que le syndicat réclamera à la Société les salaires de tous les agents présents à qui il ne serait pas donné service. - 

DESORGANISATION DES SERVICES. - En même temps une désorganisation méthodique des services se produit. - 

Les horaires sont rendus impossibles, sur une même ligne, certaine convois roulent à des vitesses dangereuses, tandis que ceux qui le suivent roulent à 1 ou 2 contacts, brûlant les résistances des boîtes régulatrices, et produisant des retards considérables dans les services. - 

ACCIDENTS. - Les accidents se multiplient: déraillement de remorques, collisions, tamponnements, prises en écharpe, non seulement on détruit le matériel, mais il y a des victimes. - 

Les agents du contrôle sont impuissants devant l'indiscipline générale, ou bien, syndiqués également, craignent les représailles s'ils font leurs devoirs. Certaines sont délibérément complices. - 

Après les incidents provoquant des arrêts de service, le personnel retarde volontairement le rétablissement des services, cherchant de prétendus témoins, s'absentant, soulevant des discussions et de nouveaux incidents. Un déraillement a produit récemment 2 heures d'interruption en pleine place Bab-el-Hadid. A Mot Bey, une interruption s'est prolongée 45 minutes après l'enquête de la Police et l'ordre de celle-ci de rétablir la circulation. - 

INSUBORDINATION. - Les actes d'indiscipline deviennent d'une gravité extrême. Un manoeuvre prête, il y a cinq ou six jours, riait des efforts d'un inspecteur à faire dégager la voie à la suite d'un accident grave dû à la négligence du personnel et insultait cet inspecteur des mots les plus orduriers. - 

INTIMIDATION. - Le mois dernier c'était le bureau d'enquête mis par deux fois en interdiction par le syndicat. Celui-ci a imposé son autorité à tous les agents par les moyens habituels bien connus.
ai_content.english_translation:
PROVOCATIONS. - While, due to the lack of equipment for the reasons above, forced unemployment increases among conductors and motormen, the union posts a notice in the depots giving first a copy of a letter addressed to the Company Management by the lawyer Kamel Hussein, a letter in which the latter claims that the Company has committed to giving work to all agents and must pay them even if they do not go out, in the same way as if they were working. The notice then adds that all agents must present themselves in mass and that the union will claim from the Company the wages of all agents present to whom service would not be given. - 

DISORGANIZATION OF SERVICES. - At the same time, a methodical disorganization of services is occurring. - 

Schedules are made impossible; on the same line, certain convoys run at dangerous speeds, while those following them run at 1 or 2 contacts, burning out the resistors of the regulator boxes, and producing considerable delays in services. - 

ACCIDENTS. - Accidents are multiplying: derailment of trailers, collisions, rear-endings, side-swipes; not only is equipment destroyed, but there are victims. - 

Control agents are powerless in the face of general indiscipline, or else, being unionized themselves, they fear reprisals if they do their duty. Some are deliberately complicit. - 

After incidents causing service stoppages, the staff voluntarily delays the restoration of services, looking for alleged witnesses, absenting themselves, raising arguments and new incidents. A derailment recently produced 2 hours of interruption in the middle of Bab-el-Hadid square. At Mot Bey, an interruption lasted 45 minutes after the Police investigation and their order to restore traffic. - 

INSUBORDINATION. - Acts of indiscipline are becoming extremely serious. A maneuverer, five or six days ago, laughed at an inspector's efforts to clear the track following a serious accident due to staff negligence and insulted this inspector with the most vulgar words. - 

INTIMIDATION. - Last month, the investigation office was banned twice by the union. The latter imposed its authority on all agents by the usual well-known means.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative report detailing a period of labor unrest and industrial sabotage within a public transport company (likely a tramway or railway network). It describes a systematic campaign by a labor union to disrupt operations through 'methodical disorganization,' including the deliberate creation of accidents, refusal to follow schedules, and intimidation of management and non-unionized staff. The text highlights the role of legal counsel (Kamel Hussein) in formalizing labor demands and notes specific geographic locations like Bab-el-Hadid, suggesting an urban setting in a French-influenced colonial or mandate territory (likely Cairo, Egypt, given the location and the context of early 20th-century labor movements).

ai_content.transcribed_text: VOLE. - Les vols ont augmenté dans des proportions énormes. Un service de surveillance secrète institué nous rend compte de ce qu'il constate à ce sujet. - ABSTENTION VOLONTAIRE DE PERCEVOIR. - Un mot d'ordre a été donné de profiter de l'encombrement extraordinaire des trains pour que les receveurs prétendent être dans l'impossibilité de percevoir. - Nous avons fait procéder à des pointages d'où il résulte que sur des trains bondés de plus de 100 voyageurs 20 ou 30 billets seulement ont été délivrés. - Sur la ligne de Gizeh, un receveur déclarait ouvertement que seuls les Européens devaient payer, que les Égyptiens avaient le droit de voyager sans payer. - ABUS DES SOINS MEDICAUX ET DES INDEMNITES. - Le nombre d'agents blessés en service a augmenté en dehors de toute raison. Les Docteurs nous déclarent être convaincus dans nombre de cas avoir affaire à des simulateurs. Un des procédés les plus courants consiste à se laisser tomber sur la chaussée lorsque le train marche à vitesse réduite. - RECLAMATIONS DU PUBLIC. - Nous recevons des plaintes très nombreuses des voyageurs, et souvent de personnes dont la parole ne peut être mise en doute, dénonçant les actes de brutalité dont le public est victime de la part du personnel. - Les causes les plus fréquentes sont à l'origine: les signaux de départs intempestifs; le défaut d'arrêt aux stations; le refus d'arrêter aux stations facultatives; la remise aux voyageurs de vieux billets ayant déjà servi; le fait de ne pas remettre le change; souvent la grossièreté de l'agent sans que rien n'y ait donné prétexte. - Nous avons dû nous borner à référer les plaignants à la Police dans la plupart des cas. - L'exposé complet des actes d'indiscipline serait très long. - A plus forte raison une énumération de faits précis est elle difficile. Nous en possédons néanmoins tous les éléments, qui nous permettraient de justifier au besoin ce rapport.
ai_content.english_translation: THEFT. - Thefts have increased in enormous proportions. A secret surveillance service instituted reports to us what it observes on this subject. - VOLUNTARY ABSTENTION FROM COLLECTING. - An order was given to take advantage of the extraordinary crowding of the trains so that the conductors claim to be unable to collect fares. - We have had counts made from which it results that on crowded trains of more than 100 passengers, only 20 or 30 tickets were issued. - On the Gizeh line, a conductor openly declared that only Europeans had to pay, and that Egyptians had the right to travel without paying. - ABUSE OF MEDICAL CARE AND INDEMNITIES. - The number of agents injured on duty has increased beyond all reason. The doctors declare to us that they are convinced in many cases to be dealing with simulators. One of the most common methods consists of letting oneself fall onto the road when the train is moving at reduced speed. - PUBLIC COMPLAINTS. - We receive very numerous complaints from travelers, and often from people whose word cannot be doubted, denouncing acts of brutality of which the public is a victim on the part of the staff. - The most frequent causes are at the origin: untimely departure signals; failure to stop at stations; refusal to stop at optional stations; giving passengers old tickets that have already been used; the fact of not giving change; often the rudeness of the agent without any pretext. - We have had to limit ourselves to referring the complainants to the Police in most cases. - A complete account of the acts of indiscipline would be very long. - A fortiori, an enumeration of precise facts is difficult. We nevertheless possess all the elements, which would allow us to justify this report if necessary.

The text highlights systemic issues including theft, conductors intentionally failing to collect fares from Egyptian passengers, fraudulent medical claims by staff to obtain indemnities, and frequent public complaints regarding staff brutality and poor service. The report serves as an indictment of the personnel's conduct and suggests a breakdown in management control, likely dating to the late 19th or early 20th century during the period of British influence in Egypt.

The position with regard to the Cairo Tramways which has been referred to in my periodical situation reports is coming to a crisis.
In the absence of any Egyptian legislation governing Trades Unions, an association of employés of the Cairo Tramway Company was constituted two months ago in the form of a Civil partnership. This extraordinary device which, as far as I know, is without precedent, and would be difficult to achieve in any other country, is of a nature, if its legality is sustained, to place this important Public Service Company entirely at the mercy of Kamel Effendi Hussein, the ambitious lawyer who is fomenting the movement.

ai_content.english_translation: This is a diplomatic cable from the British Foreign Office regarding the labor situation at the Cairo Tramway Company. It reports that in the absence of labor laws, employees formed a 'Civil partnership' union. The manager was notified that 800 employees (half the workforce) had registered an 'irrevocable assignment' of their future wages to the union. The author describes this as an 'extraordinary device' and 'without precedent,' noting that if legal, it would place the company under the control of Kamel Effendi Hussein, a lawyer accused of fomenting the labor unrest.

Cairo Tramway Company.

This Company has had difficulties with its labour since 1919. At the time of the political disorders in 1919 in Cairo, their services became disorganised and a strike occurred on August 1919 and partially on February 1, April 17 & December 16- 1920. The men returned to work on the advice of the Minister of Interior after receiving some concessions as to increased pay. A more serious strike occurred in August 10-1919 and lasted till October 5-1919.

The Labour Conciliation Board which had then only been established, intervened and after examination, advised the Tramway Company to grant some very radical concessions. The men returned to work and their delegates expressed themselves as quite satisfied.

But the Tramway Company had been selected by political agitators as a fruitful ground on which to operate and to create trouble, so a series of minor conflicts were constantly arising between the Company and the men.

Every attempt was made by the Government to keep a fair balance between the Company and the workmen, and on the whole this has been successful, as both parties have shown trust in the Government whenever there has been a clear issue. Unfortunately, as stated above, other factors besides purely labour ones have been introduced.

For instance, when the question of the then and die-mient of staff was raised, a special permanent Committee of enquiry was instituted on which the workmen were represented by a delegate and on which an independent Government official also sits, and this arrangement was accepted by both parties.

Of late the syndicate of the Cairo Tramp has been...

It details a series of strikes, the intervention of the Labour Conciliation Board, the role of the Minister of Interior, and the influence of political agitators on labor relations, concluding with the establishment of a permanent committee to resolve staff disputes.

Since then an attempt to resume the notion of doing no work in the workshop was made at the commencement of February and for several days no work was done. The reason given by the men for this was that some of their comrades had been unfairly suspended, but on enquiry, the cases of suspension were found to be fully justified. For instance, one man has been suspended because he had been found making a scene in the shops, and another, a foreigner, for gross insolence to the General Manager.

The Government, after making quite sure that work was not being done in the shops, authorised the Company to take what measures it considered necessary either by a lock-out or replacing the men, so as to meet the situation, and to ensure the continuation of the Tramway service, which is an essential transport service.

The Company announced its intention of not paying workmen who did no work and asked for an undertaking that they would carry out their duties. The movement at once collapsed and the work has been normal since.

The European section had been more guarded, but the native workmen who are the large majority had quite obviously signed away all their rights without knowing what they were doing.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Enclosure in No. 1. Report by Dr. Granville on the Cairo Tramway Company. (Extract.) THIS company has had difficulties with its labour since 1919. At the time of political disorders in 1919 in Cairo, their services became disorganised, and again occurred on August 1919 and partially on the 1st February, the 17th April and the 15th December, 1920. The men returned to work on the advice of the Ministry of Interior after receiving some concessions as to increased pay. A more serious strike occurred on the 10th August, 1919, and lasted till the 5th October, 1919. The Labour Conciliation Board, which had then only been established, intervened and, after examination, advised the tramway company to grant some very real concessions. The men returned to work, and their delegates expressed themselves quite satisfied.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
A tram strike took place in Cairo yesterday afternoon. The facts are as follows:-
Early in the afternoon a native mechanic at the workshops assaulted one of the overseers. He was accordingly sent for by the Head Office to explain his conduct. Instead of obeying the order, he went round his friends in the shop, and they all decided to stop work on the advice of Kamel Hussein. It was definitely independent and the syndicate was ignorant that anything was wrong. The result was, the trams were suspended during the afternoon and evening of yesterday, but to-day a restricted service is on the streets, and 135 out of 300 workmen are present at the Abbassia workshops. On hearing of what had happened, Rushdi Pasha sent for Kamel Hussein and gave him a sound rating, telling him that his action was quite unjustified and that as the company had expressed no intention of dismissing the man, he deserved no sympathy from his fellow-workers.
ai_content.english_translation: The document describes a tram strike in Cairo that occurred after a mechanic assaulted an overseer. When the mechanic was summoned to the Head Office, he incited his colleagues to stop work under the guidance of Kamel Hussein. The strike was unauthorized by the syndicate. Tram services were suspended, but resumed on a restricted basis the following day. Rushdi Pasha reprimanded Kamel Hussein for his unjustified actions, noting that the company had not intended to fire the mechanic, thus rendering the strike unnecessary.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official report from the British High Commissioner's office in Egypt, dated April 1921. It details a labor dispute involving tram workers in Cairo, highlighting the tension between the colonial administration, local labor syndicates, and political figures like Rushdi Pasha. The report serves as an administrative record of civil unrest and the British effort to monitor labor movements and maintain public order in post-WWI Egypt.

No. 333
19.5.21. 12 noon

Protracted anti-government demonstrations occurred in Cairo yesterday. They were only dispersed with difficulty by the police who whoever did not fire in spite of being severely handled. Further demonstrations on the same scale are expected to-day.

Late yesterday eveing a bomb was thrown at the last tram of the day entering the Shubra Depot. The tram contained blackleg drivers. Nine persons were wounded, three seriously two of whom belonged to the police guard protecting depot against the strikers. A third policeman was knifed in crowd and his assailant arrested. Two men have been arrested under suspicion of complicity in bomb outrage.

ai_content.english_translation:
Some facts concerning the violence exercised with impunity by tramway agents.

On April 12, several agents of the Company, including Mr. Van der Hecht, head of movement, were attacked and wounded.

Following representations by Mr. Dauge, the Government promised that the perpetrator of the aggression would be prosecuted.

On April 26, individuals armed with nabouts (clubs) forcibly entered the premises of the central factory and struck and wounded the agents whose names follow:

1) Ernesto Ferrari (Italian) Chief Mechanic, beaten, wounded, treated at the Public Assistance.
2) Christo Vlaviskie (Greek) Second Mechanic, beaten, wounded.
3) Mohamed Helaouani (Egyptian) laborer, beaten, wounded.
4) Mahmoud Abou Cheraba (Egyptian) laborer, beaten, wounded.
5) Domenico Benedetti (Italian) 3rd mechanic, beaten.
6) Marzouk Mohamed (Egyptian) Chief Stoker, beaten.
7) Said Hassan was also beaten near the factory.

On April 28, new aggressions, of which these are the victims:
1) Salzer, Driver at the management (serious condition - at Kasr-el-Eini hospital).

A la suite de nombreuses démarches, les autorités décident de faire garder l'usine par la police et l'on annonce à Monsieur Dauge qu'un substitut est chargé de poursuivre les coupables. En attendant ceux-ci sont remis en liberté.
Tout récemment, la compagnie ayant fait circuler quelques voitures pilotées par des conducteurs, ceux-ci sont attaqués et blessés. Ceux des assaillants qui ont été appréhendés sont aussitôt remis en liberté et peuvent venir se montrer devant l'usine pour prouver que l'impunité leur est assurée.
L'assaillant de Monsieur Van der Hecht fut cité à comparaître devant le tribunal de l'Ezbékieh le 17 mai pour répondre du délit commis par lui le 12 avril. L'affaire fixée à 8 heures du matin fut appelée à 2 heures de l'après midi et l'accusé ayant demandé une remise le juge renvoya la cause au 5 juillet.
Enfin hier, dans la soirée des coups de feu ont été tirés sur une voiture ramenant du travail des agents de la Compagnie. Il y a un tué et plusieurs blessés.
ai_content.english_translation:
Following numerous efforts, the authorities decided to have the factory guarded by the police and it was announced to Monsieur Dauge that a substitute prosecutor is in charge of pursuing the culprits. In the meantime, they have been released.
Quite recently, the company having had a few cars driven by drivers circulate, they were attacked and wounded. Those of the assailants who were apprehended were immediately released and can come to show themselves in front of the factory to prove that impunity is guaranteed to them.
The assailant of Monsieur Van der Hecht was summoned to appear before the Ezbékieh tribunal on May 17 to answer for the crime committed by him on April 12. The case, set for 8 o'clock in the morning, was called at 2 o'clock in the afternoon and the accused having requested a postponement, the judge adjourned the case to July 5.
Finally, yesterday evening, shots were fired at a car bringing company agents back from work. There is one dead and several wounded.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
NOTE DE LA SOCIETE DES TRAMWAYS DU CAIRE
SUR LE MILLIEME D'AUGMENTATION DE TARIF
- ANNEXE III -
Au cours de l'année 1919, la Société a fait des sacrifices énormes, représentant une charge annuelle d'environ £ 80.000, pour améliorer le sort de son personnel. En 1920 le Gouvernement était désireux d'accorder à ce personnel des conditions encore plus favorables. La Société invoquait sa situation financière d'après laquelle non seulement elle ne pouvait faire davantage, mais elle avait déjà fait trop de concessions.
D'accord avec la Société, le Gouvernement fit examiner les livres de comptabilité et conclut à une augmentation de tarif de 1 millième qui fut appliquée à partir du 5 Juin 1920.
Le produit de ce millième est porté à un compte spécial sur lequel la Société préleva de nouveaux avantages pour son personnel: 25% d'augmentation de salaire et un supplément de vie chère.
Ces avantages représentent £ 36.000 par an.
En 1921, le Gouvernement engage avec Monsieur de Lanoker, Directeur Général de la Société des pourparlers en vue de la suppression de l'augmentation de tarif de 1m/m. Il est de tout évidence que la Société ne pourrait plus même faire face à ses obligations financières telles que paiement de l'intérêt des obligations si cette augmentation de tarif était supprimée sans compensations ou bien sans la suppression des avantages qui en découlent pour le personnel.
Monsieur de Lanoker est en Europe et s'occupe précisément d'étudier la question avec le Conseil d'Administration de la Société d'après les préliminaires posés au Caire avant son départ. Mr. Haswell, Directeur Général
ai_content.english_translation: NOTE FROM THE CAIRO TRAMWAYS COMPANY ON THE ONE-MILLIEME TARIFF INCREASE. ANNEX III. During the year 1919, the Company made enormous sacrifices, representing an annual burden of approximately £80,000, to improve the lot of its personnel. In 1920, the Government was eager to grant this personnel even more favorable conditions. The Company invoked its financial situation, according to which not only could it not do more, but it had already made too many concessions. In agreement with the Company, the Government had the accounting books examined and concluded on a tariff increase of 1 millième which was applied starting June 5, 1920. The proceeds of this millième are carried to a special account from which the Company drew new benefits for its personnel: 25% salary increase and a cost-of-living supplement. These benefits represent £36,000 per year. In 1921, the Government engaged in talks with Monsieur de Lanoker, General Manager of the Company, with a view to the suppression of the 1m/m tariff increase. It is quite evident that the Company could no longer even meet its financial obligations such as the payment of bond interest if this tariff increase were suppressed without compensation or without the suppression of the benefits resulting from it for the personnel. Monsieur de Lanoker is in Europe and is currently studying the question with the Company's Board of Directors based on the preliminaries established in Cairo before his departure. Mr. Haswell, General Manager.

It outlines the tension between the Egyptian Government's desire to improve labor conditions for the company's staff and the company's financial constraints. The text explains how the revenue from the 1920 tariff hike was directly earmarked for a 25% salary increase and cost-of-living adjustments for employees. The document serves as a briefing for ongoing negotiations in 1921, where the government sought to roll back the tariff increase, a move the company argued would jeopardize its ability to pay bond interest unless the labor benefits were also rescinded.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPY
EGYPT GENERAL MISSION
Fzbet-el-Zeitoun
March 17th 1919.

H.B.M. Consul
Cairo.

Dear Sir,

The above mentioned missionary Society has missionaries at Belbeis and Shebin-el-Kanater. As they are the only British subjects in these two towns you will understand that I, as Secretary to the Society, am not at rest with regard to them seeing that all communications are cut. As there is a large British garrison at Belbeis I am more or less assured of their safety, our two ladies there being well known to the military. At Shebin-el-Kanater however there are no military and as in many places I understand the mob has given away to wanton murder and pillage, I should be grateful if some steps could be taken for their protection.

At Belbeis:- Miss F.A. Langford & Miss S.W. Pim
At Shebin-el-Kanater:- Mr. & Mrs. A.Y. Steel and 2 children
Miss Liblik & Miss A.M. Hay

We also have missionaries at Alexandria, Ismailia & Suez but as these will naturally benefit from the steps being taken in those places to protect British subjects, I take it to be unnecessary to mention them here.

Thanking you in anticipation for any steps you see fit to take.

Believe me,
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd) George Swan
Sec.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a copy of a letter sent by George Swan, Secretary of the Egypt General Mission, to the British Consul in Cairo on March 17, 1919. The author expresses concern for the safety of missionaries stationed in Belbeis and Shebin-el-Kanater during a period of civil unrest (the 1919 Egyptian Revolution), noting that communication lines have been severed. He requests British military protection for the missionaries in these towns, while noting that missionaries in larger cities like Alexandria, Ismailia, and Suez are likely already under the protection of existing British forces.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a primary source record from the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, a period of widespread anti-colonial uprising against British rule. The letter highlights the vulnerability of foreign missionary outposts in rural Egypt when communication and transport infrastructure were disrupted by the nationalist movement. It provides specific names of British subjects residing in the Nile Delta and illustrates the reliance of civilian expatriates on the British military garrison for security during the height of the unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text: BRITISH CONSULATE, CAIRO. 22nd March 1919. Sir, I have the honour to forward herewith a list of British Subjects living outside Cairo and its immediate suburbs. The list further does not include British Subject resident in the district of the Consular Agencies at Mansourah, Zagazig & Birke-t-es-Sab. All the people mentioned in the enclosed list have registered at this Consulate during the present year. It is possible that there are other British Subject in these places and in other localities, but as they are not registered here, they are unknown to the Consulate. I am sending in this list as it may be of use to you or to the Military Authorities at the present juncture. The names and addresses of British Subject living in the districts of the Consular Agencies will no doubt be furnished to the nearest Military Authority by the Consular Agents. I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient servant, James Morgan, Acting Consul. The Chancery, The Residency, Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official letter from the British Consulate in Cairo, dated March 22, 1919, addressed to the Residency. The Acting Consul, James Morgan, is transmitting a list of registered British subjects residing outside of Cairo and its immediate suburbs. He clarifies that the list excludes residents of the consular districts of Mansourah, Zagazig, and Birke-t-es-Sab. He notes that the list is incomplete as it only includes those registered at the Consulate, and suggests that the military authorities should contact the local Consular Agents for information regarding British subjects in those specific districts.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence from the British Consulate in Cairo during the immediate aftermath of World War I, specifically during the period of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. ai_content.transcribed_text:
General Staff Intelligence (3rd Echelon)

His Majesty's Consular Agent at Zagazig has asked whether it would not be possible for a Guard to be placed on the British Consulate in that town.

I understand this was done in the case of the British Consular Agency at Mansoura; so Mr. Nixon's request seems justifiable. At the same time, his letter is dated April 23rd, and as everything has quieted down so much since then, the Military Authorities may not consider such a precaution now necessary.

[Handwritten note:]
Would not consider leaving the British Consulate - sure there is no ground of complaint if so, I shall be very grateful if you can reply wire "urgent", on receipt of this at present, answering your letter "yes", (having a guard with local police).

Yours sincerely,
[Signature: A.D. Alban]
A.D. Alban Esq.
14.IV.19, Consulate
Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: The document consists of a typed memorandum from the General Staff Intelligence regarding a request for military guards at the British Consular Agency in Zagazig, citing a precedent in Mansoura. This is followed by a handwritten response from A.D. Alban, who suggests that while he would not consider abandoning the consulate, he would appreciate a wire response regarding the provision of a guard, potentially utilizing local police.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document captures the administrative and security concerns of British diplomatic officials in Egypt during the volatile period following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It highlights the coordination between the British military (General Staff Intelligence) and consular staff regarding the protection of diplomatic outposts in provincial towns like Zagazig and Mansoura. The correspondence reflects the British effort to maintain a presence and ensure the safety of their agents amidst the civil unrest of the post-WWI era.

ai_content.transcribed_text: With reference to your memorandum No 8882/4 of May 1st 1919, I have to inform you that your request was forwarded to the O. C. Troops, Segazig Section who writes that he does not consider it necessary to post a guard at the residence of the Consular Agent in that town. The power house guard is only a short distance from the house in question, and can easily afford any protection necessary. In view of the state of the town during the last six weeks, there is very little chance of any trouble arising necessitating the protection of the Consulate. RESIDENCY, CAIRO. 15th May, 1919. 2462/5. ai_content.transcribed_text:
TELEGRAM.
To HIGH COMMISSIONER FOR EGYPT
Ramleh.
Received 25.11.19. 1.55pm
Dated: 25.11.19.
General Blake commanding troops here has asked me to inform British subjects that in case of a serious rising here and extreme danger they can take refuge temporarily at certain points which he will communicate to me later where they will be under military protection. He wishes this to be done this week. As such a step cannot be taken without publicity and may cause alarm I think it advisable to inform you.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a telegram sent to the High Commissioner for Egypt in Ramleh, received on November 25, 1919. It conveys a message from General Blake, who commands the local troops. The General requests that British subjects be informed that, in the event of a serious uprising and extreme danger, they may seek temporary refuge at designated locations under military protection. The General intends for this to be arranged within the week. The sender expresses concern that implementing such a plan would inevitably become public knowledge and cause alarm, hence the need to inform the High Commissioner.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1919 diplomatic telegram reflecting the volatile security situation in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution against British colonial rule. The correspondence between General Blake and the High Commissioner for Egypt highlights the British military's contingency planning for the protection of British nationals amidst widespread civil unrest. The document underscores the colonial administration's sensitivity to public perception, as the sender explicitly notes the risk of causing panic by preparing evacuation or refuge points for British subjects during a period of intense nationalist agitation.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SECRET.
TO:-
First Secretary,
The Residency,
Cairo.

I have received attached letter.
It raises the whole question of local self defence schemes, which I believe have been put in hand. If so probably by this time the Consular Agent at Mansurah has been quieted.
Will you answer the British Consul please, and inform me what steps have been taken, as I am at present ignorant on the subject.

(Sd) W.N. Congreve.
Lt. General,
General Officer Commanding,
E.E.F.

G.H.Q., E.E.F.
May 25th, 1921
ai_content.english_translation: This is a secret memorandum addressed to the First Secretary at the British Residency in Cairo. The author, Lieutenant General W.N. Congreve, acknowledges receipt of an attached letter regarding local self-defense schemes. He notes that he believes these schemes are already being implemented and that the Consular Agent in Mansurah should have been reassured by now. He requests that the First Secretary reply to the British Consul on his behalf and update him on the specific actions taken, as he is currently uninformed on the matter.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official internal communication from the General Headquarters (G.H.Q.) of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force (E.E.F.) during the British occupation of Egypt. Dated May 1921, it reflects the administrative and security concerns of the British military authorities regarding civil unrest and the organization of local self-defense measures in provincial towns like Mansurah. The document highlights the hierarchical communication between the military command and the diplomatic Residency in Cairo, illustrating the intersection of military oversight and consular administration in post-WWI Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
BRITISH CONSULATE
CAIRO
23rd May 1921.

Sir,

I have the honour to refer to an enquiry from the British Consular Agent at Mansourah which I first passed on to the Residency but I have now referred to you.
He writes "In view of the unrest at present prevalent in the country and especially in regard to recent events at Tantah I should esteem it a favour if you would kindly inform me what precautions are going to be taken for the safety of the British Subjects in my Province in the event of dangerous riots and demonstrations."

I do not know if there is anything to tell him, but I pass on his enquiry as a matter of form.

I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient Servant,
(sd) W.B. HEARD
ACTING CONSUL.

To
General Sir W. Congreve,
General Officer Commanding,
Egypt,
Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official letter from the British Consulate in Cairo, dated May 23, 1921, addressed to General Sir W. Congreve. The Acting Consul, W.B. Heard, is forwarding an inquiry from the British Consular Agent in Mansourah. The agent is concerned about the current civil unrest in Egypt, specifically referencing recent events in Tanta, and is requesting information regarding what security measures the British military authorities intend to implement to protect British subjects in the province should dangerous riots or demonstrations occur. Heard notes that he is passing this request along as a formal administrative procedure.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document reflects the tense political climate in Egypt during the early 1920s, a period marked by the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 and ongoing nationalist agitation against the British Protectorate. The correspondence highlights the anxiety of British consular officials stationed in provincial cities like Mansourah regarding the safety of British nationals in the face of widespread civil unrest and anti-colonial demonstrations, particularly in the Nile Delta region (Tanta). It illustrates the administrative communication between the British civil consular service and the British military command (General Officer Commanding) responsible for maintaining order during the transition toward the 1922 declaration of Egyptian independence.

Mr. Furness.

Captain Heard called to see me this morning and made certain suggestions with regard to emergency defence schemes for the various consulates in the country which could be put into operation pending the arrival of British Troops. He suggested for the Consulate with him and discuss its vulnerability and how best it could be defended by the staff in case of a sudden attack by a mob. The Consulate is on the street and the lower windows are only protected by wooden shutters.

As regards the other Consulates and Consular Agencies in the country he suggested that each should be given a stand of arms and a supply of ammunition which would be under the sole control of the Consulate and used solely for the defence of Consular buildings and of such British Nationals as had taken refuge there in in time of stress. He had in mind particularly the case of the small British Consular agencies at Mansourah and Zagazig which would in time of riot become the assembly point of the small British Colonies in those two towns.

Captain Heard's suggestions with regard to the supply of arms to the Yonmis has obvious points in its favour. I do not however know whether the various Foreign Consuls in this country are allowed to keep arsenals for emergencies. If they are not, action on our part on the lines suggested by Captain Heard / might

The text details security concerns for British Consulates in Egypt during potential civil unrest. Captain Heard proposes that Consulates be equipped with arms and ammunition for self-defense and as a refuge for British nationals, specifically highlighting the vulnerability of the Mansourah and Zagazig agencies. The author expresses caution regarding the diplomatic implications of providing arms to foreign consulates.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1921 diplomatic memorandum from the British administration in Egypt during a period of significant political instability and nationalist agitation following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It reflects the British colonial anxiety regarding the safety of their consular staff and expatriate communities in provincial towns like Mansourah and Zagazig. The text highlights the logistical and diplomatic dilemmas faced by British officials in balancing the need for security against the potential international repercussions of arming consular outposts.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Sir,
I am directed by the High Commissioner to inform you that H.M. Acting Consul in Cairo has recently raised the question with the Residency of the safety of the various Consulates and Consular Agencies throughout the country in the event of their being attacked in time of riot. Captain Heard suggested that each Consulate should be given a stand of arms and a supply of ammunition which would be under the sole control of the Consulate and used solely for the defence of Consular buildings and of such British Nationals as had taken refuge therein in time of stress. He had in mind particularly the case of the small British Consular Agencies at Mansourah and Zagazig which would in time of riot become the assembly point of the small British colonies in those two towns.
His Excellency would be grateful if you would furnish him in due course with your views on Captain Heard's suggestions on the subject with the General Headquarters of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force.
I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient servant, H.M. Consul-General, Alexandria.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter from the British Residency in Cairo to the Consul-General in Alexandria, dated May 30, 1921. It discusses a security proposal made by Captain Heard regarding the protection of British Consular Agencies in Egypt. The proposal suggests arming these agencies with weapons and ammunition to defend British nationals during potential civil unrest or riots, specifically highlighting the vulnerability of small agencies in Mansourah and Zagazig. The Residency requests the Consul-General's professional opinion on this matter, in consultation with the General Headquarters of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document reflects the volatile political climate in Egypt during the early 1920s, following the 1919 Revolution and the lead-up to the Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence in 1922. The British administration, represented by the Residency in Cairo, was actively concerned with the security of its diplomatic outposts and the safety of British subjects residing in provincial towns. The request for arms and ammunition for Consular Agencies underscores the British perception of the Egyptian nationalist movement as a direct threat to their personnel and the necessity of maintaining a militarized defensive posture within diplomatic facilities.

ai_content.transcribed_text: H.B.M's Consul, British Consulate, Cairo. 5th June 1921. Sir, I have the honour to refer you to a letter recently received from the Rev. Allan Moore of the Holiness Movement Mission, Assiut, a copy of which has been passed to this Department for necessary action. I should be grateful if this gentleman could be informed that if he thinks any danger is threatening, either to him or his fellow missionaries, he should at once go to the Mudir and ask him to make the necessary arrangements for protection. It is true that there is no English Inspector belonging to this Ministry attached to Assiut Province at the present time, but there are two Egyptian Inspectors who are now carrying out the duties formerly undertaken by British Inspectors. I have spoken to Major Gayer-Anderson, the Acting Chief Inspector, and he is arranging for one of these Egyptian Inspectors to see Mr. Moore on his next visit to Assiut, which will take place shortly, and he will be prepared to advise Mr. Moore. I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient servant, (Signed) C. F. RYDER, for DIRECTOR GENERAL.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official letter from the British Consulate in Cairo dated June 5, 1921. It addresses a concern raised by Reverend Allan Moore of the Holiness Movement Mission in Assiut regarding his safety. The author advises Mr. Moore to contact the local Mudir (provincial governor) for protection if he feels threatened. It clarifies that while there are no British inspectors currently in Assiut, Egyptian inspectors are performing those duties, and Major Gayer-Anderson has been consulted to ensure one of them visits Mr. Moore to provide guidance.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence from the British colonial administration in Egypt during the post-WWI period. It reflects the transition of administrative responsibilities from British to Egyptian officials, as noted by the replacement of British inspectors with Egyptian ones in the Assiut province. From: The General Officer Commanding, EGYPTIAN EXPEDITIONARY FORCE.
To: His Excellency, THE HIGH COMMISSIONER FOR EGYPT, THE RESIDENCY, RAMLEH, ALEXANDRIA.
General Headquarters, Cairo, 3rd August, 1921.
Your Excellency,
I have the honour to inform you that a proposal has been put forward to form a Civil Guard from amongst the employees of the Eastern Telegraph Company at SUEZ.
2. There are about 40 men willing to volunteer for this Guard all of whom are British subjects.
The role of the Guard would be for the defence of the Eastern Telegraph Company buildings in the event of emergency when required by the Military authorities.
3. I consider that such a Force might be of great assistance in an emergency, and should be glad to know whether you approve of its formation.
If you approve the proposal I will proceed with the question of the provision and storage of arms and ammunition, and will draw up rules for the guidance of this Guard.
[Signature: E.H.H. Allenby]

It proposes the creation of a 'Civil Guard' composed of approximately 40 British employees of the Eastern Telegraph Company in Suez. The purpose of this guard is to defend company infrastructure during emergencies. The General requests the High Commissioner's approval to proceed with arming and regulating this volunteer force.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document reflects the security concerns of the British administration in Egypt during the post-WWI period, specifically regarding the protection of critical communications infrastructure. The Eastern Telegraph Company was a vital link in the British Imperial communications network. The proposal to arm British civilian employees as a 'Civil Guard' highlights the reliance on private British subjects to maintain order and protect strategic assets amidst the volatile political climate of 1921 Egypt, following the 1919 revolution and the ongoing negotiations for Egyptian independence.

Adviser, Ministry of the Interior.

I am directed by the Acting High Commissioner to transmit to you herewith a copy of a letter from the G.O.C. Egypt on the subject of a proposal to form a Civil Guard from amongst the employees of the Eastern Telegraph Company at Suez.

In conversation on the subject of this proposal General Congreve pointed out that the telegraph station is a vital centre in our line of communication, that there are precedents for the proposal in the Abu Zabal wireless station near Cairo and the Civilian Rifle Club at Alexandria both of which have armed civilian guards. Mr. Scott is inclined to agree with this view and subject to any observations /you

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Sir,
It has now become quite evident that some Egyptian persons have decided to shoot down the English members of the staff who work at Bulak. Four of them have already suffered, one of whom is dead, and the others who have not yet been shot at are disheartened and cannot do their work properly.
Nothing appears to have been done to compensate those already struck down and the remainder feel that if it should be their turn next, again nothing will be done; and if they are killed their widows will only get the usual one-third of the pension - even if that.
We therefore beg you will, before you go on leave this month, see the High Commissioner - who is the only person to whom we can appeal - and suggest that British subjects (including those who have already been shot) shall be at once given the following compensation:-
I. If slightly wounded: FIVE YEARS PAY
II. If crippled or killed: FIFTEEN YEARS PAY
This should not be left to the Egyptian Government to decide but should be insisted upon by the High Commissioner, the money being so collected as only to affect the pockets of Egyptian Subjects.
If this could be done the Staff here would work cheerfully, knowing that provision had been made for their families and future.
No word of regret has reached us up to the present from the Ministers and we feel that these cases of assassination may continue until we are all gone and that in this way Egypt will avoid paying any compensation to get rid of us; but, on the other hand, if the High Commissioner will insist on the above compensation being paid at once in each case it will immediately put a stop to these attacks.

It details a series of targeted shootings against English employees, noting that one has died and others are demoralized. The authors request that the High Commissioner intervene to secure specific compensation packages (five years' pay for injuries, fifteen years' pay for death) for British subjects, arguing that the Egyptian government is indifferent and that financial pressure on Egyptian subjects is the only way to stop the violence.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal petition from British staff members of the Egyptian State Railways, dated March 1922, addressed to Sir Blakeney. It reflects the volatile political climate in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution and the lead-up to the Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence in 1922. The staff express deep insecurity due to a campaign of assassinations targeting British officials and employees. The document highlights the colonial administration's struggle to maintain order and the staff's demand for the British High Commissioner to bypass the Egyptian government to enforce punitive financial compensation, illustrating the strained relationship between the British colonial apparatus and the Egyptian nationalist movement during this transition period.

TELEGRAM.
To HIGH COMMISSIONER FOR EGYPT, Cairo.
FOREIGN OFFICE.
No. 209.
Dated: 16.8.22.
Received: 16.8.22. 9.50pm.
Your telegram 280.
It seems clear that Englishmen are being shot at or assassinated simply because they are English and incidents cannot fail to greatly increase the uneasiness of British officials of Egypt whose faith in the Prime Minister's willingness and ability to safeguard their position will not be strengthened by the failure of the Government to prevent the perpetration of these political crimes.
In light of the warning conveyed in your note to the Prime Minister of July 20th such an incident cannot be allowed to pass with impunity. On the contrary, the cowardly assault on Brown calls for drastic action on the part of His Majesty's Government to protect the interests of British officials whose lives are in constant and increasing peril through their connection with the Egyptian Government. I should be glad to learn your views as to the matter. In my immediately following telegram I make a definite suggestion.

It addresses the assassination and shooting of British officials in Egypt, expressing deep concern that these acts are targeted specifically at British nationals. The Foreign Office notes that the Egyptian government's failure to prevent these crimes undermines the confidence of British officials in the Egyptian Prime Minister's ability to protect them. It references a previous warning issued on July 20th and demands 'drastic action' following a specific assault on an individual named Brown, signaling a shift toward a more assertive British policy in the face of political violence.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1922 diplomatic cable from the British Foreign Office to the High Commissioner for Egypt during the volatile period following the Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence (1922). The text reflects the intense pressure exerted by the British government on the Egyptian administration to protect British officials serving in the Egyptian civil service. The mention of 'Brown' likely refers to a specific victim of the anti-colonial violence that characterized the period, which the British used as a pretext to maintain influence and security control over the newly nominally independent Egyptian state.

Sarwat Pasha does not, perhaps, realise the full force of the public opinion in England which is roused by these outrages, and there is no doubt that H.M.G. will take drastic measures if they continue. I suppose the P.M. still does not realise that these crimes are the thing in Egypt which at present interests England and Europe and that their continuance jeopardises the whole future of the country: otherwise he would be more active, especially in mobilising public opinion against them. These outrages are designed to have the indirect effects of driving British officials out of Egypt, upsetting the Government, and making friendly relations between the two countries impossible. I think we should if possible avoid playing our adversaries' game.
Counter-measures should in my opinion be primarily directed towards stopping the outrages. We should attack the criminals and those who encourage them, endeavour to mobilise Egyptian opinion against them, and to protect and reassure the British Colony.
Besides improvement of police precautions, action already taken has been
(1) Formation of political crimes bureau, with powers under martial law, which is actively at work revising old inquiries, initiating new ones, and rounding up possible perpetrators of this sort of crime. I am satisfied with work it has done so far. Arrests under martial law of prominent agitators.

PRÉSIDENCE DU CONSEIL DES MINISTRES.

Bulkeley - le Caire, le 23 Août 1922

Excellence,

Je tiens à réitérer par la présente l'expression des plus vifs et plus sincères regrets du Gouvernement Egyptien que j'ai eu l'occasion d'exprimer dans ma conversation avec Votre Excellence à la suite de l'attentat commis sur la personne de Mr. Brown et de sa famille.

En transmettant ces regrets à Votre Excellence, je crois pouvoir affirmer que je suis le fidèle interprète tant des sentiments du Gouvernement Egyptien que de ceux de toutes les classes du peuple Egyptien.

Cet odieux attentat a d'autant plus provoqué l'indignation du Gouvernement et du peuple Egyptiens qu'il a atteint des femmes et des enfants.

L'enquête au sujet de ce crime se poursuit avec un zèle et une vigilance extrêmes sous le contrôle du nouveau Service dont j'ai annoncé la création à Votre Excellence par ma lettre du 23 juillet dernier.

Il est à espérer que les recherches aboutiront à la découverte des auteurs de l'attentat et qu'en nous éclairant sur les circonstances du crime, elles nous permettraient de nous prononcer avec certitude sur la nature de cet attentat.

Il ne me paraît que juste de signaler à Votre Excellence que la Presse Anglaise, en énumérant et en commentant les crimes

Son Excellence
Le Haut-Commissaire
du Gouvernement Britannique.
ai_content.english_translation:
PRESIDENCY OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS.

Bulkeley - Cairo, August 23, 1922

Excellency,

I wish to reiterate by this letter the expression of the deepest and most sincere regrets of the Egyptian Government that I had the opportunity to express in my conversation with Your Excellency following the attack committed against the person of Mr. Brown and his family.

In conveying these regrets to Your Excellency, I believe I can affirm that I am the faithful interpreter of the sentiments of the Egyptian Government as well as those of all classes of the Egyptian people.

This heinous attack has provoked all the more indignation from the Egyptian Government and people because it targeted women and children.

The investigation into this crime is being pursued with extreme zeal and vigilance under the control of the new Service whose creation I announced to Your Excellency in my letter of July 23 last.

It is to be hoped that the searches will lead to the discovery of the perpetrators of the attack and that, by shedding light on the circumstances of the crime, they will allow us to pronounce with certainty on the nature of this attack.

It seems only fair to me to point out to Your Excellency that the English Press, in enumerating and commenting on the crimes

His Excellency
The High Commissioner
of the British Government.

The letter highlights the Egyptian government's commitment to investigating the incident through a newly established security service, reflecting the tense political climate in Egypt during the transition toward nominal independence (1922) and the ongoing British occupation. The mention of the 'English Press' suggests a concern for international perception and the pressure exerted by British media on the Egyptian administration.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Department of Public Security, Special Section, War Office, Cairo, 26th/8/1922. Personal & Confidential. Dear Major Tweedie, your letter to Bennett, the position is: 1. Attacks on Sadr el Din: 2 persons identified, one in each case of assault, but it is premature as yet to say anything. Investigating this, important information has been tapped. 2. Murder of Brown - Ingram is very hopeful that they have got four of the gang; the clues are good, but not yet sufficient evidence for a court; a fifth person believed to be the instigator has also been traced. If the case works out along present lines it will also be established that it was not a political murder but due to a private grudge. Three of the four are members of a provincial murder gang brought up to Cairo for the crime. Capper asked me to write the above. Yours, Wills.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a personal and confidential letter from the Department of Public Security in Cairo, dated August 26, 1922, addressed to Major Tweedie. It provides updates on two ongoing investigations: the assault on Sadr el Din, where two suspects have been identified, and the murder of Brown, where four members of a gang have been apprehended and a fifth, the alleged instigator, has been traced. The letter notes that the murder of Brown appears to be motivated by a private grudge rather than political reasons, and that the suspects are part of a provincial gang brought to Cairo.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of internal intelligence correspondence from the British-administered Egyptian War Office during the volatile period following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution and the 1922 declaration of independence. It highlights the administrative focus on maintaining public security through the monitoring of criminal gangs and political violence. The distinction made between 'political murder' and 'private grudge' is significant, as British authorities frequently sought to categorize anti-colonial violence as common criminality to delegitimize the nationalist movement.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
TELEGRAM.
To FOREIGN OFFICE.
COMMISSIONER FOR EGYPT Cairo.
29 AUG 1922
No. 306.
Confidential.
My telegram No. 362.
The newly constituted bureau for the investigation of political crime has furnished me with the following information, which I consider hopeful, though it is premature at present to pronounce any opinion.
Among persons now under arrest Bedreddin Bey has identified the two who attacked him in 1920 and 1921 respectively, and the investigation of their cases has revealed important clues which are being followed up in connexion with other cases.
It is thought that four of the five persons who attacked Mr. T. Brown and his family have been apprehended. Three are stated to belong to a provincial murder gang and are believed to have been hired for the crime. A fifth person believed to be the instigator has been traced.
The evidence in this case is considered promising but not yet sufficient for prosecution before a Court: it indicates that the motive for the crime was a private grudge.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a confidential telegram sent from the High Commissioner for Egypt in Cairo to the Foreign Office in London, dated August 29, 1922. It provides an update on the progress of a newly formed bureau tasked with investigating political crimes. The document notes that Bedreddin Bey has identified his attackers from 1920 and 1921, leading to further leads. It also reports that four out of five suspects involved in an attack on Mr. T. Brown and his family have been apprehended, with the fifth (the instigator) identified. The telegram concludes that while the evidence is promising, it is not yet sufficient for a court prosecution, noting that the motive for the Brown attack appears to be a private grudge rather than political.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential diplomatic cable from the British High Commissioner in Egypt to the Foreign Office, reflecting the volatile security situation in Egypt during the early 1920s. Following the 1919 Revolution and the subsequent declaration of Egyptian independence in 1922, the British administration remained deeply concerned with the safety of British subjects and officials. The establishment of a 'bureau for the investigation of political crime' highlights the British effort to maintain order and suppress anti-colonial violence through intelligence-led policing. The mention of 'provincial murder gangs' and the distinction between political and private motives underscores the complex intersection of nationalist unrest and criminal activity during the transition period of the British Protectorate's end.

138, City Road,
Birmingham.
August 30th, 1922.

Sir,
My son Mr. Trevor Trought, B.A., Cantab, until recently, if not still, a Captain in 4 Ry. West Kent Reg., occupies the post of Plant Breeder to the Egyptian Government. Mr. Brown of the Horticultural Section of the same department of the Egyptian Government has recently been the victim of an attempted assassination within a quarter of a mile of my son's home (Maison Amato, Giza, Egypt). The attempted murder took place on the road which my son follows daily on his way to the Laboratories. My son was at the time in the Laboratories at Giza. In view of this outrage I apply on my son's behalf to the British Government to take steps for the safeguarding of my son's life and those of his wife and son, who are British subjects.

I have the honour, etc.,
(signed) J.W. Trought,
B.A., Birmingham.
Member of the Magistrates Association (Council and Sub Committee),
Member of the Cinema Commission Education Sub etc.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter written by J.W. Trought from Birmingham to an official body (likely the British Foreign Office), dated August 30, 1922. The author expresses grave concern for the safety of his son, Trevor Trought, a British subject and Plant Breeder for the Egyptian Government, following an attempted assassination of a colleague, Mr. Brown, near their residence in Giza, Egypt. The author formally requests that the British Government intervene to ensure the protection of his son and his son's family.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of diplomatic correspondence from the early 1920s, a period of significant political instability in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution and the lead-up to the Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence in 1922. The letter highlights the precarious position of British expatriates and civil servants working for the Egyptian government during this volatile transition period. It serves as a primary source for understanding the security concerns of British colonial officials and their families residing in Egypt, specifically in the Giza area, amidst a climate of anti-colonial violence and political unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
THE RESIDENCY
RAMLEH
September 20th, 1922.

My Lord,

With reference to my despatch No. 594 of July 24th, 1922, I have the honour to report that the Prime Minister informs me that he has now received from all the Provincial Councils in Egypt resolutions condemning the assassination of British subjects.

These resolutions are being published in the Local press as and when they are received.

I have the honour to be,
My Lord,
Your Lordship's most obedient, humble servant,

HIGH COMMISSIONER.

The Most Honourable
The Marquess Curzon of Kedleston,
K.G., G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E., etc., etc., etc.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official diplomatic communication from the British High Commissioner in Egypt to the British Foreign Secretary, Lord Curzon. It confirms that the Egyptian Prime Minister has successfully collected and is publishing formal condemnations from all Egyptian Provincial Councils regarding the recent assassinations of British nationals in the country.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal despatch sent from the British Residency in Ramleh, Egypt, to the British Foreign Office in London during the period of the British Protectorate in Egypt. It reflects the tense political climate of 1922, characterized by the rise of Egyptian nationalism and frequent attacks on British officials and residents. The High Commissioner is reporting to Lord Curzon that the Egyptian government, under British pressure, has secured and publicized formal condemnations of these violent acts from local administrative bodies to demonstrate a semblance of order and cooperation with the British authorities.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
PRESIDENCE DU CONSEIL DES MINISTRES. 
Bulkeley le Caire, le 20 Septembre 1922. 
Excellence, 
Dans ma dernière lettre du 24 août 1922 adressée à Votre Excellence, je m'étais fait l'interprète de l'indignation générale que les attentats contre les sujets Britanniques avaient provoquée dans le pays. 
Je viens maintenant d'en recevoir la confirmation : tous les Conseils Provinciaux, organes représentatifs des Moudiriehs, les Municipalités des villes ainsi que les notabilités du commerce du Caire et d'Alexandrie m'ont communiqué des résolutions dont j'ai cru devoir faire part à Votre Excellence. Tous regrettent et réprouvent ces attentats, et en appellent à la nation pour venir en aide aux Autorités en vue de découvrir leurs auteurs. 
En me faisant l'écho de ce sentiment unanime, je suis persuadé que Votre Excellence y verra une attestation nouvelle de l'esprit loyal et paisible qui anime le peuple Egyptien à l'égard de ses hôtes Etrangers. 
Veuillez agréer, Excellence, l'assurance de ma très haute considération. 
Le Président du Conseil des Ministres, 
Sarwat 
Son Excellence 
le Haut-Commissaire 
du Gouvernement Britannique.
ai_content.english_translation:
PRESIDENCY OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS. 
Bulkeley, Cairo, September 20, 1922. 
Excellency, 
In my last letter of August 24, 1922, addressed to Your Excellency, I acted as the interpreter of the general indignation that the attacks against British subjects had provoked in the country. 
I have now received confirmation of this: all the Provincial Councils, representative bodies of the Moudiriehs, the Municipalities of the cities as well as the notables of the commerce of Cairo and Alexandria have communicated to me resolutions which I felt I should share with Your Excellency. All regret and condemn these attacks, and appeal to the nation to come to the aid of the Authorities with a view to discovering their authors. 
In echoing this unanimous sentiment, I am convinced that Your Excellency will see in it a new attestation of the loyal and peaceful spirit that animates the Egyptian people towards their Foreign guests. 
Please accept, Excellency, the assurance of my very high consideration. 
The President of the Council of Ministers, 
Sarwat 
To His Excellency 
the High Commissioner 
of the British Government.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official letter from Abdel Khalek Sarwat Pasha, the Prime Minister of Egypt, to the British High Commissioner in Egypt (likely Sir Edmund Allenby). Written in September 1922, shortly after the formal declaration of Egyptian independence (February 1922), the letter addresses the political instability and violence directed against British nationals in Egypt. Sarwat Pasha seeks to demonstrate the Egyptian government's cooperation and desire for order by citing resolutions from provincial councils and municipal bodies that condemn these attacks. The document serves as a diplomatic effort to maintain the fragile Anglo-Egyptian relationship during the transition period following the end of the British Protectorate.

ai_content.english_translation:
Excellency,
I have the honor to acknowledge receipt of the letter, dated September 20, by which Your Excellency has kindly communicated to me the resolutions taken by all the Provincial Councils, as well as by the municipalities of the cities and the notables of Cairo and Alexandria, disapproving of the attacks committed against British subjects.
I thank Your Excellency for having shared with me these expressions of regret and indignation. I do not doubt the friendly and peaceful sentiments harbored by the Egyptian people towards their foreign guests; and I like to believe that the energetic measures taken by the Egyptian Government, supported by the public opinion of the country, will have put an end to these deplorable attacks.
Please accept, Excellency, the assurance of my high consideration.
HIGH COMMISSIONER
His Excellency Abdel Khalik Sarwat Pasha, President of the Council of Ministers.
September 24, 1922.
THE RESIDENCY, EGYPT

To His Excellency F. M. Viscount Allenby, G.C.B., G.C.M.G., H. M.'s High Commissioner, The Residency, Ramleh.

Excellency,

I have the honour to forward herewith copy of letter received from the Commandant of the Cairo City Police in regard to the importation of automatic pistols by this Chamber for distribution to members of the British Community in Cairo.

I am directed by my Committee to thank you for your kind offer to ensure every facility to the Chamber, and to ask Your Excellency to be good enough to inform me of the procedure to be followed in order to obtain the necessary permission for the importation of these arms.

I have the honour to be, Your Excellency's obedient servant, [Signature: J. H. B.]

[Handwritten note at top]: Mr. Murray, Ref. attached Fuad Pasha's enclosed letter - do you recollect him? I should have thought that the normal procedure on a application to the Police, if arms are required on a large scale, would be a demand to be filed. H. M. Embassy's intervention might shed light in difficulty. I am doubtful whether there would be a demand to be filed. H. M. Embassy might ask Chamber of Commerce before perhaps. [Signed] J. H. B.

A handwritten marginal note discusses the potential involvement of Fuad Pasha and the appropriate administrative channels for such a request.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
THE RESIDENCY.
I regret to have to inform you that several of the prisoners at present in the European lock-up in connection with the murders of British subjects have attempted to commit suicide. These men are all degenerates and have been accustomed to taking drugs and otherwise living viciously. I have little doubt that their detention in prison and the prevention of their usual habits is to a large extent the cause of these attempts, for in no respect have they been treated badly in prison and, on the other hand, they have received privileges not given to ordinary prisoners.
I am now arranging that these prisoners should not be kept in separate cells, but that there should be two in every cell and I am making every effort to arrange for proper exercise.
I enclose a letter from Russell Pasha which, more or less, explains the situation for your information.
I should be obliged if you would return to me this letter at your convenience.
R. S. Mounsey
DIRECTOR-GENERAL.
1 encl.
N. Kerr.
N. Mounsey - N. Russell
I think this is rather to be had confinement than can.
differs as the desirability of solitary
RF 23/x
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official communication from the Director-General (R. S. Mounsey) at The Residency in Egypt, dated October 21, 1922. It reports that several prisoners held in the European lock-up for the murder of British subjects have attempted suicide. The author attributes this to the withdrawal of drugs and the cessation of 'vicious' habits rather than mistreatment, noting that they have actually received special privileges. He is adjusting their confinement to house them in pairs rather than solitary cells to prevent further attempts. The document includes a handwritten note by N. Kerr regarding the desirability of solitary confinement versus the current arrangement.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential administrative record from the British Residency in Egypt during the post-WWI period (1922), a time of significant political unrest and anti-colonial activity in Egypt. It highlights the British colonial administration's management of high-profile prisoners accused of murdering British subjects. The text provides insight into the intersection of colonial security, prison management, and the medicalized view of 'degeneracy' and drug addiction used to characterize political prisoners of the era. The mention of 'Russell Pasha' refers to Thomas Wentworth Russell, the influential British commandant of the Cairo City Police, who played a central role in Egyptian internal security and anti-narcotics efforts.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. November 20th, 1922. SOME TIME AGO THE BRITISH CHAMBER OF COMMERCE HERE ASKED US TO HELP THEM TO IMPORT A CERTAIN NUMBER OF AUTOMATIC PISTOLS, FOR DISTRIBUTION TO MEMBERS OF THE BRITISH COMMUNITY, FOR PURPOSES OF SELF-DEFENCE. The request to bypass standard customs procedures by addressing the shipment to the High Commissioner underscores the extraterritorial influence and administrative shortcuts utilized by British officials during the transition to the Fuad I monarchy.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
FOREIGN OFFICE
189.445
27.12.22. 10.30 p.m.
Mr. Bondy Johnson, professor at the Law School was returning at 1.30 p.m. today from the school on a bicycle when he was shot at and killed on the main road between Giza Austria and the Pont des Anglais. The assailants are stated to have been three offenders who also shot at but missed another British official who passed on a motor bicycle immediately afterwards. They then escaped down a side street and across some land where it is alleged that they entered a motor car and drove off.
I want a number of my staff (being armed) laid up with a cold) to see the Prime Minister and to make the following communication:
(1) That Martial Law would not be abolished so long as these attacks continue.
(2) That an indemnity, fixed by myself, should be immediately paid to the widow.
(3) That British cavalry would again patrol the streets.
(4) That greater rigour must be shown in suppressing demonstrations.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a diplomatic cable from the British Foreign Office regarding the assassination of Mr. Bondy Johnson, a professor at the Law School in Egypt. It details the circumstances of his death on December 27, 1922, while cycling between Giza and the Pont des Anglais. The text outlines the British administration's proposed retaliatory measures, including the continuation of Martial Law, the imposition of an indemnity for the victim's widow, the deployment of British cavalry for street patrols, and a crackdown on public demonstrations.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a high-level diplomatic cable from the British Foreign Office in Cairo, dated December 1922, during the period of the British Protectorate in Egypt. It records the assassination of a British academic, Mr. Bondy Johnson, which served as a flashpoint for British authorities to demand stricter security measures and the maintenance of Martial Law. The handwritten annotations on the attached slip reflect internal administrative deliberations between officials (Keown, Taylor, and Petrie) regarding the handling of the investigation and the political response to the incident, illustrating the tense atmosphere of the Egyptian nationalist movement against British colonial presence.
