ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. December 30th, 1922. British Chamber of Commerce of Egypt. Colonel A. F. Ryder, C.B.E. You are hereby charged by me to undertake the investigation of political crimes and attacks on Europeans, with a view to the detection of the criminals and their prosecution before a Military Court. You have my full authority to take or steps as you may consider necessary for the investigation and prosecution of all these cases. You should arrange that all information in regard to any crimes of this nature is immediately communicated to you and you should issue the necessary instructions as to how the investigation is to be carried out in every case. You should select for yourself such staff as you consider you require and you are authorised to call upon any official or Department at any time for any assistance you require. You are further authorised to draw upon the Finan fund for any sum of money needed. You should keep His Excellency the Prime Minister informed in regard to your arrangements for giving effect to these instructions.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official directive issued from The Residency in Cairo on December 30, 1922, addressed to Colonel A. F. Ryder. It grants him the authority to investigate political crimes and attacks against Europeans in Egypt, with the power to prosecute suspects before a Military Court. He is given broad administrative powers to select his own staff, request assistance from any government department, and access the 'Finan fund' (likely a reference to a secret or special service fund) for financial needs, while maintaining communication with the Prime Minister regarding his progress.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal administrative directive issued during the British occupation of Egypt, shortly after the declaration of Egyptian independence in 1922. It reflects the continued British influence over internal security and the legal system, specifically the use of Military Courts to handle political crimes and attacks on foreign nationals. The document highlights the 'Residency' system, where the British High Commissioner exercised significant control over Egyptian governance, and illustrates the mechanisms used to suppress political unrest during a period of intense nationalist agitation.

The text includes reports from Reuters and Havas agencies, noting that the British community was demanding better protection and the right to arm themselves, while criticizing the official handling of previous incidents, such as the Alexandria riots.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a collection of 'Strictly Confidential' diplomatic cables from the British Residency in Cairo, dated January 1923. The text highlights the growing tension between the British expatriate community and the Egyptian authorities, as well as the British administration's concern over maintaining order. The document reflects the colonial anxiety of the period, where British residents felt increasingly vulnerable to nationalist unrest, leading to demands for self-defense measures and a more aggressive security posture by the British-controlled administration.

Headquarters,
British Troops in Egypt.

URGENT.

January 4th, 1923.

With reference to your letter No. CR.EGYPT.22082/Q of the 3rd instant, I am directed by the High Commissioner to express His Excellency's thanks for your assistance in the matter of issue of the arms in question.

I am to say that His Excellency concurs in the arrangement proposed for the issue of these weapons.

I am to request that you will be so good as to depute an officer to interview Mr. Rabino as soon as possible with a view to the settlement of details as to delivery etc. Mr. Rabino has been acquainted with His Excellency's views on the subject of the imposition of a fine in the event of loss, and the suggestion that holders of weapons should report their continued possession from time to time.

I am to enclose herewith a form of receipt which it is proposed to adopt.

First Secretary.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official communication from the Headquarters of the British Troops in Egypt, dated January 4, 1923. It acknowledges a previous letter regarding the distribution of arms. The High Commissioner approves the proposed plan for issuing these weapons. The recipient is requested to send an officer to meet with Mr. Rabino to finalize delivery details. Mr. Rabino has been informed of the High Commissioner's policy regarding fines for lost weapons and the requirement for holders to periodically report that they still possess them. A draft receipt form is attached for review.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official administrative communication from the British military authorities in Egypt during the period of the British Protectorate (shortly after the Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence in 1922, but while British military presence remained significant). It concerns the controlled distribution of weaponry, likely to local officials or specific personnel, and highlights the British administration's focus on accountability, inventory control, and the imposition of punitive measures for the loss of military-grade equipment. The mention of the 'High Commissioner' refers to the British representative in Egypt, who held significant executive power during this transitional political era.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
RESOLUTIONS
PASSED AT THE PUBLIC MEETING OF THE BRITISH COMMUNITY IN EGYPT
HELD ON TUESDAY JANUARY 2nd, 1923 AT SHEPHEARDS HOTEL

1. That this meeting expresses its abhorrence of the assassination of Dr. Robson and charges the Chairman to express to Mrs. Robson its heartfelt sympathy with her in her terrible bereavement.

2. That this meeting consisting of the British official and unofficial Community in Egypt views with indignation and abhorrence the unpunished but systematic murdering of British subjects.

3. That the strongest representation on the subject should be made to H.B.M.'s High Commissioner requesting him to use such measures as are in his power to assist the Egyptian Government to put an end to such crimes and to detect the criminals.

4. That this meeting resolves that a British Committee be formed for the purpose of organising the British Community with a view to taking such steps as may be necessary for the protection of the lives of British subjects in this country, and in particular to ensuring that the members of the British Community arm themselves for their mutual protection as a public duty, as has also been advised by H.B.M.'s Consul.

5. That this meeting is of opinion that the Public Security Department is inadequate and that the Police should be reinforced by a further and adequate European element.
ai_content.english_translation: The document contains five resolutions passed by the British Community in Egypt at Shepheards Hotel on January 2, 1923. The resolutions condemn the assassination of Dr. Robson, express sympathy to his widow, denounce the systematic murder of British subjects in Egypt, call upon the British High Commissioner to pressure the Egyptian government to stop these crimes, propose the formation of a British Committee to organize self-defense and arming of British citizens, and demand the reinforcement of the Egyptian Public Security Department with European personnel.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document records the formal resolutions of a public meeting held by the British expatriate community in Egypt on January 2, 1923, at the iconic Shepheards Hotel in Cairo. The meeting was convened in the wake of the assassination of Dr. Robson, reflecting the heightened political instability and anti-colonial sentiment in Egypt following the 1922 Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence. The resolutions highlight the deep anxiety among the British population regarding their safety, their lack of confidence in the Egyptian police force, and their desire to organize paramilitary-style self-defense measures under the guidance of British consular authorities, illustrating the tense atmosphere of the British presence in Egypt during the early interwar period.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
MINISTRY OF THE INTERIOR.
EUROPEAN DEPARTMENT.
BY THE DIRECTOR GENERAL
No. 3/52(4)
Cairo, 1st February 1923
Sir,
I have to acknowledge receipt of your letter No. B/16 of 29th January.
In regard to the first paragraph, as soon as you can let me know the exact description and quantity of pistols required and of ammunition for them, I will put forward a recommendation to the Residency that the cost should be borne in equal shares by the Egyptian and British Governments.
As to paragraph 2, I should prefer not to press, at present, the question of an allowance for practice ammunition, but to wait till the pistols and ammunition referred to in paragraph 1 have been ordered from England.
With reference to paragraph 4, the expense of an instructor does not appear to be very great, and I suggest that it would be preferable not to approach the Egyptian Government on so small a matter.
DIRECTOR GENERAL.
The President,
British Committee of Self-Defence,
Cairo Station.
Copy to the Residency.
[Handwritten note]: M. Ken. I feel that this British Committee of Self-Defence is many 450 miles away. I want this as a community matter. I am not sure if they want. Please ask. 3/2/23 [Signature]
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter from the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior (European Department) to the British Committee of Self-Defence in Cairo. It addresses the procurement of pistols and ammunition, suggesting that costs be split between the British and Egyptian governments. It advises delaying requests for practice ammunition until the initial order arrives from England and suggests handling the cost of an instructor internally rather than involving the Egyptian government. A handwritten marginal note expresses skepticism regarding the committee's distance and relevance to the local community.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative record from the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior, dated February 1923, during the period of the British Protectorate in Egypt. It reflects the bureaucratic coordination between British colonial authorities and local committees regarding security and armament. The correspondence highlights the delicate political balance of the era, specifically the attempt to share financial burdens between the British and Egyptian governments while managing the activities of British-aligned self-defence groups in Cairo. The handwritten annotation provides a rare glimpse into the internal administrative scrutiny applied to these requests, questioning the necessity and local integration of the British Committee of Self-Defence.

CONFIDENTIAL. P. 52 (4)
4th February 1928
Dear Grant,
With reference to the attached: Arrangements have been made for the arming of British subjects in Cairo, and a supply of .450 Service revolvers has been put at the disposal of the British Consul for issue on loan to British officials.
So far, no wish has been expressed for similar arrangements to be made in Alexandria: nor do I consider it desirable that any semi-official organisation should be granted them unless absolutely necessary, the Cairo arrangements being abnormal measures arising out of the series of political crimes which have been confined to the Cairo area.
I should be grateful if you would ascertain and inform me whether there is any general desire amongst British residents in Alexandria for official assistance in obtaining arms, bearing in mind that, for the moment, only .450 Service revolvers are available.
Yours sincerely,
Sgt. W. Kerr

Kaimat A.C. Grant Bey,
Commandant, Alexandria City Police,

The Chancery for information

CAIRO, 10th March 1925.

Messrs Webley and Scott Ltd.,

Birmingham.
Dear Sirs,
I beg to confirm my cable sent you to-day as follows:
'I have the following order for immediate shipment
Government Police Stores, Cairo: 500 .32 Automatic Pistols
M.P. model £2.16.9d minus 25%. Also rounds Ammunition
Automatic 19,000 .32; 1,000 .38. Also 2,000 .38. Telegraph when
delivery can be made'.
(Sent in Code).
The above order has nothing to do with the Government
Police Tender for which you have already sent patterns of
revolvers. These automatic pistols are required for
arming the English officials of the Egyptian Government,
and are most urgently required. It is hoped that you can
supply these pistols from stock and I trust that you have
duly cabled me when delivery is being made.
Please do not fail to send them by the first boat
either via Alexandria or Port Said and send the Bills of
Lading with Invoices in Triplicate to me at the above
address.
The ammunition will, of course, be included in the
shipment.
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) P.C. Palmer.

It confirms a telegraphic order for 500 .32 caliber automatic pistols and associated ammunition for the Egyptian Government's police stores. The author clarifies that this is a separate, urgent order for arming English officials, distinct from a previously discussed government tender for revolvers. It provides specific shipping instructions, requesting delivery via Alexandria or Port Said and the provision of triplicate documentation.

It highlights the reliance of the Egyptian government on British arms manufacturers (Webley and Scott) for the equipment of its police forces and the specific arming of British personnel serving within the Egyptian administration. PALIAMENTARY. [QUESTION]. 28th Feb. 1923.
EGYPT (ASSASSINATION OF BRITISH OFFICIALS).
3. Sir HENRY BRITTAIN asked the Under Secretary
of State for Foreign Affairs if he will state the
number of British officials and subjects who have been
killed in Egypt since 28th February, 1922, and not on
the British tax-payer?
Mr. MORELL: Since 28th February, 1922, seven
British subjects have been murdered in Egypt. In
addition to these, there have been attacks on the
lives of British subjects in Cairo resulting in the
death of two persons and the wounding of six others.
One attempt proved abortive. In no case have the
criminals been brought to justice. His Majesty's
Government will take every necessary step with
the Egyptian Government to ensure the responsibility
for maintaining law and order in Egypt will rest
with the Egyptian Government.
Captain Viscount CURZON: Does the figure
given include the latest outrages reported in
the Press?
Mr. MORELL: No, it does not include those.
I have not official information of them as yet.
Mr. HINDS: Has there any demand on the
Government the advisability of leaving Egypt to
the Egyptian?
Mr. HINDS: I am sorry that my question
was not clear. I meant the advisability of leaving Egypt to
the Egyptian Government.
ai_content.english_translation:
This document records a parliamentary exchange. It begins with a heading "PALIAMENTARY. [QUESTION]. 28th Feb. 1923." followed by the subject "EGYPT (ASSASSINATION OF BRITISH OFFICIALS)."
Question 3 is posed by Sir Henry Brittain to the Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, asking for the number of British officials and subjects killed in Egypt since 28th February 1922, and whether this cost falls on the British taxpayer.
Mr. Morell responds, stating that since 28th February 1922, seven British subjects have been murdered in Egypt. Additionally, there have been attacks on British subjects in Cairo, resulting in two deaths and six injuries. He notes that one attack was unsuccessful, and crucially, that none of the criminals responsible for these acts have been brought to justice. He concludes by stating that His Majesty's Government will work with the Egyptian Government to ensure that the responsibility for maintaining law and order in Egypt rests with the Egyptian Government.
Captain Viscount Curzon then asks if the figures provided include the most recent outrages reported in the press.
Mr. Morell replies that they do not, as he does not yet have official information on those incidents.
Mr. Hinds asks if there is any demand on the Government regarding the advisability of leaving Egypt to the Egyptian.
Mr. Hinds then clarifies his question, stating he meant the advisability of leaving Egypt to the Egyptian Government.
ai_content.historical_summary: This parliamentary record from 28th February 1923 details a series of questions and answers concerning the security situation for British subjects and officials in Egypt following the unilateral declaration of Egyptian independence by Britain in February 1922. Sir Henry Brittain initiates the inquiry, seeking statistics on British casualties and the financial implications. Mr. Morell, representing the Foreign Office, reveals that seven British subjects had been murdered and several others attacked in Cairo since February 1922, with no perpetrators brought to justice. This highlights the volatile political climate and the challenges to British authority and the safety of its nationals in post-independence Egypt. The exchange underscores the British government's commitment to working with the Egyptian government to restore law and order, while also revealing ongoing concerns about the effectiveness of Egyptian governance and the potential for further British withdrawal, as hinted by Mr. Hinds's question. The document serves as a primary source illustrating the complex and often violent transition of power in Egypt during the early 1920s.

ai_content.transcribed_text: My Lord, In my telegram No. 5 of 2nd January I had the honour to inform Your Lordship that, in view of the series of outrages against British subjects, I had directed that the carrying of arms by all male members of the British community would be a desirable measure. 2. In view of the original arrangement made by Lord Allenby and having regard to the probability that most of the revolvers will shortly be returned as unsuitable, the request for full payment of about one thousand seven hundred Egyptian pounds made by General Headquarters is in any case premature. The actual cost of any revolvers not returned to store would, of course, be

to the Army Council.

The letter argues that the Army's request for £1,700 in payment is premature, as the weapons are likely to be returned, and asserts that the cost should not be charged to the Foreign Office budget, as the protection of British citizens in Egypt is a military responsibility.

MEMORANDUM ON FIREARMS ISSUED TO CIVILIANS BY BRITISH CONSULATE, CAIRO.
APRIL 20TH 1923.
1. I consider that the issue of arms and ammunition should cease forthwith and those issued should be immediately withdrawn.
2. All British civilians have by now had time to procure by purchase through the Self Defense Committee automatic pistols of an approved type. If they have not done so it is presumably their own fault.
3. The longer the revolvers etc issued by the Consulate remain distributed the more impossible it will be to recall them as the persons holding them move from Cairo, go on leave, etc and it is quite out of the question for each one to be kept track of. Even now it will probably prove impossible to regain possession of more than about 90% of those issued.
4. The excessive price at which they are charged by the Army authorities, which is understood to be much more than their market value, also makes it desirable.
5. Losses have occurred, and with the passage of time will become more frequent, and it will be a very difficult task to obtain payment for the value of the articles.
6. The Consulate was given the task of issuing these firearms as an emergency measure and I do not consider that it should come to be considered a part of its normal functions either to continue in this role or to bear the responsibility to some undetermined and indefinite date for those already issued.
7. In conclusion, I consider that unless the firearms are immediately given up considerable and increasing financial loss will have to be faced for which I am unable to accept any responsibility.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official memorandum written by H.L. Mackie at the British Consulate in Cairo on April 20, 1923, regarding the policy of issuing firearms to British civilians. The author argues that the practice should be stopped immediately and existing weapons recalled. He cites several reasons: civilians have had sufficient time to purchase their own weapons through the Self Defense Committee; the transient nature of the civilian population makes tracking the weapons impossible; the high cost charged by the Army makes the current arrangement undesirable; and the Consulate should not be burdened with the administrative and financial responsibility of managing these weapons as a permanent function.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1923 administrative memorandum from the British Consulate in Cairo during the period of the British Protectorate in Egypt. It reflects the post-WWI security climate and the transition from emergency measures—where the Consulate provided arms to British subjects for self-defense—to a more normalized administrative stance. The document highlights the logistical difficulties of state-managed civilian armaments, the role of the 'Self Defense Committee' in the British expatriate community, and the friction between consular duties and military supply chains in colonial administration.

Minutes of a Meeting held at H.B.M. Consulate, Cairo on Friday, May 25th 1923, at 10.30 am.

ARMING OF BRITISH SUBJECTS.

Present: Mr H.L. Rabino, H.B.M. Consul.
Mr R.O. Rapp, H.B.M. Vice-Consul.
Mr A.W. Knowl Boyd, Director General, European Department, Min. of Interior.
Major R.G. Griffin, representing the British Committee for Self Defence.
Mr G.H. Patrick, of the Residency.
Mr G.W. Bennett, European Department, Min. of Interior.

MR. KNOWL BOYD explained that the object of the meeting was to discuss (1) the calling-in of Army revolvers issued on loan to British subjects through the Consulate and (2) the issue of 300 Automatic Pistols and ammunition which had been received, consigned to the Egypt Government on the order of the British Committee for Self-Defence. These automatic pistols and ammunition were now in store at Kasr el Nil Barracks, and he suggested that they should be issued against delivery of the Army Revolvers.

Major GRIFFIN objected to this, as his Committee had not been responsible for the issue of Army revolvers, while, on the other hand, the Automatic pistols were nearly all bespoke for individual orders.

It was agreed that the automatic pistols and ammunition at Kasr el Nil should be forthwith put at the disposal of the British Committee for Self Defence.

Mr RABINO stated that, apart from about 30 revolvers issued to the staff at ABOU ZABAL, and which might be transferred to Army account, there were about 100 to be called in.

It was decided that the Consulate would issue a circular calling for the return of all revolvers to the Consulate not later than 31st July next, and referring the holders to the British Committee for Self-Defence, which would be in a position to supply a certain number of weapons, against payment, out of the surplus of the 300 automatic pistols recently arrived, and out of their stock of weapons derived from Customs seizures.

The discussion focused on two main points: the recall of British Army revolvers previously loaned to civilians, and the distribution of 300 new automatic pistols that had arrived for the British Committee for Self-Defence. The committee decided to store the new weapons at Kasr el Nil barracks and facilitate an exchange, where civilians would return their army-issued revolvers in order to acquire the new automatic pistols. The Consulate agreed to issue a circular to all holders of army revolvers to return them by July 31, 1923.

Sir,
His Excellency
The High Commissioner,
The Residency, Cairo.

Um Bogma,
Sinai,
23rd August, 1924.

We have the honour to inform you that when the Governor of Sinai Province visited Um Bogma on the 19th June, the question of the supply of ammunition for 10 service pattern rifles was discussed and the Governor agreed to issue to the Company the necessary permit for us to import the ammunition required.

An application for this permit was forwarded to the Governor of Sinai on the 27th June, 1924, as per copy enclosed, and an acknowledgment of this application was received dated 23rd July, a copy of which is also enclosed.

This Company indented on its Head Office in Middlesbrough for
1000 rounds S.A. Ammunition, .303 ball - for rifle, short, magazine, Lee Enfield, Mark III, and
100 rounds Ammunition, .450, for pistol, Webley, Mark VI.

We have to-day received a cable from our Head Office which reads, in part, as follows :-
" Ammunition shipped Tawliwa 15th. Necessary " you apply His Majesty's High Commissioner " Cairo before can obtain delivery."

In view of the above cable, we have the honour to hereby make application to Your Excellency to grant us the necessary permit for the importation of the above mentioned ammunition.

For Your Excellency's information, there are at Abu Zenima 7 Britishers, of whom one is a lady, and 1 Italian; and at the Mines at Um Bogma there are 29 Britishers, of whom 7 are ladies and 5 are children; 2 Germans of whom 1 is a lady; 4 Spaniards; 1 Italian and 1 Greek.

As mentioned in our previous letter to the Governor of Sinai Province, the Company assumes full responsibility for the care and safe keeping of this ammunition.

We, have, etc. etc.
(sgd) ALEX. BOWIE,
Manager.
FOR THE SINAI MINING COMPANY, LTD.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SUBJECT :- Civil unrest.

From :- The Colonel on the Staff, General Staff, Commanding, British Troops in Egypt.
To :- H.E. The High Commissioner, The Residency, Ramleh.

Your Excellency,

With reference to the arrangements for the protection of British subjects which are now being considered in accordance with the terms of paragraph viii of the memorandum giving the records of a meeting held at these Headquarters dated 12th July, a copy of which has been forwarded to you, the question of providing rifles and ammunition has been raised.

2. It appears that few of the British civilians notably in isolated places are adequately armed and requests have already been received for a supply of rifles and ammunition, and as progress is made in defensive arrangements it is probable that further requests of a similar kind will be made.

3. In places where the British subject responsible for making defensive arrangements can give a reasonable assurance that rifles and ammunition will be adequately protected and maintained in good condition, I consider it desirable that rifles and ammunition should be provided, as any arrangements for defence will be very much strengthened.

4. The issue of rifles and ammunition may present certain difficulties and it is suggested that a similar procedure may be adopted as was approved by Your Excellency in your letter No. 8882/101 dated 4th January, 1923, for the issue of revolvers and ammunition.

5. It is also thought that for many reasons it would be desirable to issue rifles and ammunition only to places where a British Rifle Club could be formed, the president of which would accept the responsibility for their safe custody.

I have the honour to be,
Your Excellency's obedient servant,
Charles Gwynn
Colonel on the Staff, General Staff,
Commanding,
BRITISH TROOPS IN EGYPT.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official military memorandum from the Colonel on the Staff of the British Troops in Egypt to the British High Commissioner. It addresses the security of British civilians in Egypt amidst civil unrest. The author proposes a policy for arming British civilians, suggesting that rifles and ammunition be provided to those in isolated areas, provided they can ensure the weapons are stored securely. He recommends following a previous precedent set in 1923 regarding the issuance of revolvers and suggests that such arms should only be distributed to locations where a 'British Rifle Club' can be established to manage the custody of the weapons.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 'Very Secret' military memorandum dated August 26, 1924, originating from the Headquarters of the British Troops in Egypt. It reflects the volatile security environment in Egypt during the post-WWI period, specifically following the rise of the Wafd Party and the assassination of Sir Lee Stack later that year. The document highlights the British military's concern regarding the vulnerability of British expatriates and colonial officials living in isolated areas. By proposing the formation of 'British Rifle Clubs' to manage the distribution of arms, the document illustrates the British colonial administration's reliance on paramilitary self-defense measures to maintain order and protect its subjects during periods of heightened nationalist civil unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text: BRITISH CONSULATE, CAIRO. 27th November, 1924. Sir, I have the honour to report that I receive daily a considerable number of requests for the issue of firearms and ammunition from British subjects, particularly from those British subjects whose duties lead them into the Provinces or the native quarter of this city. Applicants invariably point out that they have tried to purchase revolvers without success since the sale of firearms without licence is prohibited. I have replied, so far to the various applicants, that measures will doubtless be taken to issue revolvers as was done before, should there be any reason to anticipate further attacks on Europeans. I consider it advisable, however, to bring these applications to your notice and to express my readiness to make arrangements for distribution of small firearms on loan to British subjects, should you consider it necessary. I have the honour to be, Sir, Your most obedient Servant, [Signature: Lomas] The First Secretary, The Residency, CAIRO. [Handwritten note at top]: I've explained the DOED arrangement by telephone to Mr. Lomas. We also spoken to Mr. Kid who will send him 12 match to sell as a start.

The Consul notes that the sale of firearms is currently prohibited and suggests that the Residency consider a loan program for small arms to British subjects as a precautionary measure against potential attacks on Europeans. A handwritten marginal note indicates a follow-up telephone arrangement involving a 'Mr. Lomas' and a 'Mr. Kid' regarding the supply of 12 'match' (likely a reference to matchlock or specific firearm type) to initiate the process.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document provides insight into the security climate in Egypt during the interwar period, specifically 1924, a time of heightened political tension following the assassination of Sir Lee Stack. The correspondence highlights the British colonial administration's concern regarding the safety of its subjects in Cairo and the provinces, and the bureaucratic control over the distribution of weaponry. It illustrates the intersection of consular administrative duties and the broader imperial security policy in Egypt, reflecting the precarious position of British expatriates during the rise of Egyptian nationalism.

THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO, 13th April 1928.

Many thanks for your letter of March 27th, and for the action which you are taking in the matter of the co-operation of your Company's representatives in the precautionary measures here. We know that we can always count on your assistance.

I would add that the position at Suez is now quite satisfactory.

(Signed) NEVILLE HENDERSON

Vice-Admiral H.W. Grant C.B.,
Eastern Telegraph Company,
Electra House,
Moorgate, E.C.2.

Grant of the Eastern Telegraph Company for their cooperation regarding precautionary measures being taken in Egypt. He notes that the situation in Suez is now satisfactory.

ai_content.transcribed_text: SECRET. CR/Egypt/20503/20/G. From: The General Officer Commanding, British Troops in Egypt. To: The Under Secretary of State, War Office, London, S.W.1. Headquarters, Cairo, 12th January, 1928. Sir, With reference to War Office letter No. 57/Egypt/1879 (A.3.), I have the honour to report that I have recently reviewed the situation as regards the protection of British residents on the Nile and consider that certain additional issues of arms are required in view of changes which have occurred since my predecessor examined the question in 1925. (a). NAG HAMADI. Sir John Jackson and Company's contract for the Nag Hamadi Barrage will result in the presence at this place of a British Community of about 35 men for the next two years. In order to make this Community capable of self defence and also able to render assistance in the evacuation of another small Community I request permission to issue:- 10 Rifles S.M.L.E. 2000 Rounds S.A.A. 10 12 bore Guns. 600 Rounds Buckshot. These will be on the personal charge of the principal representative of Sir John Jackson and Company and will only be issued in case of emergency. They will be returned as soon as the barrage is completed and the British personnel leave. (b). SOHAG. There is a small British Community at this place and I consider that rifles are necessary for the defence of the place selected for concentration in the event of disturbances. Mr. S.C. Regnier. All is now well at Suez. Mr. K.B. fixed up the buckler when he visited Suez last September, and Muir Bey, who was here yesterday, tells me that the rifles are still stored by the B.M.O. 11/4/28
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official military memorandum from the General Officer Commanding British Troops in Egypt to the War Office in London. It requests authorization to issue firearms and ammunition to British personnel working on the Nag Hamadi Barrage project and at Sohag to ensure their self-defense during potential civil unrest. It also includes a handwritten marginal note regarding the status of rifles stored at Suez.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a secret military minute from the British Headquarters in Cairo, dated January 1928, concerning the security of British nationals working on infrastructure projects in Egypt, specifically the Nag Hamadi Barrage. It reflects the British military's concern for the safety of its citizens during a period of political instability in Egypt, requesting authorization to arm civilian contractors. The document provides insight into the intersection of colonial infrastructure development and military security protocols in the interwar period, with an added handwritten note from April 1928 confirming the status of arms storage in Suez.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Notes on navigation of the Nile.
(See also Military handbook on Egypt - Page 96 et seq)
Normally the Nile as far as Aswan is navigable by steamers drawing 2 feet 6 inches from about the middle of August (in Cairo) to the end of February.
In a bad year navigation difficulties may begin as early as the end of December.
In a normal year the river is not navigable by tourist steamers from the end of February till the end of July.
The reservoir at Aswan is usually filled during November and December, the water being held until the end of April when it is gradually let out, the demand for water being particularly heavy at the end of June.
It will be seen therefore that to despatch a flotilla up the Nile between mid-February and mid-June will necessitate an abnormal outlet of water from the Aswan Dam which might seriously prejudice the cultivation of crops in all parts of the country dependent on perennial irrigation.
As an example during March 1919 in order to raise the river level two feet at Cairo a quarter of the contents of the Aswan dam was emptied. Fortunately for the cultivators a good and early flood came down and no ill effects were suffered.
The most critical period at which to heighten the river sufficient for navigation is early May if this was done it might cause the sacrifice of a great part of the cotton crop.
The question of opening the Aswan dam for purposes of navigation might have such far reaching economic effects that a decision on the question is a matter of high policy.
From the military point of view an early decision would have to be sought as it takes from 8 to 10 days for water released at Aswan to reach Cairo.
The importance of retaining a British Engineer in charge of the Aswan Dam cannot be exaggerated.
ai_content.english_translation: This document provides technical notes regarding the navigability of the Nile River for military and transport purposes, specifically focusing on the constraints imposed by the Aswan Dam. It details the seasonal water levels, the impact of dam operations on agricultural irrigation (particularly cotton crops), and the strategic necessity of maintaining British engineering oversight for water management.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an excerpt from a British military handbook concerning the strategic management of the Nile River in Egypt, likely dating to the post-WWI period (c. 1919). It highlights the tension between military logistical requirements—specifically the need to move flotillas upriver—and the economic necessity of maintaining water levels for Egyptian agriculture. The text underscores the British colonial administration's control over the Aswan Dam and the critical role of British engineers in managing the water supply, which was essential for both the Egyptian economy and the British military presence in the region.

Remarks on Visit to SUEZ by Colonel-on-the-Staff, General Staff, and Director General, European Department, Ministry of Interior, on 19th August, 1926.
1. As the Director General is responsible for the coordination with the Military Authorities for all arrangements in connection with the safety of the European population, he is the proper channel for communications from the Vice Consul with regard to any points connected with the Local Defence Scheme, (so far as the civilian community is concerned).
The Director General consults Headquarters, British Troops in Egypt, who in due course inform the Canal Brigade of any changes affecting them and issue the necessary orders.
2. Suez Defence Scheme. Action on part of civilian community.
(a) Asiatic Petroleum Company Oil Refinery. Scheme of Defence did not appear sound. To distribute the fourteen Europeans available all over the various departments of the huge area contained by the refinery with a view of preventing destruction, would, in case of serious trouble, be perfectly useless and only asking for trouble and probably result in serious loss of life. It was arranged with Mr. Taylor that it was obvious that an attack from a Suez mob was about to take place, the women and children would be withdrawn to the jetty, where the men would be ordered to concentrate. A good position is available and cover for women and children and in due course the whole party would be taken off by launches.
[Handwritten note:] Paragraph 3 is being copied and placed in the relevant file - British Rifle Club in Egypt. Mr. Henderson 11/9.

It outlines the chain of command between the Director General of the European Department, the British military authorities, and the local Vice Consul. It specifically critiques the defense plan for the Asiatic Petroleum Company Oil Refinery, deeming the dispersal of personnel ineffective and proposing a new strategy of concentrating civilians at a jetty for evacuation by boat in the event of an attack by a local mob.

MINUTE on Residency paper No. 8882/245
HIGH COMMISSIONER EGYPT
2 JUN 1927
H.E. Mr. Lee.
Colonel Burchall came to see me this evening. He wanted to know how things were going, in order to realise what chance there was, if any, of Imperial Airways machines being called upon to transport troops to, or British civilians from outlying places.
2. In reply to a question he said that the subject had not been raised.
3. I told him that I thought it highly improbable that such a proposal would ever be made; that it was obviously undesirable that private machines should be used for either purpose but particularly for troops; that, should he at any time be called upon to take such action, he should refer the matter to Y.E. and should do nothing until he had obtained Y.E.'s views.
4. Colonel Burchall agreed.

It records a meeting between the author and Colonel Burchall regarding the potential use of Imperial Airways aircraft for military transport or the evacuation of British civilians. The author advised Colonel Burchall that such a proposal was highly unlikely and undesirable, and instructed him to consult with His Excellency (Y.E.) before taking any such action.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal minute from the British Residency in Egypt during the interwar period. It reflects the British colonial administration's cautious approach to the integration of private commercial aviation (Imperial Airways) into military or emergency logistics. Dear Peterson,
On my return from leave I read the reports of Clerk and Blunt made after their visit to Upper Egypt and sent to the various Defence schemes. These reports were sent to the department under cover of your G.H./Egypt/060/2/U of May 21st. I notice that they make particular reference to a point which I have turned unofficially into a suggestion of using sea-planes or flying boats particularly for the evacuation of British residents in Upper Egypt towns.
The present scheme of evacuation under which residents will hold the concentration points until such time as the Nile flotilla arrives to take them away, though it was adopted on my suggestion which was 1st in 1919 to avoiding the obvious dangers of residents attempting to evacuate themselves - attempts which led in 1919 to serious consequences - involves a delay of several days during which the residents may have a very bad time holding the concentration points. First, the fleet has to arrive, then, the boats have to be named and got ready and finally they have to get to the various towns.
All this delay might be avoided, I suggest, and our responsibilities much lightened if the force were provided with a number of flying boats as far as I remember the conditions the landing grounds for flying planes on the river, whereas the landing grounds for flying boats are either on, or close to the river, and either bad or inaccessible. It would not be near difficult for a flying boat to land on the river, taxi in the residents with machine gun, if necessary, and take off the residents to under cover of support by a couple of ordinary machines with bombs. I understand any machine gun, but this, of course, is entirely a matter for expert opinion.
From previous conversations it seemed that difficulties existed as to the actual provision of the navy flying boats, as this came within the province of the Navy, but from enquiries which I and at home, I understand any such difficulties have now been settled and that the provision of flying boats for the R.A.F. in Egypt is quite within the region of possibility.
Perhaps you would be good enough to bring this matter to the attention of the G.O.C., who might care to summon a meeting of the Defence Committee to discuss it.
Yours sincerely,
A.W.B.
Colonel A.D. Paterson, D.S.O.,
General Staff.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal letter addressed to Peterson regarding the evacuation strategy for British residents in Upper Egypt. The author, A.W.B., critiques the existing reliance on the Nile flotilla, noting that the delay in the fleet's arrival leaves residents vulnerable. He proposes the use of flying boats or sea-planes to expedite the evacuation process, arguing that they are more versatile than standard river craft and that previous logistical hurdles regarding their provision by the Navy have been resolved. He requests that the matter be brought before the General Officer Commanding (G.O.C.) and the Defence Committee.

SECRET. REPORT ON VISIT TO SUEZ BY G.S.O.II ON 8-9-27. 
Itinerary: 
Left Cairo 0600 hrs. 
Arrived Suez 1130 hrs. (delayed by mechanical trouble). 
Inspected range and rifles in Suez. 1230 hrs. 
Inspected rifles in Consulate. 1430 hrs. 
Visited Refinery. 1530 hrs. - 1730 hrs. 
Left Suez 1745 hrs. 
Arrived Cairo 2145 hrs. 

The visit was made with the object of carrying out the annual inspection of the Suez Rifle Club in accordance with G.H.Q. instructions. Opportunity was also taken of discussing the Local Defence Scheme with the Director General, European Dept., and Gatrynd Bey of the Frontier Administration. 

Suez Rifle Club. 
The Club was only revived in January, 1927. The number of members on the books is 77 out of which 40 belong to the G.H.Q. The total number of British born adult males in Suez is about 130. Shoots are carried out on Fridays and Sundays from October to May. The average attendance is between 10 and 30. The competition of games makes it difficult to increase the membership. 

The Honorary Secretary, J.P. Stroy, Esq. (E.F.C.) promised to make an effort to raise a team for the Egypt & Sudan Trophy and to arrange matches with the Cairo Rifle Club. 

The range (600 yards) is situated north of the Suez aerodrome. Little money has been spent on it i.e. firing points and butt gallery are not finished but it is very well kept. Target numbers, firing point notices, etc., are all run/bad.

SUEZ DEFENCE SCHEME.
Some modifications to the Suez Defence Scheme were suggested by Colonel Turner last year. The Acting Vice Consul was asked:
(a) to mend the present scheme to include the modifications.
(b) to consider the question of the employment of armed civilians after the arrival of a military detachment.
This should be discussed with a representative from Canal Brigade.
The Refinery of the A.P.C. was visited by launch. Landing at the jetty at which the women and children were to be promoted [embarked].
The distance from the bungalows was over a mile and the route is exposed to fire from the bungalow enclosure which it is proposed to evacuate.
The area of the Refinery and vulnerable nature of the huts and the plant makes the question of its defence by a staff of 13 men a difficult problem. I suggested to the Acting Vice Consul that by pooling of the resources of Suez and Port Tewfik more men might be made available for the defence of the Refinery.
The present scheme of evacuating the bungalow compound is open to the objection that the mob will be given an initial success at the outset which will increase the difficulty of getting control at a later stage.
This question will be discussed further with the Colonel on the Staff, General Staff, on his return.
Reduction of Staff of E.P.C. at Suez.
The present staff is 77. Owing to the introduction of automatic plant this number will be reduced to 30 by March and by September 1928 to 14 (7 married and 7 single). To a certain extent the defence problem will be simplified as the whole reduced staff will live in or close to the E.P.C. compound. The plant can be kept going by 2 or 3 men the rest 111/

Sir,
I am directed by the Acting High Commissioner to state that he would be glad of your assistance in connection with the following matter.
2. The Director General of the European Department, who has recently paid a visit to Suez, reports that present arrangements for the action to be taken in the event of possible future disturbances would be greatly improved if the Superintendent of your Company at Suez were willing to allow certain rifles to be stored in an armoury which actually exists on the Company's premises. The Superintendent has been approached on the subject on two occasions, but has refused to agree to the above proposal on the ground that the good relations existing between the Company and the Egyptian authorities might thereby be jeopardised.
3. Mr. Henderson appreciates the motive which has actuated the Superintendent, and which, in general, has his entire approval. He does not, however, consider that in the particular case under discussion your Company need have any fear of the consequences and he would accordingly be glad if you would use your influence.
J. Davis Esq.,
Superintendent,
Eastern Telegraph Company,
Cairo.

ai_content.transcribed_text: OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR-GENERAL, EUROPEAN DEPARTMENT, MINISTRY OF THE INTERIOR. Cairo, 16th January, 1928. No. DS/24/9 (Secret). Dear Smart, With reference to your letter of January 6th, intimating the desire of H.S. the High Commissioner for information about the arrangements for evacuation of British colonies in case of need: I enclose herewith a copy of Lt. Colonel's Paterson's notes on the G.O.C's recent trip in Upper Egypt, embodying notes on evacuation, together with a copy of a memorandum by Colonel Paterson on navigation of the Nile, with which subject the question of evacuation is closely associated, in so far as concerns residents in Upper Egypt. Broadly speaking, the bases of the Defence Scheme for British residents in the Provinces are: a) Military occupation of towns along the Cairo-Ismailia Railway Line. b) Timely evacuation of small isolated colonies - by the means at their disposal (rail, motor-cars, river-craft, etc.) - to larger centres. c) Self-defence of larger colonies, pending relief, at selected points of concentration. Local Defence schemes are "vetted" by H.Q. Arms and ammunition are supplied by H.Q. and this Department. Communications are not dependent only on the telegraph and telephone; every centre is also provided with a code of air-signals for communicating with aeroplane patrols and periodic flights are made for testing purposes. d) Relief by expeditionary forces. In Upper Egypt, relief would proceed by rail or road; in Lower Egypt, the railways would be used if available, but main reliance is placed on the Nile Flotilla of commandeered river-steamers. In either case, such aid as is possible would be rendered by aeroplanes. Yours sincerely, R. M. Graves. B. S. Smart Esq., Oriental Secretary, The Residency.

It outlines the strategic defense and evacuation plans for British citizens residing in Egypt during potential civil unrest or emergency, detailing the use of the Cairo-Ismailia railway, the reliance on the Nile Flotilla for river transport, and the coordination of air support and local defense schemes.

SECRET.
NOTES ON G.O.C's TOUR - UPPER EGYPT 25.12.27 - 5.1.1928.
ASWAN.
Arrived 28th December, left 30th December 1927.
The dam was visited on the morning of 29th December and Mr Watt, Resident Engineer, interviewed.
No change as regards plans of concentration and general arrangements.
The following points were discussed:
(a) The river via WADI HALFA must be relied on for evacuation should the occasion arise, evacuation by air which was discussed in 1925 and 1926 is impracticable with present resources.
If an aeroplane is required over ASWAN for demonstration or communication it would probably be more easily found from Khartoum. An advanced landing ground would be more easily established in Sudanese territory than Egyptian. This will be discussed with H.E.
(b) It is essential to maintain communication with the resident engineer at the ASWAN Dam in case a flush of water is required to heighten the river for the Nile flotilla. (see separate note)
Means of communication:
1. Telegraph from Cairo.
11. W/T to Khartoum thence by telegraph or aeroplane.
111. Aeroplane from Cairo.
111. Is probably the most reliable.
(a) Not much trouble need be anticipated here especially among dam employees the majority of who have 15 years service and are drawing maximum pay.
A pro-forma was handed to Mr WATT for completion.

SECRET.
NOTES ON G.O.C's tour - Upper Egypt. 28.12.27 to 5.1.1928.
NAG HAMADI. (Construction of barrage 16 Km North of Nag Hamadi town)
Mr. P. du Santoy and Mr. R. Ellison (Organizer and Deputy Organizer) came on board 1700 hours 1st January 1928.
The notes on the pro-forma was agreed in principle. The following points were discussed:
(a) Attitude of local population.
It was agreed that the labourers employed on the dam would probably continue to work in the event of political troubles where no economic issues were involved and that if events in the provinces took a really serious turn the men would go back to their villages (mostly in the Sohag district).
The Egyptian engineers at the dam were said to be of a very good type.
(b) Evacuation
This community must be prepared to defend themselves until relief by an armed flotilla. They will also have to be prepared to look after 100 non-British European employees at the dam itself and a further 100 who may come in from the quarries at Isawiyah.
Nag Hamadi will also be prepared to assist in evacuating Sohag with craft from the dam (see Sohag)
(c) Arms and ammunition.
The following arms and ammunition will be supplied: by H.Q., B.T.E. 10 Service Rifles and 2,000 rounds of S.A.A. (War Office authority required)
By Ministry of Interior. 10 Sautier guns, 600 rounds buckshot, 12 pistols, 500 rounds.
(d) Air.
The signal stripe will be made of black cloth and will be displayed on the white roof of one of the large buildings near the river front. An aeroplane should fly over when the stripe are ready to photograph them.
There seemed to be sufficient prospects of finding a landing ground near the site of the works to justify a visit by a R.A.F. officer. In any case a message picking up station would be arranged.
Aircraft should be warned of cable ways which stretch over the site of the dam. The towers supporting them at each end are 180 feet high. H.Q., R.A.F., Middle East will be informed.
(e) Quarries at Isawiyah (East Bank)
100 Europeans (non-British) and 1000 Egyptians are employed at the quarries of Isawiyah, 50 miles north of the dam (near Sohag). The nearest villages are said to be hostile. The European employees would probably come up to Nag Hamadi in stone barges in case of trouble.

SOHAG.

G.O.C's tour - UPPER EGYPT. 25.12.27 to 5.1.1928.

Mr Oulton, Peel & Co's agent, came on board 1700 hours on 3.1.1928.

1. Place of concentration.
The following points were discussed:
This was changed on 30th Dec to Peel's new ginning factory on left bank about 1/2 mile up-stream of the town near mouth of Sohag Canal. Oulton has sent memoranda with plan to Ministry of Interior and promised to send large scale map showing exact location.

2. Arms and ammunition.
Oulton is confident of being able to hold out indefinitely provided his resources in arms are increased. It was agreed to form an initial small supply of one box of S.A.A. (1000 rounds). He was prepared to pay for the S.A.A. War Office authority will be required.

3. Policy regarding evacuation.
Should the occasion arise Sohag will now evacuate South to Nag Hamadi and not Asyut as previously arranged. Nag Hamadi will be responsible for supplying the craft required but the decision whether to evacuate or not will rest with the Sohag organiser. The question of communication with Nag Hamadi was discussed. Various means such as native messengers, a launch from Sohag or aeroplane was suggested. No satisfactory solution was found and it was agreed that Oulton should discuss the matter direct with the Nag Hamadi organiser.

4. Mr. Oulton is prepared to lay out both black and white stripes as a comparative test on the next occasion on which the air code is tested.

5. (a) Information obtained were made (applicable to all places) should be dropped on any others passed subsequently in the same flight.
(b) General situation reports should be dropped on isolated communities whenever flights are made over them in a period of crisis.

6. Attitude of Egyptian Officials.
The G.O.C. emphasised that the responsibility for law and order rested with the Amir and that his co-operation should be demanded.

7. The G.O.C. deprecated aggressive action such as taking of hostages.

8. Foreign Communities.
Oulton is prepared to take control of the Greek Community - the bulk are employed by Peel.
Mr Graves explained the principle that as much as possible should be done for non British communities but that assistance rendered to them should not be allowed to prejudice the security of the British community.

SECRET.

ASSIUT
Mr Foster (Egyptian State Railways) and Mr Grent (Barclays Bank) the newly appointed Assistant British Consular Agent came on board at 0800 hours 3.1.1928.
On close examination the scheme for conveying a platoon to Assiut by air proves to be so full of difficulties that it will only be adopted under the following combination of circumstances.
(a) that it is not possible to send troops by other means.
(b) that there is no likelihood of opposition from the Egyptian army battalion stationed at Assiut.
The policy will be adopted of despatching a platoon by rail as soon as trouble appears imminent.
If the concentration of the British community has already taken place the platoon will join them in the Assiut. If not a suitable camp site exists on the North side of the Ibrahimyeh Canal near the Railway Bridge.
The following suggested amendments to the Assiut Defence scheme embody the remaining points discussed:
(a) delete para. 14.
(b) cancel notes on the help which may be expected from British G.H.Q. Cairo, and substitute:
1. H.M. B.M. are arranging for the despatch of a platoon to assist by rail when trouble becomes imminent. This detachment will be located in the aerodrome space on the North side of the Ibrahimyeh Canal near the railway bridge.
Under certain circumstances the platoon may be despatched by air in which case the organiser will arrange for the provision of a guide and transport for the platoon from the landing ground to the camp site.
The senior British railway official at Assiut will be prepared to arrange:
(a) for the train conveying troops to be stopped at the bridge over the Ibrahimyeh Canal in the event of their arrival by rail.
(b) for the provision of a shunting engine and coaches at Assiut in the event of the arrival of the platoon by air.
The following additional signals for aeroplane code will be arranged with the B.M. Middle East and notified as soon as possible:
Egyptian army friendly and assisting in our protection.
Egyptian army hostile.
Egyptian army not yet disclosed intentions or Egyptian army neutral.

SECTION 2.
NOTES ON NAVIGATION OF THE NILE.
(See also Military Handbook on Egypt - Page 96 et seq)

Normally the Nile as far as Aswan is navigable by steamers drawing 4 feet 6 inches from about the middle of August (in Cairo) to the end of February.

In a bad year navigation difficulties may begin as early as the end of December.

In a normal year the river is not navigable by tourist steamers from the end of February till the end of July.

The reservoir at Aswan is usually filled during November and December, the water being held until the end of April when it is gradually let out, the demand for water being particularly heavy at the end of June.

It will be seen therefore that to despatch a flotilla up the Nile between mid-February and mid-June will necessitate an abnormal outlet of water from the Aswan Dam which might seriously prejudice the cultivation of crops in all parts of the country dependent on perennial irrigation.

As an example during March 1919 in order to raise the river level two feet at Cairo a quarter of the contents of the Aswan dam was emptied. Fortunately for the cultivators a good and early flood came down and no ill effects were suffered.

The most critical period at which to heighten the river sufficiently for navigation in early May if this was done it might abuse the sacrifice of a great part of the cotton crop.

The question of opening the Aswan dam for purposes of navigation might have such far reaching economic effects that a decision on the question is a matter of high policy.

From the military point of view an early decision would have to be sought as it takes from 8 to 10 days for water released at Aswan to reach Cairo.

The importance of retaining a British Engineer in charge of the Aswan Dam cannot be exaggerated.

It details the seasonal navigability for steamers, the impact of reservoir management on agricultural irrigation, and the strategic military implications of water level control.

It highlights the tension between colonial military logistics (moving flotillas) and the economic necessity of maintaining the Aswan Dam for Egyptian agriculture, particularly cotton production. The mention of the 1919 incident underscores the political sensitivity of water management in Egypt during the British occupation, emphasizing the strategic importance of British engineering control over the dam to balance navigation needs against the risk of crop failure.

MINUTE on Residency Paper No. 8882/250.
Evacuation of British Colonies.
Mr. Peterson.
All this confusion has been caused by the fact that my letter of the 6th instant was not attached to the papers. It is now attached, and you will see from it how the whole question arose.
As you will see from my letter, I asked Mr. Graves to talk to the G.O.C. and then with H.E. Instead of taking the matter up direct with H.E., he appears to have only sent us the report enclosed in his letter of the 16th instant. The Oriental Secretariat has never handled this question. Indeed I believe that the Head of the Chancery has hitherto seldom done more than act as post-office between H.E. on the one hand and the G.O.C. and the European Dept. on the other.
Perhaps Mr. Graves had better be asked to discuss this matter with H.E. Would you prefer to write to him yourself?
30th January, 1928.

ai_content.transcribed_text: NOTE ON ATTITUDE OF THE FOREIGN AGENCIES. 27 MARCH 1919. 8932/1. Sir Milne Cheetham. GREECE. Monsieur Sactouris has repeatedly professed his sympathy with the Residency and has advised his Colony to do all they can to keep quiet and act with the English. He said that the majority of the Greeks possessed fire arms and would, if necessary, place themselves under British officers. Their zeal has indeed had some rather undesirable results as General Watson reports several cases of their having fired on the crowd. I have begged Monsieur Sactouris to restrain this war-like ardour, and he has asked me to furnish him with the names of the offenders in order to punish them. I think there is little doubt that the Greeks are on our side. For one thing they have everything to lose by disorders in the towns and country districts, where they are universally detested, and for another the mere fact that the Italians are believed to have displayed sympathy towards the Nationalists is in itself enough to bring in the Greeks on the other side. They are obviously extremely nervous, and indeed I heard last night at the Savoy that many Greeks were endeavouring to leave the country. I have had excellent relations with the Greek Agency ever since the Venizelists have come into power, and I think Monsieur Sactouris is genuinely grateful for the support he has received both at the time of his nomination and in the matter of the optés. He has always shown himself ready to receive and act on any advice proffered by the Residency. I do not know how far the disaffected Royalist element is still strong in the country - but if it still exists...
ai_content.english_translation: This is a diplomatic memorandum written by Sir Milne Cheetham, the British Acting High Commissioner in Egypt, dated March 27, 1919. It details the political stance of the Greek community and their representative, Monsieur Sactouris, during a period of unrest in Egypt. The report notes that the Greek community is aligned with the British, though their over-zealousness has led to incidents of firing on crowds, which General Watson has reported. Cheetham notes the Greeks' fear of the local population and their rivalry with the Italians, who are perceived to support the Egyptian Nationalists. The document highlights the strong relationship between the British Residency and the pro-Venizelist Greek Agency.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential diplomatic report from the British Residency in Cairo, written in the immediate aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. It provides a contemporary assessment of the Greek diaspora's political alignment in Egypt, illustrating the complex web of foreign interests during the British Protectorate. The report highlights the strategic alliance between the British authorities and the Greek community (loyal to Eleftherios Venizelos) against the backdrop of rising Egyptian nationalism and the perceived pro-Nationalist sympathies of the Italian community. It serves as a primary source for understanding the security concerns and diplomatic maneuvering of British officials during the volatile spring of 1919.

Monsieur Lefèvre-Pontalis informed me a few days ago that some twenty Royalist Greek emissaries arrived here in January with a view to fomenting unrest and Bolshevism. I have, however, no confirmation of this, though I notice in an interesting article in the current round table that Egypt is one of the countries where the Russian Bolshevik Government intends to conduct propaganda. It has been persistently rumoured that the Italian Colony has been very unfriendly to us. I have no direct proof of this, but judging from what I know of the Italians in Egypt since my arrival in 1911, it is more than probable. Monsieur Bectouris complained that in the looting of shops and breaking of shop windows, the Italians had been spared by the students and roughs, whereas the Greeks had been singled out for unpleasant attentions. I have never personally credited the Italian agency itself with any hostile intentions. Marquis Negrotto Cambiaso is a gentleman, and, I think, too well trained a diplomatist to meddle lightly in a difficult internal situation in which his interference would necessarily sooner or later come to light. His secretaries do not strike me as sufficiently intelligent young men to play a serious role even if they wished to do so. Moreover, the Italian house is so full of glass windows, Cyrenaica, that it would be unspeakably foolish to stir up a movement here which if successful could not fail to react detrimentally on their own colonial and general position.

NOTE ON ATTITUDE OF THE FRENCH AGENT.

Monsieur Lefèvre-Pontalis, the French Minister, has, as I have already reported in my despatch no. 302 of December 27th, taken himself to his office at the Residency to see me. He landed with the fixed idea that the British officials in Egypt had in some way changed since the time of Fashoda, and were constantly creating unnecessary difficulties for the French. He particularly pointed out that his arrival and before he had time either to meet that official or form any opinion for himself as to what was going on here, he was directed by the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, then on the Egyptian Local Authorities in general, and finally the complaints having been directed from Egypt to Syria via the complaints were against the military authorities, charged with the affairs of that country.

I desired to see him at the time the Cheetham's request to the outbreak of the present disturbances, but failed to discover what he thought of the situation or in what sense he had been reporting to the Government. I saw him again not long ago and a somewhat more satisfactory conversation with him. He did not express any sympathy with us in our present difficulties.

ai_content.transcribed_text: It has been persistently rumoured that the Italian colony has been actively unfriendly to us and have done their best to promote and encourage the present movement. The Italian representative, Marquis Negrotto Cambiaso, admitted to me that in the earlier stages his compatriots had in fact favoured the new ideas partly on sentimental and liberal grounds, partly from soreness at the approaching abolition of the Capitulations to which local foreigners cling with fanatical if misplaced tenacity. Another reason may be that a considerable number of the Italian residents are poor workmen, who are doubtless to some extent influenced by socialist, possibly anarchist, sentiments. Marquis Negrotto added that he had summoned the leading members of the colony and warned them to avoid mixing themselves up in a political situation which in no way concerned them. He is himself fully aware that any large measure of nationalist success here must inevitably react most unfavourably on the Italian position in Albania, and might indeed prejudice Italian aspirations in the Adriatic and Levant as well. I think that, now that the seriousness is better appreciated, the educated and well to do foreign element - both Italian and French - are revising their first impressions and earlier sympathies for the nationalists. The only Italian who has actually been unfavourably reported on by the military authorities, is a certain [name obscured].

The French Admiralty informs the Maronite Archbishop of Cairo secretly, for necessary action, that, as a result of the Arab insurrection at PORT SAID, during which some scores of natives were killed by the British troops, the English Authorities, pretexting that the said natives had been killed by some Syrian Maronites in the course of a collision with them, immediately imprisoned then some of 30 of the latter. I saw Mr. Gary recently and asked whether he had received any disquieting news from the American missionaries in Upper Egypt. He told me that the natives were enquiring whether the United States were on the side of England or Egypt. If the former, they threatened to remove their children from the Missionary Schools. He believed the natives in question were mainly Protestant Copts.

He regarded the situation in Cairo with some misgivings, and begged me to allow the few Americans in the town to be treated as British for purposes of protection in the event of further rioting. This the Military authorities have gladly arranged to do and are taking the necessary measures.

Mr. Jackson, American Vice-Consul at Aleppo is here and is anxious to return to his post and take up his former Consular duties as soon as the Military Authorities permit the opening of foreign Consulates in Syria. He told me that Mr. Gary was anxious to call for Paris at the end of the month, leaving him in charge of the American Agency here. This he was most anxious to avoid, and begged me to do all I could to allow him to return to his post as Consul. He has apparently already received permission to go there for purposes of residence. He made a thinly veiled attack on Mr. Gary, who he implied was a fraud, and would do us no good at Paris. He struck me as being an objectionable young man, and General Staff "Intelligence".

I saw the Belgian Chargé d'Affaires, Monsieur de Royer, yesterday morning. He told me his colony, both missionaries and commercial people, were very uneasy at the turn things had taken and feared that Europeans had lost all prestige here. I said the leading European Colonies in encouraging the movement at the commencement had done all they could to bring about the situation they were now beginning to find so unpleasant, and that some of the responsibility for what had happened lay on their shoulders. Monsieur de Royer assured me that the Belgians - save possibly in Alexandria - had never had any illusions as to the natives, and had all along foreseen that an anti-British movement would rapidly turn into an anti-foreign one. I said the present policy of the Residency could not be judged in one or two days. After a week we should all know better where we stood.

Monsieur de Royer informed me that the famous German Agent OPPENHEIM was said to be in Cairo. The Savoy and also had information to that effect.

Monsieur Enctouris, the Greek Minister, called to see me in the evening, and said four of his compatriots, had been murdered in the course of the day - two of them being mere boys who had been taken out of a house in the Mahommed Aly Street and beaten.

ai_content.transcribed_text: I had a satisfactory conversation with Monsieur Lefevre Pontalis yesterday who for the first time discussed the situation in a sympathetic and human manner. He began by saying that he could not sufficiently praise your wisdom in allowing the delegation to go to Europe, and that even if this concession failed momentarily to restore order, he was convinced that it was the only possible action that could have been taken in the circumstances and would have an admirable effect abroad. He spoke in the warmest terms of Your Excellency and said that he had only not been to call at the Residency as he had had nothing in particular to say and knew you were intensely occupied. He said that the anti-Christian trend of the movement and, above all, the massacre of inoffensive Armenians, was a most alarming feature, and he showed me a letter addressed to him on April 9th by the Sheikhs and Ulemas of the Azhar which he considered highly provocative and above all, significant, as it followed and did not precede the permission for Zoghlul and his friends to proceed to Europe. I could not help saying that it was a pity that the foreign colonies had in some measure aided and abetted the movement in the beginning, and were thus, to a certain degree, responsible for the disagreeable position in which every European and, above all, every Christian now found himself.
ai_content.english_translation: The text is a report detailing a conversation between the author and Monsieur Lefevre Pontalis regarding the political situation in Egypt. It discusses the wisdom of allowing a delegation to travel to Europe, the anti-Christian sentiment and Armenian massacres, and the provocative nature of a letter from the Sheikhs and Ulemas of Al-Azhar. It also touches upon the perceived responsibility of foreign colonies in exacerbating the movement.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a diplomatic report from the British High Commission in Cairo, dated April 11, 1919. It captures the tense political atmosphere in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution. The text highlights the British administration's perspective on the Wafd delegation's travel to Europe, the sectarian tensions (specifically the targeting of Armenians), and the role of Al-Azhar leadership in the nationalist movement. The mention of 'Zoghlul' refers to Saad Zaghlul, the leader of the Wafd Party, whose exile and subsequent permission to travel to the Paris Peace Conference were pivotal moments in the Egyptian struggle for independence from British colonial rule.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
that one had to go further back for the explanation of this attitude and referred to the quarrel between Sir W. Brunyate and the foreign and native Bars.

He asked me if we objected to his receiving petitions and letters from the Nationalists. I said that we did not, as his Agency, like any other, was necessarily a post-box in such respects. He spoke with great scorn of Rushdi, and with respect of Adly Pasha, who struck him as a serious man with definite principles. He added that Rushdi was a mere 'pantin' without policy or statesmanship, and that he objected to his incessant attempts to compromise his, in small ways, agency.

He said nothing about the military measures taken to defend Europeans beyond criticizing the smallness of British patrols [at night] which were a mere incitement to a large and angry mob to display their anti-British sentiments. I said that I understood you yourself shared this view and had given orders that the size of the patrols should be increased.

I got the impression that Monsieur Lefèvre Pontalis, like Marquis Negrotto Cambiaso, was thoroughly and genuinely alarmed at the turn things had taken, and that he was prepared to afford us a much larger measure of support than a week ago in the event of our asking for his assistance. ...is rather smug and self satisfied tone had quite vanished.

Robert Greg

April 11, 1919.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is originally written in English. It records a conversation regarding the political situation in Egypt, noting a dispute between Sir William Brunyate and the legal bars. It discusses the receipt of nationalist petitions, expresses disdain for the Egyptian politician Hussein Rushdi Pasha (calling him a puppet or 'pantin') while showing respect for Adly Yakan Pasha. It notes criticisms of the small size of British military patrols at night during the civil unrest, and observes that French diplomat Monsieur Lefèvre Pontalis and Italian diplomat Marquis Negrotto Cambiaso were deeply alarmed by the unfolding events, making them far more cooperative with British authorities than they had been previously.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official diplomatic memorandum signed by British diplomat Robert Hyde Greg on April 11, 1919, during the height of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919. The revolution, sparked by the British exile of nationalist leader Saad Zaghloul and his colleagues, led to widespread strikes, demonstrations, and clashes across Egypt. This report highlights the anxieties of European diplomatic representatives in Cairo, specifically the French Minister Lefèvre Pontalis and the Italian Minister Marquis Negrotto Cambiaso, who feared for the safety of European communities amidst the anti-British uprisings. The text reveals the internal political maneuvering and British assessments of key Egyptian figures, such as the Prime Minister Hussein Rushdi Pasha and Adly Yakan Pasha, illustrating the complex colonial administration and international diplomatic dynamics during a pivotal moment of Egyptian nationalist resistance against the British Protectorate.
