ai_content.transcribed_text: Monsieur Sactouris came to see me last night and appeared much less pessimistic than when I last saw him some three days ago. He had received three deputations from the nationalists, one on the 10th and two yesterday, the last one being composed of notables and fairly important persons. He pointed out to them the folly of allowing Greeks and Armenians to be massacred, a policy which could not fail to have the worst possible effect on European opinion in Paris, and they appeared to understand and undertook to do all they could to restrain popular feeling. They promised to send emissaries at once into the native quarters to tell the people not to molest foreigners, and at the same time they suggested that a delegation composed of Egyptians and foreigners of all kinds should be formed for the same purpose. Monsieur Sactouris did not take this up, and I told him I was sure it would not meet with Your Excellency's approval.
ai_content.english_translation: Monsieur Sactouris visited me last night and seemed significantly less pessimistic than he was three days ago. He had met with three nationalist delegations—one on the 10th and two yesterday, the latter including notable and influential figures. He warned them against the folly of allowing the massacre of Greeks and Armenians, noting that such actions would severely damage their standing in European public opinion in Paris. The delegates appeared to understand and pledged to restrain popular sentiment. They promised to dispatch emissaries to the native quarters to instruct the populace not to harm foreigners, and suggested forming a joint delegation of Egyptians and foreigners for this purpose. Monsieur Sactouris declined this suggestion, and I informed him that I was certain it would not receive Your Excellency's approval.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a diplomatic report from the British High Commission in Cairo, dated April 12, 1919, during the period of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919. It details a meeting between the author and Monsieur Sactouris regarding the rising nationalist sentiment and the safety of minority populations (Greeks and Armenians) in Egypt. The text highlights the British concern over how anti-foreigner violence would be perceived by the Allied powers at the Paris Peace Conference, and reflects the ongoing efforts by British officials to manage nationalist agitation and maintain order in Cairo through local intermediaries.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
In the 'Temps', 'Débats' and 'Journal de Genève', the only foreign newspapers with which I keep in touch, the allusions to the Egyptian crisis have been few and far between and confined to the reproduction of a few Reuter telegrams and Lord Curzon and Mr. Dudley Ward's speeches in parliament; also Mr. Winston Churchill's.

The foreign colonies here were at the outset far from ill disposed to the nationalist movement, and as far as their letters to Europe have escaped censorship are not likely to contribute to putting our case in a favourable light on the continent. There is, I understand, at present a marked change in their tone and attitude but it comes a little late in the day. I consider Arkel Bey the best person to carry on British propaganda in Paris through his father Boghos Pasha, if he were so disposed. Our own newspapers are ill informed, and it is scarcely to wonder at that foreign ones are no better.
ai_content.english_translation: The document discusses the limited and often secondary coverage of the 1919 Egyptian crisis in major European newspapers like 'Le Temps', 'Le Journal des Débats', and the 'Journal de Genève'. It notes that these outlets primarily relied on Reuter telegrams and official British parliamentary statements from figures like Lord Curzon, Dudley Ward, and Winston Churchill. The author observes that foreign colonies in Egypt were initially not hostile to the nationalist movement, but their correspondence to Europe—if it bypassed censorship—likely did not favor the British perspective. The author suggests that while there is a shift in the attitude of these foreign colonies, it is too late, and proposes utilizing Arkel Bey, through his father Boghos Pasha, to conduct British propaganda in Paris.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a diplomatic dispatch from the British High Commission in Cairo, dated April 13, 1919, during the height of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919. It reflects British anxiety regarding international public opinion and the effectiveness of their propaganda efforts in Europe. The text highlights the British administration's struggle to control the narrative of the nationalist uprising, noting the reliance on official parliamentary speeches and the failure of foreign press coverage to support the British position. The mention of Boghos Pasha, a prominent Armenian-Egyptian politician and diplomat, underscores the British attempt to leverage influential local figures to sway European political circles.

FROM: C.G.S., G.H.Q., E.E.F.
TO: The Residency.

Captain Comte di Sambuy, Italian Military Attaché, called on me on 12th April, and, with reference to a conversation between the High Commissioner and the Consul General for Italy stated :-
1. The two Italian officers who took part in the Egyptian demonstrations and signed an Egyptian manifesto for Independence are :-
Lieut. Sacco, 77th Infantry.
Lieut. Carlagnano, 2nd Grenadiers.
2. Captain Sambuy has evidence on the above points.
3. These two officers excused themselves by saying they were caught by the procession and could not get away from it and that they signed the document at or near the Sultan's Palace because everybody else did so, and they were ignorant of its purport.
4. Captain Sambuy expressed his regret for the behaviour of these officers and stated that he proposed to have them sent to the Italian Base for transport to Italy. They would be ordered to report at the W.O. in Italy and a report on their conduct would be sent.
5. Both these officers were on leave from Italy, their homes or relations being in Egypt.

Cairo.
14th April 1919.
[Signature: C.G.S.]
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official military memorandum from the Chief of the General Staff (C.G.S.) of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force (E.E.F.) to the British Residency in Cairo. It details a meeting with the Italian Military Attaché, Captain Comte di Sambuy, regarding two Italian officers (Lieut. Sacco and Lieut. Carlagnano) who participated in Egyptian independence demonstrations and signed a manifesto. The officers claimed they were caught in the crowd and signed the document out of ignorance of its contents. The Italian authorities proposed sending them back to Italy for disciplinary review, noting that both officers were on leave in Egypt where they had family ties.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document provides insight into the political volatility of Egypt during the 1919 Revolution against British colonial rule. It highlights the diplomatic sensitivity of the British authorities in Cairo regarding foreign nationals (in this case, Italian officers) participating in nationalist demonstrations. The document serves as an administrative record of the British military's attempt to manage international relations while suppressing the Egyptian independence movement, specifically documenting the identification, excuse, and proposed repatriation of the two Italian officers involved.

THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO.
I saw the Italian Minister this morning. He said that as far as he was aware the situation in Cyrenaica was quiet but that there was a certain measure of unrest in Tripoli. The Italian Government he told me had displayed little or no interest in the internal situation here. His Colony were, however, growing nervous, and asked him whether they would not do well to leave the country where possible. He had advised them to keep quiet. Personally he was not optimistic as to a peaceable settlement of the present unrest and he feared that as soon as it became clear that the Peace Conference were not going to intervene in favour of the nationalist cause, there would be a big flare up, massacres and corresponding military repression, which, of course, could have only one end.
Marquis Negrotto said that apart from a certain number of Pashas with whom he played bridge at the Mohammed Aly Club, he saw very few Egyptians and that in general, information was mainly derived from his dragoman. The tone of the Club, he said, was growing more and more moderate and apprehensive, and general appreciation was shown by the tact and spirit of conciliation shown by Your Excellency since your arrival.
Marquis Negrotto Cambiaso added that he had a real esteem for Adly Pasha, whom he believed to be His Excellency.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a diplomatic report from the British Residency in Cairo, dated April 15, 1919. It details a meeting between a British official and the Italian Minister, Marquis Negrotto. The Minister discusses the political climate in Italian-held Tripoli and Cyrenaica, noting local unrest and the anxiety of the Italian colonial community. He expresses pessimism regarding the Egyptian nationalist movement, predicting violence if the Paris Peace Conference fails to support their cause. The report also mentions the social atmosphere at the Mohammed Aly Club in Cairo, where Egyptian elites were expressing appreciation for the diplomatic approach of the British High Commissioner (referred to as 'Your Excellency') and their high regard for the politician Adly Pasha.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential diplomatic dispatch from the British Residency in Cairo during the volatile period of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It provides a contemporary European perspective on the internal security situation in Egypt and neighboring Italian North Africa. The text highlights the intersection of local nationalist aspirations, the influence of the Paris Peace Conference, and the social dynamics of the Egyptian political elite (the 'Pashas') who frequented the Mohammed Aly Club. The mention of 'Your Excellency' likely refers to Field Marshal Edmund Allenby, who had recently arrived as the British High Commissioner to Egypt, marking a shift in British administrative policy.

Cairo April 16th, 1919
Dear Mr. Greg
I enclose herewith General Poli's (28932/3) record, which is quite accurate. I must point out though, that the two officers am not entitled to fund the Italian Base in Port Said. The H.O. will decide of their further destination, after reception of my report. It was understood that their departure would be postponed until I knew whether they were to be heard as witness.
Sincerely yours,
Major J. A. Hanbury
I was the that [sic] manifest mentions in General Poli's report was not for claiming independence.

Hanbury, forwards a record from General Poli, noting its accuracy. He clarifies that two officers are not authorized to fund the Italian base in Port Said and that their future movements depend on the High Commissioner's (H.O.) office following his report. He also mentions a delay in their departure pending their potential role as witnesses and adds a postscript regarding a manifest mentioned in General Poli's report.

It reflects the administrative and military oversight maintained by the British in Egypt during the period of the British Protectorate. The letter concerns the movement and status of Italian officers in Port Said, highlighting the bureaucratic coordination required to manage foreign military personnel and intelligence reporting in the region during a time of significant political transition and unrest in Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
My Lord,
It was reported to me on April 9th that two Italian officers, having previously signed an independence manifesto, took part in a big demonstration, which pushed its way into Abdin Palace.
I sent for the Italian Minister and informed him that this reprehensible behaviour on the part of two Italian officers had come to my knowledge. Marquis Negrotto expressed great surprise at this misconduct which had already come to his notice and he was having the matter investigated at once.
On April 12th he sent his Military attaché to see my Chief of Staff. Count di Sambuy informed Sir Louis Bols that he had found out the names of the two officers - Lieutenant Germano (Second Grenadiers) and Lieutenant Sacco (77th Infantry) - and that the report of their behaviour which had reached me was correct. They had excused themselves by saying that they were caught by the procession and could not get away from it and that they signed the document because everybody else did so, and they were ignorant of the purport. Count di Sambuy expressed his great regret at the conduct of these officers, residents
Right Honourable,
Earl Curzon of Kedleston,
K.G., G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E.,
etc. etc. etc.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a formal report addressed to Earl Curzon of Kedleston regarding the involvement of two Italian officers in a political demonstration in Cairo on April 9, 1919, which breached the security of Abdin Palace. The British High Commissioner in Egypt reports his diplomatic intervention with the Italian Minister, Marquis Negrotto, and the subsequent admission by the Italian military attaché, Count di Sambuy, that the officers (Lieutenant Germano and Lieutenant Sacco) were indeed involved, though they claimed ignorance of the manifesto's contents and that they were swept up in the crowd.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a diplomatic dispatch from the British High Commission in Cairo, dated April 16, 1919, during the period of the Egyptian Revolution of 1919. It details a sensitive incident where two Italian officers participated in an anti-British demonstration that reached the gates of the Abdin Palace, the seat of the Egyptian monarchy. The report highlights the delicate diplomatic balancing act between the British occupying authorities and the Italian diplomatic mission in Cairo, as the British sought to maintain order while managing the political fallout of foreign nationals participating in nationalist protests against British rule.

SECRET AND PERSONAL.
Following is a private conversation which took place on April 16th between Monsieur Pontalis and a member of a foreign community in Egypt.

Be,line: - That the native ministerial view of the British Protectorate had been declared arrogantly by the English and was a onesided act requiring endorsement by the Powers. Such endorsement he believed had been given "officieusement" by France and Italy but there was a wide divergence between such recognition and a formal endorsement. The English conduct of Egyptian affairs had been disastrous and they could not expect France - whose position in regard to Morocco was regular as compared with the British position in Egypt - to support them in a situation which has arisen through their mishandling. Having regard to the weakness of the British position both in its legal and political aspects he expressed the opinion that the possibility of restoring order by force - "Avec mitrailleuses" - was excluded. He admitted a certain divergence between these views and those of his Government, but believed that in view of the prejudicial effect it would have on the...
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a secret and personal diplomatic telegram reporting on a private conversation held on April 16th between Monsieur Pontalis and an unnamed member of a foreign community in Egypt. The text outlines Pontalis's critical perspective on the British Protectorate in Egypt, arguing that it was an arrogant, unilateral act that lacked formal international endorsement. He contrasts the British situation in Egypt with the French position in Morocco, suggesting that the British have mishandled affairs to such a degree that they cannot expect French support. He further argues that the British position is legally and politically weak, and that the use of military force (specifically machine guns) to restore order is not a viable option. He acknowledges that his personal views may differ from the official stance of the French government.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British Foreign Office telegram dated April 19, 1919, sent from Cairo during the period of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It captures the diplomatic tensions and the critical assessment of British colonial administration by French diplomat Monsieur Pontalis. The telegram highlights the precarious nature of the British Protectorate in Egypt following the end of World War I, reflecting the international scrutiny and the internal Egyptian resistance that challenged British authority during this volatile period of nationalist uprising.

(Private letter from Sir M. Cheetham to Sir R. Graham.)
THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO.
April 26, 1919.
I enclose copy of a letter to Brunyate
Contentieux, who has served on the Capitulations
Committee.
This letter will interest you as indicative of the movement of Italian, and no doubt also of French, opinion in Egypt and probably elsewhere. Our foreign friends here at any rate hope that the present disturbances will result in the perpetuation of an international situation in Egypt.
Recent reliable information shows that the Italian and French Colonies have egged on the nationalist movement a great deal more than we suspected, though we knew they were doing a good deal. The most glaring instance of impropriety on the part of the Italians was the conduct of the two Italian officers reported in our despatch no. 170.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a private diplomatic communication from Sir M. Cheetham at the British Residency in Cairo to Sir R. Graham, dated April 26, 1919. It discusses the political climate in Egypt following the 1919 Revolution, specifically noting the perceived interference of Italian and French nationals in the nationalist movement. The author expresses concern that these foreign powers are encouraging unrest to maintain the 'Capitulations' (the system of extraterritorial privileges for foreigners) and an internationalized status for Egypt, rather than allowing for a stable British-led administration.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British diplomatic correspondence from the Residency in Cairo during the immediate aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. It highlights the geopolitical tensions of the era, specifically the British suspicion that European powers (Italy and France) were covertly supporting Egyptian nationalist agitation to undermine British influence and preserve their own extraterritorial legal privileges, known as the Capitulations. The mention of Sir M. Cheetham (Acting High Commissioner) and the reference to the 'Capitulations Committee' place this document within the critical administrative period of the British Protectorate in Egypt.

ai_content.english_translation:
COPY
MINISTRY OF THE INTERIOR.
OFFICE OF THE SULTANATE COUNSELOR.
CAIRO, April 17, 1919.
CONFIDENTIAL.
My dear Counselor,
I hasten to return to you the report on constitutional reform. It is one of the most interesting studies I have read on the conditions in Egypt, and if it had been printed in England and addressed confidentially to the Foreign Office, I would have added that it served its purpose.
I believe that at the date of this report, I would probably have shared a number of your ideas. But I assume that you yourself, today, would hesitate to confirm them. If it is true that one must wait for the current national movement or uprising to stabilize before drawing definitive conclusions, it is nonetheless true that one must recognize already that ideas which seemed axiomatic have become debatable problems.
It seems to me debatable today whether England is not pushed to return, while keeping its special situation, to the side of the Capitulatory Powers to wait there until the suppression of the Capitulations is truly demanded by the Egyptians.
It seems to me likewise that one can discuss whether England would not have an interest in substituting the worrying formula of the protectorate with that [of...]
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential memorandum from the Office of the Sultanate Counselor in Cairo, dated April 17, 1919, during the immediate aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British occupation. The text reflects the high-level administrative anxiety regarding the British Protectorate status in Egypt. The author discusses the necessity of constitutional reform and acknowledges that the nationalist uprising has rendered previous British colonial assumptions ('axiomatic ideas') obsolete. It specifically addresses the 'Capitulations'—the extraterritorial privileges held by foreign powers—and suggests that the British position in Egypt is becoming increasingly untenable under the existing protectorate framework, signaling a shift in British imperial policy toward a more nuanced or potentially conciliatory approach to Egyptian sovereignty.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Cairo, 12th June 1919. His Excellency, THE SPECIAL HIGH COMMISSIONER. I beg to enclose a note from the Commandant of Cairo Police about the presence of Italians and Frenchmen in the "El-Azhar" meetings. I can do nothing in the matter myself, but hope the Residency may exert its influence with the Consuls General of these powers to restrain their subjects from encouraging by their presence the idea that their Governments side with the movement. I have the honour to be, Your Excellency's obedient servant, [Signature]. Doctors Villard and Chatinières came to Cairo on a visit from Palestine and are no longer here. They doubtless visited the Azhar as tourists. Monsieur Galliard who has been long in Morocco said he fully understood.

ai_content.transcribed_text: I saw Marquis Negrotto Cambiaso and Monsieur Gaillard this morning on the subject of the visit of their nationals to the Azhar Mosque. The former had already spoken to Maitre Guarnotte, who denied absolutely ever having put his foot in the Mosque, the whereabouts of which he was ignorant. There is, however, a Colonel Pezanti who occasionally comes to Cairo for the purpose, I believe, of purchasing horses. Marquis Negrotto is going to make enquiries. He further undertook to check as far as possible any visit of Italian visitors to the Azhar, and in case to insist that officers wishing to visit the Mosque should not go in uniform. Marquis Negrotto is going on leave at the end of the month and leaves the Italian Consul-General at Alexandria, Monsieur Maissa, in charge of the Italian Agency with his headquarters at that City. As Your Excellency is aware, I have always found Marquis Negrotto extremely pleasant and conciliatory to deal with, and I am convinced that he has been quite straight throughout the recent crisis. This opinion is, moreover, shared by everyone with whom I have ever talked here. Monsieur Gaillard knew nothing of Dr. Leon Khendirdjy but promised to make enquiries. Doctors Villard and Chatinières came to Cairo on a visit from Palestine and are no longer here. They doubtless visited the Azhar as tourists. Monsieur Gaillard who has been long in Morocco said he fully understood.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The Chancery
The Residency.

GENERAL STAFF - INTELLIGENCE,
HEADQUARTERS, EGYPT.
July 5th 1919.

With reference to your letter No. 7708 dated 2nd inst, there have been no actual demonstrations on the part of the Italians.

The nearest approach to a demonstration occurred on the day after the news of the signing of peace reached here. On that occasion a small group of Italians went round Cairo demanding that all Italian flags should be removed. In this they were successful with the exception of the Banco di Roma, whose manager refused to comply with their request.

There is little doubt that feeling against England and also to a certain extent America is very bitter at the present moment, and it cannot be denied that the Egyptian Extremists are trying to make as much capital out of it as possible.

Reports show that Egyptians and Italians are fraternising more openly, and it is said that they are trying to organize a counter demonstration on July 14th (Peace Celebration Day) though there is no confirmation of this.

It is difficult to estimate the effect of the Peace Celebrations on the natives generally at present. Bairam coincided with our celebrations and there was a general air of holiday making all round. A better estimate could probably be given after the celebrations of July 14th.

G.W. COURTNEY.
Major G.S.,
for Brigadier-General,
General Staff, Egypt.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an intelligence report from the General Staff in Egypt to the Chancery at the Residency, dated July 5, 1919. It addresses a previous inquiry regarding potential Italian demonstrations in Cairo following the signing of the peace treaty. It notes that while there were no major demonstrations, a group of Italians demanded the removal of Italian flags, which the Banco di Roma refused. It further reports on anti-British and anti-American sentiment among Egyptian extremists and mentions rumors of a potential counter-demonstration on July 14th (Bastille Day/Peace Celebration Day), noting that the recent Bairam holiday makes it difficult to gauge the general public mood.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British military intelligence report from the immediate post-WWI period in Egypt (July 1919). It captures the tense political atmosphere in Cairo following the Treaty of Versailles, highlighting the intersection of local Egyptian nationalist agitation ('Extremists') and the presence of the Italian community. The report reflects British colonial anxieties regarding the potential for civil unrest and the strategic monitoring of foreign nationals (Italians) and their interactions with the local population during a period of significant political transition and anti-colonial sentiment in Egypt.

1.) Mr Fernand Suarès, a youngish Jew in business closely related to the Cattaoui, Rolos, and other leading Jewish families here) came to see me this morning as representing the Italian ex-service men, of which he is one of the leaders, to enquire regarding the condition of Sir Lee Stack. He is a sensible person.
2.) He asked if he could speak plainly. The Italian colony were considerably excited over this dastardly act, and he hoped that I would not mind his saying that they were furious with the residency. Our leniency in case after case, notably that of Cpl. Ryan, had led them to believe that we should never take the drastic action which they believed to be demanded. All able-bodied Italians had now enrolled themselves into a private corps, badly armed unfortunately, but determined. They had their officers and non-commissioned officers and had a defence scheme which they were immediately going to put into operation in the event of the molestation of an Italian subject, a contingency which they regarded as only a matter of time.
3.) Suarès is a nephew of Cattaoui Pasha, the deputy. As a sequel of yesterday's news he said that several of Cattaoui Pasha's relations took him very seriously to task for remaining a member of Parliament. The Pasha was in a state of great depression and said 'L'independance de ce pays est maintenant complètement foutue'. The rest all agreed with acclamation.
ai_content.english_translation: The text is in English. The French phrase 'L'independance de ce pays est maintenant complètement foutue' translates to 'The independence of this country is now completely screwed/ruined'.

The report highlights the anxiety of the Italian expatriate community, their distrust of British 'leniency' regarding local unrest, and their formation of private militias for self-defense. It also captures the internal political turmoil within the influential Cattaoui family, reflecting the broader collapse of confidence in Egyptian independence efforts following the assassination, as expressed by Cattaoui Pasha.

Suarès added that whatever the feelings of the French colony might be (he had no reason to believe them different from those of his colony, but the relations between the two were, as usual, strained) he could assure me that the whole Italian colony would consider my measures as took, however severe and brutal, as justified by the circumstances.

I should add that the Spanish Minister (at lunch yesterday) expressed similar sentiments, and said that whatever he did he would report to his Government as less than the circumstances demanded.

In conversation yesterday the Italian Minister expressed himself hardly less strongly than the Spanish Minister, remarking that Egyptians could not have chosen a worse way to hurt from their own point of view. All Italians we regarded him as an unusually perfect gentleman.

At a large Levantine tea-party yesterday Atta Afifi, who took up a careless manner in discussing the incident, was so cold-shouldered by the various Europeans (mostly Greek, French, Belgian and Italian women, in what he pleased to call itself society here) that he left.

I pass this hurriedly dictated minute on to you for what it is worth.

NOTE.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE BRITISH CHAMBER OF COMMERCE, CAIRO COMMITTEE. SAVOY CHAMBERS, AVENUE DE LA BOURSE, CAIRO. 28th March, 1919. To H. E. General Sir E. Allenby, G.C.B., G.C.M.G., His Majesty's Special High Commissioner, The Residency, CAIRO. Excellency, I desire on behalf of this Committee and of the members of the British Chamber of Commerce in Cairo to express to Your Excellency the great satisfaction they feel in your appointment as His Majesty's Special High Commissioner, for the purpose of reinstating order and British prestige in this country. It is felt that in your hands confidence will soon be restored, and it is hoped that all commercial interests, which have been so severely affected, may thereby rapidly assume normal activity. I wish also to assure Your Excellency that my Committee are at all times entirely at your disposal for any assistance which they can render within their sphere of influence. As we presume an enquiry will be held, we venture to suggest that a useful purpose would be served for Your Excellency to avail yourself of the views of the British unofficial and commercial community as to the actual cause of the trouble which has arisen. I have the honour to be, Your Excellency's obedient servant, [Signature] Chairman.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal letter from the British Chamber of Commerce in Cairo to General Edmund Allenby, congratulating him on his appointment as Special High Commissioner to Egypt. The letter expresses the Chamber's confidence that Allenby will restore order and British prestige following a period of unrest. It offers the Committee's assistance and suggests that Allenby consult with the British commercial community regarding the causes of the recent disturbances.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal letter dated March 28, 1919, sent by the British Chamber of Commerce in Cairo to General Edmund Allenby shortly after his appointment as Special High Commissioner for Egypt. The context is the immediate aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. The letter reflects the anxiety of the British commercial community regarding the disruption of trade and their desire to influence the official inquiry into the causes of the uprising. It serves as a primary source for understanding the colonial administrative perspective and the alignment between British commercial interests and the military occupation authorities during a period of intense political instability in Egypt.

HIGH COMMISSIONER EGYPT

Our 44 Molasses trucks loaded from Upper Egypt before trouble and stored at Minia are about to be perished. Our life depends upon this kind of trade and we are poor and absolutely out of political affairs and always looking forward to peace. Will kindly order for moving to destination.

Merchants of Molasses.

The message states that 44 trucks loaded with molasses from Upper Egypt were stored in Minia before the onset of 'trouble' (likely referring to the 1919 Egyptian Revolution). The merchants claim the goods are about to perish, emphasize their poverty and lack of involvement in political affairs, and request an order to allow the transport of their goods to their final destination.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a telegram sent during the height of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against the British occupation. The 'Merchants of Molasses' are appealing to the British High Commissioner for Egypt to facilitate the movement of their commercial goods, which were stranded in Minia due to the widespread civil unrest, strikes, and disruption of transport networks that characterized the 1919 uprising. The document highlights the economic impact of the political instability on local merchants and the reliance on British administrative authority to restore commercial logistics during the period of martial law.

Reference I.19887/D of 30/4/1919 :-
The principal economic loss in Damanhour owing to the insurrection has been caused by the interruption and restriction of railway travel.
(1) In the villages served by the Delta Rly., articles such as sugar and matches rose 300% in price; petroleum was unobtainable at 100 a tin.
(2) Merchants in Damanhour have found their business much interfered with by being unable to visit Cairo or Alex., and in some cases have lost by failing to fulfill contracts etc.
(3) The parasitic class of trader who makes a living by buying a season ticket on the E.S.Ry. and buying on commission for other people, has had his livelihood completely cut off.
Agriculturally, the chief drawback has been the impossibility of sending manure by rail, whether artificial or the natural manure from 'Town': it is thought that this will affect the cotton, and still more the durra crop if restrictions continue.
(Sd) Lt. A. Hugh Jones
Political Officer, attached
No. 3 Section Damanhour.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official report regarding the economic impact of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution on the Damanhour region. It details how the disruption of the Delta Railway system caused severe inflation in essential goods like sugar, matches, and petroleum. It further notes that local merchants were unable to conduct business in Cairo or Alexandria, and that small-scale commission traders were put out of work. Finally, it highlights the agricultural crisis caused by the inability to transport manure by rail, which threatened the upcoming cotton and durra harvests.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a post-insurrection administrative report from the British occupation period in Egypt, specifically following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British rule. It provides a granular look at the socio-economic consequences of the civil unrest, specifically focusing on how the disruption of transport infrastructure (the Delta Railway) crippled local commerce and agricultural productivity in the Beheira Governorate. The report serves as a primary source for understanding the logistical and economic pressures faced by the British administration during the nationalist uprising.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
VICKERS LIMITED.
Shepheards Hotel,
CAIRO.
June 8th 1919.
To General Sir Edmund H.H. Allenby, G.C.M.G., K.C.B., etc.
H.M. Special High Commissioner,
The Residency,
CAIRO.
Sir,
I have the honour to enclose herewith a translation of the Arabic pamphlet, which has been circulated calling for a boycott of British trade.
I reported the existence of this pamphlet to the Residency early yesterday afternoon and stated that a copy had been handed in to the Military Headquarters at the Savoy.
The pamphlet was first brought to my notice by British Commercial interests concerned asking me the best course to pursue. I was at the same time informed that on a previous occasion when information was given to the Military Headquarters at the Savoy that a distributer of pamphlets could then be pointed out to the authorities, the informer was discouraged through the little importance in his opinion with which his information was received.
Whether this information was given to the Officials directly concerned I am unable to say.
I venture to suggest that there are unofficial means of dealing with this propaganda which are probably better not referred to in this letter.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient Servant,
(sd) F.B. POULEY,
Representative Messrs Vickers Ltd,
Egypt etc.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal letter from F.B. Pouley, representing the British firm Vickers Ltd, addressed to General Sir Edmund Allenby, the British High Commissioner in Egypt. The author informs Allenby about an Arabic pamphlet circulating in Cairo that advocates for a boycott of British goods. Pouley notes that he has already alerted the Military Headquarters at the Savoy Hotel, but expresses frustration that previous reports of anti-British agitation were met with indifference by the authorities. He concludes by suggesting that there are 'unofficial means' to counter this propaganda that are too sensitive to be put in writing.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of colonial administrative correspondence from the immediate post-WWI period in Egypt, a time of significant political unrest leading up to the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It highlights the anxiety of British commercial interests (Vickers Ltd) regarding the rise of nationalist sentiment and economic resistance (boycotts) against the British occupation. The letter provides insight into the communication channels between British business representatives and the British High Commissioner, as well as the perceived failure of the military authorities to effectively suppress anti-colonial propaganda.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The various reports and evidence are, as usual, conflicting, but I can forward the following evidences as being probably the truth.

Persons Murdered. It is very difficult to speak with certainty as to this. There were undoubtedly seven bodies found at MINIA. One may say with certainty that these included POPE Bey, Inspector of Prisons, a major (said to be Major JARVICE, as I hear that his identity disc was found, though there is no statement to that effect in this file), a lieutenant and four N.C.Os or privates.

The three witnesses on the train whom I examined all persist that there were no other soldiers on the train, or at any rate in the 1st Class coach, except the six mentioned above, and MAHMOUD IBRAHIM holds to his statement that the fifth soldier who started from LUXOR got out at ASSIUT. Of these witnesses GIRDI Eff. struck me as trustworthy, but his knowledge is chiefly derived from what the others told him. The other two are typical Egyptian witnesses, and though their stories are probably true on the whole, they would be very likely to try to keepthe crime down to its smallest limits possible, i.e. to the seven bodies which they were found.

On the other hand, the witness BISH ISMAIL, who was questioned first, speaks of eight officers (presumably two or three officers and five or six men) or possibly POPE is included), there is the telegram from Mallawi to Mr. Foster at ASSIUT on the day itself, definitely stating that a body was thrown off there, and there seems to have been a telegram from the Mamour of DEIRUT to Mudir of MINIA that a soldier's body was found there. The statement that the bodies had been thrown into the water seems to be unconfirmed. Mr. Hark says he heard that one body was put out at RODA. It seems to me that enquiries should be made at MALLAWI, Roda and Deirut as soon as possible to endeavour to trace these bodies. Of course it is quite possible they were not soldiers, but other persons, either English or native, who were killed in the mêlée.

As regards identification of the bodies at Minia, it is stated in the Minia diary that every precaution was taken to keep anything that would serve to identify the victims, but what this amounts to I do not know. It may be that further information will be obtained when we get the enquiry made by the Chef de Paquet at Minia, as well as the clothes which are being abnt for, and also from the Greek doctor who made a post mortem on the bodies, and Rifaat Eff. Hafiz, the Prisons officer in the train. It will probably in any case be desirable to take steps to exhume the bodies.

General history of the case. Train No. 89 left LUXOR at 8.10 p.m. on 17th March. On board there were two British officers, five N.C.Os. or privates, and there may have been others. At Nag Hamadi crowd surrounded train and threatened the soldiers, who were in 2nd class coach. Officers therefore took them into the 1st Class coach.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official investigative report regarding the murder of British military personnel on a train in Egypt during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It details the conflicting witness testimonies regarding the number of victims, the locations where bodies were allegedly discarded (Minia, Mallawi, Deirut, Roda), and the logistical challenges of identifying the deceased. It notes the movement of the soldiers from a 2nd class to a 1st class coach at Nag Hamadi following threats from a crowd.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British High Commission report dated March 26, 1919, concerning the violent events of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. It serves as an internal administrative inquiry into the deaths of British officers and soldiers on Train No. 89, which departed Luxor on March 17, 1919. The report highlights the chaotic nature of the uprising, the difficulty in establishing a definitive casualty count, and the administrative efforts to identify the victims through post-mortem examinations and witness interrogations. It provides critical insight into the security situation in Upper Egypt during the height of the nationalist unrest.

ai_content.transcribed_text: During the night the train was boarded at several stations by persons asking if there were English there. ASSIOUT was reached after mid-night, and the train remained there till the morning and started again at 7.10 a.m. on 18th as No.77. It is stated - though I feel some slight doubt as to this - that one of the soldiers left the train at ASSIOUT, and it is certain that POPE Bey and RIFAAT Effendi HAFIZ joined it, travelling in the same coach as the British officers and men. All was apparently quiet at ASSIOUT, but in view of what had happened in the night I confess that I am surprised that the soldiers did not take some steps to arm themselves there, which might have been possible. All accounts agree that they were unarmed. There were crowds at BENI HUSSEIN and HOWALKA and BENI KERA stations, who were threatening and threw stones. Some persons from BENI KERA seem to have forced their way on to the train and travelled to DEIROUT. At DEIROUT a large number of rioters armed with nabuts (said to be fellahine, and not Bedouins or Sheikhs, though all sorts were in the crowd, including boys and women) attacked the train. Accounts vary, but it appears that POPE and one or two of the soldiers were killed at DEIROUT. The engine-driver who had been driven from his engine, succeeded in returning and starting the train again, but a great number of the rioters remained on board and travelled to DER MOEZ. Here also there was a large crowd which again stopped the train, and drove the driver and fire-men from the engine. Two of the soldiers made their way to the engine, apparently in order to try to start the train again, and were killed there, the rest were killed either in the train or alongside it. The bodies were then all thrown in a heap into the van, not stripped as originally stated, and the train started about 1 1/2 hours later. There were crowds at the other stations, and it appears that one of the bodies was taken out at MALLAWI, and perhaps another at RODA. At ABU KERKAS also apparently plans had been made to attack the train, if it had not already been done. The train actually reached MINIA about 12.30 p.m., when enquiries were made. RESPONSIBILITY for the Murders. It seems fairly clear that the main responsibility lies with the inhabitants of DEIROUT. Attacks were made at other places, and it is possible that some of the BENI KERA people got on the train and went to DEIROUT and joined in the fight there. Also the inhabitants of DER MOEZ are directly guilty of the greater number of the actual murders, but I suggest that their guilt is slightly less than that of the people of DEIROUT, who were the true cause of everything.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is written in English and describes the sequence of events during a violent attack on a train in Egypt, likely during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It details the movement of the train from Assiout through various stations where rioters boarded and attacked British soldiers, culminating in the deaths of the soldiers at Deirout and Der Moez. The author assesses the culpability of the local populations at these various stations.

MAHMOUD ABDURAGECH stated to Judge HILL that the explanation given by the nationalists for the murders was that a notable of DEIROUT (whose name was not given) had had a son in CAIRO killed by the soldiers in the streets.
As regards other places such as MELLAWI and ABU KERKASS, the intention was certainly as bad, but as the while matter was over, they did not do anything. It will probable by quite impossible to give any individual responsibility with any certainty; though later on doubtless people will be found to say that they saw individuals actually beating, such individuals being probably their personal ennemies. Futher inquiry required. The above note is made on the information now before me. When I have examined the proés verbal of the MINIA Chef de Parquet, and questioned RIAAT Effendi HAFIZ it may be that a few more facts may coe out.

ai_content.english_translation: This is an urgent diplomatic telegram sent from the High Commissioner for Egypt in Cairo to the Foreign Office in London, dated April 4, 1919. It reports on a violent incident during the Egyptian Revolution of 1919. A train carrying British military personnel left Luxor on March 17th. At Nag Hammadi, local Egyptians boarded and harassed the soldiers. At Assiut, Kaimakam Pope Bey of the Egyptian Prisons Department joined the train. On March 18th, hostile crowds gathered at various stations, throwing stones and trying to board. At Deirout, a large crowd attacked the train, entered the first-class carriage, and killed one or two British passengers. At the next station, Der Moes (Deir Mawas), reinforced crowds armed with stones, sticks, and knives killed all remaining unarmed British passengers. Their bodies were put back on the train, except for one, and the train continued amidst further crowds.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a highly urgent diplomatic telegram sent by the British High Commissioner for Egypt to the Foreign Office in London, dated April 4, 1919, detailing a notorious and tragic incident during the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 (the Deir Mawas incident). The telegram describes the journey of a train that departed Luxor on March 17, 1919, carrying British officers and soldiers, which was repeatedly beset by nationalist crowds protesting British colonial rule. As the train traveled north through Upper Egypt, passing Nag Hammadi and Assiut (where Kaimakam Pope Bey joined), it was violently attacked at Deirout and Deir Mawas (Der Moes) on March 18. Unarmed British personnel, including Pope Bey and several soldiers, were brutally killed by crowds armed with sticks, stones, and knives. This report highlights the intense anti-British sentiment and violent unrest that characterized the 1919 revolution, which ultimately forced Great Britain to unilaterally declare Egyptian independence in 1922.

TELEGRAM.
2.
COMMISSIONER FOR EGYPT
Cairo.
Native ticket inspector and two native officials travelling made unsuccessful efforts to deceive and divert attention of mob but on arrival at Deirut they battered at closed doors and windows. Colonel Pope and two others who got out on other side were murdered, and bodies put in brake van. Though Acting station master had sent message to local police on seeing threatening attitude of mob one hour before train was due, Police Officer only arrived about 20 minutes after arrival of train with some six unarmed men out of 40 armed men available. He did nothing and sent no warning ahead. Acting station master in spite of opposition eventually got train away, natives swarming all over it, and remaining British at bay in two compartments. At Deir [Deirut] another dense mob attacked train. Two British managed to reach engine and they and native driver tried to start train but vacuum brake had been applied. Driver fled and two British were overpowered and battered to death. Three remaining British also gained engine, and made no effort to work levers, but fought till overpowered. Five bodies battered beyond recognition were thrown on the platform, stripped, and subjected to worst indignities. Sixty Egyptian soldiers returning from Sudan by train to join reserve leaned out of windows cheering. Their officers took no effective action. Police again arrived late and did nothing.

The report highlights the failure of local police to intervene, the mob's attack on the train, the killing of British passengers, and the complicity or inaction of Egyptian soldiers returning from Sudan who cheered as the violence occurred.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The Residency
15-4-19
For the last week I have been working on the Deir-Mawas murder case. First it has been very difficult to procure any evidence at all. Not a single Police officer can be trusted; for instance the Mamur of Police who was acting Mamur, took no steps at all to stop the hostile demonstration in the station on the day of the murder. The few murderers who were arrested and sent to the Markaz he released shortly afterwards without even taking their names; in the case of the attack on the steamers, certain notables were allowed to speak to the villages on the steamers, telling them to come on and attack; one notable was wounded in the attack, he now producing a letter purporting to be written by the noting Mamur asking him to go to the river to stop the people. I am convinced that this letter is fabricated and was written after the event to shield the notable. Similarly in a lesser degree with the other Markaz officials. I have had to imprison four of them. The murder of the officers was even a more brutal affair than is at first supposed, for two hours the officers were being gradually murdered, they had nothing to defend themselves with except a luncheon basket, soda-water bottles and lumps of coal. At Deir-Mawas, the crowd were breaking in the carriage windows with nabuts, dragging Pope boy into the platform and murdering him with sticks and knives, boarding the train to set at the other officers and beating the carriages with stones. From Deir-Mawas the first class carriages must have been full - inside and outside - with a howling mob, and finally the scene at Deir-Mawas defies description, Major Bayer Anderson is reporting fully on this, there is little doubt that while the women were drinking with delight and urging on the men, their husbands after ordering the Englishmen stripped them and subjected them to every form of insult. Besides the Egyptian Army officers who were travelling on the train, the police officers at both stations did practically nothing to protect the Englishmen.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official report from the British Residency in Egypt regarding the investigation into the Deir-Mawas murder case during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It details the complicity of local police officials, the fabrication of evidence by notables to avoid prosecution, and the brutal nature of the attack on British officers, describing the mob violence and the failure of local authorities to intervene.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential report from the British Residency in Cairo, dated April 1919, concerning the investigation into the Deir-Mawas incident—a violent episode during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution against British colonial rule. The report highlights the systemic failure of local Egyptian police and officials to protect British personnel, alleging that they were either complicit in the violence or actively obstructing the investigation by releasing suspects and fabricating exculpatory evidence. It provides a harrowing account of the mob violence against British officers, reflecting the intense anti-colonial sentiment and the breakdown of order in Upper Egypt during the uprising.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Inquiry along the line from MINIA to ASSIUT into the MURDER of 9 BRITISH OFFICERS & N.C.Os at DEIRUT & DEIR-MOWIE on the morning of March 18th 1919.

For at least 24 hours before this incident crowds had collected between MINIA & BENI QORRA and probably also further N & S of these places.

These were doubtless influenced by news of the VASTA riot and murder on the 15-3-19 and of the rioting in Cairo since the 9-3-19.

It is said that inflammatory accounts of the "shooting of school boys" by British troops in Cairo had aggravated the already critical condition of affairs.

These station crowds at first contented themselves by meeting in coming and out-going trains with patriotic cries of "Long Live Egypt" "Zaghlul" "Down with the English", and by travelling free from station to station.

In a few instances where they encountered English Inspectors ( as in the case of Mr. Burnand, at MALLAWI on the 17th ) they were markedly hostile.

On the 17th also there was a considerable exchange of peoples travelling free between stations from MINIA & BENI QORRA ( where the up and down trains meet and pass ). This seems to have been an organised movement between MALLAWI and DEIRUT which latter place was strongly reinforced from the former.

These reinforcements remained at DEIRUT until next day, staying in and about the station and taking part in a procession of students held there.

The 8.30 p.m. Express No 77 from LUXOR on the 17th left with the 8 or 9 officers and N.C.Os, since murdered - together with some other Europeans who fortunately quitted the train on its arrival at ASSIUT ( 12.20 a.m. 18-3-19 ) where there must have been a rumour if not actual warning of trouble ahead.

The express did not proceed beyond ASSIUT so that the 8 or 9 concerned caught the 6.55 a.m. local train on the 18th for CAIRO which was booked to stop at every station on route. There were no other Europeans and no women on this train as has been rumoured.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an intelligence report detailing the events leading up to the murder of nine British officers and non-commissioned officers near Deirut and Deir-Mowie on March 18, 1919. It describes the spread of civil unrest following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, noting how crowds gathered at railway stations, influenced by reports of riots in Cairo and Vasta. The text highlights the organized nature of the protests, the hostile treatment of British officials, and the movement of agitators between stations. It concludes by tracing the final movements of the British personnel who were killed after transferring to a local train at Assiut, noting that they were the only Europeans on board.

As far as one can gather the actual party consisted of 3 or 4 officers (including Colonel Pope, Major Jarvis, a staff officer) and 4 or 5 N.C.Os., amongst them C.S.M. SUMMERSGILL, 6th Manchesters attd. I.C.C., an Australian and 2 I.C.C. other ranks. The N.C.Os. were probably travelling 2nd class from Assiut where there seems to have been no hostile gathering but being received later by threatening crowds which boarded the train at ABU GOHHA they all collected in the single first class carriage at the head of the train which was only separated from the engine by the break-van. None of the party was armed.
Before reaching BEIRUT at the scheduled time 0825 all doors and shutters had been closed and the train 'Farrash' put in the adjacent second class carriage, with instructions from the ticket inspector HAJJ ALI to tell the crowds that the 1st class was unoccupied.
The train was now packed however, even the carriage roof being covered with men, news had been travelling ahead and there were many informers so that the mob at BEIRUT were not deceived, and at once began battering at the doors and windows.
On this a native KAIMAKAM SHUKRI Bey of the Prisons Department who was travelling with said Colonel Pope and a ticket inspector and, Guda opened one shutter and putting out their heads assured the people that the Bey and his family were the only ones present.
This had no effect however. The carriage was rushed and entered by rioters armed with knives and pikes, amongst them was one abd el Zaki Ali and his partner, poultry dealers of BEIRUT, these two and others remained in the carriage and went with it as far as DEIR LOLIE. Shukri Bey and the ticket inspector escaped to the 2nd class while Col Pope got out on the opposite line and was last seen, crawling under the train to escape and concentrated attack - his body was afterwards placed in the break-van, some say, still alive.
It is stated also that the body of 1 murdered Englishman was put into the engine furnace and consumed at Beirut. The engine driver denies this stating that he was present in the engine room the whole time at Beirut though absent from it at DEIR LOLIE where this might have happened.
The rioters had won broken in all the doors and windows of the carriage with stones, sticks, axes and pikes.

The acting station master Sidhom Eff., Hanna who was on duty (in the presence of the station master Gindi Eff., Yusuf on a few days' rest from whom he could hear the riot but was to overcome to assist) as he says - spent as a matter of fact in his room above Deirut Station, where he sent a message for assistance (a copy is filed in the station wake) to the markaz at 07:30 a.m., (i.e., one hour before the train was due), but only 20 minutes after the train's arrival did the kulahis of police (quleis Taha Eff., Nier a couple of policemen and a few ghafirs, all unarmed - these took little or no active part in the fighting.
The late arrival of the police and ghafirs, their inadequate numbers, ill-disciplined, unarmed condition and apathy - together with the fact that with a possible force of some dozen, armed police and 30 or more ghafirs, at his disposal, the police officer did not provide an adequate escort, either to travel on with the train, or to conduct the party to the markaz at Deirut for safety, and did not wire warning the markaz at Deirut or Mallawi, seems criminal neglect of duty, which implicates any at Deirut, these remarks are equally applicable to markaz authorities at Deir Moris. Gindi Eff himself eventually forced his way to the river, but found that his electric staff had been taken from the matter.
This he recovered with difficulty and gave him, but it was again snatched away. Finally Yall being now willing that the train should start, the staff was produced, they cleared away from on top, and from in front of the engine, and let it proceed, half an hour late to Deir Moris.
The time of departure was wired ahead and the condition of affairs had been already made known to Deir Moris and Mallawi stations by H.S.R. telegraph and telephone. The train left the station with an excited mob swarming on the roof gangways, etc., and the remaining British at bay in a couple of compartments of the 1st class.
On reaching Deir Moris at 9:30 a.m., (30 minutes late) there were still 9 of the party alive in the carriage. Two, possibly 3 others besides Col. Pope having been killed at Deirut or between it and Deir Moris and their bodies stowed away in the adjacent break-van.

ai_content.transcribed_text: The Kulahiz of Police, Mustafa Tani, Hilmi on being summoned at once from the Markaz by the station master, arrived half an hour later with the Omda, 3 mounted and 4 unmounted police, all unarmed, but as at Deirut, there was no effort to assist. Steam, however, was low and it took over 10 minutes to stoke-up, when, as at Deirut, by general consent the train was allowed to proceed, before it did so, all the bodies, some half clad, but mostly naked, were thrown into a sort of break-van where several of the murderers remained with them. The train reached Mallawi (station master Tadros Ef. Boktor) at 10.16 nearly an hour late. The station was packed with the usual excited mob. The first class carriage was quite empty, but in the break-van were the 7 bodies, one of them dangling out of the door, another body had been dropped or dragged out just at the beginning of the Mallawi platform. This was that of O.K.B. Summergill 6th Lancers etc., M.G. It has since been buried at Ashmunein by the Hamur and reports made on it by the Wakil Nimba and police doctor. When the train drew up, people surged forward to see and execute the murderers, but before they could get at them it was steamed out of the platform at 10.20 (i.e. after 4 minutes). A stop was made at the next station Roda to take on water. There as at subsequent halts, a large crowd pressed forward to see, and execrate the murdered English. By order of the E.S.R. Inspector at Mallawi (Abu El Ghani) it was missed as also Abu Kerkas where there was a huge demonstration and many mounted men carrying banners, swords, ploke etc., but beyond Abu Kerkas the vacuum break-van was again applied. Kaisi with great forethought, had the van containing the bodies together with the wrecked 1st class compartment uncoupled, and shunted off straight away. Conclusion.

It seems apparent from the above that events at Cairo and Wasta (sequent to the deportation of the Nationalist leaders) were followed by a carefully planned and systematic destruction of the railway in Upper Egypt, in the mechanical details of which the technical officials seem themselves to have been largely implicated.

Everything seems to point to the murder of the 18th, being an organised concentration of murderous peasantry on the train and at the stations concerned.

Guissaries apparently travelled by the train itself, and got out at Deirut and Deir Moute.

The complete destruction of every Englishman seems to have been insured. Had any survived beyond Deir Moute he would certainly have been killed later at Mallawi or Abu Kerkas or elsewhere.

The connivance of the police and markaz authorities must have been obtained. They allowed themselves to be disarmed, the strongly defensible markaz at Deirut to be sacked without the slightest resistance, and not only no steps were taken to defend those attacked or escort them to safety, but they were actually sent on to certain death unguarded.

The administrative staffs of the station concerned seem to have been powerless to act but appear to have done the best they could.

The behaviour of the Egyptian soldiers in the train at the time was cowardly and disgraceful in the extreme, and the inaction of the 2 or 3 Egyptian officers deserves the severest censure. The present condition in this area, seems to me volcanic.

COPY.
The Residency
Deirut, 18-4-19.
Dear Mr. Haines,
I have just got back from Cairo. After that pessimistic feeling that is so infectious in Cairo, everything up here is full of hope. The people appear very subdued, extraordinarily different from the insolence of the Cairo effendi. I do not think I can do better than stay here and watch the inquiry into the murder case, and collect new evidence.
At present the evidence is coming in very well.
I expect to go to Assiut on Sunday or Monday to see Gen: Shea who is expected back from Kena.
The troops are continuing to visit villages every day in search of arms. We have got 550 in five days, and in the course of the next week I hope to get another 2000. The same is being done at Assiut.
Of course this is not much, but it is better than nothing and I hope we may soon start fining the villages.
I forgot to tell you how well the Mudir of Girga has done in keeping his province quiet. If you could spare the time to write him a word of praise, it would be much appreciated and well deserved.
I am, Sir,
Yours sincerely,
(Signed) N.D. Macnaghten.
Copies to:
Residency,
G.S. "I" (b),
Mr. Morice,

He praises the Mudir (governor) of Girga for maintaining order and requests that a commendation be sent to him.

CONFIDENTIAL
General Headquarters,
Egyptian Expeditionary Force.

With reference to the attached report, this appears to be a matter which involves officials who are responsible for the Public Security. What information they received and what they conveyed to Higher Authority, and as to whether their immediate superiors, is a matter which may require investigation.

I am of opinion that the Military Authorities are involved, but should an enquiry be instituted, it is essential that they be represented and not restricted in a hearing.

Headquarters,
Cairo,
24th April 1919.

(a) The railway officials at Assiut had very definite evidence of serious unrest on the line on the 17th (as is shown by copies of wires they received which are now in the possession of the G.O.C. Huddleston's Force), yet no action appears to have been taken.

Taking these facts into consideration, I am of opinion that there is a reflection on the action of British officials of the Egyptian Government both at Assiut and Cairo in this affair, and therefore consider that it would be more appropriate should this enquiry be ordered by you than locally by me.

Further, I desire to clear up a suggestion which has been made, of conspiracy amongst Egyptians at Assiut to prevent the murdered officers and other ranks being informed of the state of affairs to the north.

Rear H.Q. Upper Egypt,
April 19th 1919.

W.H. Huddleston
Major-General,
Cmdg. Upper Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
CONFIDENTIAL
G.O.C., Egypt.
I beg to request that a Court of Inquiry may be convened for the purpose of enquiring into:-
1. Reasons why British Officers and O.Rs. were allowed to proceed north from Asyut on Train 77 on the morning of the 18th March, although the area north of Asyut had been in a state of dangerous unrest since 15th March.
2. The behaviour of Civil officials between Asyut and Minia during the period 15th to 18th March, both dates inclusive, regarding the matter of warnings of danger to their superiors.
The investigation of the Deirout Murder Case, shows that the murdered Officers and men should never have been allowed to travel on Train 77 on the 18th taking into account the following:-
(a) Asyut was never out of touch with Cairo by wire via WADI HALFA, but no wires suggesting the prevention of Europeans travelling appear to have been received or sent.
(b) Officials barely escaped with their lives on the 17th and reached Asyut on that date, but the train no. 77 was nevertheless allowed to run on the 19th.
(c) The railway officials at Asyut had very definite evidence of serious unrest on the line on the 17th (as is shown by copies of wires which are now in the possession of the G.O.C. Huddleston's Force), yet no action seems to have been taken.
Taking these facts into consideration, I am of opinion that there is a reflection on the action of British officials of the Egyptian government both at Asyut and Cairo in this affair, and therefore consider that it would be more appropriate should this enquiry be ordered by you than locally by me.
Further, I desire to clear up a suggestion which has been made, of conspiracy amongst Egyptians at Asyut to prevent the murdered officers and other ranks being informed of the state of affairs to the north.

H. H. Huddleston
Major-General,
Cmdg. Upper Egypt.
Rear H.Q. Upper Egypt,
April 19th, 1919.

It also addresses the conduct of civil officials and investigates potential conspiracies among the local Egyptian population to withhold information from the British military.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
A Commission is instituted to inquire into:-
1. The reasons why British officers and other ranks were allowed to proceed north from Asyut by train No. 77 on the morning of March 19th.
2. The measures of precaution taken by the responsible civil officials during the days immediately preceding March 19th in view of the dangerous condition of the country between Asyut and Minia.

The Commission is composed of:-
Sir Alexander Wood Renton, Kt., - Chairman.
Judge H. W. Baynes, K.C.,
Lieut. Colonel H. Laurie, D.S.O., R.F.A.

The Commission is authorised to summon before it and to interrogate all persons, civil or military, whose evidence it may consider it desirable to take. All persons so summoned are required to attend before the Commission and to give their evidence accordingly.

The Commission will report to the Commander-in-Chief.

1st May, 1919.

It lists the appointed members of the commission and grants them the legal authority to summon and interrogate witnesses, with the final report to be submitted to the Commander-in-Chief.

MINISTRY OF THE INTERIOR
Cairo.
(2)
191
Education, improved communications, telephones, etc. than to the Mudir being made responsible for public security, I cannot say.
Recent events may compel the English Government to return to the system of English Commandants as Sir John Shea suggests. I should view this with great regret, and am of opinion that it would be intensely unpopular with the classes interested in securing a greater share in their own Government, and, needless to say, with the officers of the Police. Any decision on this point, which I think is of great political importance, should be deferred for the present.
As regards the summary dismissal of all police officials in Assiut town and those in the Provinces, guilty of misconduct but not brought before Military Tribunals, I cannot agree with Sir John Shea. The Ministry proposes, however, to try these officers by a Special Council of Discipline in the Ministry of Interior on evidence supplied by the Military Authorities. An appeal from this would lie with the Superior Council of Discipline.
I am strongly against the proposal to retire Allam Pacha and the sub-Mudir on the evidence I have seen. Up to March 23rd he seems to have shown real ability in carrying out a policy which after all was acquiesced in by his Inspector and the Military Authorities in Assiut. Had General Huddleston reached Assiut on March 22nd instead of March 25th, there would have been no riot, and the Mudir's record would have been considered excellent. I am afraid most of the other fourteen Mudirs would have behaved like Allam Pacha, badly served as he was by his Commandant of Police and the Mamour Bandar, and I do not consider it just that he alone should suffer.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official memorandum from the Ministry of the Interior in Cairo, discussing administrative and security policies in Egypt. The author evaluates the suggestion by Sir John Shea to reinstate English Commandants, expressing concern that such a move would be politically unpopular. The text addresses the disciplinary actions against police officials in Assiut following a riot, rejecting summary dismissals in favor of a Special Council of Discipline. Finally, the author defends Allam Pacha, the Mudir of Assiut, arguing that his actions were reasonable given the circumstances and the lack of support from his subordinates, and that he should not be unfairly penalized for the riot.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an internal administrative memorandum from the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior, likely dating to the early 20th century (post-1919 revolution era). It reflects the tension between British colonial oversight and Egyptian administrative autonomy. The text highlights the debate over the 'English Commandant' system, the handling of civil unrest in Assiut, and the internal disciplinary processes for Egyptian officials (Mudirs) during a period of political instability. It provides insight into the British advisory role in the Egyptian police force and the complexities of maintaining public order while managing nationalist sentiment.

THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO.
24th May 1919.
Sir,
I have the honour to acknowledge your letter of to-day forwarding the evidence recorded by the Commission of inquiry into certain matters connected with the train murders in Upper Egypt, and a map showing all the material damage to the Egyptian railway system between the 15th and the morning of the 10th March last.
I am, sir,
Your obedient servant,
[Signature]
Sir Alexander Wood Renton, Kt.,
Ministry of Justice,
Cairo.
ai_content.english_translation: The Residency, Cairo. 24th May 1919. Sir, I have the honour to acknowledge your letter of today forwarding the evidence recorded by the Commission of inquiry into certain matters connected with the train murders in Upper Egypt, and a map showing all the material damage to the Egyptian railway system between the 15th and the morning of the 10th March last. I am, sir, Your obedient servant, [Signature], Sir Alexander Wood Renton, Kt., Ministry of Justice, Cairo.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official correspondence from the British Residency in Cairo, dated May 1919, addressed to Sir Alexander Wood Renton at the Egyptian Ministry of Justice. It acknowledges the receipt of evidence and a map regarding the 'train murders' and sabotage of the Egyptian railway system that occurred during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The document reflects the British colonial administration's efforts to document and investigate the widespread civil unrest and anti-colonial violence that paralyzed infrastructure in Upper Egypt during the spring of 1919.

24th May 1919.

MR. AMOS.

The Special High Commissioner has directed me to send you the enclosed report of the Commission of Enquiry in connection with occurrences near Assiut.

His Excellency will be glad if you will appoint an official of your Department to examine the report and suggest points on which action should be taken.

Will you kindly return the report as soon as possible as it is desired to pass it on to the Military Authorities for similar examination.

I send also herewith a map submitted by Sir A. Wood Renton with the report.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official memorandum dated May 24, 1919, addressed to Mr. Amos. It conveys instructions from the Special High Commissioner to review an enclosed report regarding incidents that occurred near Assiut. The recipient is requested to assign a departmental official to analyze the report and recommend necessary actions. The document also notes that a map provided by Sir A. Wood Renton is included and requests the return of the report for subsequent review by Military Authorities.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative communication from the British High Commission in Egypt, dated shortly after the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It concerns the aftermath of civil unrest and violence in the region of Assiut. The 'Commission of Enquiry' mentioned was likely tasked with investigating the disturbances that occurred during the nationalist uprising against British colonial rule. The involvement of the 'Military Authorities' and the reference to Sir A. Wood Renton (a British judge who served as Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Cyprus and later in Egypt) highlights the intersection of judicial inquiry and military governance during the British Protectorate period in Egypt.

REPORT ON THE COURT OF ENQUIRY on THE CIVIL ADMINISTRATION OF THE PROVINCE OF ASSIUT DURING MARCH, 1919.

Judge Mc. Barnett and Mr. Allam have presented, in my opinion, a most valuable report and I agree with most of their conclusions. I give my observations when necessary, paragraph by paragraph.

(6) I think Secret Service funds in the Mudirs' hands have proved of no political value. We have come to the conclusion that in future the Interior Inspectors must have more to say concerning the expenditure. Local agents are necessary in the Provinces.

(7) I do not agree that the Police force has lost efficiency and prestige during the last four years. It has now been tested and failed, but failed because the movement throughout the country has been looked upon as a political movement of far reaching importance to Egyptians.

(8) It seems clear that the Assiut Police Officers behaved very badly in the recent disturbances. There has never been any idea in the minds of police officers that fire-arms could not be used to put down disorder, but at Assiut the policy of non resistance was justified on the ground that killing members of a riotous mob would simply mean the destruction of the small force.

(9) The inadequate number of English Inspectors in the Ministry of Interior is the real reason why abuses were so rife in connection with the supply of fodder and labour for the Military Authorities. But it is only right to say that the Inspectors were up to their pre-war standard. That is to say one for every two Mudiriehs. An increase in their number may raise political difficulties, but I hope these will be surmounted.
(10-17) No remarks.
(18) The trial of some of the Notables mentioned in the Report may bring to light what has never yet been proved. I mean that there were leaders of the better class who really meant to overturn the Government by an organized insurrection.
(19) It is astonishing to me that the near approach of General Huddleston's force was not enough to deter the Mamour Bandar from any participation in an attempt to subvert the Government. News seems to have passed rapidly from place to place, and the flotilla was on its way between Minia and Asiut. Summary vengeance was a certainty if English lives were lost.
(20) Mr. Macnaghten seems to me to have acted throughout with courage and ability.
(21) I am in agreement with the report as to the conduct of Allam Pacha. Had we been able to inform him of the nearness of relief, he might have acted with greater boldness. General Huddleston's delay on route, due I suppose to the low river, was fatal to the safety of the town. He only arrived at noon on March 25th, but Mr. Burnett-Stuart visited Asiut on March 22nd.
