ai_content.transcribed_text: CONFIDENTIAL. The Residency, Ramleh, EGYPT. 1. I forward herewith for the information of His Excellency the Special High Commissioner copies of correspondence with regard to the report of the Wood-Renton Commission. 2. The Commander-in-Chief agrees with General Bulfin's view that the Military authorities did not assume any control over UPPER EGYPT until the evening of the 18th. The responsibility for communicating intelligence in UPPER EGYPT appears therefore to have rested up to that date with the Ministry of the Interior. 3. With regard to para XVI of the Wood-Renton report, it appears that attempts were made, after direct communication with UPPER EGYPT was cut on March 15, to communicate via the SUDAN; but that owing to the fact that the lines from CAIRO to SUEZ were cut at the same time, no messages actually passed by this route before March 19, when a telegram from KHARTOUM, dated March 18, was received at CAIRO. 4. The copy of the report of the Commission and Evidence is returned herewith. (Signed) A.L. Lynden-Bell, Major-General, Chief of the General Staff, Egyptian Expeditionary Force. 22nd June 1919.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official memorandum from the British Residency in Ramleh, Egypt, dated June 22, 1919. It addresses the findings of the Wood-Renton Commission regarding the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The text clarifies that British military authorities did not take control of Upper Egypt until March 18, 1919, placing prior responsibility on the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior. It also details communication failures between Cairo, Suez, and the Sudan during the unrest, noting that telegrams were delayed due to severed lines.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal administrative record concerning the British military's response to the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. The Wood-Renton Commission was established to investigate the causes and handling of the widespread nationalist uprisings against British colonial rule. This specific memorandum serves to clarify the timeline of military intervention and the breakdown of communication infrastructure during the height of the protests in March 1919. It highlights the administrative friction between the British military command (Egyptian Expeditionary Force) and the Egyptian civil government, providing critical context for the British assessment of the security situation in Upper Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text: CONFIDENTIAL. G.S. 1531/90. General Officer Commanding, EGYPT. 1. Attached is a copy of the report of the Wood-Renton Commission which was formed to enquire into the reasons why British officers and O.R. were allowed to proceed north from ASYUT on the morning of the 16th March. 2. His Excellency The Special High Commissioner has asked for remarks on the report from the military authorities concerned. 3. The paragraphs of the Commission's report which chiefly concern the military authorities are para. 16 (pages 17 and 18) and the conclusion on this paragraph (XVI, page 34). 4. It is suggested in these paragraphs that the civil authorities in UPPER EGYPT been informed from CAIRO of the seriousness of the situation in the DELTA, it might have caused them to realise the dangers threatening in their own province. 5. Will you please obtain from General Watson his remarks on the report of the Commission and forward them with any comments of the military authorities; and forward them with any comments you may wish to make. (Signed) A. P. Wavell, Major-General, Chief of the General Staff, Egyptian Expeditionary Force. 9/6/19. Copy of report to be returned. D.B.G., E.E.F. I concur in Major-General Watson's remarks. Until the arrival of Major-General Huddleston at ASYUT the Civil Government were in sole charge of the Country from that date the military took control of the situation. I can therefore only regard the Civil authorities as being entirely responsible for the state of affairs and the methods of communication and intelligence until the night of the 16th March when the Military assumed control. (Signed) Edward Bulfin, Lieut.-General, Commanding EGYPT. 22nd June 1919.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official military memorandum regarding the Wood-Renton Commission report, which investigated the circumstances surrounding the movement of British personnel from Asyut on March 16th. It includes instructions from the Chief of the General Staff, A.P. Wavell, to obtain comments from General Watson regarding the Commission's findings, specifically concerning the failure of civil authorities in Cairo to adequately warn those in Upper Egypt about the severity of the situation in the Delta. The document concludes with a formal statement by Lieut.-General Edward Bulfin, who asserts that the Civil Government held sole responsibility for the situation until the military took control on the night of March 16th.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of internal British military correspondence from the Egyptian Expeditionary Force (E.E.F.) dated June 1919, following the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It concerns the administrative and military accountability for the security failures that occurred during the unrest, specifically focusing on the Wood-Renton Commission's inquiry into the movement of British troops from Asyut. The document highlights the friction between civil and military authorities in Egypt during the British occupation, with General Bulfin explicitly distancing the military from responsibility for the intelligence and communication failures that preceded the military takeover of the region on March 16th, 1919.

ai_content.transcribed_text: CONFIDENTIAL. G.S.6/12. General Staff, EGYPT. With reference to your memo, No. G.S.47/7 dated 10th instant, and letter No. G.S.1531/20 dated 9th idem, from the Food-Ration Commission, I have the honour to make the following remarks:- 11. From the commencement of the disturbances the Military authorities were dependent entirely upon information received from the Ministry of the Interior, the Residency, and from reports received from the Director of Railways, Sir George Macaulay, with all of whom they kept in close touch. Troops despatched in the first instance to various Mudirieh towns, were sent in aid of the Civil Power, and it was presumed that the Ministry of the Interior was communicating all information on the state of the Country to its responsible officials in the Provinces, as it was to the Military authorities. Commencing from the 11th March, the Director of Railway Transport attended the daily Conferences at headquarters, Force in Egypt, and from the 16th March, Mr. [Name illegible], Liaison Officer with the Interior, Public Security Department, attended also, and were fully cognizant of the state of the Country, as far as was known to the Military authorities, as all information of importance was daily read out at the Conference. 2). Railway and Telegraphic communications into the South were cut near CAIRO on the 15th March, and news of the murder of Mr. Smith at WASTA was not received until the 16th. Arrangements were then made to despatch further Indian troops by water on the 16th and 17th to WASTA, and a British Infantry battalion on the 18th with Brigadier-General Huddlestone, whose orders were to take command of all troops in Upper Egypt and to restore order, etc. Brigadier-General Huddlestone arrived at WASTA on the evening of the 18th, and from that moment it may be assumed that the Military had taken over command of the situation in Upper Egypt. Headquarters, Abbassia, 20th June 1919. (Signed) H. D. Watson, Major-General, Commanding Cairo District. I concur in Major-General Watson's remarks. Until the arrival of Brigadier-General Huddlestone at WASTA the Civil Government were in sole charge of the Country from that date the Military took over control of the situation. I can therefore only regard the Civil authorities as being entirely responsible for the state of affairs and the methods of communication and intelligence until the night of the 18th March when the Military assumed control. 22nd June 1919. (Signed) Edward Bulfin, Lieut-General, Commanding EGYPT.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal military report regarding the command structure and communication failures during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution. It details the reliance of the British military on the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior for intelligence, the disruption of communications near Cairo, the murder of a British official at Wasta, and the subsequent deployment of troops to restore order in Upper Egypt. It concludes with a formal concurrence by Lieutenant-General Bulfin, clarifying that the Civil Government held responsibility for the situation until the military took direct control on March 18th.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential military report from the British occupation forces in Egypt, dated June 1919. It serves as an administrative post-mortem of the British response to the 1919 Egyptian Revolution (the 'disturbances'). The text highlights the friction between the British military command and the Egyptian Civil Government, specifically regarding the flow of intelligence and the timing of the military's assumption of control in the provinces. It provides critical evidence of the British transition from supporting the 'Civil Power' to direct military governance in response to the widespread nationalist uprising.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
CONFIDENTIAL
G.S. 47/7.
Chief of the General Staff,
G. H. Q.
Reference your G.S. 1531/20 dated 24th. June.
I regret the delay in replying to the above quoted letter.
I know that I gave orders for efforts to be made to communicate with UPPER EGYPT via the SUDAN, but, owing to the constant changes in my Staff, and to the fact that Major G.H. BELL, who was my only Staff Officer on the dates in question, is no longer with me, I have found it necessary to refer the matter to the D.S.O. in C. to find out what steps were actually taken.
I find that everything possible was done and that as soon as direct communication was cut, UPPER EGYPT via SUEZ, PORT SUDAN, and WADI HALFA.
The lines from SUEZ to CAIRO were out on the 15th. and again on the 16th. March. Commencing the 18th. March I arranged for aeroplanes to take telegrams to ISMAILIA or SUEZ for transmission to UPPER EGYPT.
The E.S.T. arranged to send telegrams to UPPER EGYPT via SUEZ, PORT SUDAN and WADI HALFA on the 19th. March but had to cancel this on receipt of information that the wires were out between WADI HALFA and ASSWAN. It was not until 21st. and 22nd. March that they accepted messages for ASSWAN and ASSIUT respectively.
Throughout the whole of this period communication North of WADI HALFA was very intermittent and although the E.S.T. Repair gangs were constantly at work repairing the lines it was not until the 22nd. that satisfactory touch was obtained North of ASSWAN.
I attach a report on this subject from the G.O.C., Cairo District.
With reference to para. 2 of this report I have been unable to get into touch with the SOUDAN AGENCY as their Offices were closed during BATRAN. I will send a supplementary report on obtaining information from them.
(Sgd) Edward J. Bulfin.
Lieut-General,
Commanding EGYPT.
H.Q., EGYPT.
2nd. July, 1919.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal military memorandum from Lieutenant-General Edward J. Bulfin, Commanding Egypt, to the Chief of the General Staff at General Headquarters. It addresses a delay in responding to a previous inquiry regarding communication failures in Upper Egypt during March 1919. The report details the disruption of telegraph lines between Cairo, Suez, and Upper Egypt, the use of aeroplanes to bypass these disruptions, and the difficulties faced by the Egyptian State Telegraphs (E.S.T.) in maintaining contact with stations like Wadi Halfa, Asswan, and Assiut. It notes that staff turnover, specifically the departure of Major G.H. Bell, hindered the initial investigation into the communication breakdown.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British military administrative correspondence from the post-WWI period in Egypt, dated July 1919. It provides insight into the logistical challenges faced by the British occupation forces during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution, specifically regarding the maintenance of telegraphic and military communications between Cairo and the southern provinces (Upper Egypt and the Sudan). The document highlights the reliance on alternative transport methods, such as aeroplanes, when ground-based telegraph infrastructure was sabotaged or disrupted, and reflects the administrative friction and staff instability within the British military command during this volatile period.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
CONFIDENTIAL.
GS. 22/14.
Headquarters
EGYPT.

Reference your No. GS. 47/7 dated 25th. inst.

I greatly regret that I can find no trace of any communication with the Sudan between the 15th. and 18th. March or of any attempt to send any message.

"G.S." 2nd. Echelon were I believe in communication with the Sudan through the Sudan Agency in Cairo - and perhaps enquiry may be made from both as to whether any message passed on those dates.

From information received up to the 16th. March when news of the murder of Mr. Smith at Wasta reached me I had no great anxiety in regard to the Provinces South of the Fayoum and Beni Suef.

On receipt of the above news arrangements for the prompt despatch by water of further troops to Upper Egypt were made - and the remainder of the 46th. Punjabis left the same day.

Headquarters.
Abbassia.
29-3-1919.
(Sgd) H.D. Watson
Major General,
Commanding CAIRO District.

(1) I have read the Report of Sir Alexander Wood Renton's Commission and the minutes of evidence taken before it.
(2) As regards the conduct of Interior Officials in the Mudirieh of Assiut, I agree with the finding of the Commission that if the ordinary police officials in the Markazes North of Assiut had only done their duty the outrages would never have taken place. By this I mean that if proper intelligence had reached the Mudir or Mr. Macnaghten no English passengers would have been allowed to travel north and even the train itself would have been detained at Assiut. The police officials, guilty of this criminal neglect, are, I understand, under trial.
(3) The Commission may well express astonishment that the Mudir did not know more about what was going on in his province, but I should gather there was a criminal conspiracy to keep him in ignorance. He was known to be in the closest touch with the English Inspector and Capt. Cowell.
(4) It is obvious that, in spite of Mr. Morice's circular of January 1913, the Commandant of Police showed no initiative and seemed glad to shelter himself behind the Mudir without whose express orders he declared he could not take any action.

My Lord,
The good impression given by the Mohamed Said Ministry as reported in my telegram No. 635 of March 23rd, 1919, has been confirmed. Mohamed Said Pasha himself and his colleagues have shown a firm front, in face of many difficulties, and this attitude has undoubtedly contributed greatly to the return of the country to its present condition of quiet, and to the restitution of the normal activities of the civil power.
Both the Prime Minister's desire to avoid popularity among Egyptians and his anxiety to placate his countrymen by measures involving a show of concession obtained from myself have led at times to position of some difficulty. As an example I have the honour to quote the following incident which occurred during my recent absence in Syria.
The Prime Minister heard on July 2nd, through the Adviser to the Ministry of the Interior, that 45 executions
/An
The Right Honourable
Earl Curzon of Kedleston, K.G., G.C.S.I., etc., etc., etc.
ai_content.english_translation: My Lord, The positive impression created by the Mohamed Said Ministry, as previously reported in my telegram No. 635 dated March 23, 1919, has been validated. Mohamed Said Pasha and his associates have maintained a firm stance despite numerous challenges, which has significantly helped restore order and normal civil governance in the country. The Prime Minister's balancing act—trying to avoid being seen as too popular with the Egyptian public while simultaneously attempting to appease them by seeking concessions from me—has occasionally created difficult situations. For instance, while I was away in Syria, the Prime Minister learned on July 2nd from the Interior Ministry Adviser that 45 executions were planned.

The author (likely the British High Commissioner) evaluates the stability of the government, noting the tension between the Prime Minister's efforts to maintain British-mandated order and his need to manage Egyptian nationalist sentiment through perceived concessions. The mention of '45 executions' refers to the ongoing judicial and military suppression of nationalist unrest during the period of the British Protectorate.

ai_content.transcribed_text: CONFIDENTIAL. Cairo, 4th December 1920. A.W. Keown-Boyd Esq., Private Secretary, The Residency. Dear Mr. Keown-Boyd, I am now beginning to collect material for the final report of the Indemnities Commission. If my recollection serves me aright, Colonel Lloyd, Mr. Baynes and I, in our Report, gave a somewhat careful the Deirut Train Murders, gave a break and spread of the historical summary of the outbreak and spread of the riots throughout Egypt, and we also annexed to the Report a large map showing the dates and scenes of all the disturbances. It would be a great assistance to me if His Excellency would allow me to have confidential access to these documents for a short time. I shall be greatly obliged if you can help me in the matter. Yours sincerely, A. Wood.

The author specifically requests to consult a previous report co-authored with Colonel Lloyd and Mr. Baynes, which detailed the 'Deirut Train Murders' and included a map documenting the timeline and locations of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution riots. ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. 6th July, 1928. Dear Bennett, Thanks for your letter No. SF/A.1(10) of June 30th. Would you do something for us in this connection? Hanem Aref wrote to us a short time ago, giving as her address EL-FIFRIE, ABU KORKES, MINIA, and enquiring what had become of the money which she understood had been deposited in a bank at her disposal after the events of 1919. As far as we know, there is no such money, and if Hanem Aref had really been under the impression that a deposit was awaiting her at one of the banks, I think she would have ascertained particulars at an earlier date than this. (Since she was given, in 1920, a collection of gold bracelets, which had been subscribed for among the British public in Cairo, the Residency at least has had no communication from her). It is just possible of course that some interested relative or friend has suddenly thought that there is money to be made out of Hanem Aref's good act. I have written the above to give you an idea of how the case stands. Now what we should like to know is this: Is Hanem Aref in real need? Could you have confidential and trustworthy enquiries made on the point? Yours sincerely, (sgd) Norman Mayers. G.W. Bennett Esq., European Dept.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal diplomatic letter from the British Residency in Cairo to G.W. Bennett regarding an inquiry from a woman named Hanem Aref. The author, Norman Mayers, explains that Hanem Aref, residing in Abu Korkes, Minia, is inquiring about funds she believes were deposited for her following the 1919 events. Mayers expresses skepticism about the existence of such funds, noting that she had previously received a collection of gold bracelets from the British public in Cairo in 1920. He suspects that a relative or friend might be prompting her to seek money. He concludes by asking Bennett to conduct a confidential investigation into whether Hanem Aref is in genuine financial need.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of internal British colonial administrative correspondence from the Residency in Cairo, dated July 1928. It highlights the British authorities' management of individuals involved in the political unrest of 1919 in Egypt. The letter reveals the intersection of humanitarian aid (the 1920 gold bracelet collection) and the bureaucratic scrutiny applied to Egyptian subjects who sought financial restitution or support from the British administration. It provides insight into the Residency's investigative methods and their cautious approach to claims of financial hardship among the local population in the Minia region.

MINUTE on Residency paper No. 8940/56
Mr. Smart.
Hanem Aref.
We have now obtained some information from Bennett regarding the financial condition of this Hanem Aref whose name came before the public in 1919 in connection with a generous gesture to a dying British soldier on Mellawi railway station.
The memorandum which I put up to you in June is not in the file. You will remember that Hanem Aref appealed to us for the remainder of the amount due to her. It was evident from Judge McBarnet's pamphlet (17880/1), the only paper we had to go on, that no fund existed for the benefit of Hanem Aref. The set of gold bracelets she received in 1920 being the end of the matter as far as money collected from British admirers of her generous act went. We can of course confirm this from some British official present in Cairo at the time, but I don't think there is much chance that any bank deposit exists.
We decided to enquire into Hanem Aref's finances, and /54 was written to Bennett accordingly. We have now got his reply. It is not particularly valuable, as it seems to have been obtained from Hanem Aref as it seems to have been obtained from Hanem Aref as it seems to have been obtained from Hanem Aref as it seems to have been obtained from Hanem Aref (see paper attached to -/56). It does frankly state, however, that the object of Hanem Aref's petition was 'to obtain a subvention'.
The question now seems to be: Does H.E. consider this is a case warranting expenditure from No.5 Account?
N.M.
28th. Decr. 1928.
I suggest that we might send her, through the British Consular Agent at Minia, £E.10 from No.5 fund, as she can be considered as a 'distressed Egyptian'.
28th. Decr. 1928.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. 31st. Decr., 1928. Dear Mr. Shirley, A certain Hanem Aref, living at El Fikria, Markas Abu Korkas, wrote to us some time ago asking for financial assistance. She said that she understood a sum of money stood to her credit in one of the Cairo banks. She turns out to be the Hanem Aref whose name was well-known in Cairo at the time of the Dirout train murders in 1919, when, alone out of a raging mob on Mellawi station, she showed pity to a dying British soldier and murdered therefore. You probably remember the details of the case. In 1920 Hanem Aref was presented with a set of gold bracelets which had been subscribed for by British admirers in Cairo of her generous action. It appears that she married a cartwright after the troubles, but that she was divorced in 1925. She is now destitute and earns her living as a domestic servant. His Excellency has considered the case, and would like to make Hanem Aref a present of the £E.10 enclosed herewith. Would you kindly summon the woman therefore, and explain that the fund collected for her in 1919 was given to her in full at the time and that we have no knowledge of any bank deposit such as she suggests. His Excellency wishes however to accept the present gift in token of his appreciation of her charitable deed. Sgd. W. Smart. F.W. Shirley Esq., British Consular Agent, c/o Messrs John Peel & Co., Minia.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal letter from the British Residency in Cairo to the British Consular Agent in Minia, dated December 31, 1928. It concerns a woman named Hanem Aref, who had previously gained notoriety and British admiration for her humanitarian actions during the 1919 Egyptian Revolution (specifically the Dirout train murders). The letter clarifies that she is currently destitute and divorced, and instructs the Consular Agent to deliver a gift of 10 Egyptian Pounds from the Residency, while correcting her misconception regarding a non-existent bank deposit from 1919.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British colonial administrative correspondence from the interwar period in Egypt. It highlights the British authorities' continued interest in individuals who assisted British personnel during the 1919 nationalist uprising. The letter serves as both a charitable gesture and a bureaucratic clarification, illustrating the intersection of personal welfare and political memory in the context of the British occupation of Egypt. The mention of the 'Dirout train murders' places the subject within the violent events of the 1919 revolution, where Hanem Aref's intervention was framed by the British as a 'charitable deed' worthy of recognition.

To. The British Consular Agent.
From. F.H. Butler Esq.
10. I. 28.
With reference to your letter of the 4th inst. with enclosures. I visited El Yiakrieh to-day and through the medium of the Omdah Elwalli Bey Abdel Maqsoud, Hamen Aref was found and brought to his house.
She recognised me immediately as the intermediary through whom communication had been made with British authorities previously in 1920.
I explained fully that no funds remained for her in any Bank, nor did she know having received the balance of the cash remaining over and above the cost of the bracelets, with the MaBarnett.
I receipt taken at the time by me and sent to Judge years ago since when apparently her husband divorced her four years ago since when she has been in difficulties which have increased through some slight disability to use her right arm, damaged in a brawl in which she insolently shouted down the late National Hero. She has an Amazon's heart at least.
Of her jewels she had a very considerable quantity, apart from those given her by the English sympathisers, who has lived through a period of excessive debauch, it is not that of a drug taker and there is about her something very gentle. She wept when she heard of his Excellencies kindness and expressed sincere gratitude.
Enclosed find receipt, by Hamen Aref (Thumb) The Omdah the Sarruf and self.
I recommend the Omdah whose courtesy and tact left nothing to be desired.
Signed. F. H. Butler.

It concludes with a recommendation for the Omdah's conduct and mentions enclosed receipts signed by thumbprint.

It illustrates the role of British consular agents in managing the welfare and financial affairs of individuals under their protection, often involving local administrative figures like the 'Omdah'. From Hanem Aref bin Arer Ali.

Minia.

Hanem Aref has the honour to inform His Excellency that she has received the money (£E.10) which His Excellency kindly caused to be given to her as an act of sympathy. His Excellency's representative came to Abu Korkus and handed the money to her in the presence of the Omda, at the latter's house. She recounts that the money was delivered by a representative in the presence of the Omda (village headman). Upon leaving, she publicly proclaimed her loyalty to the King of England and Great Britain. She emphasizes that the small sum feels as significant as 10,000 pounds due to the gesture of kindness, and notes that local villagers incorrectly rumored that she had received 100 pounds.

ai_content.transcribed_text: There is a group who, at this present juncture, desire to call into question the international character of the Egyptian question; and tries to imply that the dispute is solely between Egypt and England, i.e. a Crown Colony and its Mother Country. We can understand Englishmen propounding such a theory but we fail to understand how a group of Egyptians, however much imbued with the desire to arrive at a solution, could so pervert the facts of the Egyptian situation - facts supported by historical evidence now a period of 40 years. (Here follows samples of 'facts' alluded to.) If we were to admit that the question could be settled between England and Egypt we should, by implication, accept the Protectorate; and all that would remain to us would be to ask England to decide on the form of her government of our country. Those persons, therefore, who admit this theory and at the same time demand complete independence are guilty of manifest inconsistency. The British conductor waits by saying that the Zaghlulist delegation will to London. It is implied, but (owing to the censorship) not stated in so many words, that the invitation extended to these constituted formal recognition by London of the potential status of this mission. The excellence of his tactics, the circumspection displayed by him, the previous dispatches, the three delegates, his anxiety to consult the Egyptian public at every stage, and all subjects of constant arrangement. Emphasis is laid on the need of Great Britain to arrive at an amiable agreement with Egyptians, and on the tentative and non-committed character of the negotiations by the head of Zaghlul. Zaghlulist statements that the mere fact of negotiations being held in London derogates the international character of the Egyptian question are hotly denied. The Hon. Zaghlulist papers of the time from Eulogize the services of Adly Pasha Yeghen as mediator between Zaghlul and the British authorities in London. The 'Mokattam', which has made a welcome reappearance in the field of political discussion has given cautious encouragement to the 'Accommodationist' thesis. The 'Mimbar' and 'Watan' have adopted a similar attitude. The 'Irreconcilable' press consists of the two Wafdist papers, 'Omma' and 'Mahroussa', and the 'Ahaly'. It is very vocal but, at present, it seems to represent merely a minority composed of extremists and bitter personal foes of Zaghlul who are disquieted at the idea of a policy of reconciliation and eager to destroy Zaghlul's prestige and his policy.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is written in English. It discusses the political climate in Egypt regarding the status of the Egyptian question, specifically debating whether it is an international issue or a domestic matter between a colony and its mother country. It analyzes the role of Zaghlul and his delegation, the negotiations in London, and the stance of various Egyptian newspapers ('Mokattam', 'Mimbar', 'Watan', 'Omma', 'Mahroussa', 'Ahaly') regarding the potential for an accommodation or settlement with the British authorities.
ai_content.historical_summary: This manuscript appears to be a contemporary political analysis or diary entry from the early 1920s, likely written by a British official or observer in Egypt. It provides a detailed account of the political maneuvering surrounding the Egyptian nationalist movement, the Wafd party led by Saad Zaghlul, and the diplomatic efforts of Adly Pasha Yeghen. The text highlights the tension between 'irreconcilable' nationalists who rejected any British presence and 'accommodationists' who sought a negotiated settlement. It reflects the complex administrative and diplomatic context of the British Protectorate era in Egypt, focusing on the internationalization of the 'Egyptian Question' and the internal divisions within the Egyptian press and political elite.

In regard to the latter the Censorship, whilst insisting on moderation of language, has allowed practically complete freedom of expression. This distinction is recognized - and appreciated - by the journalists concerned.

TURKEY & ISLAM. Condemnation of the Turkish peace conditions and of the Allies' treatment of Turkey is frequent, but rarely passionate. There have been several extracts from Turco-phil (and Anglo-phobe) writers in the French press in support of this condemnation. It is clear that Egyptian sentiments in favour of Turkey has been much diminished by the spread of modern Nationalist theories and the realization that the Ottoman Empire is no longer a Military power. An interview with the notorious agitator Abdel Aziz Shawish, who extolled Enver, and some propagandist matter about the ex-Khedive and his son, were suppressed.

MISCELLANEOUS. "La Bourse" has published a series of articles by a Maltese lawyer (G. Mifsud) criticizing Mr. Mirat's proposals for judicial reforms which the writer regards as unsatisfactory.

The proceedings of the Nile Projects Commission are being published in English and Arabic papers, who have hitherto refrained from comment upon them. The reports of these proceedings are not censored before publication.

The Zaghlulists have decided to participate in the reception to be organized by the Watanists in connection with the arrival of Farid Bey's body next week.

Cairo.
5 June 1920.
(Signed) G.S.SYMES.

It mentions the suppression of an interview with agitator Abdel Aziz Shawish praising Enver Pasha, as well as propaganda regarding the ex-Khedive. Under 'Miscellaneous', it reports on local press articles criticizing judicial reforms, the publication of the Nile Projects Commission proceedings, and the cooperation between the Zaghlulist and Watanist political factions for the repatriation of Farid Bey's body.

The report highlights the shifting loyalties of the Egyptian public, noting a decline in pan-Islamic or pro-Ottoman sentiment in favor of localized Egyptian nationalism following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire. It also documents the active British censorship of nationalist figures like Abdel Aziz Shawish and the ex-Khedive Abbas Hilmi II, alongside the tactical cooperation between the mainstream Zaghlulist movement (led by Saad Zaghloul) and the more radical Watanist party during the repatriation of the nationalist leader Mohamed Farid's remains.

PRESS 8TH FEBRUARY

Repetition of almost all points dealt with during the last three days about the Sudan and the Dustour, and the Ministry's resignation.

AL-AHRAM Extract from a leading Article "Editorial"

If we criticise the actions of Ministers, we only do this owing to our keen desire to safeguard the country's interests. It is possible that we make criticisms in order to replace Ministers by others who could realize our desire in favour of the country, but as long as the interests of the country are in danger, everybody should only pronounce the name of "EGYPT" in which every Egyptian has a right and a duty. We have been united as a bundle of sticks tightly tied up, but political intrigues played its part and the English policy succeeded in breaking us one by one. We are still inattentive and suffer the consequences of politics. We recommend that all parties should explain their points of view in connection with the promulgation of the Dustour, because we feel sure that the postponement of its publication is the reason of crisis and calamities which fell on this country. There are wise men in this country but they are scattered, so that they should mobilize their lines in order to present a united front. The Ahram addresses same appeal to its colleagues the journalists.

ai_content.historical_summary: This archival document is a British Foreign Office registry cover sheet (Registry Number E 1623/10/16) from February 1923, detailing discussions on British imperial policy in Egypt during a period of intense nationalist agitation. Following the unilateral declaration of Egyptian independence in 1922, Britain maintained a heavy military and political presence under martial law, overseen by High Commissioner Lord Allenby. The minute records an inquiry by prominent left-wing British politicians Ben Spoor and E.D. Morel, who advocated for an end to repressive measures and a reconciliation with Egyptian nationalist factions. ai_content.transcribed_text: ON the 8th February Mr. McNeill received at the Foreign Office Mr. Ben Spoor, M.P. and Mr. E. D. Morel, M.P., who had asked for an interview in order to discuss the situation in Egypt. Mr. Murray and Mr. Cooper were also present. Mr. MOREL said that the Labour Party did not regard Egypt as a party question. They only desired to discover a solution of the present anomalous position in which martial law remained in force although the independence of Egypt had been recognised. There was a widespread feeling in Egypt that there was a general consensus of opinion in favour of a more liberal policy and that His Majesty's Government were not ill-disposed, but that the stumbling block in the way of progress was His Majesty's High Commissioner. In the subsequent course of the conversation he returned repeatedly to this point and added that, according to the information which reached him, Lord Allenby had at first been extremely liberal-minded, but had lately come under other influences which had altered his point of view. The two changes which Mr. Morel wished to see in Egypt were the abolition of martial law and the return of Zaghlul.

Morel and Mr. Ben Spoor, members of the British Labour Party, met with Mr. McNeill to advocate for a shift in British policy toward Egypt. They argued that the continued imposition of martial law was incompatible with the recognition of Egyptian independence. They specifically requested the lifting of martial law and the permission for the nationalist leader Zaghlul to return to Egypt, suggesting that Lord Allenby, the British High Commissioner, had become an obstacle to these liberal reforms.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. February 3rd, 1923. No. 64. 7988/1693. My Lord, I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of Your Lordship's despatch No. 7 (E. 14459/1/16) of the 2nd of January, and to state that the question of closing the house of Zaghlul Pasha was carefully examined at the time of the murder of Mr. Robson. The considerations advanced in Your Lordship's despatch were not lost sight of, but the Prime Minister strongly represented to me that the adoption of this measure would embarrass his Government, and throw additional odium upon ourselves, without probable benefit either to Public Security or to Egyptian and British interests generally. 2. Since Tewfik Pasha Nessim showed himself ready to meet any reasonable demand for the adoption of measures designed to bring the authors of past outrages to justice, and to prevent the renewal of murder in the future; and since the attitude of the Wafd itself towards the murder of Mr. Robson was not unsatisfactory, I decided to meet the Prime Minister's views in the matter. Circumstances, however, may at any time make the reconsideration of my attitude necessary. The Most Honourable The Marquess Curzon of Kedleston, K.G., G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E., etc., etc.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official diplomatic dispatch from the British Residency in Cairo to the British Foreign Secretary, Lord Curzon. The author acknowledges receipt of instructions regarding the potential closure of Zaghlul Pasha's residence following the assassination of Mr. Robson. The author explains that he deferred to the Egyptian Prime Minister, Tewfik Pasha Nessim, who argued that such an action would be counterproductive, causing political embarrassment and public resentment without improving security. The author notes that he accepted this advice because the Egyptian government and the Wafd party had shown a cooperative attitude regarding the investigation of the murder, though he reserves the right to change his position if circumstances dictate.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal diplomatic dispatch sent from the British Residency in Cairo on February 3, 1923, addressed to the British Foreign Secretary, Lord Curzon. It concerns the British administration's response to the assassination of Mr. Robson in Egypt and the subsequent pressure to take punitive measures against the Wafd party, specifically the closure of Zaghlul Pasha's house. The document highlights the delicate balance of power between the British occupation authorities and the Egyptian government under Prime Minister Tewfik Pasha Nessim, illustrating the British policy of managing Egyptian nationalist sentiment while maintaining security and colonial interests in the post-1922 independence era.

Notes on preceding and other precautionary measures.

I. The following orders have been issued by the Commandant Cairo City Police:-
In future, on the report being received of a political murder or attempted murder in Cairo or Giza, all staff, men and traffic officers who are not on duty at the time, or who are on leave in Cairo, will assemble at once at their offices and await orders.
Staff officers of the division concerned and officers of the Qism concerned will naturally go to the scene of the crime.

II. The Commandant Cairo City Police has issued instructions for a special detachment of Police to be ready immediately to proceed to the scene of the crime for the purpose of carrying out instructions under I.1.b (1).

The Mamour Mubahith at the Ministry will telephone the report of the crime as soon as possible after receiving it to all Divisional Assistant Commandant, Inspectors and Qisms.

III. The Commandant Cairo City Police has arranged for the services of a tracker to be available at any time he is required.

IV. On commission of a crime a section of the Special Section Staff will immediately proceed to the Special Section office for duty. Mr. Mackintosh will be in charge.

V. Arrangements are being made by the Director of Personnel and Equipment for staff to be immediately available for printing notices etc.
Action through Special Section to Department in question.

VI. Telephonic communications (by courtesy of the Director of Telephones, Cairo).
If a crime takes place officers of the Public Security Services on the scene of the crime or elsewhere, e.g., officers of the Cairo City Police, or the Special Section, may wish to make urgent calls. If any officer cannot get through at once from any telephone, he should ask for 6711 and then to be put through at once to the number required.

It details six immediate punitive measures: 1) Appointment of a Military Governor for Cairo and Giza. 2) Closure of public meeting places, including 'The House of the Nation' (Zaghlul's House), and an absolute ban on public meetings. 3) Imposition of a heavy fine on the district where the murder occurs. 4) Simultaneous arms searches in specific Cairo quarters by British forces. 5) Immediate arrest of suspects and uncooperative witnesses, with Judge Holmes preparing lists for charges. 6) Preparation of a scheme for immediate compensation to the victim's relatives. The memorandum then discusses two broader considerations: I) The proposal to exact a £E.25,000 fine from the Egyptian Government was examined by the High Commissioner and rejected for three reasons: a) Egypt is not an enemy country. b) The Egyptian Government would have a legitimate grievance because British officials largely conducted murder inquiries without consulting them. c) Such a fine would have little impact on the 'Sedered public.' II) The question of whether to liquidate the positions of all British officials and re-employ those wishing to stay on contract had not yet been considered.

It also reveals internal deliberations, such as the High Commissioner's decision to discard a proposal for a large fine on the Egyptian Government, citing reasons related to Egypt's status (not an enemy country), the lack of consultation with Egyptian authorities in investigations, and the perceived ineffectiveness of such a fine on the general public. The final point indicates an ongoing discussion about the employment status of British officials in Egypt. The content strongly reflects the tense political climate in British-occupied Egypt during a period of heightened nationalist sentiment, likely in the aftermath of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution or subsequent unrest in the 1920s or early 1930s, where British authorities sought to assert control and deter violence against their nationals amidst calls for greater Egyptian independence. The mention of 'Zaghlul's House' is a key indicator of this post-1919 context.

ai_content.transcribed_text: EGYPT AND SOUDAN. CONFIDENTIAL. [February 16.] SECTION 1. No. 1. The Marquis della Torretta to the Marquess Curzon of Kedleston.—(Received February 16.) Italian Embassy, London, February 11, 1923. My Lord. AS you are aware the British delegation at the Lausanne Conference after having proposed to the co-ordinating committee for the draft treaty new clauses in substitution for articles 101-113 of the Treaty of Sevres, later on, requested the insertion of two articles in the new treaty, indicated as (A) and (B), to deal with the Egyptian question in its entirety. Article (B) runs as follows:— "The questions arising from the recognition of the State of Egypt shall be settled by agreements to be negotiated subsequently in a manner to be determined later between the Powers concerned. The provisions of the present treaty relating to territories detached from Turkey under the said treaty will not apply to Egypt." By this article the British Government have relegated the whole question to an agreement to be concluded at a later date. In compliance with instructions received I have the honour to confirm that the Italian Government have accepted the above text, but, when the clause comes into force, they expect to participate in the discussions and signature of the agreement relating to questions arising from the independence of Egypt. Among the questions referred to, the Italian Government are especially interested in the settlement of that relating to the Suez Canal, since the Italian Government were a signatory to the Constantinople Convention of 1888. I beg that your Lordship may be good enough to give me assurances in this connection, and in expressing my thanks in anticipation, I have, &c. TORRETTA.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official diplomatic dispatch from the Italian Ambassador, the Marquis della Torretta, to the British Foreign Secretary, the Marquess Curzon of Kedleston, regarding the status of Egypt during the Lausanne Conference negotiations. The document outlines the British proposal for new treaty clauses (A and B) to replace the Treaty of Sèvres regarding Egypt, specifically excluding Egypt from the general provisions applied to territories detached from the Ottoman Empire. The Italian government accepts this text but explicitly reserves its right to participate in future negotiations concerning Egyptian independence, specifically citing its interest in the Suez Canal as a signatory to the 1888 Constantinople Convention.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential diplomatic communication from the British Foreign Office archives, dated February 1923. It captures a critical moment in the post-WWI settlement where the status of Egypt—which had been declared independent by Britain in 1922—was being formally decoupled from the broader Treaty of Sèvres negotiations at the Lausanne Conference. E 1909/10/16
No. 1.
[February 16.]
EGYPT AND SOUDAN.
CONFIDENTIAL.
SECTION 1.
(Translation.)
Italian Embassy, London, February 11, 1923.
My Lord,
AS you are aware the British delegation at the Lausanne Conference after having proposed to the co-ordinating committee for the draft treaty new clauses in substitution for articles 101-113 of the Treaty of Sèvres, later on requested the insertion of two articles in the new treaty, indicated as (A) and (B), to deal with the Egyptian question in its entirety.
Article (B) runs as follows:—
"The questions arising from the recognition of the State of Egypt shall be settled by agreements to be negotiated subsequently in a manner to be determined later between the Powers concerned. The provisions of the present treaty relating to territories detached from Turkey under the said treaty will not apply to Egypt."
By this article the British Government have relegated the whole question to an agreement to be concluded at a later date.
In compliance with instructions received I have the honour to confirm that the Italian Government have accepted the above text, but, when the clause comes into force, they expect to participate in the discussions and signature of the agreement relating to questions arising from the independence of Egypt. Among the questions referred to, the Italian Government are especially interested in the settlement of that relating to the Suez Canal, since the Italian Government were a signatory to the Constantinople Convention of 1888.
I have, &c.
TORRETTA.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal diplomatic communication from the Italian Ambassador (Torretta) to the British Foreign Secretary (Marquess Curzon of Kedleston) regarding the status of Egypt in the context of the ongoing Lausanne Conference. The Italian government accepts the British proposal to defer the settlement of Egyptian status to a future agreement, but explicitly reserves the right to participate in those future negotiations, specifically citing their interest in the Suez Canal as a signatory to the 1888 Constantinople Convention.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an excerpt from a British Foreign Office confidential print series concerning Egypt and the Sudan, dated February 1923. It captures a critical moment in post-WWI diplomacy where the status of Egypt—formerly under Ottoman suzerainty and then a British protectorate—was being redefined in the wake of the Treaty of Sèvres and the subsequent Lausanne Conference. The correspondence highlights Italy's insistence on maintaining its legal standing regarding the Suez Canal, rooted in the 1888 Constantinople Convention, as the British Empire sought to formalize its new relationship with an independent Egyptian state.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Cairo, February 2, 1923. Field-Marshal Viscount Allenby to King Fuad. Enclosure 1 in No. 1. I AM directed by the Marquess Curzon of Kedleston to present to your Majesty the documents annexed hereto and numbered respectively 1 and 2. I need not dilate to your Majesty upon the grave nature of the first of these two communications. I earnestly hope that your Majesty and your Majesty's Government will not persist in an attitude which so serious a view is taken by the British Government, and will see your way to authorise me without any delay to give the necessary assurances to His Britannic Majesty's Government. The form in which His Britannic Majesty's Government invites your Majesty to give these assurances is set forth in Annex No. 2, which I am to ask your Majesty to sign. Should your Majesty fail, after consideration, to affix your signature to this document, my instructions are that the essential parts of the first document are to be forthwith published. What further action His Britannic Majesty's Government may take in this case I shall not endeavour to anticipate, but I venture to call your Majesty's attention to the last paragraph of Annex No. 1.

Allenby expresses the gravity of the situation, urging the King and his government to provide specific assurances to the British government as outlined in 'Annex No. 2'. He warns that if the King fails to sign the document, the British government will publish the contents of the first document ('Annex No. 1') and implies further, unspecified consequences.

If, therefore, the Constitution is promulgated with the articles amended in the manner suggested by Lord Allenby in para. 7 (b) of this telegram, we need no longer press for the enactment of the Indemnity Law before the promulgation of the Constitution, provided the Indemnity Law is enacted before the Constitution "comes into effect".

As far as I can make out Lord Allenby and Adly Pasha seem to contemplate a programme on the following lines:-
A. Early or immediate promulgation of Constitution with special provisions inserted in it that it will not come into effect till Parliament meets.
B. Enactment of an ordinary Egyptian decree giving the Egyptian Government additional powers to deal with disturbances and to effect preventive arrests.

E. Enactment of an electoral law promulgated under powers possessed by Government under existing Constitution (see passage marked in Cairo despatch No. 858 (flag C)

G. Enactment of Indemnity Law and conclusion of agreement connected therewith.
H. Holding of elections.
I. Meeting of Parliament and coming into force of Constitution.

It appears from para. 8 of Lord Allenby's telegram that the steps indicated at F, G and H above are all intended to take place within a period of about ten days.

If the above inferences are correct it remains to examine the various issues which they raise.
(1) The Sudan. I imagine Adly intends to exclude the contentious Sudan articles from the Constitution, but to insert in their stead a provision whereby it will be left to Parliament to frame articles defining the position of that country in regard to the King and the Constitution of Egypt. POLITICAL
Decypher. Lord Allenby, (Cairo), February 28th 1923.
D. 1.0 a.m. March 1st 1923.
R. 8.30 a.m. March 1st 1923.
No. 83.
Your telegram No. 61.
King has again invited Adly Pasha to form government.
Adly Pasha is acting with great caution and has attempted to test public opinion by issuing statement of policy which his party would support if such a policy were adopted by any government taking office.
This statement contemplated:-
1. Removal of restrictions imposed by His Majesty's Government upon liberty of Egyptian government in respect of Sudanese articles in constitution.
2. Abolition of martial law and release of Zaghloul and other internees.
3. Establishment of union and harmony in the country.
Confidential. I have been in touch with Adly Pasha who indicated in regard to 1. that if he took office he might find means to exclude from text of constitution any pre-judgment of status of Souden and to refer question to parliament when it meets. He would then use whole influence of his party to induce parliament to let question stand over until final negotiations.
Obvious dangers of this course have been pointed out.

It also notes Allenby's confidential discussions with Adly Pasha regarding a compromise on the status of the Sudan to avoid pre-judging the issue before parliamentary negotiations.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Memorandum by Mr. Murray.

During the course of the past few days I have had an opportunity of having long conversations with two members of the Egyptian Civil Service who have only just returned to England, and I have also received a long letter from a friend of mine in the Ministry of Interior in Cairo. All three are men with about 15 to 20 years service in Egypt.

The views expressed appear to me of sufficient interest to warrant their being summarised briefly and put on record, especially as for some little time past we have had rather scanty indications from Lord Allenby of the development in the situation in Egypt.

(1) My first informant, who has been largely responsible for the organisation of the force of village watchmen numbering some 50,000 and who travels extensively throughout the provinces, told me that the fellahin are no longer the apathetic and docile people that they were a few years ago. On the average, seven of his watchmen get shot in every week. I asked him whether they did not shoot back and he replied in the affirmative, but added that they selected their victims from amongst their own personal enemies.

He told me that the Governors of provinces and the subordinate officials are taking not the faintest interest in their work. The Governors generally, and commandants of the provincial police frequently, are absent 10 or 15 days in every month from their provinces and the rot has spread to the headmen of the villages who are doing whatever seems good in their own eyes.

He thought that the Residency was most unduly optimistic....
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a memorandum written by Mr. Murray summarizing intelligence gathered from British officials recently returned from Egypt. It details a decline in administrative oversight, a rise in rural unrest among the fellahin (peasantry), and a breakdown in the effectiveness of the village watchmen system. The author expresses concern that the British Residency in Cairo is failing to accurately report the deteriorating security and administrative situation to London.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential memorandum, likely from the British Foreign Office archives, concerning the state of British-occupied Egypt. It reflects the anxieties of British civil servants regarding the post-WWI political climate in Egypt, specifically the erosion of British control over the provinces and the perceived failure of Lord Allenby's administration to address the growing defiance of the rural population. The text highlights the 'rot' in the provincial administration, where officials were neglecting their duties, and notes the increasing violence involving the village watchmen (ghaffirs), signaling the broader nationalist unrest that would characterize the period leading up to the 1922 declaration of Egyptian independence.

ai_content.transcribed_text: In fact the whole show has degenerated into a sort of silly diplomatic game which the Egyptians enjoy playing before an audience of newspapers and which they play rather better than Allenby. Remember that the very few Egyptians who have any idea of patriotism are now out of the game, not that they out much ice when they were in it. The rest of the nation, especially the Ministerial lot, are not bothering in the least about their country and cannot be persuaded that the English are either. They have no reason to think so that I can see. Every ministry goes in now on the 'eat, drink and be merry' line and does not even want to stay in long enough to do their country any good, as long as they get all the jobs they want for their relations and score off their enemies who were in the last Ministry. If they did want to stay in any one of them could stand up to the newspapers and when Parliament comes in things will be worse and I don't think any Ministry will have more than three months life, during which time no useful administration can be done. The whole thing now is a vicious circle and we ought to get out of it. Nobody thinks anything of the English nor have they any confidence in any Ministry. All idea of stability has disappeared. In the old days ministers and the country did believe that the occupation was a stable element and that if anything happened there was always the Agency to turn to. But now they don't look....

Your telegram No. 65.
I do not think it would be judicious for me to proceed to London. Such a move at present moment would cause sensation here and would be interpreted as indicating that His Majesty's Government were embarrassed by the situation and were contemplating change of policy. I am advised that any such impression would lead to intensification of outrage campaign. It would moreover fortify the King in belief in his ability, of which he is believed to have boasted before the Soudan controversy, to secure my recall. In the event of the situation improving within the next few weeks, above-mentioned objections would be less pertinent.
I shall endeavour to make to Your Lordship full report of every aspect of the problem but it would be of considerable assistance to me if you would take an early opportunity of addressing to me the definite questions Your Lordship has in view.
Meanwhile I would venture to offer certain comments on earlier part of your telegram under reference.
It is much to be regretted that political progress has for the present been rendered impossible by outrages. Their natural effect upon British opinion here

26. The explosion of 1919 has spent its force. Some of the London papers compare the present situation with that of 1919. I am convinced that they are much mistaken. In that year the grievances felt during the war by the whole population at last found their vent in a general and quite genuine explosion of anger, mainly directed against the British Army. That explosion has ever since been fading away, and there is now, I think, little force left in it. Here, as in other countries, there is always the possibility of fresh trouble arising, but there seems little reason for anticipating anything at all resembling the disturbances of 1919.

27. The delay in forming a ministry has been due, not to a movement of national protest, but rather to the following causes:
(a) the dilemma over the Soudan clauses, which it is hoped may be eased by the passage of time;
(b) the feeling that, while the suspension of martial law is not for the moment politically possible, it would be somewhat difficult for ministers to appear to be partners in its enforcement. It is one thing to be laissez imposer and another to co-operate.

32. What of the suggestion that we have been lacking in courageous consistency? It is urged by the second school of critics that the essence of the Declaration of February was that we should stand aloof from Egyptian internal politics, and, resting on our positions, await the day when an Egyptian government would come forward able and willing to make a treaty with us. Whereas, it is said, we have continued to interfere, have supported our supposed friends, and waged war against our apparent enemies, with corresponding injury to the policy of disentanglement and alliance.

33. Our immediate concern is not with the past, but with the present and with the future, the temptation must therefore be resisted to examine in further detail the justification for the course adopted by His Majesty's Government in Egypt since the failure of the London negotiations. The question to be examined is whether or not it is possible and expedient to take a further definite step forward in the direction of conciliation with Egypt.

Such a step might consist either
(a) in seeking to come to a definite understanding with the Zaghlulists, or
(b) in permitting them to return to Egypt unconditionally, and leaving events to take their course.

ai_content.transcribed_text: 34. As already indicated, I find it difficult to believe that any bargain could, at the present time, be made with the Zaghloulists. It is not necessary, in examining this question, to ask ourselves what exactly are the minimum British requirements. The Zaghloulists appear to be completely pledged to the repudiation of the Declaration of February, and the unconditional evacuation of Egypt and the Soudan. Can they possibly retire from this position? It seems most doubtful whether, as a party, they can do so. It may very well be that the stream of secession will continue to flow in the future as in the past - nobody can work with Zaghloul for long, and his probable successor, (his nephew Atif Bey Barakat - now in the Seychelles) is not unlikely to continue this disruptive tradition. There are many indications that the people at large are inclined in an increasing degree to peace rather than to war, ( :/: ) - but any person who entertains or expresses such sentiments removes himself, by so doing, from the ranks of the incorruptibles. ( :/: ) There is some justification for the suspicion that this lukewarmness is partly due to the firm attitude of H.M.G. towards the Zaghloulists and towards the King. Egyptians are not wholly insensitive to symptoms of vivacity in an opponent. A recent writer in a vernacular paper thought it necessary to rebuke those who say that Zaghloul is already forgotten.

(a) It would tend to restore the political purity of our position.
(b) It would relieve H.M.G. of the burden of responsibility for measures uncongenial to our political traditions, and likely to give rise to strong and increasing criticism at home.

ai_content.transcribed_text: Memorandum by Sir W. Shuter. 24.3.23. E 3454. 1. It is a curious illustration of Egyptian political mentality that they still incline to the policy of 'non-cooperation' in order to bring pressure to bear upon His Majesty's Government to get rid of Martial Law and to secure the return of Zaghloul. This takes the form of pressure to prevent the formation of Ministries - of whatever colour. Castro has pointed out the futility of this in 'La Liberté', and argued that the only rational line for the Zaghloulists to take is to press for a Zaghloulist Cabinet - not for no Cabinet at all. So long as His Majesty's Government claimed general responsibility for the administration of the country, non-cooperation was a rational policy. Today His Majesty's Government no longer makes that claim. All that the Nationalists can logically complain of is that in spite of our declaration of disinterestedness, we still in fact interfere too much. But the method proposed for making us withdraw further is illogical, since it rests upon the implication that His Majesty's Government is more concerned than are the Egyptians to keep the machinery of Government in working order; in other words it amounts to a refusal of independence, and to an invitation to His Majesty's Government to extend rather than to diminish the field of its responsibilities.

It discusses the political strategy of Egyptian Nationalists who were employing 'non-cooperation' to force the British government to end Martial Law and allow the return of the nationalist leader Zaghloul. The author notes that while this policy made sense when the British were directly administering the country, it is now illogical because the British have renounced that claim. The author argues that the Nationalists' current tactics actually invite continued British interference rather than achieving the independence they seek.

II. Egypt has at the present time no serious internal problems - at least none that interest the public. The finances are flourishing; there are no labour or industrial troubles of any consequence; the peasantry is prosperous; Egypt alone (?) everywhere being pushed forward actively. The finances she has derived considerable political advantages, without any increase in her debt or in her direct taxation, and with only very moderate increases in her indirect taxation - and these latter cannot be attributed to war expenses.

This being so, the only possible subject matters of political strife are (a) the constitution and (b) relations with England. The problems of the constitution are reasonable subjects of concern and controversy, involving as they do the future balance of power in the country - King v. people and go on. But it is difficult not to think that the continuance of the campaign against England is largely due to the convenient weapons it offers for inter-party strife. The 'Sudan clause' furnish an example of this. And whenever we on our side give signs of attaching importance to 'negotiations' we play into the hands of those who for the purposes of internal politics desire to make use of the conflict with His Majesty's Government. One of the main objects of the unilateral declaration of February 1922 was to deprive the question of negotiation of its urgency. Lord Milner's policy of a treaty with Egypt, though statesmanlike in conception, had the defect that its announcement appeared to place His Majesty's Government in the position of suitors, seeking for a diplomatic advantage. It inspired suspicion in the minds of many Egyptians, while in the minds of others it excited exaggerated notions of the value of the favour they were asked to grant.

The subject of Martial Law in Egypt has been much misunderstood. Strictly speaking some element of Martial Law has always existed in Egypt since the occupation, for the reason that the British Army was not and could not be subject to Egyptian Law, and in the last resort must be deemed to have at all times possessed all powers necessary to defend itself and its members. But since the relations of the two Governments British and Egyptian were cordial, amounting almost to relations of alliance, this reserve power was kept entirely in the background.
On the outbreak of the war with Turkey new problems presented themselves. It became necessary not only to assert in a definite form the almost forgotten power of the British Army to defend itself, but - what was from a practical point of view more important - it became necessary for the British authorities to take in the common interest wide powers of government. The chief cause of this necessity was the fact that the powers of the Egyptian government in its own territory are severely limited by the Capitulations. Few if any of the numerous measures rendered imperative by a state of war could be effectively taken by the Egyptian government without bringing it into conflict with the capitulary privileges of the foreign colonies: - such measures were the deportation or internment of enemy subjects, the sequestration of enemy property, the prevention of communication commercial or otherwise with enemy countries, the suppression of espionage, postal and press censorship, the control of food supplies, the control of drink, traffic and so on.

But it may be taken as certain that the foreign states concerned would have viewed with much greater suspicion and apprehension a claim of exceptional powers made by the Egyptian government than a similar claim made by the British government. In point of fact British Martial Law has met with very slight criticism from foreigners, though it has touched and controlled their lives in countless ways; indeed it would be fair to say that it has enjoyed and still enjoys their moral support.
In a proclamation of November 2, 1914, which accompanied the notice whereby Martial Law was established, the Commander in Chief announced that "the powers to be exercised by the Military authorities are intended to supplement and not to supersede the Civil administration".
It was in this spirit that Martial Law was in fact administered, wherever possible resort was had to civil machinery; while the machinery of Martial Law was as far as possible assimilated to that of a civil administration, with regular courts, and explicit legislative acts. To a large degree the machinery was operated by civilians, both English and Egyptian. In fact Martial Law displayed itself as a device whereby under British supervision the powers of the Egyptian government were expanded to the extent which, save for the Capitulations, would have been their normal domain in times of war and civil disturbance.
Why has Martial Law been kept on so long?

ai_content.transcribed_text: UNREST IN EGYPT. Murder of Professor Robson. Interesting Letter. A letter received by his parents, in Adelaide, from Dr. Bret Day, of Cairo, written on January 6, contains the following:—'We kept Christmas and New Year in our own flat. We were invited to a dance at midnight on Christmas Eve, and dined at the Peninsula and Heliopolis. This Heliopolis Palace has been re-opened as a General Hospital during the war, and is now a magnificent hotel, and I am revisiting it; surely the most magnificent hotel in the world. There are none in Europe or U.S.A. to touch it. The King himself holds a fair pocket of the stock, but though they will fill up in a week or so with tourists for four months, they are empty now. The assassinations continue here. Last week Professor Robson, of the Law School, was cycling home on the outskirts of the city just after mid-day when four gun-men, who had been in hiding, jumped out, and emptied their revolvers into him, killing him instantly. I carry a Mark II, 45, as well as a patient, he did not merit so sad a tragic. An eye-witness gentleman, who was in a tram, is said to have seen the fight, and written a song of device who was in a motor car, and saw the whole thing, in order to escape—life. A man was shot in the back, and died a few days afterwards at Shepheard's. There were 20 wounded, yet not even caught. These plain truths are uttered for the benefit of Lord Allenby, who is trying to keep a thousand Britishers here at the present time. I came here to study the history of Egypt. Last year Lord Allenby, who is the only man who knows the situation, saying that 407 natives found with bombs would be shot. He gave the natives a week to turn in their arms to the police, and after that what natives were found with arms he either gave them three months' prison or let them off. Can you imagine it? Lord Allenby is the best known, and a French officer in Aleppo, in Syria. The French intend to be in Egypt. Since then there has been no shooting of French soldiers or officers. That was the stuff to give them in the Orient. Points to the Arabs is a line from home. At present the troops are crowded, and the food is bad and the water is bad and the food is very dear, and it is difficult to find in the famine condition of the country at the present time. I also see the only thing reported by the Arabs is a famine, a war to be watched by an army supervisor at the country borders, and I am printing no mortal fear was to have been lifted this week, but the Home Government have refused to carry out until more peaceful conditions reign here. The police have been doubled here, and military cavalry patrols circulate day and night. It is the Egyptian themselves who are so much afraid of all this. They are to be much afraid of all this. I am going to watch the assassins. There is a reward of £5,000 for whoever will find the murderers, but if an Egyptian knew who they are he would be afraid of his skin. I feel convinced that in an other three or four years the plan will be intolerable to Europeans, and it will be time to pull up stakes and clear out. No matter which way one looks, there is at the present time in the future of Egypt. The British officials are being in fair numbers and helping them—good luck to them—a good deal. Indemnities for giving £5,000 to £8,000 being the rule for reporting officials. The country's finances will be rock in another year, as practically no cotton has been sold for three seasons. The British sold the Sudan cotton off Egypt, which was supply when they can cut off Egypt's water supply, which they are doing, and this can kill the cotton, crop to fail here when they like. Now that Britishers are getting controlling agriculture here, the crop being too lazy, there is no system here, which they are doing, and this can kill the quality of the cotton, and cotton is the only source of income for the country, so they can easily deduce that Egypt is the finished.'

It transmits a copy of the "Official Journal" containing the Royal rescript promulgating the Constitution and Electoral Law for Egypt. Allenby notes that the text is largely what was drafted by Sarwat Pasha's committee, but significant modifications were introduced by King Fuad under the régime of Nessim Pasha. These changes were designed to enhance the King's powers and control over the government, notably by suppressing the article stating that power sprang from the nation, allowing the King to nominate half the Senate members and all Ministers, and granting him legislative initiative. Allenby expresses concern that an "Oriental sovereign" might abuse these powers, potentially undermining democratic ideals. The document also mentions the King's willingness to modify the wording of the constitutional committee, with a reference to "Bolshevik Govern-" in a comparison.

Handwritten annotations indicate internal review and commentary. One note by "R.C.L." on May 9, 1923, states that while "nobody imagines that an advanced democratic constitution like this is the least bit suitable for a country like Egypt," it is "preferable to allowing King Fuad any real power." This suggests a preference for a flawed constitution over an autocratic monarchy. Another note by "C.R.C." on May 10, 1923, confirms it was "SEEN BY." A marginal note points to "Mr. McNeill" and another comments that "King Fuad shows up in an even worse light here," reinforcing the critical view of the King's actions.
ai_content.historical_summary: This confidential British government memorandum, dated April 23, 1923, from Field-Marshal Viscount Allenby, the British High Commissioner for Egypt, to Foreign Secretary Marquess Curzon, details the promulgation of Egypt's new Constitution and Electoral Law. The document highlights significant concerns regarding King Fuad's amendments to the original draft, which were perceived as consolidating royal power at the expense of democratic principles. Specifically, King Fuad removed the clause asserting national sovereignty, gained the right to appoint half the Senate and all Ministers, and secured legislative initiative. Allenby expresses apprehension that these expanded powers could be abused by an "Oriental sovereign," undermining the nascent democratic framework in Egypt. Handwritten annotations by British officials further underscore these concerns, with one noting that while a fully democratic constitution might not be suitable for Egypt, it was still preferable to granting King Fuad "any real power," indicating a pragmatic acceptance of a less-than-ideal constitutional monarchy over outright autocracy. The document reflects the complex political landscape of post-1922 independent Egypt, where British influence remained significant, and the struggle between monarchical authority and constitutional governance was a central issue.
