ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. No. 276 (7988/1913). May 1st, 1923. My Lord, I have the honour to enclose herein a French translation of a Manifesto published by the Zaghlulist Wafd in protest against the promulgation of the Constitution. 2. Its publication was the signal for the inauguration in the Zaghlulist press of a rather laboured though none the less persistent attack on the terms of the Constitution. This campaign does not, however, appear seriously to have affected the opinion which is held in most circles that the Constitution is likely to prove, in spite of certain shortcomings, of genuine benefit to the Egyptian people. In fact the "Liberté" a paper noteworthy among the European press for its constant support of Zaghlul, went so far as to say that the fears entertained in Zaghlulist circles were exaggerated and due to misinterpretation of the text of the Constitution. 3. The manifesto has in fact fallen flat, and it is worthy of remark that whereas all previous manifestoes of the Wafd have been followed by numerous letters of support in the newspapers, this manifesto has found hardly any such backing. The public, even those of strongly Zaghlulist tendencies, have found little in the text of the Constitution which can be attacked to the benefit of the Zaghlulist party. 4. I understand that the Wafd having realised that their campaign against the Constitution is unlikely to command, The Marquess Curzon of Kedleston, K.G., G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E., etc., etc., etc.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal diplomatic dispatch from the British Residency in Cairo to the Marquess Curzon of Kedleston, dated May 1, 1923. The document reports on the political reception of the newly promulgated Egyptian Constitution. It notes that the Wafd party, led by Zaghlul, published a manifesto in protest, but that this campaign failed to gain public traction. The author observes that even pro-Zaghlulist newspapers, such as 'Liberté', found the Wafd's criticisms to be based on misinterpretations of the constitutional text, and that the public generally viewed the Constitution as a positive development for Egypt.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a diplomatic report from the British Residency in Cairo during the period of the Egyptian struggle for independence and the transition to a constitutional monarchy. It highlights the internal political friction between the British-backed administration and the Wafd party, led by Saad Zaghlul, following the 1923 Constitution. The dispatch provides contemporary insight into the failure of the Wafd's initial attempts to mobilize public opinion against the new constitutional framework, reflecting the British assessment of the political climate in Egypt at the time.

Les Wafd et la Constitution
La Constitution a été promulguée, et à l'étiquer.
La Constitution a été promulguée, mais les limites de l'État égyptien n'y ont pas été indiquées et il n'y a pas été stipulé que le Soudan, qui est la source de vie pour l'Égypte, en fait partie, ni que le Roi de l'Égypte est Roi du Soudan.
« Il n'est pas de droit qu'elle reconnaît à côté de lui un lien le diminuant ou le démolissant. Même la responsabilité ministérielle, base de toute Constitution et de par laquelle se manifeste le contrôle de la nation sur la gestion du gouvernement, est restreinte de façon à fournir aux ministres un échappatoire chaque fois que le cabinet serait en danger. Et le Parlement ne peut rien amender dans la Constitution, car les conditions de la révision sont telles qu'elle devient impossible.
De plus, l'application de cette Constitution est suspendue, la loi martiale est maintenue, les enfants de l'Égypte sont dispersés par l'exil, la prison et la détention, les tribunaux militaires anglais continuent à disposer du sort des Égyptiens, que la Constitution reconnaît comme indépendants ! »
ai_content.english_translation:
The Wafd and the Constitution
The Constitution has been promulgated, and labeled.
The Constitution has been promulgated, but the limits of the Egyptian State were not indicated therein, and it was not stipulated that the Sudan, which is the source of life for Egypt, is part of it, nor that the King of Egypt is King of the Sudan.
'There is no right that it recognizes alongside it a link diminishing or demolishing it. Even ministerial responsibility, the basis of any Constitution and through which the nation's control over the management of the government is manifested, is restricted in such a way as to provide ministers with an escape route whenever the cabinet is in danger. And Parliament cannot amend anything in the Constitution, because the conditions for revision are such that it becomes impossible.
Furthermore, the application of this Constitution is suspended, martial law is maintained, the children of Egypt are dispersed by exile, prison and detention, and English military courts continue to dispose of the fate of the Egyptians, whom the Constitution recognizes as independent!'
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a clipping from the French-language Egyptian periodical 'La Liberté', dated April 23, 1923. It provides a critical analysis of the 1923 Egyptian Constitution from the perspective of the Wafd Party. The text highlights the Wafd's grievances regarding the document, specifically the failure to define Egypt's territorial boundaries to include the Sudan, the lack of true ministerial accountability, the impossibility of parliamentary amendment, and the continued presence of British military courts and martial law despite the nominal declaration of independence. It serves as a primary source for understanding the political tensions between the Egyptian nationalist movement and the British-backed monarchy during the early years of the Kingdom of Egypt.

With reference to our conversation of the 12th

salient features of the information obtained up to the
6th December from Cachia, the intermediary employed by

As regards Part I, it would seem likely that the

in this summary to the notice of the Colonial Office. You
may, however, see fit, in the meanwhile, to draw the attention
of the Colonial Office to the information regarding the
connection between Hassan Khaled Aboul-Houda and the
ex-Khedive.

S.I.S. Section I.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
SUMMARY OF INFORMATION RECEIVED UP TO 6TH DECEMBER 1923
REGARDING THE ACTIVITIES OF THE EX-KHEDIVE.
PART I.
I. GENERAL OUTLINE OF THE PLAN.
The plot was apparently conceived in the first instance by an individual who went by the name of "IBRAHIM", but whose real name has been since revealed as MEHMET ALI EYULU. Between the latter and the ex-KHEDIVE a form of contract was drawn up by which the ex-KHEDIVE engaged to bear the whole costs of the venture. "IBRAHIM", or MEHMET ALI, to give him his real name, was to receive L.E.120 a month for his expenses whilst carrying out the arrangements. In the event of failure he was to receive some unspecified reward, whilst if it succeeded he was to receive £20,000 and a position in EGYPT compatible with the services he had rendered.
It was the accidental perusal by the Informant of this contract which first made him cognisant of the ex-KHEDIVE'S plans.
Broadly speaking the plan is as follows:-
(a) To carry out propaganda in favour of the ex-KHEDIVE by the employment of young students in EGYPT, and by carrying out propaganda in EGYPT itself of a purely pacific nature on Pan-Islamic lines. This was to take the form that the ex-KHEDIVE had remained faithful to EGYPT and to the CALIPH, in consequence of which he had lost his throne.
(b) A disaffected element in TANTAH was to be gradually organised, advantage being taken of the fact that certain individuals in this quarter had suffered in various ways by the repression of the late disorders, with the object of eventually arming them with a view to their creating a demonstration in force.
(c) The arms necessary for the above purpose were to be purchased in GERMANY, shipped to DALAMAN, and eventually transported from the latter place to TANTAH.
(d) Meantime, elsewhere in EGYPT, propaganda was to be directed against KING FUAD, and not definitely against the English. When it was considered that the ground had been sufficiently prepared a violent demonstration would take place, and rumours would be spread to the effect that EGYPT'S real KHEDIVE and Deliverer was actually in EGYPT.
Emphasis must be laid on this aspect of the affair, as Informant has repeatedly stressed the fact that this provides the key to the whole plot. It is hoped that if in TANTAH a violent outburst occurs in favour of the ex-KHEDIVE; and that the ground here and elsewhere has been carefully prepared by propaganda, that this will give the ex-KHEDIVE the opportunity of entering the country by storm, and he will be able to present ENGLAND with a "fait accompli". If attempts are made to suppress this outburst, recourse will be made to the arms provided. Thus by a wide preparation it is hoped that the TANTAH outburst will, in the excitement of the moment, carry the mass of the population of EGYPT with it, and if it succeeds in this respect the ex-KHEDIVE, in the ex-states, will actually be in hiding on Egyptian soil, will make his/
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an intelligence summary detailing a plot orchestrated by the deposed Khedive of Egypt, Abbas Hilmi II, to regain power. The plan involved hiring an agent named Mehmet Ali Eyulu (alias 'Ibrahim') to conduct a multi-pronged campaign. This included Pan-Islamic propaganda, organizing disaffected groups in Tanta, and smuggling arms from Germany via Dalaman to incite a violent uprising. The ultimate goal was to create a 'fait accompli' that would force the British to accept the Khedive's return to power amidst a popular uprising against King Fuad.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British intelligence report from December 1923 concerning the subversive activities of the exiled Khedive Abbas Hilmi II. Following the British declaration of a protectorate over Egypt in 1914 and the subsequent deposition of Abbas Hilmi II, the former ruler remained a significant threat to British interests and the newly established monarchy of King Fuad. The report outlines a sophisticated, albeit failed, conspiracy involving propaganda, arms smuggling, and the exploitation of local unrest in Tanta to facilitate a coup d'état. It provides critical insight into the post-WWI geopolitical climate in Egypt, the British surveillance apparatus, and the persistent efforts of the deposed Khedive to reclaim his throne.

ai_content.transcribed_text: A. PURCHASE OF ARMS. (a) The purchase of arms was entrusted to MEHMET ALI EYUBLU, who had already had experience in arms smuggling during the war in Tripoli, when he was engaged in smuggling arms to the Tripolitans from EGYPT. He is stated to have been very successful in this respect. MEHMET ALI proceeded to GERMANY in June last in an attempt to procure arms. In this he was unsuccessful. He returned to LAUSANNE at the beginning of July and met TOPAL ISMAIL HAKKI, former Intendant of the Turkish War Office. After a lengthy discussion had taken place between MEHMET ALI and TOPAL ISMAIL HAKKI, the former returned to GERMANY, and after his departure the ex-KHEDIVE stated to informant that ISMAIL HAKKI would procure the arms.

Following their meeting, the ex-Khedive informed the source that Ismail Hakki would handle the procurement.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
INTRODUCTION.

Devant la seconde phase de la Conférence de Lausanne et au moment où on discute les questions touchant en partie l'Egypte, la délégation nationale Egyptienne a pensé qu'il serait utile de présenter à la Conférence de Lausanne un mémoire faisant ressortir les divers états de ces questions au point de vue égyptien.

Bien qu'il ne nous soit guère permis d'entretenir quelques illusions sur le sort réservé à l'Egypte par cette Conférence, la délégation Nationale Egyptienne considère comme un devoir de tenter un nouvel effort en faveur de l'indépendance de son malheureux pays.

On persiste en effet à vouloir disposer de son sort sans l'avoir même consultée.

L'Egypte ressent d'autant mieux l'affront fait à son histoire qu'elle a toujours lutté pour son indépendance et que depuis un siècle ses efforts ont été incessants pour se libérer.

LES EGYPTIENS ONT TOUJOURS LUTTE POUR MAINTENIR LEUR INDEPENDANCE.

Grâce à ses conquêtes et aux victoires brillantes de ses armées, l'Egypte redevenait elle-même. En 1807 elle battait les Anglais à Abou Kir, en 1818 elle prenait l'Arabie et rentrait en possession des lieux saints de l'Islam, tombés entre les mains des wahabits, en 1823, elle établissait l'ordre et la sécurité au Soudan.

Elle n'est plus serve de la Turquie, elle est son alliée et joue un rôle glorieux dans la guerre Turco-Grecque de 1826-29.

Toujours....
ai_content.english_translation:
INTRODUCTION.

Before the second phase of the Lausanne Conference and at the moment when questions partly affecting Egypt are being discussed, the Egyptian National Delegation thought it would be useful to present to the Lausanne Conference a memorandum highlighting the various states of these questions from the Egyptian point of view.

Although we are hardly allowed to entertain any illusions about the fate reserved for Egypt by this Conference, the Egyptian National Delegation considers it a duty to make a new effort in favor of the independence of its unfortunate country.

Indeed, they persist in wanting to dispose of its fate without even having consulted it.

Egypt feels all the more the affront made to its history because it has always fought for its independence and for a century its efforts have been incessant to free itself.

THE EGYPTIANS HAVE ALWAYS FOUGHT TO MAINTAIN THEIR INDEPENDENCE.

Thanks to its conquests and the brilliant victories of its armies, Egypt was becoming itself again. In 1807 it defeated the English at Aboukir, in 1818 it took Arabia and re-entered into possession of the holy places of Islam, which had fallen into the hands of the Wahhabis, in 1823, it established order and security in Sudan.

It is no longer a serf of Turkey, it is its ally and plays a glorious role in the Turco-Greek war of 1826-29.

Always....
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official memorandum submitted by the Egyptian National Delegation during the second phase of the Lausanne Conference (1922–1923). The delegation protests the fact that international powers are deciding Egypt's political fate and sovereignty without consulting the Egyptian people or their representatives. To justify their claim to complete independence, the memorandum outlines Egypt's modern military and political achievements under Muhammad Ali Pasha's dynasty, citing the defeat of the British at Aboukir in 1807, the campaigns in Arabia against the Wahhabis in 1818, the pacification of Sudan in 1823, and Egypt's autonomous role as an ally rather than a vassal of the Ottoman Empire during the Greek War of Independence (1826–1829). The text reflects the intense diplomatic struggle of Egyptian nationalists seeking recognition of their sovereignty in the post-World War I international order.

3) De céder à l'Angleterre la garde du Canal du Suez, confiée à l'Egypte et à la Turquie associées, par le traité de 1888. Ce transfert menace à la fois la souveraineté de l'Egypte et les intérêts des autres Puissances, ayant le libre passage au canal.
En outre, ces dispositions seraient contraires au Pacte National d'Angora qui dit que tous les territoires séparés de la Turquie seront reconnus par elle indépendants et que cette indépendance sera remise à la nation elle-même.
Maintenant que la Turquie renonce à ses droits sur l'Egypte conformément à son pacte national, ainsi qu'il résulte des différentes déclarations de principe de ses hommes d'Etat à Angora et au cours de la Conférence de Lausanne, c'est aux Egyptiens, sans aucun doute, que la Turquie cède directement le reste de ses droits sur l'Egypte.
ai_content.english_translation: 5. 64. Because of a community of religion which removed any idea of vassalage, it is for Egypt to receive from its former ally the affirmation of its independence and the restitution of its rights, which no one has the power to dispose of outside of the two nations directly concerned. Any other way of acting would have as a result: 1) The recognition of all measures taken by England since its illegal occupation in 1882 until today. 2) The recognition of the 1889 Sudan agreement by which England arrogated to itself the right to associate with Egypt in the possession of the Sudan, an integral part of the Nile Valley. A treaty whose nullity cannot escape any man of good faith. 3) To cede to England the guard of the Suez Canal, entrusted to Egypt and Turkey jointly, by the treaty of 1888. This transfer threatens both the sovereignty of Egypt and the interests of other Powers, having free passage to the canal. Furthermore, these provisions would be contrary to the National Pact of Angora which says that all territories separated from Turkey will be recognized by it as independent and that this independence will be returned to the nation itself. Now that Turkey renounces its rights over Egypt in accordance with its national pact, as results from the various declarations of principle of its statesmen in Angora and during the Lausanne Conference, it is to the Egyptians, without a doubt, that Turkey directly cedes the rest of its rights over Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
KASSALA RAILWAY & COTTON GROWING SCHEME
Note for Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs.
A Loan is being raised with the Guarantee of the British Government under the Trade Facilities Act 1921 to provide funds for the building of an extension of the Sudan Government Railways about 217 miles in length to Kassala in the Eastern Sudan and so connect that district with Port Sudan the Sudan's port of export on the Red Sea.
One of the main objects of building the line is to render possible the development of the cotton growing area in the Gash Delta (which is in the Kassala district) where excellent long staple cotton of the Egyptian type has been grown for a number of years but no expansion of the industry was feasible without railway transport. The line will also open up the Eastern Sudan for the export of cereals and cattle.
As the Treasury considered it preferable that the loan should not be raised by the Sudan Government itself and decided that as a condition of granting the guarantee the co-operation must be obtained of people with experience of cotton growing in the Sudan who would undertake to finance and carry out the irrigation and development of the cotton growing area in the Gash Delta, the following arrangements have been entered into by the Sudan Government with the Sudan Plantations Syndicate Ltd., which has been growing cotton in the Sudan for years past.
(1) A Concession has been granted to the Kassala Cotton Company Ltd., which has been formed for the purpose by the Sudan Plantations Syndicate Ltd., for the financing supervision and management, in consultation with the Sudan Government, for a period of 40 years, of the irrigation and development of the cotton growing area in the Gash Delta.
The terms of the concession are on lines similar to those upon which the Sudan Plantations Syndicate Ltd., has undertaken the management of the cotton growing in the Gezira District of the Sudan.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official memorandum regarding the Kassala Railway and Cotton Growing Scheme. It outlines the financing of a 217-mile railway extension to Kassala, guaranteed by the British Government under the 1921 Trade Facilities Act, to facilitate the export of cotton, cereals, and cattle. It details the creation of the Kassala Cotton Company Ltd. by the Sudan Plantations Syndicate Ltd. to manage irrigation and development in the Gash Delta for 40 years, mirroring the management model used in the Gezira District.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal administrative note concerning the infrastructure and economic development of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan in the early 1920s. It highlights the strategic intersection of British imperial trade policy (the Trade Facilities Act 1921) and the commercial exploitation of the Gash Delta. The text explains the necessity of railway connectivity to Port Sudan for the viability of long-staple cotton production, a cornerstone of the colonial economy. It also documents the institutional role of the Sudan Plantations Syndicate, a major private entity that dominated agricultural development in the region, and establishes the administrative framework for the Kassala Cotton Company's concession.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
EMPIRE COTTON GROWING CORPORATION.
Changes made in the Corporation's investments since the last meeting of the Board of Trustees on December 14th, 1922.
The Finance Sub-Committee at their meeting on April 17th, 1923, reviewed the Corporation's securities, and after careful consideration decided to recommend to the Executive Committee that they should make certain alterations in these securities, and that the action taken should be reported to the Board of Trustees.
It was pointed out by the Corporation's financial advisers that holders of National War Bonds had the option of transferring within 14 days after the payment of any half-yearly interest into National War 5% Loan at 95; by investing in this security, therefore, the Corporation could ensure against capital depreciation, the conversion rights which might entail a considerable appreciation in value if as appeared likely a yield of 4% on gilt-edged securities became the normal return.
The recommendations were adopted by the Executive Committee on April 17th, and the following list gives the securities sold, the prices obtained, and the total realised after the deduction of commissions:-
£250,086.9.5. Local Loans 3% @ 66 1/8 £169,751. 12. 4.
£52,250 Conversion Loan 3 1/2% @ 79 5/8 £41,407. 2. 6.
£100,000 Funding Loan 4% @ 91 1/2 £90,874. 0. 0.
£302,012. 14. 10.
The sale of these investments resulted in a net profit of over £28,000 after deducting commission, whilst an increase in annual revenue of about £780 is secured.
The sum thus realised was invested in National War 5% Bonds 1927 and 1929, the nominal value of the Bonds purchased being £291,784: 15: 1.
In order to avoid purchasing a broken amount of these Bonds the British Overseas Bank bought £141,000 1927 Bonds and a similar amount of 1928 Bonds. The cost of these Bonds at 104 18/32 exceeded the amount realised from the sale of the investments by £230:4:10. The Finance Committee decided that this sum be most easily adjusted by investing this sum from surplus income, and their suggestion was adopted by the Executive Committee at their meeting on May 8th. The nominal value of the Bonds purchased with this sum is £215: 4: 11.

It outlines the strategic sale of various government securities (Local Loans, Conversion Loan, and Funding Loan) to reinvest in National War 5% Bonds, aiming to hedge against capital depreciation and secure a better yield. The text provides a detailed accounting of the sale proceeds, the resulting profit of over £28,000, and the subsequent purchase of 1927 and 1929 National War Bonds, including a minor adjustment for a surplus payment handled by the British Overseas Bank.

EMPIRE COTTON GROWING CORPORATION.
COTTON PRODUCTION IN THE EMPIRE.
MEMORANDUM PREPARED AT THE REQUEST OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE BOARD OF TRADE.
INTRODUCTION.
In compliance with the request of the President of the Board of Trade that the Corporation would furnish him with a memorandum setting out the main directions in which, in their opinion, cotton growing in the Empire could best be expedited, if the necessary financial assistance could be arranged, the Corporation have the honour to submit the following statement:—
In their opinion, given the requisite finance, a very large increase of the supplies of raw cotton within the Empire can be secured. The addition would immediately begin to be felt and would extend over a considerable period. The Corporation have attempted to deal with the question comprehensively in their note, of which this introduction is a summary. The primary factors in augmentation of production are comprised under the heads of Transport, Research, Political Support, Administration and Personnel, and Financial Support.
1. Transport.—This is treated in detail later; in the main it is an African problem. The following railways, if constructed, will help cotton growing:—
(a) In the Sudan—
(i) Sennar-Gedaref.
(ii) Suakin-Tokar light railway.
(iii) Nuba Mountains—El Obeid railway.

It outlines strategies to increase raw cotton production within the British Empire through financial assistance. It identifies key areas for development, specifically focusing on transport infrastructure, research, political support, and administration. It highlights specific railway projects in the Sudan, including lines connecting Sennar to Gedaref, a light railway between Suakin and Tokar, and a line connecting the Nuba Mountains to El Obeid, as essential for facilitating cotton cultivation.

The text reflects the colonial economic policy of the interwar period, specifically focusing on the Sudan as a strategic hub for cotton production. Research.—This is only second in importance to communications and includes the improvement of cultivation methods, elimination or mitigation of pests and disease, the provision of approved and suitable strains of seed, and if possible, the evolution of improved types of cotton, from the standpoint of yield, resistance to unfavourable climatic conditions and to pests, and of suitability to manufacturing requirements.
3. Political Support.—If the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan is to play an adequate part in cotton production, it is essential that she receive equitable treatment so far as the provision of water from the Nile is concerned. The subject is to come up for discussion between the Governments of Great Britain and Egypt at an early date. It is at present reserved.
Relations with Abyssinia are involved in the proposed irrigation from Lake Tsana, while it is possible that some of the terms of the Congo Convention might require modification if certain promising experiments in the way of cotton cultivation are to have a fair chance.
4. Administration and Personnel.—The Corporation are to take the share in schemes of cotton development that it appears from the President’s note the Government desire that they should, and if any share in direct responsibility for results is to be assigned to them, their relationship to the Departments of State concerned needs more exact definition.
An enquiry into the personnel, average capacity and organization of the various African Departments of Agriculture is urgently called for. Steps to augment or reinforce personnel are now being taken in the Union of South Africa and in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan.
5. Financial Support.—If cotton growing is to be developed on sound lines, financial support, varying in degree and in kind, will have to be provided. Definite proposals in this direction will shortly be submitted from South Africa, and the industry is probably sufficiently developed in the Sudan for the requisite funds to be provided through normal financial channels; but it appears to the Corporation to be probable that the provision of a certain amount of initial credit would enormously facilitate rapid development. The Corporation will shortly have at their disposal reliable technical advisers in all parts of Africa, whose reports on commercial propositions might with some confidence be accepted. The Corporation fully recognise the difficulty of rendering such assistance. Anything which might cause a boom, or speculative floating of doubtful ventures is to be avoided at all costs, and yet the provision of some kind of help is unavoidable if the requisite rapidity of progress is to be assured.
As regards the amount of cotton that can be hoped for, the Corporation direct attention to the note prepared by their Director for the Imperial Economic Conference, in which some estimate is attempted.

ai_content.transcribed_text: 1. There are two methods by which the supply of cotton can be increased, (a) by rendering existing areas under cotton more productive, and (b) by enlarging the areas in which cotton is cultivated, and multiplying their number. The first can be attained by methods which can be grouped under the head of 'Research', resulting in the improvement of cultivation methods or the reduction of insect pests. For example, in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan at present cotton is grown on a three years' rotation: a cotton crop, which is followed in the second year by a green leguminous crop ploughed in for manure, and in the third, by a bare fallow. Such a system constitutes an agricultural nightmare. The Corporation have arranged for a scientific mission to proceed to the Gezireh, and if as a result of their report a crop of any value can follow the cotton, or the bare fallow be eliminated, it is obvious that the aggregate production will be much increased. To give another illustration, well nigh a third of the Nyasaland crop is at present damaged by the red boll worm. If entomological work should succeed in controlling this pest the result in increased cotton production would be obvious. More important still, if reinforcement of the argument be needed, if as the result of the establishment of a really first-class Empire Plant Breeding Station a type of cotton should be evolved which does not shed its bolts, a very notable increase would be recorded. Work of this kind the Corporation have in hand or under consideration, and it should be within their resources; but no success which can be hoped for from such methods can do more than alleviate the scarcity unless an enormous increase of areas under cultivation can be secured. 2. The areas which can be developed are, in Africa, the Sudan, Uganda, including the Kavirondo District of Kenya Colony, Tanganyika, large tracts in the Union of South Africa, Nigeria, Nyasaland and, very likely Northern and Southern Rhodesia outside Africa, India, Australia, and Mesopotamia. 1. Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. Dealing with these placed in order of importance, priority would appear to belong to the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. With a view to accelerating cotton growing in the Sudan the British Government could help in the following ways: (I). By guaranteeing Sudan Government Loans for an extension of the Gezireh scheme beyond the present 300,000 feddans. Work could not commence until Autumn, 1925, so that money would not be required till then, but the Sudan ought to know that it can count on getting the money when required. Extension would be based on present storage capacity at Makwar, probably justifiable up to 600,000 feddans. The extension beyond 300,000 feddans would be undertaken in two stages of 150,000 feddans each, the first to cost £1,250,000 for main canalization, the second probably more, but by the time the second unit was ready for development there should be proved results from the first 300,000 feddans, and then further money ought to be procurable from the ordinary channels. It is to be noted, however, that this raises a question with Egypt. In 1920 Lord Allenby gave an undertaking in writing to Sirry Pasha, then Minister of Public Works, that the area of 300,000 feddans would not be exceeded without examination of the whole project by an expert commission, on which both Egypt and the Sudan were to be represented. A public announcement appeared in the press that the area would not be exceeded without reference to Egypt; but the Foreign Office can, of course, state the exact position. (II). By assisting the Sudan to obtain and finance Lake Tsana Concession from Abyssinia. The obtaining of this Concession, which has no conceivable value to anybody else, by, in the opinion of the Corporation, a matter of the most urgent moment. The possible obligation might be put at from £50,000 to £100,000 annual rent, and two million capital.
ai_content.english_translation: The text outlines two primary strategies for increasing cotton production: improving existing cultivation through research (e.g., crop rotation and pest control) and expanding the total area under cultivation. It identifies the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan as the highest priority for expansion, specifically through the Gezireh scheme. It proposes that the British Government guarantee loans for expanding the Gezireh project beyond 300,000 feddans, noting the political sensitivity of this expansion due to a 1920 agreement with Egypt involving Lord Allenby and Sirry Pasha. It also suggests securing the Lake Tsana Concession from Abyssinia to support irrigation and development.

(iii) Assistance in financing railway development, (a) Sennar-Gedaref say two million, (b) Suakin-Tokar light railway say £50,000, (c) Nuba Mountains light railway.

As regards labour, the Corporation incline to think, judging from past Sudan experiences, that the necessary labour would be forthcoming for all the schemes referred to. The immigration into the Sudan from other parts of Africa is a most interesting phenomenon.

(iv) Political Aspect—His Majesty's Government would have to come to an agreement with Egypt which would ensure the Sudan a fair opportunity for development of irrigation schemes, and for drawing water from the Nile, subject only to not interfering with such rights as Egypt can fairly claim to have established by past use, and which are necessary to her own continued existence. This question is of supreme importance. The really big opportunity of development in the Sudan depends on Nile water, and if Egypt claims the right to veto all projects which involve the utilization of such water, the Sudan can never play a really important part as a cotton producing country. Given reasonable co-operation between the two countries, and if the money can be found for the necessary works on the Nile, there is ample water for both. The British Government should be prepared (a) to make Egypt a fair offer guaranteeing her undisturbed use of such water as she can justly claim, and (b) if Egypt will not accept any reasonable offer, to back up the Sudan in going ahead without Egypt's acceptance.

Either alternative may involve financial commitments for the British Government. As regards (a) a settlement with Egypt might be facilitated if the British Government were to put at the disposal of the Sudan a sum of money in order to enable the latter to repay to Egypt a part of the advance made to the Sudan in the past for development, say half the development debt, 3 million, or such sum as may be deemed just. Until an equitable arrangement is made as regards this money lent by Egypt to the Sudan the position of both the Sudan Government and the British Government is a fundamentally weak one. As regards (b) a definite break with Egypt would compel the Sudan Government to face the necessity of providing her own military forces and involve her in some other financial loss. 2. Union of South Africa and Swaziland.
A railway ought to be constructed joining up Komatiport to Komatiport, thereby opening up Swaziland, and the Union Government and the High Commissioner ought to be asked to set forth their views as to how the development of the cotton belt, both in the Union of South Africa and in Swaziland ought to be undertaken. The necessity of setting up ginning, transport and financial facilities must form an integral part of any comprehensive scheme. The provision of a certain amount of money under Imperial guarantee would be a necessary part of both schemes, and General Smuts and his Government ought to be asked to formulate a scheme as, indeed, they have already promised to do. Properly conceived, the second part of this proposition ought to be interest-bearing well nigh from the start, and a Swaziland railway might reasonably be expected to be an interest-bearing proposition before very long.
3. Uganda and Kenya
The principal cotton-growing area in Uganda is the country in the vicinity of Lake Choga. The Governor of Uganda has recommended that this area be linked up with the Jinja Railway by an extension from that railway in the direction of Mbale. While such a railway is desirable, it would be far better to extend it south of Mount Elgon and through Northern Kavirondo in Kenya Colony to connect with the extension of the Uganda Railway which has now reached Turbo. This would enable the railway to be commenced from both ends simultaneously. Northern Kavirondo is an area of great agricultural possibilities and one in which cotton might be grown in large quantities. Intimately connected with this extension is the repair and improvement of the Uganda Railway and harbour facilities at Kilindini.
4. Tanganyika.
The repair and possible extension of the Lindi tramway would open up a potential cotton-growing country with a large native population.
The area south of Mwanza and Lake Victoria is a proved cotton-growing area, and it is suggested that the Governor of Tanganyika be asked whether a railway from Mwanza southwards eventually to be extended to Tabora would assist and develop cotton growing in the former neighbourhood.
5. Nyasaland.
An extension of the existing railway northwards to Lake Nyasa is now under consideration, but much difference of opinion exists as to the route to be followed. That hitherto favoured by the Colonial Office would leave the Shire Highlands Railway at Luchenza and follow an eastern route to Lake Nyasa near Fort Johnston on the Lake. A large and very vocal body of opinion, however, recommends that the new railway should leave the existing one at Chirono and follow the line of the Shire Valley where the most promising agricultural land is found. It is a matter of urgency that this question now held up should be decided, and in making a decision a subsequent extension to North-Eastern Rhodesia should be borne in mind. In any case the existing railways north and south of the Zambesi ought to be connected by a bridge.
6. Nigeria.
The Nigerian Government are carrying out the construction of the eastern railway as rapidly as labour conditions permit, and it is understood that they do not desire to do more than this for the present; but it is not known whether this would be their attitude if they were offered a loan free of interest for a term of years.

It is felt that the possibilities of a considerable increase, particularly of the type of cotton of which the shortage in Lancashire is most acutely felt, exist in India, but the Corporation have always been advised that on account of the political situation in that country, considerable caution was advisable as to the line of approach. The late Sir William Meyer, to whom the Corporation were much indebted, always expressed himself in this sense. A highly-developed organization, the Indian Central Cotton Committee, now exists for handling cotton questions. It works on much the same, though smaller, lines as the Corporation, and derives its means from an export duty on cotton as well as on cotton consumed in Indian Mills. The Corporation are in constant touch with the Indian Committee, and meet any requests for assistance to the best of their ability. So far as practical recommendations go, they can only suggest that the Secretary of State call the attention of the Viceroy to the urgency of the present situation, and to the fact that a ready demand exists for surplus Indian cotton of the requisite quality and length of staple; and that, if and when the Government of India invite either technical or financial assistance, so far as possible it will be accorded. The Corporation note with satisfaction that the gigantic Sukkur barrage has at last been approved, and that the work will be started forthwith. A scheme for Indian settlement on a large scale in British Guiana, a subject on which the Indian Government possess full information, would appear to be worthy of their consideration. 8. Australia. A considerable amount of cotton can be grown in Australia, notably in Queensland and in New South Wales. Want of population is the limiting factor. A considerable proportion of the funds which the British Government have earmarked for emigration purposes might be devoted to this object, though some changes in the Act might be necessary if the best results are to be obtained. Supplementary to this, the Australian Government might consider the advisability of trying some Italian immigrants, particularly those who have been born and brought up on the Lombard plain. It is understood that Italian labour is beginning to appear in considerable numbers on Queensland sugar estates.

LOANS.
It is essential that if His Majesty's Government decide to proceed with any or all of these extensions they should be constructed with a loan free of interest, and that no interest should be paid until the Colonies in which they are situated are in a position to do so without crippling their resources and stifling their normal development. To give a Colony a railway and starve its educational or medical services in an attempt to secure premature payment of interest might prove a very doubtful blessing, even from the standpoint of immediate cotton production.

METHOD OF DEVELOPMENT TO BE ADOPTED.
South Africa and Australia apart, a very careful experiment on the lines of the partnership existing in the Sudan would appear well worthy of a trial by the Colonial Office. At present European ownership is strictly limited in their cotton-growing areas, but if the advantage of capitalistic development could be obtained, and exploitation of the native landowner avoided, progress would be speedier. Kavirondo would appear an ideal spot in which such an experiment could be made, unless the Conventional Congo Agreement render such a policy impossible. It is difficult to see how it could be worked without a guiding monopoly.

NECESSARY STAFF.
This is a matter of extreme difficulty. It must be borne in mind that cotton-growing is only one aspect of tropical agriculture, and that the ideal officers, whether in the employment of the Governments concerned, or of cotton-growing enterprises, or of the Corporation, ought to be trained tropical agriculturists. The Corporation, after consulting most eminent technical advice, have adopted a scheme of training, and are giving a certain number of Studentships, this year eleven in all; but the Colonial Office and the Governments interested ought to be asked most carefully to consider whether they are satisfied with their present method of recruitment, or whether their agricultural cadets ought not to receive the same advantages as are open to the Corporation's Students. In such an enquiry the Corporation would gladly co-operate. The Corporation are strongly of opinion that a decision ought to be adopted if the very difficult agricultural problems are to be satisfactorily solved. Such a decision would probably entail the enlargement of the new Imperial College of Agriculture in Trinidad. Furthermore, the Corporation have been driven to the conclusion that on account of the miserable rates of pay offered in the past by various tropical Dependencies, many of the existing staff are quite incapable of tackling the problems presented to them, and that a vigorous weeding out is called for. The problem is beset with difficulties, as at present the supply of capable men, even to fill existing vacancies, is in no sense equal to the demand.

RELATIONS BETWEEN THE CORPORATION AND DEPARTMENTS OF STATE.
If it is the policy of His Majesty's Government to hold the Corporation responsible or even partially responsible for any share in the working out of this programme, it ought to be definitely laid down that they can call for any information which is necessary to enable them to judge of the merits of a situation from the broadest possible standpoint, and that they should receive such information not as a matter of courtesy, but in the ordinary course of routine.

General Smuts has already acceded to such a condition, and has further promised that the Senior Cotton Specialist to be appointed to his Department of Agriculture by the Corporation shall have free right of communication with the Corporation, of course, through the responsible Minister.

ai_content.transcribed_text: WHEREAS His Majesty's Government, in accordance with their declared intentions, desire forthwith to recognise Egypt as an independent sovereign State; And whereas the relations between His Majesty's Government and Egypt are of vital interest to the British Empire: The following principles are hereby declared: 1. The British protectorate over Egypt is terminated, and Egypt is declared to be an independent sovereign State. 2. So soon as the Government of His Highness shall pass an Act of Indemnity with application to all inhabitants of Egypt, martial law as proclaimed on the 2nd November, 1914, shall be withdrawn. 3. The following matters are absolutely reserved to the discretion of His Majesty's Government until such time as it may be possible by free discussion and friendly accommodation on both sides to conclude agreements in regard thereto between His Majesty's Government and the Government of Egypt: (a) The security of the communications of the British Empire in Egypt, (b) The defence of Egypt against all foreign aggression or interference, direct or indirect, (c) The protection of foreign interests in Egypt and the protection of minorities, (d) The Soudan.

ai_content.transcribed_text: EGYPT AND SOUDAN. CONFIDENTIAL. No. 1. Admiralty to Foreign Office.—(Received February 13.) Admiralty, February 12, 1923. Sir, I AM commanded by my Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to acquaint you that in drawing up their arrangements for the control of shipping in any future war the Admiralty had contemplated arrangements for the establishment at Port Said of a staff for the examination of cargoes of neutral vessels possibly carrying contraband. 2. In view, however, of the altered conditions following on the recognition of the independence of the Kingdom of Egypt and the proposal to institute a 'Canal zone,' the details of which have not yet been settled, it appears that this contemplated arrangement will have to be altered. In such case it would be necessary that this Control Service should be moved to a point further south, probably to Perim and Aden, with an auxiliary station at Port Soudan. 3. I am accordingly to enquire whether in the view of the Secretary of State— (1.) Under existing circumstances a contraband control might be set up at Port Said or Suez, or (2.) In the event of a war of first-class importance it is thought that His Majesty's Government would resume control of the Canal zone as in the late war. I am, &c. P. E. MARRACK. (For Secretary).
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal communication from the British Admiralty to the Foreign Office regarding the strategic control of shipping and contraband in the Suez Canal zone following the recognition of Egyptian independence. It discusses the logistical necessity of moving contraband inspection stations from Port Said to more southern locations like Perim, Aden, or Port Sudan due to the changing political status of Egypt, and seeks clarification on whether the British government intends to re-occupy the Canal zone in the event of a major future conflict.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential diplomatic dispatch from the British Admiralty to the Foreign Office, dated February 1923. It reflects the post-World War I geopolitical transition in Egypt, specifically following the Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence in 1922. The Admiralty is concerned with maintaining maritime security and contraband control in the Suez Canal, which was a vital artery for the British Empire. The text highlights the tension between recognizing Egyptian sovereignty and the British desire to maintain strategic military control over the Canal zone, illustrating the 'reserved points' of British policy in Egypt that would continue to cause friction throughout the interwar period.

If, therefore, Egypt becomes a member of the League of Nations in the near future and presses for an early settlement by agreement with His Majesty's Government of the question of the British garrison, we cannot refuse to open negotiations without delay. It is, however, altogether beyond the bounds of probability that any Egyptian Government would agree to a settlement which would admit the presence of a British garrison in the localities laid down in Lord Derby's memorandum. With the failure of the negotiations it would only be natural that Egypt should bring the matter to the notice of the League, claiming that she had done her best to settle the matter amicably with His Majesty's Government and had failed, owing to the latter refusing to apply the general proposition which they had themselves laid down in the case of the French occupation of the Ruhr. As against this claim we could only argue that the Anglo-Egyptian question which must be decided in the manner laid down in our Declaration of February 28th, 1922, and that until agreement was reached, the status quo must be maintained. We might also invoke our intimation to all foreign Powers following the withdrawal of the Protectorate that we would regard outside intervention in the affairs of Egypt as an unfriendly act. It is, however, to be feared that before an impartial court the Egypt claim would appear to be the stronger one, and it would certainly be embarrassing for us to refuse an offer of arbitration by the League or reference of the dispute to the Permanent Court of International Justice.

The naval staff in a paper submitted separately in E.7640 have shown clearly the enhanced importance of the Suez Canal and how relatively easy it would be for the Japanese to block it by sinking a ship in a suitable place immediately before the outbreak of war.

It is, however, evident from paragraph 12 of the memorandum that what the War Office want in Egypt is a strategic place d'armes - a sort of near eastern Aldershot - and rightly or wrongly they appear to attach quite as much importance to this object as to the defence of the Canal.

They are, in fact, more intent on proving the necessity for keeping British troops in the interior of Egypt than on evolving counter measures to ward off the danger, which the admiralty regard as threatening the safety of the Empire. Thus in order to strengthen their case they enunciate in paragraph 6 the new doctrine that "our position in the Sudan.......... cannot be considered secure unless we are able to control Egypt".

The view taken in this department has been the precise converse provided that the Suez Canal remains free from obstruction viz. that as long as we control the Sudan, Egypt is at our mercy. Again in paragraph (3) of the memorandum reference is made to the conclusion of the Standing Defence Sub-Committee of the Committee of Imperial Defence in regard to the strategical importance of Palestine.

That conclusion was based upon memoranda by the Colonial Office, Air Staff, General Staff, and Naval....

It analyzes the conflict between British military requirements (maintaining a garrison and a 'strategic place d'armes') and the diplomatic risks of refusing arbitration by the League of Nations. It also contrasts the views of the War Office, the Admiralty, and the Colonial Office regarding the strategic necessity of controlling Egypt to secure the Sudan and the Suez Canal.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a high-level British inter-departmental memorandum, likely dating to the early 1920s, concerning the post-Protectorate status of Egypt. It reflects the tension between the British military's desire to maintain a strategic military presence in Egypt (viewing it as a 'near eastern Aldershot') and the diplomatic constraints imposed by the 1922 Declaration and the potential for international arbitration via the League of Nations. The text highlights the strategic importance of the Suez Canal and the Sudan to the British Empire, while documenting internal disagreements between the War Office, the Admiralty, and the Colonial Office regarding the necessity of a permanent military occupation of Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text: E 9134/1761/16 No. 1. Field-Marshal Viscount Allenby to Mr. Lindsay.—(Received September 12.) Dear Lindsay, YOUR letter dated the 6th September, 1923. I concur in your proposal to send a copy of Scott's despatch No. 566 of the 18th ultimo to the War Office, pointing out to them the situation as regards our obligations to surrender Kasr-el-Nil Barracks, and advising them that, unless the barracks can be given up immediately, which is presumably not possible, we shall have to offer to pay rent pending arrival at an agreement with the Egyptian Government. You have correctly interpreted the views I expressed when you and I discussed the question of barrack accommodation in Egypt. We can and should let the Egyptian Government regain possession of Kasr-el-Nil when it can be economically done; but the operation must perforce be gradual, as we cannot turn our troops into the streets. Yours sincerely, ALLENBY.

Suggested Reply.
On 27th February and on 4th March bombs were thrown in Cairo with the result that 8 British soldiers were wounded. I have no doubt that all sensible and patriotic Egyptians sincerely deplore these crimes, the perpetration of which is encouraged by the political excitement engendered and kept alive by agitation.
A week before the first of these outrages the members of the Wafd issued a manifesto which, in Lord Allenby's opinion, was calculated to disturb public order. He accordingly had them warned that they would be held personally responsible for any disorders that might result from their action, and when the second outrage occurred they were arrested.
In imposing fines Lord Allenby is attempting to bring home to the public the need for collaborating with the police in effecting the arrest of terrorists. The apathy with which not merely the recent outrages but the long series of attempts on the lives of British subjects have hitherto been regarded by native eye-witnesses has enabled the criminals in every case to make good their escape. His Majesty's Government have not, therefore, interfered with any measures which Lord Allenby, in his appreciation of the local situation, has felt bound to adopt in order...

It details specific incidents of violence against British soldiers in Cairo, the issuance of a manifesto by the Wafd party, and the subsequent punitive measures taken by Lord Allenby, including the arrest of Wafd members and the imposition of fines to encourage public cooperation with the police against terrorists.

Daily Mail
7th March 1923
CAIRO ARRESTS.
EGYPT STILL WITHOUT A CABINET.
FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.
Cairo, Tuesday.
Further arrests were made to-day in connection with the throwing of two bombs at British Army Headquarters on Sunday. They include those of the editor of Al Biali, an organ of the extremists, and Sadik Bey Hanio, one of the most prominent supporters of Zaghlul Pasha, the exiled Nationalist leader.
It is reported that a new Wafd, or Executive, of the Nationalist Party has been formed to carry on the work of those arrested. Members of the Legislative Assembly to-day petitioned King Fuad and asked for an audience, which he declined to grant.
Adly Pasha, the ex-Prime Minister, states that he has definitely declined to form a Ministry. The prospects of a settlement of this crisis are therefore more remote than ever.
** Three British soldiers were wounded and an Egyptian was killed by one of the bombs thrown on Sunday. Egypt has been without a Cabinet since the beginning of February.

It reports on arrests following a bombing at British Army Headquarters in Cairo, the formation of a new Wafd executive, the refusal of King Fuad to meet with the Legislative Assembly, and the refusal of Adly Pasha to form a new government, leaving Egypt without a cabinet since February.

The text highlights the ongoing conflict between the British occupation authorities, the Egyptian monarchy under King Fuad, and the Wafd Party led by the exiled Saad Zaghlul. Parliamentary Question. Mr. Lawson, - To ask the Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, whether, seeing that the Egyptian electoral law as issued enacts that registration for the coming election must take place before the 16th of this month and that this constitutes the beginning of the electoral campaign, steps will be taken that political leaders and others imprisoned and exiled by the operation of British martial law are no longer arrested and imprisoned by British martial law without charge or trial during the electoral period. [Wednesday 9th May.]

Reply within
Answer May 9

The continuance of martial law does not affect the Seychelles deportees as they are detained under a Seychelles Order in Council. Zaghloul's return to Egypt, however, can only be prevented by the exercise of martial law. If pressed regarding either the former or the latter as well as regarding the Wafd prisoners we shall presumably have to refer to Lord Allenby.

There is nothing in the electoral law (see Flag "A") which fixes the last day of registration for an election as May 16th. Mr. Lawson is probably thinking of Article 23 of the Electoral Law which fixes 11 days from the 1st of May as the period in which the Commission is appointed to hear complaints against the electoral lists.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
THE SECRETARY OF STATE'S QUERY ON THE ATTACHED DRAFT.
Lord Allenby's despatch No. 594 of July 24th lest (E. 7611 - Flag "D") explains the machinery for dealing with the investigation of these political crimes.
Up to the end of July last the Egyptian police could not arrest anyone on suspicion or search anyone's domicile without first obtaining authority from the Parquet. The police and the parquet had long been at loggerheads, and as Lord Allenby points out, the parquet was more often than not indifferent and liable through fear of students and hooligans to allow the enquiry to break down. To eliminate this weak spot in the Egyptian machinery, Lord Allenby and Sarwat Pasha evolved a scheme whereby certain picked men were delegated to serve under the Egyptian Director General of Public Security for the sole purpose of elucidating these political outrages and were invested with certain powers under Martial Law enabling them to arrest on suspicion and effect domiciliary searches, and at the same time rendering them immune from liability for such acts under the Egyptian Code of Criminal Procedure.
What in practice happens is that the Egyptian Department of Public Security undertakes the task of investigating these crimes.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a memorandum or briefing note regarding the administrative and legal procedures for investigating political crimes in Egypt. It details the tension between the Egyptian police and the 'Parquet' (public prosecutor's office) and explains how Lord Allenby and Sarwat Pasha bypassed these legal hurdles by creating a special unit under the Director General of Public Security, empowered by Martial Law to conduct arrests and searches without the usual judicial oversight.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a British diplomatic record concerning the administrative restructuring of Egyptian law enforcement during the British occupation. It highlights the friction between the traditional Egyptian judicial system (the Parquet) and the British-led security apparatus. By invoking Martial Law, British authorities, in collaboration with the Egyptian Prime Minister Sarwat Pasha, effectively circumvented the Egyptian Code of Criminal Procedure to suppress political unrest, specifically targeting student activists and 'hooligans' by granting police immunity and expanded powers of arrest and search.

The responsibility for the investigation of these crimes is thus a joint one but when it comes to arrests and domiciliary searches, though the instruments may be the civil Egyptian police, the authority is solely that of Martial Law.

To an arrest on suspicion or a domiciliary search being necessary, one of the officials who is invested with the necessary powers under Martial Law by Lord Allenby sends the Egyptian police to effect the arrest or perform search. More often then not, if the person arrested happens to be someone of standing, he is confined in Kasr el Nil Barracks under a military guard, for the reason that ordinary accommodation in an Egyptian prison is so poor and the prisons are now so crowded that such a person could not be accommodated in a manner suitable to his position.

It clarifies that while the Egyptian police may physically carry out arrests or searches, they do so under the direct authority of Martial Law powers granted by Lord Allenby. It further notes that high-status individuals arrested under these conditions are typically detained at the Kasr el Nil Barracks rather than in standard Egyptian prisons, citing the poor conditions and overcrowding of the latter as the justification for this preferential treatment.

ai_content.transcribed_text: BOMB OUTRAGES (EGYPT). 47. Mr. MOREL asked the Prime Minister whether any of the actual perpetrators of the bomb outrages in Egypt have been arrested; how many members of the Egyptian Nationalist party are now in prison on suspicion of being concerned with those outrages; how many of them are now given for their explanations having been given for their arrest and if, in view of the long period for which some of these persons have already been detained, His Majesty's Government will recommend to the High Commissioner the advisability of expediting the trials of these persons and ensure their being brought before the Egyptian Courts. Mr. MCNEILL: I cannot, with propriety, comment on the guilt or innocence of the prisoners now on trial, nor can I indicate the political allegiance of the other 35 prisoners under detention, on the 2nd June on suspicion of complicity in the murder conspiracy. I know of no 'explanation' of their arrest has been given in reply to several recent questions in Parliament (namely that the persons are suspected of complicity in the conspiracy.) We have nothing to show that there is any delay in collecting the evidence against the arrested persons and as much of the evidence against them is coming out in the Conspiracy Trial now in progress we must presumably await the termination of this before proceeding against them. Their trial will no doubt be held as soon as the evidence is complete. (c.f. our reply to Mr. Oliver on 4th June). In reply to Mr. Morel's question of 16th May it was stated that they would be tried by Court Martial as long as Martial Law provided a better chance of bringing the guilty parties to justice than any other course; Mr. Morel, of course, would like them to be arraigned before the Native Courts, when he no doubt hopes that they would be acquitted. It is apparently the present intention of the local authorities to bring the suspects before the Native Courts if adequate evidence is forthcoming...
ai_content.english_translation: The document is a transcript of a parliamentary question and answer session regarding the arrest of individuals in Egypt following bomb outrages. Mr. Morel questions the Prime Minister on the status of the perpetrators and the detention of Egyptian Nationalist party members. Mr. McNeill responds on behalf of the government, stating that he cannot comment on the guilt of those on trial, noting that 35 prisoners were detained on June 2nd for conspiracy to murder. He defends the legal process, citing the ongoing Conspiracy Trial and the use of Court Martial proceedings as a means to ensure justice, while acknowledging the possibility of future trials in Native Courts.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a record of a British Parliamentary exchange concerning the political climate in Egypt during the period of British occupation and the enforcement of Martial Law. It highlights the tension between the British administration's use of military tribunals (Court Martial) to suppress nationalist activity and the parliamentary scrutiny regarding the due process and detention of Egyptian Nationalist party members suspected of involvement in bomb outrages and conspiracy to murder. The text reflects the administrative and legal mechanisms used by the British to maintain control in Egypt while responding to domestic political pressure in London.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
TELEGRAM.
Foreign Office
To
HIGH COMMISSIONER FOR EGYPT
Ramleh.
July 5th 9 15 pm
Received 6th 6 54 am
No. 685.
Your despatch 121. (2689/14)
H.M.G. have had under consideration assistance rendered by Egypt during war and there is strong feeling that this assistance is by no means commensurate with great advantages and prosperity she enjoys owing to British efforts and sacrifices. Question of conscription for labour has been again raised and it has been suggested that the proclamation of November 6th 1914 should be cancelled. I am reluctant to agree to this course unless no other means are open but it is essential to effectively prosecute the war that military requirements in regard to provision of labour should be met. I should be glad to learn therefore whether you can guarantee that number of egyptian labourers now employed by H.M.G. can be maintained at full figure of 100,000 further that recruitment can be secured on more permanent basis and not be subject to constant renewals owing to terms of contracts made. It is also very desirable that labour should be secured at lower rate than is being now paid.
Please consider and report as soon as possible how these objects can be best attained with due regard to native feeling. You may think it advisable to explain necessities of situation to Sultan and his ministers and enlist their advice and co-operation.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a diplomatic telegram from the British Foreign Office to the High Commissioner for Egypt regarding the mobilization of Egyptian labor for the war effort. The text expresses British dissatisfaction with the level of support provided by Egypt, suggesting that Egypt has benefited significantly from British protection. It discusses the potential cancellation of a 1914 proclamation to allow for the conscription of labor, requests a guarantee of 100,000 laborers, seeks to lower wages, and advises the High Commissioner to consult with the Sultan of Egypt to achieve these goals while managing local sentiment.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1917 diplomatic telegram from the British Foreign Office to the High Commissioner for Egypt during the First World War. It highlights the colonial administration's pressure on the Egyptian government to provide a larger, cheaper, and more permanent labor force for the British military effort, specifically the Egyptian Labour Corps. The document reflects the tension between British wartime requirements and the political necessity of maintaining stability by involving the Sultan and his ministers in the recruitment process, illustrating the complex power dynamics of the British Protectorate in Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
WAR OFFICE, LONDON, S.W. 2nd June, 1917.

Sir:-
I am commanded by the Army Council to transmit to you for the information of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs the attached extract from a telegram (No. A.M.1953 dated May 24th 1917) received from the General Officer Commanding-in-Chief, Egypt.

The Army Council are now awaiting the receipt of the copy of the High Commissioner's letter referred to in the last paragraph of the telegram and in the meantime I am to enquire if in the opinion of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs any modification of the proclamation issued by His Majesty's Government on November 6th, 1914, can be made in order to enable the Egyptian Government to render greater assistance in the prosecution of the war. In this connection I am to invite attention to the present favourable military situation and to the consequent absence of any danger of the invasion of Egypt.

I am to add that the Army Council would also be glad to receive any suggestions which may occur to the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs on the other points raised in the telegram.

I am, etc.,
(Signed) B. B. Cubitt.

Under Secretary of State,
Foreign Office.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official letter from the War Office in London, dated June 2, 1917, addressed to the Foreign Office. It conveys a request from the Army Council to the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs regarding a telegram received from the General Officer Commanding-in-Chief in Egypt. The letter asks for an opinion on whether the proclamation of November 6, 1914 (which established the British Protectorate over Egypt), should be modified to allow the Egyptian government to contribute more effectively to the war effort, citing the improved military situation and the lack of threat of invasion as justification for potential policy changes.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of internal British administrative correspondence during World War I. It highlights the strategic reassessment of the British Protectorate over Egypt in 1917. By this stage of the war, the British military command in Egypt felt that the initial restrictive measures imposed by the 1914 proclamation—which had formally severed Egypt's ties to the Ottoman Empire and established British control—could potentially be relaxed to encourage greater Egyptian participation in the war effort. The document reflects the bureaucratic coordination between the War Office and the Foreign Office regarding colonial policy and the mobilization of local resources in the Middle Eastern theater.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
S E C R E T.
EXTRACT from a telegram from G.O.C.-in-C., Egypt, to the C.I.G.S., War Office, No. A.M. 1953 of 24th May, 1917.

"As regards your question as to whether I consider that Egypt is contributing to fullest extent possible both as regards railway material and in other respects, it has always been my opinion that practically speaking Egypt has not felt the strain of war at all and I have constantly studied the question as to how to utilise Egyptian resources more fully without producing results which would so adversely affect the carrying on of the war in other ways as to counter-balance the advantages obtained by further utilisation of Egyptian resources. I had a conference with High Commissioner yesterday on the subject and we agreed that Egypt's part in the war had been unimportant. It appeared to us that possible ways in which Egypt could help further in the war might be considered under two main headings, namely personnel and railways.

"As regards personnel it must be remembered that in consequence of a proclamation issued presumably with the authority of H.M. Government by General Maxwell on November 6th, 1914, no form of compulsory recruitment either of soldiers or labour is possible in Egypt at the present time. This proclamation gave a definite assurance that "Great Britain takes upon herself the sole burden of the present war without calling on Egyptians for aid therein". However in spite of this there are serving under voluntary engagements some 15,000 men of the Egyptian Army, of whose brilliant services in the Darfur operations and in the Soudan I need not remind you,"
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a secret extract from a telegram sent by the General Officer Commanding-in-Chief in Egypt to the Chief of the Imperial General Staff in London on May 24, 1917. The text discusses the extent of Egypt's contribution to the British war effort during World War I. The author notes that Egypt has not felt the 'strain of war' and discusses potential ways to increase contributions in personnel and railway resources. It highlights a significant political constraint: a 1914 proclamation by General Maxwell, which promised that Britain would not impose compulsory recruitment on Egyptians, thereby limiting the British military to voluntary enlistment, despite which 15,000 Egyptians were serving in the Egyptian Army in Darfur and the Sudan.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document provides critical insight into the British administrative and military policy in Egypt during World War I. It highlights the tension between the British desire to mobilize colonial resources (specifically manpower and infrastructure) and the political necessity of maintaining stability in Egypt by honoring the 1914 pledge against conscription. The mention of the 15,000 volunteers serving in the Darfur and Sudan campaigns underscores the role of the Egyptian Army as a regional force under British influence, while the telegram itself reflects the internal British debate regarding the 'unimportant' nature of Egypt's contribution relative to the total war effort.

EXTRACT FROM A TELEGRAM FROM G.H.Q. TO WAR OFFICE, DATED 16TH MAY 1916.

As regards your question as to whether Egypt is contributing to the fullest possible extent, both in material and in respect of personnel, it has always been my opinion that practically all that Egypt can do in the way of war effort I have and am doing. 

As regards the question as to how to obtain more personnel without seriously affecting the services of the railways, I have considered the matter in conference with the Residency and we trust that Egypt's part in the war will be considered under two main heads, namely, the provision of labour and the provision of personnel. 

As regards personnel it must be remembered that the consequences of a premature conscription with the Egyptian fellahin would be serious. In the opinion of the Ministry of War, no form of compulsory recruitment is possible in Egypt at present. The Ministry of War states that Great Britain relies upon the Egyptian Labour Corps for the bulk of the labour without calling on the fellahin. However, in spite of this there are some 15,000 men serving under voluntary enlistment and some 3,000 newly recruited battalions for service with E.E.F. and also 98,000 manual labourers of whom 23,000 are serving overseas. There is no doubt in my opinion that no serious increase in personnel can be obtained under voluntary enlistment and the very important question arises as to whether introduction of compulsory recruiting is advisable in Egypt at the present moment. Of course large numbers of Egyptians would become available but I think it is questionable whether the advantages thus obtained would compensate for the serious check to the production of the cotton and food stuffs which Egypt is now required to supply. It is quite possible moreover that the introduction of compulsory recruitment might have an unfortunate effect on the present satisfactory internal condition of Egypt with its mixed population. As regards question as to whether we could get more help from Egyptian railways I am bound to say that Sir G. Macaulay has given me assistance in every possible way and has invariably complied with every request I have made. At the present time he is prepared to take up and place at my disposal 176 kilometres of single line between Alexandria and Dabaa. I have most carefully considered question as to whether any more lines can be taken up and at present I do not see how this can be done without seriously interfering with conduct of war in other ways. It should be borne in mind that railway arteries must be maintained in a country where wheeled traffic is practically non-existent if the produce of the country such as cotton, sugar, cereals, onions and forage is to be moved from agricultural out districts to ports and centres of consumption. Inland waterways are being developed but this comparatively slow method

It is an official report regarding the British military's assessment of Egypt's contribution to the First World War effort, specifically addressing the feasibility of conscription versus voluntary labor and the strategic use of Egyptian railway infrastructure.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a 1916 official extract from a telegram sent to the British War Office regarding the mobilization of Egyptian resources during World War I. It highlights the tension between the British military's need for manpower (laborers and soldiers) and the economic necessity of maintaining Egypt's agricultural output (cotton and food) for the war effort. It explicitly discusses the risks of implementing compulsory conscription among the Egyptian fellahin, citing potential social unrest, and acknowledges the cooperation of Sir G. Macaulay regarding the repurposing of railway lines between Alexandria and Dabaa for military logistics.

FOREIGN OFFICE,
June 8th, 1917.

Sir:-
I am directed by Lord R. Cecil to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, No. 0.1/206 (M.O.1.), of the 2nd instant, relative to the question of the assistance contributed by the Egyptian Government in the prosecution of the war.
I am to state, in reply, that the questions raised by the Army Council are receiving His Lordship's careful consideration, but that he would prefer to postpone his reply to your letter until he has been acquainted with the views expressed by His Majesty's High Commissioner for Egypt in the letter referred to in the last paragraph of Sir A. Murray's telegram.
Lord Robert would be grateful if the Army Council would furnish him with a copy of that letter as soon as it has been received.
I am, etc.,
(Signed) R. Graham.

Secretary
to the Army Council.

It acknowledges receipt of a letter from the Army Council regarding the Egyptian Government's contribution to the war effort. Lord Robert Cecil requests a delay in providing a formal response until he can review the correspondence from the British High Commissioner in Egypt, which was referenced in a telegram from Sir A. Murray. The Foreign Office asks the Army Council to provide a copy of that specific letter.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence between the British Foreign Office and the Army Council during the First World War. It highlights the bureaucratic coordination required to manage the British protectorate of Egypt and the mobilization of local resources for the war effort. The mention of Sir A.
