ai_content.transcribed_text: FOREIGN OFFICE, June 18th, 1917. W.115861/17. Immediate. Sir:- With reference to my letter of the 8th instant, I am directed by Mr. Secretary Balfour to transmit to you, herewith, to be laid before the Army Council, a copy of a despatch from His Majesty's High Commissioner for Egypt, relative to the recruiting of labour for military purposes in Egypt. Mr. Balfour is in agreement with the views expressed by Sir R. Wingate in his letter of May 23rd to the General Officer Commanding in Egypt, (which, it is presumed, is that mentioned in your letter, No. 0.1/206 (M.O.1.), of the 2nd instant) and with the conclusions reached by the Committee at Cairo to whom the matter was referred by Sir R. Wingate. With respect to the second paragraph of your letter of June 2nd, Mr. Balfour considers that it would be a grave mistake to modify the Proclamation of November 5th, 1914, and that the advantages which might be obtained by such action would not be proportionate to the bad effect which would thereby be created on public opinion in Egypt and elsewhere. I am, Sir, Your most obedient, Humble Servant, (Signed) R. Graham. The Secretary to the Army Council.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official communication from the British Foreign Office to the Army Council, dated June 18, 1917. It discusses the recruitment of labor in Egypt for military purposes, referencing previous correspondence from Sir Reginald Wingate (High Commissioner for Egypt) and the Army Council. It also addresses a request to modify a 1914 Proclamation, which the Foreign Secretary, Arthur Balfour, advises against due to potential negative impacts on public opinion in Egypt.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence from the British Foreign Office during the First World War. It highlights the delicate balance the British administration in Egypt had to maintain regarding the mobilization of local labor for the war effort. The reference to the 'Proclamation of November 5th, 1914' pertains to the declaration of a British Protectorate over Egypt following the Ottoman Empire's entry into the war. The document illustrates the tension between military requirements for labor and the political necessity of maintaining stability and avoiding civil unrest in Egypt, as advised by the High Commissioner, Sir Reginald Wingate, and supported by Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. 7th July 1917. Sir, I have the honour to forward herewith a copy of a telegram received from the Foreign Office on the subject of utilising further the resources of Egypt more especially in regard to labour and railway material. I am directing a Committee (constituted as follows) to assemble without delay to consider and report on this question:- Sir William Brunyate, K.C.M.G., President. The Hon. R. Lindsay, M.V.O., J. Haines Esq., Colonel W.H. Herbert, C.M.G., Members. I suggest that Brigadier-General Sir George Macaulay K.C.M.G., should also be appointed a member of this committee in his joint capacity of Director of Railway Transport and General Manager Egyptian State Railways. I further suggest, for your consideration, that Lieutenant-Colonel Jellicoe, A.Q.M.G. (Personal Services) become a member of the Committee and that Lieutenant-Colonel Basil be called in evidence as required. I am arranging that all necessary correspondence be placed at the disposal of the Committee. I have the honour to be Sir, Your obedient servant, General Sir Edmund Allenby, K.C.B., Commanding-in-Chief Egyptian Expeditionary Force.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official letter from the British Residency in Cairo, dated July 7, 1917, addressed to the High Commissioner of Egypt. The author, General Sir Edmund Allenby, informs the recipient that he has received a telegram from the Foreign Office regarding the mobilization of Egyptian resources, specifically labor and railway materials for the war effort. Allenby proposes the formation of a committee to oversee this, naming specific British officials and military officers to serve on the board, and requests the inclusion of key railway and transport personnel to facilitate the logistical requirements of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence from the British Residency in Cairo during the First World War. It reflects the British military's strategic focus on mobilizing the infrastructure and labor force of Egypt to support the Sinai and Palestine Campaign. The document highlights the bureaucratic process of establishing a committee to manage the extraction of resources, illustrating the intersection of colonial administration and military logistics under the command of General Sir Edmund Allenby, who had recently taken command of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force in June 1917.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Paraphrase of Telegram No. 685 dated July 5th from the Foreign Office to the High Commissioner in reference to His Excellency's Despatch No. 121 of May 30th.

"In view of the considerable advantages and prosperity which she owes to the efforts and sacrifices of Great Britain it is strongly felt that Egypt has not rendered corresponding assistance during the war. His Majesty's Government have had this assistance under consideration and in particular the question of conscription has again been raised. The war cannot be effectively prosecuted unless means are found to provide the labour requisite for military requirements and it has been suggested that we should cancel the Proclamation of November 6th 1914. This I am reluctant to agree to unless no other course can be found and I shall accordingly be glad if you will inform me whether you can give guarantees on the following points:-
"1. That the number of Egyptian labourers now employed by His Majesty's Government can be maintained at the full figure of 100,000.
"2. That recruitment can be assured on a more permanent basis and not be subject to constant renewals owing to the terms of contracts made. Further, attention is drawn to the desirability of securing labour at a rate lower than that at present paid. You should consider the best means by which, with due regard to native feeling, these objects can be attained and report at the earliest date possible.
As regards the Egyptian State Railways the efforts which they have made to meet military requirements are fully recognised; nevertheless it may be necessary that they should help even further in providing rails and locomotives to meet freight difficulties."
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a paraphrase of a telegram sent from the British Foreign Office to the British High Commissioner in Egypt regarding the mobilization of Egyptian labor for the war effort. It expresses British dissatisfaction with Egypt's contribution to the war, proposes the potential implementation of conscription, and requests the High Commissioner to secure 100,000 laborers on more permanent, lower-cost contracts. It also acknowledges the role of the Egyptian State Railways in supporting military logistics.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a diplomatic communication from the British Foreign Office during World War I, reflecting the colonial administration's pressure on Egypt to increase its contribution to the British war effort. It highlights the transition from voluntary labor to more coercive measures, such as the potential cancellation of the 1914 Proclamation, to ensure a steady supply of 100,000 laborers for the Egyptian Labour Corps. The document underscores the tension between British military requirements and the socio-economic impact on the Egyptian population, as well as the strategic importance of the Egyptian State Railways in managing wartime freight and logistics.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
THE RESIDENCY
RAMLEH
7th July 1917

Sir William Brunyate, K.C.M.G.

With reference to the attached copy of a letter addressed by the High Commissioner to the Commander-in-Chief, His Excellency would be glad if you would arrange for the Committee to assemble as soon as possible.

The Committee should submit a report on the whole question for submission to His Majesty's Government having regard to the former correspondence of which copies are attached.

You will receive in due course a copy of the Commander-in-Chief's reply to the High Commissioner.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official memorandum sent from the British Residency in Ramleh, Egypt, to Sir William Brunyate. It instructs him to convene a committee to prepare a report for the British government regarding a matter previously discussed in attached correspondence, following a communication between the High Commissioner and the Commander-in-Chief.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal administrative directive issued from the British Residency in Ramleh, Egypt, during the First World War. It reflects the high-level coordination between the British civil administration (the High Commissioner) and the military command (the Commander-in-Chief) regarding the formation of a committee to address a specific policy or strategic question for His Majesty's Government. Sir William Brunyate, a prominent British colonial official and legal expert in Egypt, is being tasked with organizing this committee, highlighting the bureaucratic machinery of the British Protectorate in Egypt during the 1917 period.

The letter discusses the inability of Egypt to provide new military troops due to current constraints, but expresses the government's willingness to provide financial support—specifically £500,000—to cover the costs of defensive works required by the British military. The document highlights the complex power dynamic between the British High Commission and the Egyptian Council of Ministers during the period of the British Protectorate.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPIE. 
Presidence du Conseil des Ministres. 
Le Caire, le 11 Janvier 1916. 
No 323. 
Monsieur le Conseiller Financier, 
Dès le début de la Guerre avec la Turquie, le Gouvernement Britannique, s'inspirant de sentiments dont le Gouvernement Egyptien ne pouvait que lui être reconnaissant a déclaré prendre la responsabilité exclusive de la défense de l'Egypte, assumant à lui seul et sans aucune participation du Gouvernement Egyptien, les charges considérables de toute nature que comportait un pareil engagement. Mais les évènements ont pris depuis une telle tournure que l'Egypte semble devoir être l'objet d'une nouvelle et plus importante offensive. 
Devant cette situation, Sa Hautesse le Sultan et Son Gouvernement considerent que l'Egypte ne saurait continuer à se désintéresser en quelque sorte d'un conflit où son existence même pourrait être en jeu et quelle se doit à elle-même de s'associer dans la plus large mesure possible à la défense de son territoire et de ses droits. 
Si de nouvelles troupes ne pouvant être levées actuellement, il ne saurait être question d'un concours militaire, l'Egypte peut tout au moins prêter son assistance financière. Les mesures prises ou à prendre par les Autorités militaires en vue de la défense ont nécessité et nécessitent encore des travaux considérables dont le coût est évalué à £500,000 environ; l'Egypte est disposée à prendre cette dépense à sa charge. 
Je vous prie en conséquence de vouloir bien étudier les voies et moyens pour assurer à cet égard la réalisation des vues du Gouvernement Sultanien. 
Veuillez agréer, Monsieur le Conseiller Financier l'assurance de ma haute considération. 
Le Président du Conseil des Ministres 
(Sd) H. RUCHDI 
S.S. Lord E. Cecil, Conseiller Financier
ai_content.english_translation: COPY. Presidency of the Council of Ministers. Cairo, 11 January 1916. No 323. Mr. Financial Advisor, From the beginning of the War with Turkey, the British Government, inspired by sentiments for which the Egyptian Government could only be grateful, declared it would take exclusive responsibility for the defense of Egypt, assuming alone and without any participation from the Egyptian Government, the considerable burdens of all kinds that such an engagement entailed. But events have taken such a turn that Egypt seems likely to be the object of a new and more important offensive. Given this situation, His Highness the Sultan and His Government consider that Egypt cannot continue to remain indifferent to a conflict where its very existence could be at stake and that it owes it to itself to associate itself to the greatest extent possible with the defense of its territory and its rights. If new troops cannot be raised at present, there can be no question of military assistance, but Egypt can at least provide financial assistance. The measures taken or to be taken by the military authorities for defense have necessitated and still necessitate considerable work, the cost of which is estimated at approximately £500,000; Egypt is prepared to take this expense upon itself. I therefore ask you to kindly study the ways and means to ensure the realization of the Sultanic Government's views in this regard. Please accept, Mr. Financial Advisor, the assurance of my high consideration. The President of the Council of Ministers (Signed) H. RUCHDI. To His Excellency Lord E. Cecil, Financial Advisor.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official communication from Hussein Rushdi Pasha, the Prime Minister of Egypt, to Lord Edward Cecil, the British Financial Advisor to the Egyptian government, dated January 11, 1916. It reflects the shifting political and military landscape of World War I, specifically the transition of Egypt from a passive protectorate to an active financial contributor to the British war effort against the Ottoman Empire. The document formalizes the Egyptian government's offer to cover £500,000 in defense costs, signaling a strategic shift in the Sultanate's involvement in the conflict to secure its own territory against potential Ottoman offensives.

ai_content.transcribed_text: COPIE. Cairo, 7 Février 1916. Monsieur le Président, J'ai l'honneur d'accuser réception de la lettre de Votre Excellence en date du 4 Janvier dernier à l'adresse de Lord Edward Cecil, par laquelle vous avez bien voulu lui faire part du désir, de Sa Hautesse le Sultan et de Son Gouvernement que l'Egypte, ne pouvant pas prêter un concours armé pour aider à repousser l'offensive dont elle est menacée, contribuât du moins à la tache de la défense en prenant à sa charge la dépense qu'entraîneront les travaux militaires actuellement en cours de construction. Il est vrai que, par suite d'une économie rigoureuse dans les administrations de l'Etat et d'une amélioration relative des revenus due en grande partie à la présence en Egypte des troupes britanniques, le Gouvernement Egyptien peut maintenant espérer, son fond de réserve aidant, qu'il n'aura pas à recourir à des moyens extraordinaires tels qu'un emprunt par exemple pour se procurer des ressources. Mais ce résultat ne sera pas atteint sans difficulté et, bien que la situation financière paraisse plus favorable à l'heure actuelle qu'elle ne l'était l'an passé, il ne faut pas oublier que jusqu'à la fin des hostilités les affaires demeureront forcément dans l'incertain. Un épuisement complet de la Réserve pourrait plus tard mettre l'Egypte dans la nécessité de chercher de l'aide financier au dehors. Je n'ai pas besoin de rappeler à Votre Excellence à quel point il est désirable d'eviter cet expédient. Pour toutes ces considerations, il ne parait pas possible de recommander au Gouvernement Egyptien la mise à éxécution directe du projet amical qu'il s'était proposé
ai_content.english_translation: COPY. Cairo, February 7, 1916. Mr. President, I have the honor to acknowledge receipt of Your Excellency's letter dated January 4th last, addressed to Lord Edward Cecil, by which you were kind enough to inform him of the desire of His Highness the Sultan and His Government that Egypt, being unable to provide armed assistance to help repel the offensive by which it is threatened, should at least contribute to the task of defense by taking on the expense that the military works currently under construction will entail. It is true that, as a result of rigorous economy in the State administrations and a relative improvement in revenues due in large part to the presence of British troops in Egypt, the Egyptian Government can now hope, with the help of its reserve fund, that it will not have to resort to extraordinary means such as a loan, for example, to obtain resources. But this result will not be achieved without difficulty, and although the financial situation appears more favorable at the present time than it was last year, one must not forget that until the end of hostilities, affairs will necessarily remain uncertain. A complete depletion of the Reserve could later put Egypt in the position of having to seek financial aid from abroad. I do not need to remind Your Excellency how desirable it is to avoid this expedient. For all these considerations, it does not seem possible to recommend to the Egyptian Government the direct implementation of the friendly project it had proposed.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal diplomatic letter from the British High Commission in Cairo to an Egyptian official (likely the Prime Minister), dated February 1916. It addresses a proposal by the Sultan of Egypt to contribute financially to the defense of Egypt against the Ottoman-led offensive during World War I. The British official, writing on behalf of Lord Edward Cecil (Financial Adviser to the Egyptian Government), politely declines the offer, arguing that while Egypt's financial situation has improved due to the presence of British troops and fiscal austerity, the government must preserve its reserve funds to avoid the necessity of seeking foreign loans during the uncertainty of the ongoing war.

Je puis ajouter que les amicales intentions du Gouvernement de Sa Hautesse ont été officieusement communiquées au Gouvernement de Sa Majesté Britannique, qui désire que l'expression de sa haute appréciation des sentiments qui ont dicté cette proposition, soit adressée à Sa Hautesse.

ai_content.english_translation:
and it would be more acceptable to His Britannic Majesty's Government that the offer not be formally presented to it.

It will be necessary, however, at the end of hostilities, to definitively settle a considerable expense that the Egyptian Government has provisionally assumed by carrying it to a suspense account. It will then be possible, if the country's financial situation permits, to charge Egypt with a greater share of this expense than that which would fall to it under the arrangements currently in force.

Moreover, I am in a position to inform Your Excellency that the Egyptian Government's proposal has been duly communicated to H.E. the High Commissioner, who has highly appreciated it, recognizing in it a new example of the excellent sentiments of His Highness towards Great Britain and a new proof - if one were needed - of the spirit of friendship and cooperation by which His Highness and His Government have always been inspired. I may add that the friendly intentions of His Highness's Government have been unofficially communicated to His Britannic Majesty's Government, which desires that the expression of its high appreciation of the sentiments that dictated this proposal be addressed to His Highness.

It is therefore an agreeable duty for me to act as the interpreter to Your Excellency of this high appreciation of His Britannic Majesty's Government, which I pray you to be so kind as to communicate to His Highness the Sultan.

Please accept, Mr. President, the assurance of my very high consideration.

THE FINANCIAL ADVISOR a.i.
(Signed) R.C.L.

THE RESIDENCY, EGYPT
25 JUL 1917
No 1615/11

The High Commissioner has received and examined the report drawn up by Lieut.-General H.M. Lawson, C.B., on the subject of man power in Egypt.
His Excellency desires that this report, copies of which could be furnished you by General Head Quarters, should be carefully studied by the committee of which you are a member.
Four points of special importance emerge from this report. They are:
(1) to review and reconsider the lists drawn up by the Classification Committee;
(2) to consider the utilisation of elements of the Egyptian Army, so as to release British soldiers;
(3) to examine the desirability of an appeal being made by the High Commissioner for women for hospital work and other female occupations;
(4) to investigate the question of providing native clerks for Army office requirements.
His Excellency wishes to draw particularly your attention to the above questions, but your terms of reference in this connection should be General Lawson's report as a whole.
With a view to facilitating the work of your Committee, the High Commissioner has requested the Commander-in-Chief to be so good as to appoint a second representative to attend its meetings with Lieutenant-Colonel Jellicoe.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official memorandum from the British Residency in Egypt, dated July 25, 1917. It conveys the High Commissioner's instructions regarding a report on 'man power' in Egypt authored by Lieutenant-General H.M. Lawson. The recipient is instructed to study the report, specifically focusing on four key areas: reviewing classification lists, utilizing Egyptian Army personnel to replace British soldiers, recruiting women for hospital and other roles, and hiring local clerks for military administrative tasks. The document also notes the appointment of Lieutenant-Colonel Jellicoe as a representative to the committee.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an administrative directive from the British Residency in Egypt during the First World War. It reflects the British military's urgent need to optimize manpower resources in the Egyptian theatre of operations in 1917. By seeking to replace British soldiers with Egyptian Army personnel and local civilian clerks, and by exploring the mobilization of women for support roles, the document illustrates the logistical pressures faced by the British Empire in the Middle East as the war entered its later stages. The mention of 'man power' and the specific focus on administrative efficiency highlights the transition toward total war mobilization in colonial territories.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. RAMLEH. July 24th 1917. Sir, With reference to my letter of July 7th, I have the honour to transmit to you herewith copy of a Minute, which I have caused to be addressed to Mr. Lindsay, as President, and to his Colleagues on the Committee appointed to enquire into Egypt's contribution to the war. You will observe that I am instructing this Committee to examine General Lawson's report as a whole - and with special reference to four points - with a view to meeting the recommendations put forward by him. In the enclosed Minute, I also inform the Committee that I am requesting you to be so good as to appoint a second officer to sit together with Lieutenant-Colonel Jellicoe on this committee. I should be grateful if you could see your way to meeting this request. I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient Servant, General Sir Edmund Allenby, K.C.B., Commanding-in-Chief, Egyptian Expeditionary Force.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Note to all members of the Committee on Utilisation of Egypt's resources during war.

As it appears that certain of the members of the Committee called upon by the High Commissioner to discuss the further utilisation of Egypt's resources during the War are still in some doubt as to the origin, composition and aims of this Committee, I am directed by His Excellency to transmit the following explanations, which, it is hoped, may elucidate any misunderstandings which may exist.

On the receipt of Foreign Office telegram No. 635 His Excellency decided to summon a Committee to discuss the questions raised therein. The principal point to be discussed was the possibility of further utilising the resources of Egypt during the War - with special reference to the Egyptian Labour Corps.

The members selected were:-
1. Sir William Brunyate, to act as Chairman.
2. Mr Lindsay. 3. Mr Haines. 4. Colonel Herbert.
5. Brigadier General MacMunn. 6. Lt-Colonel Jellicoe.

Owing to stress of work Sir William Brunyate found himself unable to accept the post of Chairman, which therefor devolved on Mr Lindsay, to whom Sir William Brunyate was requested to hand over all papers relating to the formation of the Committee and the questions to be discussed.

Since the selection of the Committee two further questions have arisen, which His Excellency considers should also be discussed by the committee. The first is General Lawson's Report on Man Power in Egypt; the second "Rolling Stock and Coal", which formed the subject of Sir George MacMunn's Note forwarded to you on July 27th.

It serves to clarify the purpose and membership of a committee established to manage Egyptian resources during World War I. It outlines the committee's original mandate regarding the Egyptian Labour Corps, lists the appointed members, notes a change in chairmanship from Sir William Brunyate to Mr. Lindsay due to workload, and adds two new agenda items: General Lawson's Man Power report and the issue of rolling stock and coal.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a primary source from the British Residency in Cairo during the First World War. It illustrates the administrative efforts of the British occupation authorities to mobilize Egyptian resources, specifically labor and infrastructure (rolling stock and coal), to support the war effort. The document highlights the bureaucratic process of committee formation and the shifting priorities of the British administration in Egypt as the war progressed, specifically referencing the Egyptian Labour Corps, which was a critical component of the British military logistics in the Middle Eastern theater.

EGYPTIAN STATE RAILWAYS AND TELEGRAPHS
MEMORANDUM.
Referring to F.O. telegram No.685 of 5-7-17, Section 2, para. 4 - "As regards the Egyptian State Railways -------- difficulties".
The State Railways have parted with all reserve permanent way material for Army purposes, only retaining just enough for urgent repairs.
Existing open lines will have to be torn up if more rails are wanted, but at present a sufficient supply for Military purposes is on order from India.
The question of engines and rolling stock is more serious:
Excluding non-effective vehicles, wagons in shops and awaiting repair, etc., there are approximately 9,200 available trucks on E.S.R.
Of these, 1170 have been sent to Military lines East of Suez Canal, and 537 are permanently marshalled in troop stocks, Armoured Trains, etc., and are not available for any other purpose.
Army traffic requirements West of the Suez Canal account for another 1,700.
Total for Military purposes 3,400.

EGYPTIAN STATE RAILWAYS AND TELEGRAPHS

When the Military line from Kantara to Gaza has been doubled, a further supply of 80 engines and 1,200 trucks will be wanted on that section, probably before January 1918. There is very little prospect of these being obtained from War Office or outside sources by the end of the year.

The E.S.R. will therefore have to furnish them and thus will have parted with just one half of its available rolling stock. i.e., 4,600 wagons.

With the existing 5,800 wagons for the public and railway service purposes it is just possible to meet public demands during the present slack season, but there will be a shortage of wagons in the Cotton Season, and the crop cannot be moved at the usual rate.

If the extra 1,200 wagons are taken at the end of the year the transport problem in Egypt will be a burning question, as even if non-essential traffic be eliminated the number of trucks available will be insufficient for necessary public requirements.

The question of engines is equally worthy of attention.

There are in stock 588
Lent to Military Railway 53
Balance on E.S.R. 535.

[Handwritten note at bottom]: Not received for registration.

THE RESIDENCY
RAMLEH
5th August 1917

HIGH COMMISSIONER
EGYPT
6AUG1917
No 1615/23

The Hon: R. Lindsay, M.V.O.

I have read your Draft Report No.2 on the Man
Power question. It seems to me a good and useful produc-
tion.

The following minor points struck me on reading
it through:-

1. Are adequate bounties paid immediately to the
relations of casualties? This to some extent might
neutralize their adverse effect on recruitment. As the
Committee will, I am sure, agree it is everything to pay
at once.

2. Has any endeavour been made to punish landowners
and employers etc. spreading false reports detrimental
to recruiting?

3. I hope the value of the Press will not be ignored
as a means of influencing public opinion. A series of
articles contrasting the present state of Egypt with
other countries, belligerent and otherwise, and depicting
the economic effects of a Turco-German military occupation
of Egypt, however temporary, in the Moslem papers could not
fail to have a certain effect. Could, under the aegis
of the Committee, a Press campaign of this nature be work
up? To be successful it would require to be subtle,
persistent and suitably disseminated. Can the Committee
suggest any leaders of public opinion besides the Ministe
and other officials whose assistance might be canvassed t
o. Not received / 1st September. ack.
ai_content.english_translation:
This document is a memorandum from 'The Residency' in Ramleh, dated August 5, 1917, addressed to 'The Hon: R. Lindsay, M.V.O.' It bears a stamp from the 'High Commissioner Egypt' dated August 6, 1917, with reference number 1615/23. The sender acknowledges receipt and review of 'Draft Report No.2 on the Man Power question,' deeming it a 'good and useful production.' However, the memo outlines three 'minor points' for consideration:

1.  It questions whether 'adequate bounties' are paid 'immediately' to the families of casualties, suggesting that prompt payment could 'neutralize their adverse effect on recruitment.' It emphasizes the importance of immediate payment, stating 'it is everything to pay at once.'
2.  It asks if efforts have been made to 'punish landowners and employers etc. spreading false reports detrimental to recruiting.'
3.  It stresses the importance of utilizing 'the Press' to influence public opinion. It proposes a 'Press campaign' under the 'aegis of the Committee' involving a series of articles. These articles should contrast 'the present state of Egypt with other countries, belligerent and otherwise,' and illustrate the 'economic effects of a Turco-German military occupation of Egypt,' even if temporary, particularly in 'Moslem papers.' The memo notes that such a campaign would need to be 'subtle, persistent and suitably disseminated' to be successful. It also asks if the Committee can suggest 'leaders of public opinion besides the Ministers and other officials' whose help could be sought. A handwritten note at the bottom reads "Not received / 1st September. ack."
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an internal British administrative memorandum from the Residency in Ramleh, Egypt, dated August 5, 1917, addressed to R. Lindsay, M.V.O. It provides critical feedback on a 'Draft Report No.2 on the Man Power question,' indicating the British administration's efforts to manage and mobilize human resources in Egypt during World War I. The memo highlights key concerns regarding recruitment, including the need for prompt payment of bounties to casualties' families to maintain morale and recruitment rates, and the necessity of suppressing false reports that undermine recruitment efforts. Crucially, it emphasizes the strategic importance of propaganda, suggesting a sophisticated press campaign in 'Moslem papers' to influence public opinion. This campaign would aim to contrast Egypt's situation with other nations and underscore the negative economic consequences of a potential Turco-German occupation, thereby garnering support for the British presence and war effort. The document reveals the complex challenges faced by the British in maintaining control and stability in Egypt during wartime, including managing public perception and ensuring adequate manpower.

first place to the ingrained distrust of the fellah for all service connected with the army and military operations. This sentiment is historic in its nature and cannot be overcome in any short period of time. The conditions of the last forty years have done little to remove it. Combined with the mental constitution and unwarlike propensities of the fellah it gives rise to countless vague fears and exposes recruiting agents from numerous unforeseeable contingencies. There is a village in Menufieh into which the Recruiting agents cannot enter because two or three of its men were taken prisoner two years ago by Turks and have not been heard of since. If any considerable number of men were to return wounded to their villages from Sinai; if a transport returning from France with Labour Corps men were to be torpedoed; if a high Nile flood were to necessitate calling out the corvée; all these/elements which would be instantly reflected in recruiting returns. Moreover, the fellah in the country districts is probably more prosperous than he has ever been before, and landowners have been paying 6 1/2 p.t. per day for labour where 3 1/2 p.t. used to suffice. It is not surprising that landowners and employers of labour interested in eliminating competition, spread stories to discourage recruiting for the army.

The short terms of service for which alone the fellah will engage, is in accordance with his usual habits as observed in the past. Contractors, except in special cases such as coaling at Port Said, were seldom able to keep their labourers for any considerable uninterrupted period, and if a man wished to go away, it was generally worth while to pay him and let him go.

ai_content.transcribed_text: The Remedies. We note from the F.O. telegram of July 5th. that the question of conscription has again been raised. On this we can but refer to the report of the Committee appointed by Your Excellency in May on this special subject. We are unanimously agreed that its conclusions are correct, and that the introduction of compulsion would have the most unfortunate results both politically, and on the actual volume of service that it would be possible to obtain from the country. As regards administrative pressure, we observe that General Sir A. Murray is more averse from this method even than from conscription and we unanimously concur in this view. Mudirs, by their loyal and energetic co-operation, have already exercised such influence as can properly be used; and where any local excesses of zeal on the part of lesser officials have occurred they have always had the opposite effect on recruiting to that aimed at. It remains to enquire whether recruiting can be improved by offering further inducements. What the Army requires is more, better, and longer service, and it is only logical to assume that a well considered scheme for increasing pay, improving bonuses, and giving leave of absence must achieve something in the desired direction. But we admit that we are not sanguine that it will solve the problem set before us. The townsman who has not profited by the agricultural boom and has suffered from the rise of prices, comes forward freely for the wages now offered; but his physique is poor, and he is not satisfactory for Army purposes. To the countryman whom we specially desire to enlist, a matter of a piastre or two per day has

Furthermore, they recommend maintaining short terms of service, as longer terms or indeterminate periods (like the duration of the war) are contrary to local customs and would likely discourage potential recruits.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COPIE
PRÉSIDENCE DU CONSEIL DES MINISTRES.
LE CAIRE, le 11 janvier 1916.
No. 323.
À Monsieur le Conseiller Financier,
Dès le début de la guerre avec la Turquie, le Gouvernement égyptien, s'inspirant de sentiments dont le Gouvernement britannique ne pouvait que être reconnaissant a déclaré prendre la responsabilité exclusive de la défense de l'Égypte, assumant à lui seul et sans aucune participation du Gouvernement égyptien, les charges considérables de toute nature que comportait un pareil engagement. Mais les événements ont pris depuis une telle tournure que l'Égypte semble devoir être l'objet d'une nouvelle et plus importante offensive.
Devant cette situation, la hauteuse le Sultan et son Gouvernement considérant que l'Égypte ne saurait continuer à se désintéresser en quelque sorte d'un conflit où son existence même pourrait être en jeu et qu'elle se doit à elle-même la défense de son territoire et de ses droits.
Et, de nouvelles troupes ne pouvant être levées actuellement, il ne saurait être question d'un concours militaire, l'Égypte peut tout au moins prêter son assistance financière. Les mesures prises ou à prendre par les autorités militaires en vue de la défense ont nécessité et nécessitent encore des travaux considérables.
E.B. Lord E. Cecil,
Conseiller Financier.
ai_content.english_translation:
COPY
PRESIDENCY OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS.
CAIRO, January 11, 1916.
No. 323.
To the Financial Advisor,
From the beginning of the war with Turkey, the Egyptian Government, inspired by sentiments for which the British Government could only be grateful, declared it would take exclusive responsibility for the defense of Egypt, assuming by itself and without any participation from the Egyptian Government, the considerable burdens of all kinds that such a commitment entailed. But events have since taken such a turn that Egypt seems likely to be the object of a new and more important offensive.
Faced with this situation, His Highness the Sultan and his Government, considering that Egypt cannot continue to remain indifferent to a conflict where its very existence could be at stake and that it owes it to itself to defend its territory and its rights.
And, as new troops cannot be raised at present, there can be no question of military assistance, Egypt can at least provide its financial assistance. The measures taken or to be taken by the military authorities for the purpose of defense have necessitated and still necessitate considerable work.
E.B. Lord E. Cecil,
Financial Advisor.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official memorandum from the Egyptian Council of Ministers, dated January 11, 1916, addressed to the British Financial Advisor, Lord Edward Cecil. It reflects the geopolitical tension in Egypt during World War I, specifically following the Ottoman Empire's entry into the war against the Allied powers. The text highlights the transition of Egypt from a state of passive defense to active financial contribution to the British war effort, as the Egyptian government acknowledges the impossibility of raising new local troops but commits to funding the extensive defensive infrastructure required to protect the territory against potential Ottoman offensives.

ai_content.english_translation: Cairo, February 7, 1911. Mr. President, I have the honor to acknowledge receipt of your Excellency's letter dated January 4th addressed to Lord Edward Cecil, by which you were kind enough to inform him of the desire of His Highness the Sultan and his Government that Egypt, not being able to provide armed assistance to help repel the offensive with which it is threatened, should contribute at least to the task of defense by taking on the expense that will be incurred by the military works currently under construction. But this result will not be achieved without difficulty and, although the financial situation appears more favorable at the present time than it was last year, it must not be forgotten that until the end of hostilities, affairs will remain uncertain. A complete exhaustion of the reserve could later put Egypt in the position of having to seek financial aid from abroad. I do not need to remind your Excellency how desirable it is to avoid this expedient. Surely if Sultan and Ministers understand the deep and painful impression here which it will take some time to eradicate that Egypt is profiting by War without endeavouring to make any adequate return, they would use every effort in the matter. I find it hard to believe increase of payment or bonuses perhaps provided by Eygptian Treasury, and any possible advantages to labourers recruited such as exemption from conscription would not assist recruitment. In any case may I suggest that if you could repeat I sic ? report a vigorous recruiting campaign had already begun, and had met with a certain measure of success, bad impression likely to be caused by your reply might be mitigated. If campaign fails, other means may have to be tried, but it is to be hoped that cancellation of Proclamation can be avoided.

Your private and confidential telegram.

Sir R. Wingate à

Le 23 août 1917.

Faisant suite à notre entretien de hier, je m'empresse de vous faire savoir que je viens de recevoir ce matin une dépêche particulière de Sir Ronald Graham. Ce télégramme est une réponse personnelle et officieuse à celui que j'ai adressé officiellement au Foreign Office hier et dont je vous ai communiqué le contenu.

Sir Ronald me dit que le Foreign Office remettra sa réponse définitive jusqu'à l'arrivée de la lettre officielle que j'ai adressée à Monsieur Balfour à ce sujet, et qui partira par le prochain courrier. Il craint cependant, que mon télégramme de hier ne soit considéré comme inquiétant. ai_content.english_translation: Sir R. Wingate to Rushdi Pasha, The Residency, Ramleh. August 23, 1917. Following our conversation yesterday, I hasten to let you know that I have just received this morning a private dispatch from Sir Ronald Graham. This telegram is a personal and unofficial response to the one I addressed officially to the Foreign Office yesterday and whose content I communicated to you. Sir Ronald tells me that the Foreign Office will postpone its definitive response until the arrival of the official letter I addressed to Mr. Balfour on this subject, which will leave by the next mail. He fears, however, that my telegram of yesterday might be considered alarming. He cannot doubt that the Ministry and the Ministers would not delay in deploying all their efforts to obtain a satisfactory solution, if they realized the deep and bad impression created by my response.

The document highlights the internal anxieties of the British administration in Egypt regarding the potential for diplomatic friction and the need to manage the 'impression' created by their correspondence with London.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Copy of letter from Rushdi Pasha to the High Consul Seloner, dated Bulkley August 22nd, 1917.
Chère Excellence,
En réponse à votre lettre de ce jour au sujet du recrutement du Labour Corps, voici les mesures prises ou en train d'être prises à cet égard :-
1o. Majoration de la solde journalière de P.T.3 au même de P.T.4 et nécessaire, le Gouvernement Egyptien prenant à sa charge cette majoration.
2o. Dispense de service militaire de tout homme qui s'engagerait pour au moins une année.
3o. Dispense de la taxe de gardiennage pour la durée de l'engagement.
4o. Propagande dans les villages par les mamours et par les omdahs en faveur des engagements.
5o. Ordres aux Moudirs et Gouverneurs d'appuyer de tout le poids de leur autorité ces engagements.
6o. Tournées dans les provinces par un haut fonctionnaire du Ministère de l'Intérieur pour contrôler l'exécution de ces ordres.
Je suis convaincu que ces mesures ameneront un afflux d'engagements et aboutiront ainsi au résultat recherché.
Le Conseil de Ministres a déjà adopté en principe les trois premières mesures. Je me charge du reste.
J'ai seulement besoin de causer par votre intermédiaire avec l'autorité militaire et de voir Hazel, que j'ai mandé par téléphone pour mettre toute la machine en branle.
Votre bien dévoué
(signed) H. Husni
ai_content.english_translation:
Copy of letter from Rushdi Pasha to the High Consul Seloner, dated Bulkley August 22nd, 1917.
Dear Excellency,
In response to your letter of today regarding the recruitment of the Labour Corps, here are the measures taken or in the process of being taken in this regard:-
1. Increase of the daily wage from P.T.3 to P.T.4, the Egyptian Government taking charge of this increase.
2. Exemption from military service for any man who enlists for at least one year.
3. Exemption from the guard tax for the duration of the enlistment.
4. Propaganda in the villages by the mamours and omdahs in favor of enlistments.
5. Orders to Moudirs and Governors to support these enlistments with the full weight of their authority.
6. Tours in the provinces by a high official of the Ministry of the Interior to control the execution of these orders.
I am convinced that these measures will bring about an influx of enlistments and thus lead to the desired result.
The Council of Ministers has already adopted in principle the first three measures. I will take care of the rest.
I only need to speak through your intermediary with the military authority and to see Hazel, whom I have summoned by telephone to set the whole machine in motion.
Yours very devotedly,
(signed) H. Husni

It outlines a series of administrative and financial incentives designed to boost recruitment for the Egyptian Labour Corps during World War I. The measures include wage increases, exemptions from military service and local taxes, and the mobilization of provincial officials (Moudirs and Omdahs) to encourage enlistment. The document reflects the collaborative administrative relationship between the Egyptian government and the British occupation authorities during the war effort.

EGYPT'S WAR INVESTMENTS.
At the outset of the war, the economic position of Egypt was seriously prejudiced by the fall in price of cotton, which is her staple crop for export. In the first year of the war, the loss in value of exports amounted to 10 million pounds. The consequent reduction in purchasing power, coupled with the restrictions on seaborne trade, caused the imports to fall by a more than corresponding amount, while, in the latter half of the period, the increase in the British forces in Egypt and therefore in the sums spent by them in the country began to exercise a favourable influence on its fortunes. The combined result of forced economy and military expenditure at the end of the first year of war was to leave the country with a balance in its favour, after payment of the interest on the Public Debt and other foreign charges, estimated at some 5 million pounds.
The second year of the war witnessed a recovery in the price of cotton and a restoration of the value of the exports almost to its pre-war figure. At the same time the expenditure by the British forces continued on a considerable scale. On the other hand, the difficulty of obtaining imports kept their quantity well below the pre-war level, and their total value, in spite of enhanced prices, fell far short of the figure representing the purchasing power of the country. For well-known reasons, gold could not be imported in substitution for goods, but a sum of 3 1/4 million sovereigns was set aside at the Bank of England for Egyptian account as part cover for the note-issue. Allowing for this gold deposit, and for foreign charges as before, the balance in favour of the country during the second year of the war may be estimated at about 10 million pounds.

-3-
The repayment of debts has increased the surplus funds in the hands of mortgage companies and merchants by several millions. These sums have been partly deposited in banks, partly invested by the companies latter in the manner above-described, partly invested by the companies and firms themselves. The two leading mortgage companies hold between them about 5 1/2 millions of British and French War Securities.
Under the head of direct investment, the Egyptian Government holds about 3 1/2 millions in British War Loan and Exchequer Bonds, over and above the amount employed in conversion of its Consols. The Public Custodian of enemy property holds £ 750,000 of the same securities. Direct investment by private persons and firms in Allied War Loans may be estimated at from 1 to 2 millions. A moderate amount has also been invested in Egyptian Unified Stock.
The broad result of this analysis is to show that practically the entire surplus income of the country since the war has been re-invested in Allied War Loans, mainly British, in various forms. In other words, the country has placed its available resources at the disposal of the Allied Powers on credit. It may be specially noted in this connection that in contrast with India, the people of this country have not received value in the shape of metallic currency for more than a small fraction of their savings, but have taken paper instead.
The fact that liabilities on this and other accounts will, as already shown, have to be met after the war, explains the preponderance of shorter-term securities in the investments on Egyptian Account.
It is worth remark that any contribution which Egypt might be called upon to make to military expenditure during the war can hardly be of any effective present utility, since she is already contributing in actual resources to the extent of her capacity, and the amount of this contribution, which is the essentially important matter, will not be increased by the conversion of a loan into a gift.
27.8.1917

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. August 31st, 1917. Private. My dear Lindsey, I have read Roussin's note with much interest - it is most helpful and I am sending a copy home - will you give him my best thanks. Apart from the purely financial aspect with which Roussin's note deals, I should like to have a general note on what Egypt has done - directly or indirectly - towards helping on the war - both from a general as well as financial standpoint. I mentioned the matter to both Rushdi Pasha and Adly Yeghen Pasha, would you talk the matter over with them? A note from the Council of Ministers and prepared with financial assistance might prove very helpful. I do not want a long official Memorandum but rather an informal note, which I could send Graham unofficially. Yours sincerely, R WINGATE. P.S. Thanks for your note re the Geographical Society.

RAMLEH.
September 2nd 1917.

Sir,

With reference to your Telegram 685 of July 5th and subsequent correspondence relative to the assistance rendered by Egypt during the war, I have the honour to forward to you herewith copy of a memorandum on Egypt's war investments, which has been prepared by Mr. G. I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your most obedient, humble servant,

Arthur James Balfour, O.M., M.P.,

ai_content.transcribed_text:
COMMITTEE OF MAN POWER ETC.
Report No. 3.
Employment of Women under the Military Authorities.
The Committee has examined the question of the substitution of women for men in various forms of employment under the Military Authorities. We have understood that what is wanted is whole time service for which the Military Authorities would pay definite salaries while the women would undertake towards them the definite obligations of paid service. They would be employed mainly in hospital work, as clerks, or in any other capacity in which women could suitably do men's work. It has been suggested that a good deal of substitution in this way might be effected and that an appeal by the High Commissioner might be fruitful of good results.
We regret to say that we are not in agreement with the view expressed above.
Apart from Englishwomen who will be dealt with later, there are in Egypt theoretically available for this purpose, Maltese and Syrian women, Levantines of various categories, Italians and French. Of the servant class who theoretically might be available as domestics in hospitals, but it is well known they do not normally make good servants and it is always considered better to use Egyptians of the suffragi class. They are naturally better educated though they do not often have such familiarity with the English language, but they are more difficult to address an appeal to and take service in domestic capacities. With all these people there are such social considerations makes it almost impossible for them to out themselves off from their home or family and engage in whole time service for any purpose, especially for such as an army.
In so far as women capable of assisting the Military Authorities exist in Egypt, it might be said that where they are educated it would be better to use Egyptian clerks and where they are not educated Egyptian suffragis will be more suitable and easier to get. Of both Egyptian clerks and servants considerable reserves exist and now are being carefully exploited through the Civilian Employment Agency.
Englishwomen are in quite a different category to those of other nationalities.
It must be remembered that inhabitants of the United Kingdom do not ordinarily come to Egypt to settle down and found families in the country. They are usually only resident here for the period during which they do the work for which they have come. The result is that there very much fewer men of the British race. According to the census of 1907 (the figures for 1917 are not yet available) there were ten men to every four women. Of the women who are in Egypt nearly all have come for some very definite purpose.

Dear Sir Reginald, I find that the last report of a meeting of the Man Power Committee was sent to you without a copy of the covering letter to the A.A.G. I attach hereto the covering letter in question, together with two further letters which have passed in the matter. The only interpretation I can place on General Adye's letter is that he has not understood in the past exactly what was implied by the carrying of sums of money to Suspense Account, and that as soon as it is put clearly to him he will realise that the method is not one which ought to continue. If that is so, I think that it ought to be much easier to get things on to a proper basis. I have not yet been able to put up to the Council of Ministers a list of the sums carried to Suspense Account because of the difficulty of getting details from the departments, but I hope that it will be ready in a few days. My idea would then be to transmit the list to the President of the Council by a letter in which I should mention that he had asked to be informed of the nature of such sums. It would then be for the Ministers spontaneously to express the desire to have the matter put on a proper basis. Very sincerely yours, [Signature]

ai_content.transcribed_text:
February 3rd, 1918.
Sir,
I am in receipt of your letter No. A(H)68 of 21st January, and note that I was in error in supposing that it was suggested that any of the expense of the Training Schools was being established at Cairo was to be charged xxxxxxxxxx to Egyptian Government account without prior consultation with that Government. The explanation of my mistake is that hitherto, so far as I am aware, Egyptian Government moneys have only been rendered available for auxiliary military purposes by the placing of sums to a suspense account by the Financial Adviser purporting to be under authority given him by the Commander in Chief. And I may note in this connection that I have quite recently been pressed by your Intelligence Department (ref. No. I.4268/3) to accept responsibility for relatively trivial sums on these lines.
As I mentioned in my earlier letter, I have every reason to believe that as soon as I can make out a complete statement of the sums already carried to suspense account, the Egyptian Ministers are prepared to recommend that they be written off as an Egyptian contribution to the cost of the war, and that thereafter provision may be made for dealing with such matters in a more normal way.
At the time the arrangement was first adopted it was adopted with the knowledge of Egyptian Ministers and was regarded by them with approval. It is now so long ago that you may have difficulty in realizing the reluctance of Ministers when the Protectorate was first declared to accept direct responsibility for anything connected with the war, and probably no better arrangement could have been made. But I am glad to see that you concur in thinking that such an arrangement is now out of date. Whatever is arranged for the future, I will see that nothing in done of a nature to prevent prompt action by the Egyptian service in matters of military urgency, but pending the settlement of the general question I should incline to advise against the putting forward of minor claims, such as the one out of which the present correspondence arose.
As mentioned in my earlier letter, the only heavy item now running is that of the cost of the Military Railways east of the Canal, into which I have not yet had time to go in detail, but in connection with which I am led to believe that we are providing at Egyptian expense coal, labour and stores. Owing especially to the rise in freights, I am advised, as I told you, by General Macaulay that the item will involve expenditure this year to an extent which may frighten Ministers and may upset our budget.
February 6th 1918.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official letter dated February 3rd, 1918, regarding the financial arrangements between the British Protectorate in Egypt and the Egyptian Government. The author clarifies a misunderstanding regarding the funding of Training Schools in Cairo and discusses the 'suspense account' mechanism used by the Financial Adviser to fund auxiliary military purposes. The author notes that Egyptian Ministers are likely to write off these costs as a contribution to the war effort. The letter also addresses the need to move away from these ad-hoc financial arrangements and expresses concern over the rising costs of the Military Railways east of the Suez Canal, which are being funded by Egyptian resources and threaten the Egyptian budget.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of official correspondence from the British administration in Egypt during the First World War. It highlights the complex financial relationship between the British Protectorate and the Egyptian Government, specifically regarding the funding of military operations and infrastructure (such as the Military Railways east of the Suez Canal). It illustrates the administrative tension of using 'suspense accounts' to bypass standard budgetary procedures and the British effort to formalize these expenditures as Egyptian contributions to the war effort, while managing the fiscal stability of the Egyptian state.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
G.H.Q., E.E.F. January 31st, 1918.
Sir,
I have the honour to acknowledge your letter of January 26th, 1918 on the subject of schools for training natives for certain employments with the E.E.F.
I am glad that the proposals met with the general approval of the Committee and have noted the suggestions on points of detail made by the Committee.
As regards the question of the cost of these classes, there is I think some misunderstanding.
It was quite understood by me that the Committee could give no decision upon this matter and all that was asked for was an expression of its opinion as to the possibility of the Egyptian Government's concurrence in the suggestion.
Nor was it suggested that you in your capacity as acting Financial Adviser should direct payment to be made out of the funds of the Egyptian Government under the powers granted to the Financial Adviser by the Commander-in-Chief E.E.F.
It is realised that this is a matter for the consideration of the Egyptian Government, and fortified by the opinion of the Committee, a request will now be forwarded through the proper channels for the favourable consideration by that Government of a suggestion which it is thought the advantages to the Egyptian native may be held to warrant.
I have the honour to be, Sir, Your obedient Servant, (Signed) JOHN ADYE, Major General, D.A.Q., E.E.F.
T. Prunyate, President, Committee on Man Power, etc., in Egypt.
ai_content.english_translation: General Headquarters, Egyptian Expeditionary Force. January 31st, 1918. Sir, I acknowledge receipt of your letter dated January 26th, 1918, regarding the training of local natives for roles within the E.E.F. I am pleased the Committee approves of the proposals and have noted their specific suggestions. Regarding the funding, there appears to be a misunderstanding; I did not expect the Committee to decide on costs, but merely to provide an opinion on whether the Egyptian Government might support the idea. I did not suggest that you, as acting Financial Adviser, should authorize payments from Egyptian Government funds using your powers under the Commander-in-Chief. I understand this requires formal consideration by the Egyptian Government. With the Committee's backing, we will now formally request the Egyptian Government to consider this proposal, which we believe will be beneficial to the Egyptian native population. I remain your obedient servant, Major General John Adye, Deputy Adjutant-General, E.E.F. To T. Prunyate, President, Committee on Man Power, Egypt.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal military memorandum from the General Headquarters of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force (E.E.F.) during the First World War. It addresses the administrative and financial complexities of establishing vocational training schools for local Egyptian natives to serve in support roles for the British military. The correspondence clarifies a misunderstanding between Major General John Adye and T. Prunyate (President of the Committee on Man Power) regarding the source of funding, emphasizing that the British military sought the Egyptian Government's cooperation rather than unilaterally drawing upon their treasury. It highlights the colonial administrative process of the British occupation of Egypt and the integration of local labor into the war effort.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
D.A.Q., G.H.Q., E.E.F. January 26th, 1918.
Sir,
With reference to your letter of 9th January 1918 as to the establishment of schools for the training of natives of Egypt as mechanical transport drivers, clerks and typists, and officers' servants, I duly assembled the Committee on Man Power etc. in Egypt as requested by you, and submitted to them your letter under reply. I now enclose a record of the proceedings of the Committee, which has been approved as correct by the members present.
You will see that, subject to some doubts as to officers' servants, the Committee were entirely favourable to the establishment of the schools in question, and were satisfied that they would be beneficial to Egypt. The Committee made certain observations on some details of the proposed scheme, but I am rather afraid that they are made too late to be of assistance to you.
As regards the acceptance of the cost of the scheme by the Egyptian Government, you will see that, as requested by you, I took the opinion of the Committee thereon, although, as I was careful to point out to them, the matter appeared to me to be one entirely outside their province.
Notwithstanding the unanimous opinion of my colleagues on the Committee, I regret that the charge is one on which I am not at present prepared to accept on behalf of the Egyptian Government. I understand the suggestion to be that I should myself take the responsibility, under the powers given me or about to be given to me by the Commander-in-Chief, to direct the payment of the sums in question out of moneys belonging to the Egyptian Government, leaving the question of the manner in which the Suspense Account is ultimately to be met for further decision. Were the schools to be under Mr. Wells - an arrangement which I in no way suggest - I should be perfectly prepared to support the whole charge thereof, as we are already paying the expenses of his office. But I am very desirous of keeping to the principle that while we bear the expenses of services rendered by us, we should not be asked to pay for individual Army expenses.
I am only waiting for details of the existing Suspense Account before submitting a report thereon to the Council of Ministers, the result of which I have reason to hope will be that the Egyptian Government should take over the whole of it, and that cause I should propose to include in the new Budget some sum for meeting on a regular footing such expenses as we incur on behalf of the Army. In the meantime, however, I am anxious to have as few charges as possible which I should [text continues] February 6th, 1918.
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official administrative memorandum from the Deputy Adjutant Quartermaster of the General Headquarters of the Egyptian Expeditionary Force, dated January 26, 1918, with a follow-up date of February 6, 1918. The document discusses the establishment of training schools for Egyptian nationals to serve as mechanical transport drivers, clerks, typists, and officers' servants. The author reports on the findings of a 'Committee on Man Power' regarding the feasibility and benefits of these schools. A significant portion of the text addresses the financial burden of the project, specifically whether the Egyptian Government should bear the costs or if it should be treated as an 'Army expense' under a 'Suspense Account.' The author expresses hesitation in committing Egyptian government funds to these military-related training programs, preferring to keep the accounts separate and awaiting a broader budget review.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document provides insight into the administrative and financial complexities of the British occupation of Egypt during World War I. It highlights the tension between the British military administration (E.E.F.) and the Egyptian government regarding the funding of training programs for local personnel. The correspondence illustrates the bureaucratic process of establishing vocational training schools for the war effort and the careful negotiation required to balance military needs with the fiscal responsibilities of the Egyptian state, particularly concerning the 'Suspense Account' and the upcoming national budget.

The High Commissioner asks me to thank you for your letter of February 4th and the interesting correspondence which you forwarded with it. Your letter makes the matter quite clear, and His Excellency concurs in your remarks. We should now send on Reports Nos. 4 and 5 of the Man-Power Committee to the Foreign Office as a matter of routine - may we have the necessary three copies of each?

As I was writing this, a further letter - copy herewith - arrived from General Allenby, enclosing copies of your correspondence with General Adye, up to January 31st, and copies of General Adye's letter to Mr. Wells of December 16th.

May we have your observations on the Commander-in-Chief's letter, which, as you see, suggests that this particular sum of £7,000 should be paid by the Egyptian Government.

When you have submitted proposals in connection with the Suspense Account to the Council of Ministers, will you let us have your report on the matter in a form that we could forward to the Foreign Office, as they are anxious to be furnished with further details as to the operation of the Suspense Account - see Foreign Office Despatch No. 328 of November 12th, last paragraph, copy of which was sent to you on December 6th.

February 6th 1918.

Finally, it asks for a report on the 'Suspense Account' to be prepared for the Council of Ministers so that the British Foreign Office can be updated, referencing a previous dispatch from November 1917.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
The Residency.
Cairo 9th February, 1918
It will probably be convenient that I should deal at one and the same time with your Minutes No. 2689 of 2/2/18 and No. 1915 of 6/2/18, as both raise the question of the bearing of Military or quasi-military expenses by the Egyptian Government.
Hitherto all such proposals, if accepted, have resulted in the expenses concerned being carried to Suspense Account by the Financial Adviser purporting to act under the powers intrusted to him by the Commander in Chief. You will be aware that General Adye has recently explained that as regards one of the two sums now in question such has never been the intention of the Military authorities, so that I presume the proposal to be that the Council of Ministers should be requested to vote the necessary credits in the two cases.
I have already explained to General Adye that as we are looking to the Council of Ministers to agree in the near future to write off the Suspense Account against the British Government, amounting now to over 2 1/2 millions, I regard the moment as an inopportune one for putting forward requests for credits for small sums, especially of a disputable character. Upon the importance of that aspect of the question, I without going so far I should wish to insist anew. I am to say that it is my duty to persuade Ministers to make proposals as to writing off the Suspense Account.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official memorandum from the British Residency in Cairo, dated February 9, 1918. It addresses two previous minutes regarding the funding of military or quasi-military expenses by the Egyptian government. The author notes that such expenses were previously placed in a 'Suspense Account' by the Financial Adviser. The author mentions a recent clarification from General Adye regarding the military's intentions and suggests that the Council of Ministers should be asked to vote on these credits. However, the author expresses concern that requesting credits for small, disputable sums is ill-timed, given that the British government is currently negotiating with the Council of Ministers to write off a larger Suspense Account debt of over 2.5 million pounds.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of administrative correspondence from the British Residency in Cairo during the British Protectorate of Egypt (1914–1922). It highlights the complex financial relationship between the British military authorities and the Egyptian government during World War I. The text illustrates the tension between military expenditure and the Egyptian state's budget, specifically concerning the 'Suspense Account'—a mechanism used to defer or obscure military costs. The document reflects the British effort to manage Egyptian fiscal policy while attempting to settle a significant debt of 2.5 million pounds, demonstrating the colonial administration's control over Egyptian financial governance during the war period.

I have already mentioned to General Adye that the supply of coal, stores and Labour to the railways east of the Canal seems likely to be next year a heavier burden than we can conveniently support and that I should be ready at any time to discuss the whole matter.

I come now to the two items actually under discussion.

The first of them relates to the expenses of keeping returning labourers for a five days quarantine/segregation camp at Kantara. I have already informed the Adviser of the Interior that if he and the D.G. Public Health are prepared to take over the entire service, I am prepared to pay for it. The D.G. Public Health considers that theoretically that would be the proper system, but states that his staff is so depleted by giving men to the Army that he is not in a position to undertake the work. That being so, the work is being carried out by the Army and I see no reason to differentiate between the necessary expenses of such segregation and the other expenses of pay, transport etc. incident to returning the labourers to their homes. I see that it is stated in the Commander in Chief's letter that the quarantine is imposed in the interests of Egypt and that therefore the expense should be borne by the Egyptian Government. The same view has already been put forward by the D.M.S.

Public Health, and I should feel it my duty to resist the charge in question, if only to make it clear that I do not concur that such quarantine is imposed in the interests of Egypt. We are finding the labourers at some expense to ourselves and allowing them, for Army purposes, to go to cholera infected districts. Were inadequate precautions taken for the prevention of the introduction of cholera into Egypt, and an epidemic followed, the whole of our staff would be far too busy to permit of further recruiting taking place for the E.L.C., and as a purely Egyptian matter we should certainly desire to prevent the sending of/further labourers, even could they be obtained. As a matter of logic, the argument put forward may, perhaps, best be met by observing that if I own a pit I am required to fence it and the fact that my doing so is in the interests of my neighbours does not prevent me being expected to pay for the fencing.

The second charge proposed is in respect of allowances made to Egyptians while undergoing courses at schools recently started by the Military authorities and as to this we are told that the result of these schools will ultimately be to provide us with better mechanical transport drivers, clerks and suffragis. It also appears that the schools were started on the suggestion of Mr. Wells who, although at present engaged on work for the Army, is an Egyptian Government official and is paid as such. As to this, I have to observe that Mr. Wells advised the setting up of these schools for the benefit of the Army and not for the benefit of Egypt and that I see no possible reason for distinguishing between the allowances made to pupils and the cost of their rations, the teaching staff and other expenses connected with the schools. If I am asked to put forward this charge to the Council of Ministers as one proper to be borne by them, I should be extremely reluctant to do so without being able to assure them at the same time that the whole cost of Mr. Wells's special office was being taken over by the Military authorities, and even in that case I should feel my position a thoroughly undignified one.

I deal with certain other points arising out of your Minute of 6/2/18 in a separate Note.

(signed) W.E. BRUNYATE.
ACTING FINANCIAL ADVISER.
ai_content.english_translation: The document is an official memorandum written by the Acting Financial Adviser, W.E. Brunyate, regarding the allocation of financial responsibilities between the British Military (E.E.F.) and the Egyptian Government. It addresses two specific disputes: first, the costs associated with quarantine measures for laborers recruited for the Egyptian Labour Corps (E.L.C.) during a cholera outbreak; and second, the funding of vocational schools for Egyptians, which were initiated by Mr. Wells. Brunyate argues that the military should bear these costs, as the schools were established for military benefit rather than Egyptian national interest, and he expresses reluctance to request the Egyptian Council of Ministers to cover these expenses.

It highlights the friction between the British military administration (Egyptian Expeditionary Force) and the Egyptian civil government regarding fiscal responsibility. The text provides insight into the logistical challenges of the era, including the management of labor corps, public health concerns (cholera), and the establishment of technical training schools for the local population, all while navigating the complex dual-authority structure of the British Protectorate in Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text: MINISTRY OF FINANCE. ADVISER'S OFFICE. The Residency. Cairo, February 10th. 1918. Sir, With further reference to your Minute No. 1615 of 6/2/18, I have to observe as follows: (a) I have given instructions that 3 copies each of Reports Nos. 4 and 5 of the Man Power Committee shall be prepared and forwarded to you. (b) Mr. Lindsay left with me a Note as to Suspense Account intended as a reply to F.O. Despatch 328 of 12/11/17, but as in my opinion he did not give the details of the Suspense Account in the form required by the War Office, I have had to be ob- prepared. The details have had to be ob- tained from the different services, some of which have set them in an incorrect form, and it is only to-day that I am obtaining the complete list. I propose as soon as possible to communicate it to the President of the Council and will then consider what cover- ing note is required to render it most useful to the War Office. ACTING FINANCIAL ADVISER

The author addresses a previous minute (No. 1615) regarding the preparation of reports. The author confirms that three copies of reports 4 and 5 from the Man Power Committee are being prepared. Furthermore, the author notes that a document provided by Mr. Lindsay regarding a 'Suspense Account' (intended as a reply to a Foreign Office despatch from November 1917) was insufficient in detail for the War Office. The author explains that they have been gathering the correct details from various services and will soon present the complete information to the President of the Council for further action.

It reflects the bureaucratic coordination between the Egyptian government, the British Residency, and the War Office in London during the final year of World War I. The mention of the 'Man Power Committee' and 'Suspense Account' highlights the intense logistical and financial scrutiny applied to military expenditures and resource mobilization in the Middle Eastern theater of the war. EGYPT
28 FEB 1918
THE RESIDENCY,
CAIRO.
February 11th 1918.
Sir,
In continuation of my despatch no. 247 of October 25th 1917, I have the honour to forward herewith, for your information, copies of reports nos. 4 and 5 of the man-power committee, which has been considering recruiting for the Egyptian Labour Corps and analogous questions.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
With the highest respect,
Your most obedient, humble servant,
[Arthur Balfour, etc., etc.]
ai_content.english_translation: This is an official diplomatic dispatch sent from the British Residency in Cairo to the Foreign Office in London. The sender references a previous communication from October 1917 and submits two reports (nos. 4 and 5) from a 'man-power committee' tasked with overseeing the recruitment of the Egyptian Labour Corps during the First World War.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal diplomatic dispatch from the British Residency in Cairo, dated February 1918, during the British occupation of Egypt. It serves as a transmittal letter for administrative reports concerning the 'Egyptian Labour Corps' (ELC). The ELC was a critical logistical component of the British war effort in the Middle East, providing manual labor for military operations in the Sinai and Palestine campaigns. The mention of a 'man-power committee' reflects the increasing pressure on the British administration to mobilize Egyptian labor resources, a policy that would eventually contribute to the social unrest leading to the Egyptian Revolution of 1919.
