Your despatch 297 (5750/2) and 328 (5750/4).
Egypt's contribution to the war.
Detailed explanations of the origin and operation of the suspense account with table of items of expenditure were forwarded in my despatch No. 44 by bag on March 8. (5751/1).
As you are aware Financial Adviser has, with knowledge and approval of Ministers, been meeting military expenses out of Egyptian monies, the amount of which expenses up to March 31 next will be approximately three million Egyptian pounds. While some of these are no doubt properly chargeable against Egyptian Government, similar payments against budgetary credits and salaries of Egyptian officials seconded to serve under British military authorities probably counter-balance them.
At request of Prime Minister, Financial Adviser has recently submitted details of the expenditure and at Council meeting yesterday the Sultan presiding Council on proposal of Prime Minister spontaneously and unanimously passed following resolution:-

It explains that the Financial Adviser, with the approval of the Egyptian Ministers, has been using Egyptian funds to cover military expenses, estimated at three million Egyptian pounds by March 31. ai_content.transcribed_text: The Residency, Cairo. 23rd December, 1919. I intend shortly to send home a final despatch dealing generally with the part Egypt has played in the War, and bringing to notice outstanding services in connection with the War rendered by departments of the Government, and by individuals, of whom for one reason or another no mention has yet been made. I shall, therefore, be glad if you will let me have, as early as you conveniently can, a statement of any such services rendered by departments of your Ministry, and by bodies under your general control (e.g. Committees, etc.) formed for special War purposes, as well as a list of names of individuals who have hitherto received no mention and whose services in Egypt, in connection with the War, you consider should now be brought to notice. The proposed despatch will be the last opportunity of bringing to notice work done here distinctively in connection with the War, and must leave here by January the 10th at the latest. I am addressing a similar letter to all the Advisers, with the exception of Mr. Haines from whom I have already received a note on the lines indicated above. Yours very sincerely, [List of names: Sir Brunyate, C.M.G., Dunlop, Esqre, M.A., LL.D., Tottenham, Esqre]

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. 20th January, 1919. My Lord, I should in any case have wished, at the close of the war to submit to you a record of the work performed by the Egyptian Government, but War Office Confidential letter 0157/5613 of November 27 of last year, a copy of which was sent to me privately, gave me the idea of doing so immediately and of reporting rather on the services performed by individual officials than on the work performed by the Department to which they belong. I do not know whether the opportunity which has been afforded me of seeing the War Office letter referred to above may be construed as an occasion for putting forward further names for decorations. If this is the case, I should be glad to be informed, and I will, without delay, submit a list of names extracted from the reports enclosed in this despatch. The notes enclosed herewith have been drawn up by the senior British officials in the different departments of the Egyptian Government. In many cases these reports contain little more than a summary of information which it has been my duty to furnish you from time to time, but I trust that, grouped in the present form, this information will enable you to reach a correct estimate of the many and valuable services performed during the course of the war. Detailed comment on these reports by me is perhaps unnecessary, but they appeal to me, although indirectly, a high tribute to the British officials, advisers and Under Secretaries in whose charge the departments concerned have lain. Right Honourable, Earl Curzon of Kedleston, K.G., G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E., etc.

He inquires whether this report should also serve as a recommendation for decorations (honors) for these officials. He explains that the enclosed notes were compiled by senior British officials and serve as a summary of their wartime contributions, which he believes reflect highly on the British advisers and Under Secretaries serving in the Egyptian administration.

LIST (B)
RECOMMENDED FOR C.B.E.
Major (Temporary Lieutenant-Colonel) James Keiro, C.M.G., D.S.O., Military Attaché, The Residency, Cairo, has afforded me great assistance, particularly in dealing with the Palace and with various Committees here with which he is in close touch. He has ably managed all ceremonial matters and has devoted himself unsparingly to the furtherance of projects in aid of the Red Cross, Y.M.C.A. and other kindred institutions.
RECOMMENDED FOR BREVET MAJORITY
Captain James Ulick Francis Canning, Coldstream Guards (Attached Egyptian Army), has done excellent work as my Aide-de-Camp and it is to be remembered that the exigencies of work here make greater demands than are involved in the ordinary duties of an A.D.C. Captain Alexander has had control of personnel. He has and has assisted me in matters of A.D.C. He has invariably carried out his duties with the greatest application and thoroughness, and I cannot speak too highly of the capacities of this officer.
RECOMMENDED FOR O.B.E.
Captain Richard Gibbings, R.A. Retired, sat on the Classification Committee which dealt with the liability of British subjects in Egypt to military service. At the outbreak of war he took a leading part in organising a Local Defence Force composed of British civilians, of which he was Commandant, at a time when the garrison in Egypt was very much depleted.
Major Fredric Eugene, Veterinary Department, Egyptian Government, acted as Pathologist to the Army; he was lent for a considerable time to the Army; was attached to the Camel Defence Force, and was present at some of the fighting on the eastern frontier.
Major Duncan Silvestro, Veterinary Department, Egyptian Government, acted as Officer Commanding the Camel Hospital at Zeitoun, in addition to his ministry work as Director of the Veterinary School.

Sir,
I have received Sir R. Wingate's despatch No. 32 of January 20th and your despatch No. 58 of February 5th transmitting reports on the war work performed by various departments of the Egyptian Government.
They form an interesting and gratifying record of the many calls which were made upon the Egyptian Civil Service, and the willing and efficient manner in which response was made thereto.
I am well aware of the difficulties with which officials in Egypt have had to contend during the war. Prolonged absence from home and the obligation to keep the machinery of Civil Government in motion when other and more attractive fields lay open might well have induced feelings of disappointment and discontent. I am happy to see that the traditions of the Egyptian Civil Service have been so worthily maintained.
Cheetham K.C.M.G., &c. &c.

MacDonald, Mr Haines and the other Heads of Departments and officials mentioned in these despatches for the valuable services which they have rendered. I am with great truth Sir, Your most obedient humble Servant, [Signed: Allenby]. [Handwritten note:] The First Secretary, The Residency. Mr Kerr. [Handwritten note:] I attach a copy of a judgment given by the Mixed Court of Cairo on November 24th in the case of [illegible] which is in the nature of a test case as it throws doubt on the legal validity of decisions taken by the Egyptian Government out of the state of war. [Red ink note:] This I think the P.M. intends to [illegible].
ai_content.english_translation: The document consists of a formal typed letter from the British High Commissioner in Egypt (Allenby) expressing the gratitude of the British Government to various high-ranking British officials serving in the Egyptian administration. The handwritten portion is an internal administrative note from a secretary or official to Mr. Kerr, attaching a judgment from the Mixed Court of Cairo dated November 24, 1924, which challenged the legal standing of certain Egyptian government actions taken during the state of war.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an archival record from the British Residency in Cairo, dated late 1924. It captures a dual administrative function: the formal recognition of British officials serving in the Egyptian government (a period of significant transition following the 1922 Unilateral Declaration of Egyptian Independence) and an internal legal concern regarding the 'Mixed Courts' of Egypt. The Mixed Courts were a unique judicial system established to handle cases involving foreigners, and the attached judgment mentioned in the handwritten note highlights the ongoing legal friction between the British-influenced administration and the Egyptian judiciary regarding the transition from wartime emergency powers to civil governance.

The litigation arises from the impact of the outbreak of World War I (August 1924, likely a reference to the state of war or subsequent sequestration/administrative actions) on his business interests. ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a legal memorandum or court submission concerning the legal status of European nationals in Egypt during the early stages of World War I. It specifically addresses the 'Capitulations'—the extraterritorial privileges granted to foreign nationals in the Ottoman Empire and Egypt. The text argues that the Egyptian Government cannot evade civil liability for the seizure of property (specifically a bookstore and funds) belonging to a German national by claiming these actions were solely the responsibility of the British Military Authority, which had occupied Egypt. The document highlights the tension between the Egyptian state's administrative actions and the legal protections afforded to foreign subjects under the Capitulatory regime, referencing a specific Council of Ministers decree from August 6, 1914, shortly after the outbreak of the war.

Attendu que soit à raison des violations par l'Allemagne ci-dessus rappelées des principes du droit des gens, soit à raison de la position géographique de l'Égypte dont le territoire est traversé par le Canal de Suez et commande les communications de l'Europe avec l'Orient, soit à raison de la présence en Égypte d'un corps d'armée Britan-nique d'occupation, il était naturel, sage et prudent de la part du Gouvernement Égyptien, en l'état de guerre entre les nations du centre de l'Europe et les Alliés, de prévoir, surtout devant les procédés de l'Allemagne jusqu'alors inutilisés dans la conduite de la guerre, une attaque de l'Égypte et de pren-dre pour y parer les moyens nécessaires à la défense de son territoire et à la sauvegarde de son existence.
Attendu que la crainte d'une attaque de l'Égypte, pourtant non alors en guerre, n'était nullement chimérique, puisque cette attaque a eu lieu en février 1915 par un corps d'armée de la Turquie commandé par des offi-ciers Allemands.
ai_content.english_translation: Whereas, either by reason of the violations by Germany mentioned above of the principles of the law of nations, or by reason of the geographical position of Egypt, whose territory is crossed by the Suez Canal and commands the communications of Europe with the Orient, or by reason of the presence in Egypt of a British army corps of occupation, it was natural, wise and prudent on the part of the Egyptian Government, in the state of war between the nations of central Europe and the Allies, to foresee, especially in view of the methods of Germany hitherto unused in the conduct of war, an attack on Egypt and to take to parry it the means necessary for the defense of its territory and the safeguarding of its existence. Whereas the fear of an attack on Egypt, although not then at war, was by no means chimerical, since this attack took place in February 1915 by an army corps of Turkey commanded by German officers.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal legal or diplomatic justification for the defensive measures taken by the Egyptian government during the early stages of World War I. It articulates the strategic necessity of protecting the Suez Canal—a vital artery for the British Empire—against the Central Powers. The text specifically references the February 1915 Ottoman offensive against the Canal, which was supported by German military advisors, as proof that the threat to Egyptian neutrality and sovereignty was real rather than hypothetical, thereby legitimizing the British military presence and the defensive posture adopted by the Egyptian authorities.

ai_content.english_translation:
Whereas the Egyptian Government did not violate the Capitulations on August 6, 1914, the day it declared war on Germany, it considered the Capitulations as suspended with regard to the Germans, according to the laws of war, and did not, for this reason, reserve for them the privileges stipulated therein when it delegated to the Chief of the British troops the power to ensure the defense of Egypt;
Whereas in summary the decision of the Council of Ministers of August 6, 1914 was in fact and in law a true declaration of war on Germany, and that by the fact of its declaration of August 6, 1914 of solidarity with England, Egypt found itself at war with Turkey when on November 5, 1914, Turkey declared its alliance with Germany, which is why the Commander of the British troops in Egypt warned Egypt, and which is why in February 1915 Egypt was attacked by Turkey.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a legalistic memorandum justifying the suspension of the Capitulations (extraterritorial privileges) for German nationals in Egypt following the outbreak of World War I. It argues that the Egyptian government's decision on August 6, 1914, to align with Great Britain constituted a de facto declaration of war against Germany, thereby nullifying the legal protections previously afforded to German citizens under the Capitulatory regime. The text serves as an administrative record of the transition from Egypt's status as an autonomous province of the Ottoman Empire to its role as a British-defended territory, detailing the chain of events that led to the Ottoman Empire's entry into the war and the subsequent military threat to Egypt in 1915.

ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a legal memorandum or diplomatic brief concerning the constitutional validity of the Egyptian government's decision to enter a state of war with Germany on August 6, 1914. This terminology is significant in administrative law, as it typically shields such high-level political decisions from judicial review. The text likely pertains to a post-WWI legal dispute or arbitration regarding damages incurred by the Egyptian state or private entities during the conflict.

ai_content.transcribed_text: EGYPT AND SUDAN. CONFIDENTIAL. [January 12, 1925.] SECTION 1. No. 1. [J 112/112/16] Field-Marshal Viscount Allenby to Mr. Austen Chamberlain.—(Received January 12.) Cairo, January 4, 1925. (No. 11.) Sir, I HAVE the honour to transmit to you herewith, for your information, copies of a judgment given by the Cairo Mixed Tribunal on the 24th November in the case of Heinrich Finck v. Minister of the Interior. This judgment is of some interest, as it turns on the legal validity of decisions taken by the Egyptian Government arising out of the state of war. 2. Finck was, prior to the war, a German bookseller in Cairo. He fled from the country on the 29th October, 1914, and his business was sequestrated and sold, the Germans, Schmidt and Hoffman, who were subsequently arrested by the two other authorities and interned in Malta. The business was sequestrated and sold, the proceeds being entirely absorbed by the costs. Finck thereupon sued the Egyptian Government for over £22,000 damages, on the ground (a) that they had delegated the defence of the country to a Power which was already at war with Germany, and (b) that in doing so they had omitted to reserve the capitulatory right of Europeans, especially in regard to arrests. 3. After considerable argument, the court, as will be observed, rejected the suit, on the ground that the action of the Egyptian Government in entrusting the defence of the country to a Power which could not afford a ground for any suit with Germany, and was an act of State which could not afford a ground for any suit at law. I have, &c. ALLENBY, F. M., High Commissioner.
ai_content.english_translation: This is a formal diplomatic dispatch from Field-Marshal Viscount Allenby, the British High Commissioner in Egypt, to the British Foreign Secretary, Austen Chamberlain. It concerns a legal case brought by a German national, Heinrich Finck, against the Egyptian government regarding the seizure and liquidation of his bookstore in Cairo during the First World War. The document summarizes the court's decision to dismiss Finck's claim for damages, citing the Egyptian government's actions as an 'act of State' taken during wartime, which shielded them from legal liability.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential diplomatic dispatch from the British High Commissioner in Egypt, Lord Allenby, to the British Foreign Office in London. It provides a summary of a legal ruling by the Cairo Mixed Tribunal regarding the sequestration of enemy property (German-owned businesses) in Egypt during the First World War. The case of 'Heinrich Finck v. Minister of the Interior' highlights the complex legal status of foreign nationals under the Capitulations system in Egypt and the extent of the Egyptian government's authority to seize property under the direction of the British military administration during the state of war. It serves as a primary source for understanding the intersection of international law, colonial administration, and wartime emergency measures in early 20th-century Egypt.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
Monsieur le Haut-Commissaire,
Je m'empresse d'envoyer ci-joint à Votre Excellence copie du projet de convention que le Gouvernement Égyptien est disposé à conclure avec le Gouvernement Allemand pour le règlement des questions qui se sont soulevées à la suite de la reprise des relations entre l'Allemagne et l'Égypte.
Le Gouvernement Allemand accepte le dit projet, (qui a d'ailleurs été établi en tenant compte de certaines modifications demandées par la Légation du Reich), sauf en ce qui concerne le paragraphe 5 de l'article 1er. De paragraphe a pour objet de faire reconnaître par le Gouvernement Allemand qu'aucune responsabilité n'incombe ni au Gouvernement Égyptien ni aux ressortissants égyptiens pour les mesures prises sur le territoire égyptien à l'occasion et à la suite de l'état de guerre.
Cependant je me vois dans l'obligation d'insister pour l'insertion de cette clause dans la convention, d'autant plus que des procès ont déjà été intentés à l'encontre du Gouvernement Égyptien par des ressortissants allemands pour obtenir la condamnation du chef du préjudice qu'ils prétendent avoir subi à la suite des dites mesures. Aussi, bien que le Ministère soit très désireux de donner satisfaction dans toute la mesure possible aux demandes du Gouvernement Allemand, il considère qu'il ne pourrait conclure l'accord sans la stipulation...
Son Excellence
Le maréchal Vicomte Allenby, G.C.B., G.C.M.G.,
Haut-Commissaire de sa majesté Britannique en Égypte.
ai_content.english_translation: Mr. High Commissioner, I hasten to send herewith to Your Excellency a copy of the draft convention that the Egyptian Government is prepared to conclude with the German Government for the settlement of questions that have arisen following the resumption of relations between Germany and Egypt. The German Government accepts the said draft, (which has moreover been established taking into account certain modifications requested by the Reich Legation), except regarding paragraph 5 of Article 1. This paragraph aims to have the German Government recognize that no responsibility falls upon either the Egyptian Government or Egyptian nationals for measures taken on Egyptian territory during and following the state of war. However, I find myself obliged to insist on the insertion of this clause in the convention, especially since lawsuits have already been filed against the Egyptian Government by German nationals to obtain compensation for the damages they claim to have suffered as a result of said measures. Therefore, although the Ministry is very eager to satisfy the requests of the German Government as much as possible, it considers that it could not conclude the agreement without the stipulation... His Excellency Marshal Viscount Allenby, G.C.B., G.C.M.G., High Commissioner of His Britannic Majesty in Egypt.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal diplomatic communication dated February 7, 1923, addressed to Field Marshal Viscount Allenby, the British High Commissioner in Egypt. It concerns the legal and diplomatic negotiations between the Egyptian government and the German government regarding the resumption of post-WWI relations. The core of the dispute involves the Egyptian government's insistence on an indemnity clause (Article 1, paragraph 5) to protect Egypt and its citizens from legal claims brought by German nationals for damages incurred during the war. The document highlights the complex transition of Egypt from a British protectorate toward a sovereign state, as it navigates international legal obligations and the protection of its own administrative actions taken during the conflict.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
THE RESIDENCY,
CAIRO, RAMLEH.
29 JULY 1917
HIGH COMMISSIONER EGYPT
No 1616/3

Mr. Haines,
General Staff - Intelligence Section.

A question was recently asked in the House of Commons as to how many Egyptians had been executed since 1914 for political offences; whether the Tribunal by which they were sentenced was Military or Civil; Egyptian or British; open or secret; how many were transported or otherwise banished from Egypt; and where they now are.

The High Commissioner will be glad if you will let him know all available facts on these points for the information of the Foreign Office.

It requests a detailed report regarding the number of Egyptians executed for political offenses since 1914, the nature of the tribunals (military/civil, Egyptian/British, open/secret), and the number of individuals banished or transported from Egypt, in order to answer a parliamentary inquiry in the House of Commons.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a confidential administrative request from the British High Commissioner's office in Egypt during the First World War. It reflects the British colonial administration's need to prepare a formal response to a parliamentary inquiry in London regarding the suppression of political dissent in Egypt. FOREIGN OFFICE, August 7th, 1917.

(For the Secretary of State)
[Signature]
Sir R. Wingate, G.C.B., G.C.V.O., &c., &c., &c.

It reflects the British government's internal process of responding to parliamentary inquiries during the First World War. Specifically, it concerns a query raised by the Irish nationalist MP Laurence Ginnell regarding the execution of Egyptians for political crimes under the British protectorate established in 1914. The document includes an official 'High Commissioner Egypt' stamp dated 26 August 1917, indicating its receipt in Cairo.

ai_content.transcribed_text:
RESIDENCY.
6th September 1917
General Staff - Intelligence,
2nd Echelon,
G.H.Q., E.E.F.
With reference to your 579 and 4271, dated 29th July and August 24th, respectively, I have been in communication with the Director General of Public Security regarding this matter, and I understand that he will address you for the period of General Maxwell's command, i.e. up to the end of March, 1916, when he was acting under powers delegated by the then Commander-in-Chief.
Confining my remarks to the period since March, 1916, when General MURRAY assumed command and this Section became responsible for these cases, I beg to inform you that the Military Authorities have not executed any Egyptians for political offences. Any executions which have taken place and with which we are concerned, have been for military offences and do not, therefore, come within the terms of the F.O. telegram.
With regard to the number of Egyptians transported or otherwise banished from EGYPT, I attach a list of persons transported for military reasons on the recommendation of this Section.
SALAMA MOHAMED EL KHOLI. MALTA.
ABDEL AZIZ MOHAMED EL NAHAS (TAGATI). MALTA.
SHAFIK MANSUR. MALTA.
W.H. Deedes, Lieut-Colonel, G.S.I.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is an official communication from the British Residency in Egypt to the General Staff Intelligence (G.H.Q., Egyptian Expeditionary Force). It clarifies that since General Murray took command in March 1916, no Egyptians have been executed for political offenses, distinguishing these from military offenses. It also provides a list of individuals (Salama Mohamed El Kholi, Abdel Aziz Mohamed El Nahas, and Shafik Mansur) who were transported to Malta for military reasons.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a piece of British colonial administrative correspondence from the Residency in Cairo, dated September 1917, during the British Protectorate over Egypt. It serves as a formal clarification regarding the treatment of Egyptian political prisoners and the distinction between political and military offenses under the British military administration. The document highlights the British policy of banishing 'undesirable' Egyptian nationalists to Malta, a common practice during the First World War to suppress anti-colonial sentiment and maintain control over the Egyptian Expeditionary Force's rear areas. The signature of W.H. Deedes, a prominent British intelligence officer, underscores the document's role in the security apparatus of the era.

ai_content.transcribed_text: The Residency, Cairo. September 19th 1917. With reference to your note of the 20th August last, No. 1616, will you please cancel this Department's letter No. P.O./M/3883/17 of the 16th August, as I understand the Adviser, Ministry of the Interior, sent you a reply No. 1674, dated the 28/8/17, to your note No. 578 of July 29th. I regret that my F.O./M/3883/17 was sent to you by mistake. It should have been addressed to the Adviser.
ai_content.english_translation: The Residency, Cairo. September 19th, 1917. Regarding your note from August 20th, number 1616, please disregard this Department's previous letter (P.O./M/3883/17) sent on August 16th. I understand that the Adviser to the Ministry of the Interior already provided a response (No. 1674) on August 28th, 1917, concerning your inquiry from July 29th. My previous letter was sent in error and should have been directed to the Adviser instead.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is an official administrative communication from the British Residency in Cairo, dated September 1917, during the British Protectorate of Egypt. It concerns the bureaucratic management of political prisoners and the internal coordination between the British Residency and the Egyptian Ministry of the Interior. The correspondence serves as a formal retraction of a misdirected letter regarding the status of Egyptians executed, transported, or banished for political offenses since 1914, highlighting the complex administrative oversight of the British authorities over the Egyptian judicial and security apparatus during the First World War.

ai_content.transcribed_text: THE RESIDENCY, CAIRO. October 21st 1917. SIR, I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Despatch No. 209 (151495/16) of August 7th, forwarding a copy of a Parliamentary question by Mr. Ginnell regarding the executions and other punishments inflicted on Egyptian subjects during the war for political offences. I now transmit herewith lists, which have been compiled at my request by the Ministry of the Interior in conjunction with the Military authorities. List A. gives the names of the only two Egyptians who have been executed for political offences since the beginning of the war. Both these individuals were tried by an open British Military Court. List B. contains the names of those Egyptians who have been banished from Egypt and not allowed to return. The places mentioned after their names are those in which they are believed to be at present. List C. gives a list of all Egyptians who have been transported from Egypt, down to December 1916. All those mentioned in this list are in Malta. I also have the honour to enclose a long list (List D.) of Egyptians who have been interned in Egypt since the war started, and a supplementary list etc. etc. The Right Honourable Arthur James Balfour, O.M., M.P.
ai_content.english_translation: This document is a formal diplomatic dispatch from the British Residency in Cairo to the British Foreign Secretary, Arthur James Balfour. It acknowledges a parliamentary inquiry regarding the treatment of Egyptian subjects during World War I and provides four categorized lists (A, B, C, and D) detailing Egyptians who were executed, banished, transported to Malta, or interned by British military authorities for political offenses.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a significant piece of British colonial administrative record-keeping during the British Protectorate over Egypt (1914–1922). It reflects the British military's efforts to suppress Egyptian nationalist dissent during the First World War. The dispatch categorizes the punitive measures taken against the local population, including capital punishment, exile, and internment, in response to a parliamentary inquiry in London. It highlights the intersection of British military law and Egyptian civil administration, specifically documenting the use of British Military Courts to try Egyptian subjects for political activities deemed threatening to the war effort.

ai_content.transcribed_text: (D.2.) showing the names of Egyptians deported to their villages, or removed from the Canal Zone. List D.3. I regret the delay which has occurred in answering your despatch, but some of the Cadre have not yet sent in their lists D.2. and D.3. are interior, and for this reason lists D.2. and D.3. are not complete. In view, however, of your telegram no. 984 of October 16th, I have thought it best to forward the lists to you as they are. As soon as the remaining names are received from the Ministry of the Interior, I will forward them to you. I also venture to draw your attention to my despatch no. 215 of September 24th (in reply to your despatch no. 182 of July 14th), in which I forwarded a full report on the case of Georges Phillippides Bey, ex chief of the Cairo secret police, and detailed replies to two Parliamentary questions raised by Mr. King, of a somewhat similar nature to that under reply. I have the honour to be, Sir, In the highest respect, your most obedient, humble servant,

It also references a previous report concerning Georges Phillippides Bey, the former head of the Cairo secret police, in relation to Parliamentary inquiries raised by a Mr. King.

title: Rental Agreement / Lease Contract (Kira Mukavelenamesi) ? 26 Rabi' al-Awwal 1329 (Hijri) / 14 Mart 1327 (Rumi) [27 March 1911]
academic_citation: "DSC00136", Private Academic Collection / Ottoman Document (Sep 2022) 1 Collection.

ai_content.english_translation:
This lease contract has been drawn up regarding the rental of the shop located in the Sinan Pa?a neighborhood of Be?ikta?.
The monthly rent agreed upon in piastres (kuru?) shall be paid and delivered in accordance with the specified conditions.
Written on 26 Rabi' al-Awwal 1329 and 14 Mart 1327 [27 March 1911].
Resident of Sinan Pa?a neighborhood in Be?ikta?.
ai_content.historical_summary: This document is a formal lease contract (Kira Mukavelenamesi) for a commercial shop located in the historic Sinan Pa?a neighborhood of Be?ikta?, Istanbul. Dated March 1911 (late Ottoman period), the agreement outlines rental terms, monthly payment obligations, and legal responsibilities, affixed with imperial Ottoman revenue stamps.

title: Sharia Court Record / Legal Deed (H?ccet) ? 20 Recep 1330 Hijri [10 January 1912 Gregorian]
academic_citation: "IMG 1061", Private Academic Collection / Ottoman Document (Sep 2022) 1 Collection.

ai_content.language: Divani / Riq'a script in Ottoman Turkish
ai_content.english_translation: Regarding property in the central province city of Izmir, located in the Karata? quarter, belonging to the Ottoman Rolandiye Bank, from the women of the Greek nation, Espina daughter of Pavli Apostolo?lu from Kayseri... in the presence of the honorable ?smet at the Sharia Court of Appeal... Written on 20 Recep 1330 [10 January 1912].
ai_content.historical_summary: Sharia court deed concerning property transactions in the Karata? and Vandoniye quarters of Izmir involving a Christian Ottoman woman from Kayseri, Espina bint Pavli Apostolo?lu, and the Ottoman Rolandiye Bank.

title: Tapu Land Title Deed (Tapu Senedi) ? 20 Shawwal 1320 Hijri [19 January 1903 Gregorian]
academic_citation: "IMG 1062", Private Academic Collection / Ottoman Document (Sep 2022) 1 Collection.

ai_content.language: Divani / Riq'a script in Ottoman Turkish
ai_content.english_translation:
General Directorate of Land Registry and Cadastre
Land Title Deed
To be possessed with full ownership, a house and adjacent plot in A?a?? Mahalle of ?erkezk?y village, Saray Nahiye, Vize Kaza, K?rkkilise Sanjak, Edirne Vilayet... Boundaries: North: Road; South: House of Mustafa Efendi; East: House of Mehmed Efendi; West: House of Ahmed Efendi. Owners: Mehmed son of Ali and his wife Fatma daughter of H?seyin (half share each). 20 Shawwal 1320 [19 Jan 1903].
ai_content.historical_summary: Imperial Ottoman land title deed issued by the Cadastral Directorate for a house and land in ?erkezk?y, Edirne Vilayet, recording full parcel boundaries and co-ownership by Mehmed bin Ali and his wife Fatma.

title: Sharia Court Record / Power of Attorney (Vek?letn?me) ? 13 ?evval 1330 Hijri [25 September 1912 Gregorian]
academic_citation: "IMG 1063", Private Academic Collection / Ottoman Document (Sep 2022) 1 Collection.

ai_content.document_type: Sharia Court Record / Power of Attorney (Vek?letn?me)
ai_content.transcribed_text:
Ayd?n Vilayeti merkezi olan Medine-i ?zmir'de k?in mahkeme-i ?er'iyye huzuruna
Tebaa-i Devlet-i Aliyye-i Osmaniyye'den Rum milleti nisvan?ndan Kayseriyeli Yani binti Pavli Apostol o?lu meclis-i ?er'-i ?erife gelip
Mahkeme-i ?stinaf Hukuk Dairesi azas?ndan ?smet Bey haz?r oldu?u halde takrir-i kel?m
Atina d?hilinde Ba?dad pazar?nda k?in sened-i hakan? uhdemizde olan bil-c?mle emlak...
vek?let-i mutlaka-i sahihe-i ?er'iyye ile Atina'da sakin Bosnal? nam kimesneyi vekil tayin eyledim.
F? 13 ?evval sene 1330
ai_content.english_translation: In the presence of the noble Sharia Court in Izmir (Ayd?n Vilayet)... Yani daughter of Pavli Apostol, an Ottoman Greek subject from Kayseri, in the presence of Appeals Judge ?smet Bey, appointed Bosnal? in Athens as absolute representative to manage and transact all real estate in the Baghdad market in Athens. 13 Shawwal 1330 [25 Sept 1912].
ai_content.historical_summary: Official Izmir Sharia Court power of attorney allowing a Christian Ottoman woman from Kayseri to manage commercial real estate assets in Athens, Greece, registered just prior to the First Balkan War.
